events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1714, King George I of Great Britain and Ireland arrived in London for the first time, having sailed from the Netherlands after his accession to the throne. His arrival marked the beginning of a new era in British monarchy under the House of Hanover.
events.name: George I arrives in Britain

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1714, the Cossacks of the Russian Empire perpetrated a massacre on the Finnish island of Hailuoto, killing approximately 800 people overnight. This event is part of the broader context of conflicts involving the Russian Empire during this period.
events.name: The Great Hatred on Hailuoto

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1714, George I was crowned in Westminster Abbey, marking his formal acceptance as the monarch of Great Britain and Ireland. This event solidified his rule and the transition of power from the House of Stuart to the House of Hanover.

locations.name: Westminster Abbey, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Coronation of George I

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1714, Dutch investors led by brothers Nicolaas and Hendrik van Hoorn purchased the South American colony of Berbice from French mercenary Jacques Cassard. This acquisition played a significant role in the colonial dynamics of the region.
events.name: Purchase of Berbice

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1714, King Philip V of Spain issued a decree to reorganize the Spanish government, establishing four ministries with the Secretary of State as the chief minister. This marked a significant step towards modernizing the Spanish administration.
events.name: Reorganization of the Spanish government

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1714, the Ottoman Empire declared war on the Republic of Venice, initiating hostilities that would last until 1718. This conflict was part of the larger struggle for control over territories in the Mediterranean.

image.caption: Oil painting depicting Venetian troops capturing Ottoman-occupied Vonitsa and Preveza.
image.credit: Antonio and/or Giuseppe Stom, died in the 1700s. See the relevant article by Miltos Karkazis. — National Historical Museum , Athens, Greece
image.date_qualification: The depicted capture is dated November 1717 in the image description; the painting is dated c. 1720s. It is not a contemporary photograph of the December 1714 declaration of war.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ottoman Empire declares war on Venice

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1715, a devastating fire broke out in London, described as the worst since the Great Fire of 1666. The fire started on Thames Street and consumed over 100 houses before it was brought under control.
events.name: Fire in London

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1715, voting commenced for the British House of Commons, continuing for 46 days across various constituencies. This election was significant in shaping the political landscape of Britain.
events.name: Voting begins for the British House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1715, the Tuscarora and their allies signed a peace treaty with the Province of North Carolina, agreeing to relocate to a reservation near Lake Mattamuskeet. This treaty effectively ended the Tuscarora War, which had significant implications for Native American relations in the region.

locations.name: Lake Mattamuskeet, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Peace treaty ends the Tuscarora War

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1715, voting for the British House of Commons concluded, resulting in a significant victory for the Whig Party, which won 341 out of 558 seats. This election marked a pivotal moment in British political history.
events.name: Voting for the British House of Commons concludes

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1715, James Stuart, known as the Old Pretender, met with Pope Clement XI to seek support for his claim to the British throne. This meeting was part of his efforts to restore the House of Stuart to power during the Jacobite rising.
events.name: James Stuart meets Pope Clement XI

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1715, Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke, fled from Great Britain to France due to suspicions regarding his involvement in secret negotiations with France. His departure marked a significant moment in the political turmoil of the time.

image.caption: Portrait of Henry St John, 1st Viscount Bolingbroke.
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is “18 th century date QS:P,+1750-00-00T00:00:00Z/7”; this is a portrait date, not the date of the 1715 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Henry St John flees to France

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1715, the Battle of Gurdas Nangal commenced during the Mughal-Sikh Wars, as the Mughal Army laid siege to a fortress near Gurdaspur where Sikh General Banda Singh Bahadur and his men were holed up. This battle was part of the larger conflict between the Mughal Empire and the Sikh forces.
events.name: Battle of Gurdas Nangal begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 15, 1715, the Yamasee Confederation launched a surprise attack on English settlements in the Province of South Carolina, marking the beginning of the Yamasee War. This conflict arose from tensions over land and trade between Native Americans and European settlers.
events.name: Yamasee Confederation attacks English settlements

events.enhanced_description: On April 24, 1715, the Battle of Fehmarn took place in the Baltic Sea during the Great Northern War, where Danish forces under Christian Gabel captured five Swedish warships. This battle highlighted the naval conflicts between Denmark and Sweden during this period.
events.name: Battle of Fehmarn

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1715, a total solar eclipse was observed across southern England, Sweden, and Finland, with astronomer Edmond Halley documenting the phenomenon known as 'Baily's beads'. This event was significant in the study of astronomy and eclipses.
events.name: Total solar eclipse observed

events.enhanced_description: On May 28, 1715, riots erupted in London on the birthday of King George I, as supporters of the Old Pretender, James Stuart, protested against the Hanoverian rule. This unrest reflected the deep political divisions in Britain at the time.
events.name: Rioting in England on King George I's birthday

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1715, King Philip V unified the governments of the Kingdom of Castile and the Kingdom of Aragon into a single state, centralizing the rule of a unified Kingdom of Spain. This consolidation was a significant step in the formation of modern Spain.
events.name: Unification of the Kingdom of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1715, Tsar Peter I of Russia observed the unsuccessful attempt of 45 Dutch and English ships to enter the small harbor of Saint Petersburg. This event prompted him to recognize the necessity for additional harbors to facilitate the import of Western goods into Russia.
events.name: Tsar Peter I of Russia witnesses the attempt of 45 Dutch and English ships

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1715, the Treason Act 1714 came into effect in the Kingdom of Great Britain, allowing for the forfeiture of property owned by individuals convicted of treason. This law remained in force until June 24, 1718, significantly impacting the legal landscape regarding treason.
events.name: Britain's Treason Act 1714 takes effect

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1715, the fall of Nauplion, the capital of the Venetian Kingdom of the Morea, marked a significant turning point in the Ottoman–Venetian War (1714–18). This event sealed the fate of the Peloponnese Peninsula, which was soon completely retaken by the Ottomans.
events.name: Fall of Nauplion during the Ottoman–Venetian War

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1715, a Spanish treasure fleet consisting of 12 ships, commanded by General Don Juan Ubilla, set sail from Havana, Cuba, bound for Spain. Tragically, just seven days later, 11 of these ships sank in a storm off the coast of Florida, leading to significant treasure salvage efforts in subsequent centuries.
events.name: 1715 Treasure Fleet departs Havana

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1715, the Old Dock in Liverpool, England, opened as the world's first enclosed commercial wet dock, designed by engineer Thomas Steers. This innovative structure revolutionized maritime trade and shipping logistics in the region.
events.name: Old Dock opens in Liverpool

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1715, King Louis XIV of France passed away after a remarkable reign of 72 years. His death led to the ascension of his five-year-old great-grandson, Louis XV, with Philippe d'Orléans appointed as regent during the young king's minority.
events.name: Death of King Louis XIV of France

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1715, the first major Jacobite rising erupted in Scotland against the rule of King George I of Great Britain. The Earl of Mar raised the standard of James Edward Stuart, the son of the deposed King James VII, and marched towards Edinburgh.
events.name: First major Jacobite rising in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1715, Daniel Voysin de la Noiraye, who had served as France's Secretary of State for War since 1709, resigned at the request of the new regent, Philippe d'Orléans, following the death of King Louis XIV.
events.name: Daniel Voysin de la Noiraye resigns

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1715, during the Jacobite rebellion in Great Britain, supporters of James Edward Stuart raided the Scottish parish of Burntisland. They captured an arsenal of weapons and began an occupation of the area, declaring Stuart as King James VIII of Scotland.
events.name: Jacobite raid on Burntisland

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1715, William Mackintosh of Borlum, a leader of the Jacobite rising, landed in Scotland with 1,500 men after crossing the Firth of Forth from France. This marked a significant moment in the Jacobite efforts to reclaim the throne.
events.name: William Mackintosh lands in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1715, the Treaty of Greifswald was signed between Russia and the Electorate of Hanover. This agreement recognized Russia's annexation of Swedish Ingria and Estonia while Hanover claimed the Bremen-Verden duchies.
events.name: Treaty of Greifswald signed

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1715, the Battle of Sheriffmuir took place, where the forces of the Kingdom of Great Britain, led by John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll, confronted the Jacobite army. The battle was indecisive, halting the Jacobite advance but failing to deliver a clear victory.

image.caption: Monument to Clan MacRae at Sheriffmuir.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2016-06-04; the date is the image date, not the battle date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Sheriffmuir

events.enhanced_description: On November 14, 1715, the Battle of Preston concluded with government forces defeating the Jacobite incursion after a five-day siege. This battle was a significant setback for the Jacobite cause.
events.name: Battle of Preston

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1715, the Third Barrier Treaty was signed between Britain, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Dutch Republic. This treaty aimed to address territorial and military concerns in the region.
events.name: Third Barrier Treaty signed

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1715, the application of the Nueva Planta decrees in Majorca and the Balearic Islands brought these territories under the laws of the Crown of Castile, marking a significant shift in governance.

image.caption: Royal Greater Coat of Arms of Spain, common version with the collars of the Golden Fleece and the Holy Spirit.
image.date_qualification: The depicted arms are dated 1700–1761 in the image description; the image file itself dates to 2011-05. Neither date identifies a depiction of the 1715 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Nueva Planta decrees applied in Majorca

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1715, James Edward Stuart rejoined the Jacobite rebels in Scotland, but his efforts to rally support for the cause were unsuccessful, reflecting the waning momentum of the Jacobite uprising.
events.name: James Edward Stuart rejoins Jacobite rebels

events.enhanced_description: In 1716, the notorious English pirate Edward Teach, better known as Blackbeard, was given command of a sloop in the Bahamas. His leadership marked a significant moment in the Golden Age of Piracy, as he became one of the most feared pirates of the Caribbean.
events.name: Blackbeard's Command

events.enhanced_description: In 1716, Tsar Peter the Great of Russia studied medicine under the renowned physician Herman Boerhaave at Leiden University. This experience was part of Peter's broader efforts to modernize Russia and improve its medical practices.
events.name: Peter the Great Studies Medicine

events.enhanced_description: The Kangxi Dictionary was published in 1716, establishing a comprehensive reference for Han characters that would be used for centuries. This monumental work laid the groundwork for the study and understanding of Chinese characters in subsequent generations.
events.name: Publication of the Kangxi Dictionary

events.enhanced_description: The Nueva Planta decrees were enacted to centralize the administration of Spain under Philip V, effectively abolishing the Principality of Catalonia as a distinct political entity. This marked a significant step in the unification of Spain and the consolidation of royal power.
events.name: Application of the Nueva Planta decrees to Catalonia

events.enhanced_description: The Tugaloo massacre was a pivotal event in the Yamasee War, leading to an alliance between the Cherokee Nation and the British province of South Carolina against the Creek Indian nation. This shift significantly altered the power dynamics in the region.

locations.name: Tugaloo River, South Carolina, United States

events.name: Tugaloo Massacre

events.enhanced_description: Following the Battle of Sheriffmuir, Jacobite forces burned the town of Crieff to the ground, reflecting the intense conflict and reprisals characteristic of the Jacobite uprisings in Scotland. This act of destruction was part of the broader struggle for Scottish independence.
events.name: Burning of Crieff

events.enhanced_description: The 1716 Algiers earthquake sequence began with a powerful Mw 7.0 mainshock that devastated the city, resulting in significant loss of life and property, with estimates of around 20,000 fatalities. This earthquake highlighted the seismic vulnerability of the region.
events.name: 1716 Algiers Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: After the failure of the Jacobite rising of 1715, James Edward Stuart fled from Scotland to France, seeking refuge and support for his cause. His departure marked a significant moment in the ongoing struggle for the Jacobite claim to the British throne.
events.name: James Edward Stuart flees to France

events.enhanced_description: In a significant act of retribution following the Jacobite uprising, leaders James Radclyffe and William Gordon were executed in London. Their deaths symbolized the harsh consequences faced by those who opposed the Hanoverian government.
events.name: Execution of Jacobite leaders

events.enhanced_description: On the night of March 6, 1716, an extraordinary aurora borealis was observed across Europe, from Ireland to Italy. This natural phenomenon captivated the attention of many and was documented by various observers of the time.
events.name: Aurora Borealis seen across Europe

events.enhanced_description: In March 1716, Charles XII of Sweden led an invasion of Norway, crossing the border at Basmo, near the modern-day town of Marker. This military action was part of the larger conflict known as the Great Northern War.
events.name: Charles XII of Sweden invades Norway

events.enhanced_description: Simon Fraser, a former Scottish rebel, was granted a pardon by King George I of Great Britain, reflecting the shifting political landscape following the Jacobite uprisings. His pardon was significant for those who had opposed the Hanoverian rule.
events.name: Simon Fraser receives pardon

events.enhanced_description: Italian Jesuit missionary Ippolito Desideri arrived in Lhasa, becoming one of the first Europeans to attempt to introduce Christianity to Buddhist Tibet. His mission marked a significant moment in the history of religious exchange between East and West.
events.name: Ippolito Desideri arrives in Lhasa

events.enhanced_description: Jeremias III was elected as the new Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, becoming the leader of the Eastern Orthodox Christian Church. His leadership was pivotal during a time of significant change and challenge for the Orthodox community.

image.caption: Portrait of Ecumenical Patriarch Jeremias III.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Εθνικό Κέντρο Τεκμηρίωσης , Γεδεών, Μανουήλ, Αποσημειώματα Χρονογράφου 1800-1913, Αθήνα 1932
image.date_qualification: No depicted date is supplied; the upload timestamp is not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Jeremias III becomes Ecumenical Patriarch

events.enhanced_description: In April 1716, Austria, under the rule of Charles VI, renewed its alliance with the Republic of Venice, prompting the Ottoman Empire, led by Ahmed III, to declare war. This alliance was a crucial factor in the geopolitical tensions of the time.
events.name: Austria renews alliance with Venice

events.enhanced_description: John Law established the Banque Générale Privée in Paris, which played a significant role in the financial system of France. His banking innovations were pivotal in the development of modern financial practices.
events.name: John Law founds Banque Générale Privée

events.enhanced_description: By Royal Warrant of King George I, two companies of field artillery were raised in Woolwich, each comprising 100 men. This formation was part of the ongoing military reforms in Britain during the early 18th century.
events.name: Formation of artillery companies

events.enhanced_description: John Churchill, the 1st Duke of Marlborough, suffered a paralytic stroke, marking a significant decline in the health of one of Britain's most celebrated military leaders. His condition affected the political and military landscape of the time.

image.caption: Oil portrait of John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough, by Enoch Seeman.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated July 1716; the event is dated 28 May 1716. The image is a portrait, not an event photograph or illustration of the stroke.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Duke of Marlborough suffers stroke

events.enhanced_description: In a brutal crackdown, 600 imprisoned members of the failed Sikh Khalsa rebellion against the Mughal Empire were executed on the orders of Emperor Farrukhsiyar. Banda Singh Bahadur, the rebellion's leader, faced a particularly gruesome fate.
events.name: Execution of Sikh Khalsa members

events.enhanced_description: Tokugawa Yoshimune assumed control as the new Shogun of Japan following the death of the six-year-old Ietsugu, marking the beginning of the Kyōhō Era. His leadership would influence the direction of the Tokugawa shogunate during a time of internal and external challenges.
events.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune becomes Shogun

events.enhanced_description: Prince Eugene of Savoy arrived in Brussels as the first Governor-General of the Austrian Netherlands, following its cession from Spain. His administration would set the stage for significant political changes in the region.
events.name: Prince Eugene of Savoy arrives in Brussels

events.enhanced_description: Prince Ernest Augustus was created Duke of York and Albany in the peerage of Great Britain, reflecting the ongoing consolidation of titles and power within the British aristocracy during this period.
events.name: Prince Ernest Augustus created Duke

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Dynekilen saw the Swedish fleet defeated by a combined Danish-Norwegian fleet, marking a significant naval engagement during the Great Northern War. This battle underscored the shifting naval power in the region.
events.name: Battle of Dynekilen

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, during the Seventh Ottoman-Venetian War, the Ottoman Empire laid siege to Corfu, the last bastion of the Republic of Venice in the Greek islands. The siege ultimately failed, preserving Venetian control over the island.
events.name: Siege of Corfu

events.enhanced_description: Natchez, one of the oldest towns on the Mississippi River, was founded by French civilians at the site of Fort Rosalie. This establishment marked an important development in the French colonial presence in North America.
events.name: Founding of Natchez

events.enhanced_description: George Seton, the 5th Earl of Winton, escaped from the Tower of London, where he was under sentence of death for his involvement in the Jacobite rising of 1715. His flight into exile underscored the ongoing tensions between Jacobites and the Hanoverian government.

locations.name: Tower of London, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: George Seton escapes from Tower of London

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Petrovaradin, 83,300 Austrian troops under Prince Eugene of Savoy defeated 150,000 Ottoman Turks led by Silahdar Damat Ali Pasha, who was killed in the battle. This victory was a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between the Habsburg Monarchy and the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Battle of Petrovaradin

events.enhanced_description: Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, returned to Vienna from Italy, marking a significant moment in his reign as he navigated the complex political landscape of Europe during the early 18th century.
events.name: Charles VI returns from Italy

events.enhanced_description: In September 1716, Maria, an enslaved African woman on the Dutch West India Company's plantation in Curaçao, revolted against her overseer, Christiaan Muller, killing him and several members of his family. The rebellion lasted ten days before it was suppressed, leading to Maria's execution by burning at the stake on November 9, 1716.
events.name: Maria's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1716, Alexei Petrovich, the Tsarevich of Russia and son of Tsar Peter the Great, fled Saint Petersburg with his mistress and several companions. After spending over a year in Austria, he returned to Russia, where he was arrested and ultimately died in prison in 1718.
events.name: Alexei Petrovich's Flight

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Temeșvar, which lasted six weeks, concluded on October 12, 1716, when the Ottoman defenders surrendered to the Austrian forces led by Prince Eugene of Savoy. This marked a significant territorial gain for the Habsburg Empire, as the Turks were forced to leave behind their artillery and relinquish claims to Hungary.
events.name: Siege of Temeșvar

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1716, two significant laws were enacted in the Highlands of Scotland aimed at curbing the influence of Jacobites who sought to restore the House of Stuart. The Disarming Act restricted the carrying of weapons, while amendments to the Treason Act allowed for broader jurisdiction in treason trials.
events.name: Laws Against Jacobites

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1716, a devastating fire broke out in Wapping, London, resulting in the deaths of fifty people and the destruction of 150 houses. This incident followed closely on the heels of another fire at the Spring Gardens, highlighting the ongoing challenges of fire safety in urban areas.
events.name: Wapping Fire

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1716, Charles Townshend, 2nd Viscount Townshend, was demoted from his position as Secretary of State for the Northern Department in the British government, with James Stanhope taking his place. This event was a precursor to the Whig Split of 1717, indicating shifting political alliances.
events.name: Charles Townshend's Demotion

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, Count Carl Gyllenborg, the Swedish ambassador to Great Britain, was arrested in London for his involvement in a plot to assist James Francis Edward Stuart, the Pretender to the British throne. This incident highlighted the tensions surrounding the Jacobite cause and international diplomacy.
events.name: Gyllenborg's Arrest

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, the Omani invasion of Bahrain successfully removed Persian control over the Arabian kingdom. This event marked a significant shift in power dynamics in the region, establishing Omani influence over Bahrain.
events.name: Omani Invasion of Bahrain

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, François-Marie Arouet, later known as Voltaire, was sentenced to eleven months in the Bastille for a satirical verse against the Regent of France. This imprisonment would lead to his emergence as a prominent writer and philosopher.
events.name: Voltaire's Imprisonment

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, the Tatar invasions devastated many towns in Transylvania, including Cavnic, Sighet, and Dej. These invasions contributed to the instability and suffering in the region during this period.
events.name: Tatar Invasions in Transylvania

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had her son inoculated against smallpox in Istanbul, making him the first British person to receive this treatment. This act was pivotal in introducing the practice of inoculation to Britain.
events.name: Inoculation of Edward Wortley Montagu

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, the Casa de Contratación (House of Trade) was established in Cádiz, Spain. This institution played a crucial role in regulating trade and navigation between Spain and its colonies in the Americas.
events.name: Establishment of Casa de Contratación

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, Maharaja Pamheiba of Manipur converted to Hinduism under the influence of Shantidas Goswami, subsequently declaring it the official religion of his state. This marked a significant cultural shift in the region.
events.name: Conversion of Maharaja Pamheiba

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, the most recent rupture of New Zealand's Alpine Fault occurred, resulting in an earthquake estimated to have a magnitude between 7.8 and 8.1. This seismic event significantly impacted the region's geology and landscape.

locations.name: Alpine Fault, South Island, New Zealand

events.name: Rupture of New Zealand's Alpine Fault

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, the Charleville musket was introduced into service in France. This firearm became a standard issue for French infantry and played a significant role in military engagements during the 18th century.
events.name: Introduction of Charleville Musket

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, Thomas Fairchild, a nurseryman in Hoxton, became the first person to successfully produce a scientific plant hybrid, known as Dianthus Caryophyllus barbatus or Fairchild's Mule. This achievement marked a significant milestone in horticultural science.
events.name: Thomas Fairchild's Plant Hybrid

events.enhanced_description: In 1717, Murshid Quli Khan declared himself the first Nawab of the Bengal Subah, effectively ruling Bengal with near-sovereign authority while nominally loyal to the Mughal Empire. This marked the beginning of significant regional autonomy.
events.name: Murshid Quli Khan Declares Himself Nawab

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1717, the kingdoms of Great Britain, France, and the Dutch Republic signed the Triple Alliance, aiming to uphold the Treaty of Utrecht (1713). This alliance was a strategic move to maintain peace and balance of power in Europe following the War of the Spanish Succession.
events.name: Triple Alliance

events.enhanced_description: The Silent Sejm, which took place in February 1717, marked the beginning of the Russian Empire's increasing influence over the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. This event signified a shift in power dynamics in Eastern Europe, as Russia began to assert its control over the region.
events.name: Silent Sejm

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1717, following a treaty between France and Britain, James Stuart, the Pretender to the British throne, left France seeking refuge with Pope Clement XI in Rome. This marked a significant moment in the ongoing Jacobite struggle for the British throne.
events.name: James Stuart's Refuge

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1717, a series of blizzards paralyzed what would become the northeastern United States, burying the region under heavy snowfall. This extreme weather event had significant impacts on transportation and daily life during that period.
events.name: Blizzard in Northeastern United States

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1717, dancer John Weaver performed in what is considered the first ballet in Britain, titled 'The Loves of Mars and Venus', at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. This performance marked a significant development in the evolution of ballet as a theatrical art form in the country.

image.caption: Title page of A collection of ball-dances perform'd at court.
image.credit: Mr. Isaac, John Weaver (1673-1760), James Paisible — A collection of ball-dances perform'd at court: viz. the Richmond, the roundeau, the rigadoon, the favourite, the Spanheim, and the Britannia (1706)
image.date_qualification: The title page is a publication associated with John Weaver, dated 1706; it is contextual material, not a depiction of the 1717 performance.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Ballet in Britain

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1717, Benjamin Hoadly, Bishop of Bangor, delivered a sermon that ignited the Bangorian Controversy within the Church of England. He argued against the Biblical justification for church governance, a stance that drew significant attention and debate within religious circles.
events.name: Bangorian Controversy

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1717, the Whydah Gally, the flagship of the infamous pirate Black Sam Bellamy, was wrecked in a storm off the coast of Wellfleet, Massachusetts. The ship sank with a significant treasure on board, and only two crew members survived the disaster.
events.name: Wreck of the Whydah Gally

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1717, Spain established the Viceroyalty of New Granada, carving it out from the northern section of the Viceroyalty of Peru. This new administrative division, with its capital at Bogotá, would later play a crucial role in the independence movements of Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela.
events.name: Creation of the Viceroyalty of New Granada

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1717, the Premier Grand Lodge of England was founded in London, marking the establishment of the first modern Freemasonic Grand Lodge. This organization would later merge with the Ancient Grand Lodge of England in 1813 to form the United Grand Lodge of England.
events.name: Founding of the Premier Grand Lodge of England

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1717, George Frederick Handel's 'Water Music' was first performed on a barge on the River Thames in London. This performance was notable for its grandeur and has since become one of Handel's most celebrated works.
events.name: First Performance of Water Music

events.enhanced_description: The month-long Siege of Belgrade concluded on August 17, 1717, when Austrian forces under Prince Eugene of Savoy captured the city from the Ottoman Empire. This victory was a significant achievement in the ongoing conflict between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans.
events.name: Siege of Belgrade

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1717, the Spanish conquest of Sardinia concluded with the surrender of the last Sardinian outpost, Castelsardo. This event marked the completion of Spanish military operations on the island, which was then part of the Holy Roman Empire.
events.name: Spanish Conquest of Sardinia

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1717, King George I of Great Britain issued a proclamation offering amnesty to pirates in the West Indies, encouraging them to surrender to British authorities by September 5, 1718. This initiative aimed to curb piracy in the region and restore order.
events.name: Proclamation for Suppressing of Pirates

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1717, John Toland held the first known Druid revival ceremony at Primrose Hill in London during the Autumnal Equinox. This event aimed to establish the Mother Grove, which would later evolve into the Ancient Order of Druids.

image.caption: Portrait of John Toland, an Irish philosopher.
image.credit: J. D. Philippin, born Sysang (1729 - 1791) — http://www.carboneria.it/Tolandfr.htm
image.date_qualification: Portrait of an event figure, not a depiction of the First Druid Revival Ceremony. No image date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First Druid Revival Ceremony

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1717, a devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck Antigua Guatemala, causing widespread destruction throughout the city. The disaster prompted authorities to consider relocating the capital of Guatemala to a different site due to the extensive damage.
events.name: Guatemala Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1717, King Philip V of Spain ordered the closure of all universities in Catalonia, including the historic Estudi General de Lleida. This action was part of a broader effort to suppress Catalan culture and autonomy following the War of the Spanish Succession.
events.name: Closure of Universities in Catalonia

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1717, Antonio Vivaldi's opera 'Tieteberga' premiered at the Teatro San Moisè in Venice. This event marked a significant contribution to the Baroque opera repertoire, showcasing Vivaldi's innovative musical style.
events.name: Premiere of Tieteberga

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1717, the trial began in Boston for six pirates who survived the wreck of Samuel Bellamy's ships, Whydah and the Mary Anne. The trial concluded with five of them being convicted of piracy and robbery, leading to their execution on November 15.
events.name: Trial of Pirates in Boston

events.enhanced_description: On November 28, 1717, pirates led by Edward Teach, known as Blackbeard, and Benjamin Hornigold captured the French slave transport Concorde near the island of Saint Vincent. Blackbeard renamed the vessel Queen Anne's Revenge, enhancing its armaments and making it his flagship.

locations.name: Saint Vincent, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines

events.name: Capture of Concorde by Blackbeard

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1717, King George I of Great Britain banished his son, George, Prince of Wales, and daughter-in-law Caroline of Ansbach from the royal household following a confrontation at the baptismal ceremony for their newborn son. This incident highlighted the ongoing tensions within the royal family.
events.name: Banishment of George, Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1717, a catastrophic flood struck the North Sea coast between the Netherlands and Denmark, resulting in thousands of deaths and widespread destruction of homes. This disaster is remembered as one of the most devastating floods in the region's history.
events.name: Christmas Flood

events.enhanced_description: In September 1718, forces of the Tibetan Dzungar Khanate defeated an expedition of the Chinese Imperial Army led by General Erentei at the Salween River. This battle underscored the ongoing conflicts between the Dzungar Khanate and the Qing Dynasty.
events.name: Battle of the Salween River

events.enhanced_description: In 1718, the Funj warrior aristocracy deposed the reigning mek and placed one of their own on the throne of Sennar, marking a significant shift in power and the Islamization of the region. This event was pivotal in the history of Sudan.
events.name: Islamization of Sudan

events.enhanced_description: In 1718, the white potato was introduced to New England from England, marking the beginning of its cultivation in the region. This agricultural shift would have lasting effects on American cuisine and farming practices.
events.name: Introduction of the white potato to New England

events.enhanced_description: In 1718, coffee began to be cultivated in Surinam, a Dutch colony in South America. This development contributed to the global coffee trade and the economic significance of coffee in colonial economies.
events.name: Coffee cultivation in Surinam

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1718, Sufi rebel leader Shah Inayat Shaheed was beheaded by the Mughals after being deceived into a meeting under the pretense of discussing peace. His execution marked a significant moment in the ongoing resistance against Mughal authority.
events.name: Beheading of Shah Inayat Shaheed

events.enhanced_description: On January 17, 1718, Jeremias III reclaimed his position as the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, following a brief tenure by Metropolitan Cyril IV of Pruoza. This event underscored the ongoing power struggles within the Eastern Orthodox Church.
events.name: Jeremias III Reclaims Patriarchate

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1718, the reign of Victor Amadeus over the principality of Anhalt-Bernburg ended after 61 years. He was succeeded by his son Karl Frederick, marking a transition in leadership for the principality.
events.name: End of Victor Amadeus' Reign

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1718, Manuel II (Mpanzu a Nimi) ascended to the throne of the Kingdom of Kongo following the death of King Pedro IV (Nusamu a Mvemba). Manuel's reign would last until 1743, continuing the legacy of the Kongo monarchy.
events.name: Manuel II Becomes Monarch of Kongo

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1718, Anton Florian became the new Prince of Liechtenstein, succeeding Joseph Wenzel. His ascension marked a continuation of the Liechtenstein dynasty's influence in Central Europe.
events.name: Anton Florian Becomes Prince of Liechtenstein

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1718, Daniel Overbeek arrived in Ceylon as the new Dutch Governor after a 10-month sea voyage from the Netherlands. His governance would influence Dutch colonial policies in the region.
events.name: Daniel Overbeek Becomes Governor of Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1718, Edward Wortley Montagu, the four-year-old son of the British Ambassador to Turkey, became the first British person to be inoculated with the smallpox vaccine. This event was pivotal in the history of vaccination in Britain.
events.name: First Smallpox Inoculation in Britain

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1718, the Privy Council of the United Kingdom underwent a reorganization, with Charles Spencer succeeding James Stanhope as the new First Lord of the Treasury. This change reflected the shifting political landscape of the time.
events.name: Reorganization of the Privy Council

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1718, Great Britain, France, and the Dutch Republic reached an agreement to phase out the authority of the House of Medici over the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. This decision declared Gian Gastone de' Medici as the last ruler of the Medici family, with the Spanish House of Bourbon set to take control of Tuscany in the future.
events.name: Agreement on the phasing out of the House of Medici

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1718, Father Antonio de San Buenaventura y Olivares founded San Antonio by constructing the Mission San Antonio de Valero. This mission would later become known as the Alamo, a significant site in Texas history.
figures: Antonio de San Buenaventura y Olivares
events.name: Foundation of San Antonio

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1718, the settlement of New Orleans was founded in New France. This city would grow to become a major cultural and economic center in the southern United States.
events.name: Founding of New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1718, the infamous pirate Edward Teach, known as Blackbeard, blockaded the port of Charleston, South Carolina, with a fleet of four ships. For an entire week, he plundered incoming vessels, showcasing the height of piracy in the Caribbean.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of Edward Teach, known as Blackbeard.
image.credit: Joseph Nicholls (fl. 1726–55). [1] Although James Basire (1730–1802) is attributed as the engraver based on the signature "J. Basire", unless he engraved the item at the age of 6, it is likely his father Isaac Basire (misreading of initial?) or another J. Basire. — http://jcb.lunaimaging.com/luna/servlet/detail/JCB~1~1~1785~2720004:Captain-Teach-commonly-call-d-Black
image.date_qualification: Published in 1736, after the 1718 blockade; the image description notes that the engraving may date to circa 1726.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Blockade of Charleston by Blackbeard

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1718, Blackbeard and Stede Bonnet accidentally ran aground in the ship Queen Anne's Revenge at Topsail Inlet, North Carolina. Following this incident, Blackbeard negotiated a pardon with the colonial governor, marking a significant moment in pirate history.

locations.name: Topsail Inlet, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Grounding of Queen Anne's Revenge

events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1718, the Treaty of Baden was signed, effectively ending the Toggenburg War. This treaty marked a significant resolution in the conflicts of the time.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Baden

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1718, a devastating 7.5 magnitude earthquake struck Tongwei County in Gansu, China, resulting in the tragic loss of approximately 73,000 lives. This disaster highlighted the vulnerability of the region to seismic activity.
events.name: Earthquake in Tongwei County

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1718, the Treaty of Passarowitz was signed, concluding the Austro-Turkish War. This treaty reshaped the political landscape of Southeast Europe.

image.caption: Map of the Banat of Temeswar, Kingdom of Serbia, and Military Frontier.
image.date_qualification: The map describes the region in 1718; the supplied image date is 2009 and refers to the map's creation, not the treaty signing.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Passarowitz

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1718, construction began on Kadriorg Palace in Tallinn, Estonia, at the behest of Tsar Peter the Great. The palace was dedicated to his wife, Catherine, and symbolizes the Russian influence in the Baltic region.
events.name: Construction of Kadriorg Palace

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1718, the Battle of Cape Passaro took place, where a Spanish fleet was decisively defeated by the British Royal Navy under Admiral George Byng. This battle was a precursor to the War of the Quadruple Alliance.
events.name: Battle of Cape Passaro

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1718, a duel took place at the Bois de Boulogne in Paris between Armande Félice de La Porte Mazarin and the Vicomtesse de Polignac, both mistresses of the Duc de Richelieu. The duel, initiated by Mazarin, resulted in her being wounded, highlighting the dramatic social dynamics of the French aristocracy.
figures: Armande Félice de La Porte Mazarin
events.name: Duel at Bois de Boulogne

events.enhanced_description: On September 27, 1718, the Battle of Cape Fear River commenced as pirate Stede Bonnet and his crew aboard the Royal James faced off against Colonel William Rhett and his ships. This confrontation marked a significant moment in the fight against piracy in the region.

locations.name: Cape Fear River, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Battle of Cape Fear River

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1718, Stede Bonnet and his crew were captured near the mouth of the Cape Fear River and taken to Charleston, South Carolina, where they faced trial for piracy. This event marked a significant crackdown on piracy in the region.

locations.name: Cape Fear River, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Capture of Stede Bonnet

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1718, Mughal Emperor Farrukhsiyar restored the titles and responsibilities of his chief adviser, Mir Jumla III, nearly three years after his dismissal. This restoration reflected the shifting power dynamics within the Mughal court.
events.name: Restoration of Mir Jumla III

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1718, a lightning strike caused an explosion at the powder magazine of the Old Fortress in Corfu, resulting in numerous casualties. This tragic event highlighted the dangers of storing explosive materials in populated areas.
events.name: Explosion at Old Fortress, Corfu

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1718, Voltaire's first play, Oedipus, premiered at the Comédie-Française in Paris. This marked the beginning of Voltaire's illustrious career in literature and theater.
events.name: Premiere of Voltaire's Oedipus

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1718, Blackbeard was killed in action during a battle at Ocracoke Inlet, North Carolina, after a Royal Navy contingent was sent to confront him. His death marked the decline of the Golden Age of Piracy in the Americas.

locations.name: Ocracoke Inlet, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Death of Blackbeard

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1718, a catastrophic fire broke out in Wapping, London, resulting in the deaths of fifty people and the destruction of 150 houses. This incident followed another fire just days earlier, highlighting the dangers of urban living at the time.
events.name: Fire in Wapping, London

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1718, following the death of her brother Charles XII, Ulrika Eleonora proclaimed herself Queen regnant of Sweden. This marked a significant moment in Swedish history as she became one of the few female monarchs to rule.
events.name: Ulrika Eleonora proclaims herself Queen of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1718, Stede Bonnet was hanged in Charleston, South Carolina, after being recaptured. His execution marked the end of a notorious pirate career and served as a warning to others in the pirate community.

image.caption: Print engraving depicting Stede Bonnet, attributed to Captain Charles Johnson.
image.date_qualification: Retrospective print illustration dated circa 1725, several years after Bonnet’s execution; it is not a contemporary depiction of the execution.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Execution of Stede Bonnet

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1718, the Holy Roman Empire, Kingdom of Great Britain, Dutch Republic, and Kingdom of France formally declared war on Spain, initiating the War of the Quadruple Alliance. This conflict would reshape alliances and power dynamics in Europe.

locations.historical_name: Holy Roman Empire, Great Britain, France
locations.name: Holy Roman Empire, Kingdom of Great Britain, Kingdom of France

events.name: Declaration of War on Spain

events.enhanced_description: In 1719, Prussia conducted Europe's first systematic census, a significant administrative undertaking that aimed to gather comprehensive demographic data. This census set a precedent for future population studies in Europe.
events.name: First systematic census in Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1719, miners in Falun, Sweden, discovered the apparently petrified body of Fet-Mats Israelsson, who had died in 1677. This unusual find sparked interest in the natural sciences and the preservation of organic materials.
events.name: Discovery of Fet-Mats Israelsson

events.enhanced_description: In 1719, Raine's Foundation School was established in Wapping, London, founded by Henry Raine. This institution aimed to provide education to the poor and was part of a broader movement towards educational reform in England.
events.name: Opening of Raine's Foundation School

events.enhanced_description: In 1719, James Figg opened one of the first indoor venues for combat sports in London, adjacent to the City of Oxford tavern. This venue became a significant site for the development of boxing and other combat sports in England.
events.name: James Figg opens combat sports venue

events.enhanced_description: The Carolean Death March was a disastrous retreat undertaken by the Swedish-Carolean army, primarily composed of Finnish soldiers, led by Carl Gustaf Armfeldt. The army faced severe winter conditions while crossing the Tydalen mountains, resulting in the death of approximately 3,700 men and leaving many others severely incapacitated.
events.name: Carolean Death March begins

events.enhanced_description: The Principality of Liechtenstein was officially established within the Holy Roman Empire, marking its recognition as a sovereign state. This event laid the groundwork for Liechtenstein's future as an independent principality.
events.name: Creation of the Principality of Liechtenstein

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1719, the Riksdag of the Estates formally recognized Ulrika Eleonora's claim to the Swedish throne after she consented to a new constitution. This event marked her ascension as queen regnant of Sweden, a significant moment in Swedish history.
events.name: Recognition of Ulrika Eleonora's claim to the Swedish throne

events.enhanced_description: The First Treaty of Stockholm was signed, marking a significant diplomatic agreement during a tumultuous period in European politics. This treaty aimed to address conflicts arising from the Great Northern War.
events.name: First Treaty of Stockholm signed

events.enhanced_description: Farrukhsiyar, the Mughal Emperor of India, was deposed by the Sayyid brothers, who subsequently installed Rafi ud-Darajat as the new emperor. This power shift marked a significant change in the Mughal dynasty's leadership.
events.name: Deposition of Farrukhsiyar

events.enhanced_description: A devastating earthquake, estimated to have a magnitude greater than 7, struck El Salvador, causing extensive damage including large fractures and liquefaction zones. The disaster resulted in the destruction of numerous buildings, including houses, churches, and monasteries.
events.name: Earthquake in El Salvador

events.enhanced_description: Ulrika Eleonora was crowned as Queen of Sweden in a ceremony held in Stockholm, solidifying her position as the monarch following her recognition by the Riksdag. This event was a pivotal moment in Swedish royal history.
events.name: Coronation of Ulrika Eleonora as Queen of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: The French army, commanded by James FitzJames, 1st Duke of Berwick, invaded the Basque provinces of Spain, with a force of 20,000 troops crossing into Navarre. This military action was part of the ongoing conflicts in the region during this period.
events.name: French invasion of the Basque provinces

events.enhanced_description: In Louisiana, Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville's brother Serigny arrived on a French man-of-war, bringing news of the declaration of war between France and Spain. This announcement had significant implications for colonial politics in North America.
figures: Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville
events.name: Declaration of war between France and Spain

events.enhanced_description: Daniel Defoe published 'Robinson Crusoe', a novel that would become one of the most famous works in English literature. The story of a castaway's survival on a deserted island resonated with readers and has since become a classic.

image.caption: Engraved frontispiece from the first edition of Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — First edition of Robinson Cruose
image.date_qualification: Frontispiece associated with the 1719 first edition; a book illustration, not a depiction of the act of publication.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Robinson Crusoe

events.enhanced_description: King Philip V of Spain departed from Madrid, leading 15,000 men of the Spanish Army into Navarre to confront the French forces under Berwick. This military maneuver was part of the broader conflict between Spain and France.
events.name: King Philip V of Spain leads troops into Navarre

events.enhanced_description: In Louisiana, Bienville captured Pensacola, but the city was later recaptured by the Spanish. This back-and-forth control of Pensacola highlighted the ongoing territorial disputes in the region.
figures: Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne, Sieur de Bienville
events.name: Capture of Pensacola by Bienville

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 2011, a powerful 7.2 magnitude earthquake struck near the city of Van in eastern Turkey, resulting in over 600 fatalities and significant damage to approximately 2,200 buildings. The disaster prompted a massive rescue and relief effort to assist the affected population.
events.name: Earthquake in Turkey

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Ösel Island, a Russian naval force achieved a decisive victory over the Swedish fleet. This battle was part of the larger naval engagements during the Great Northern War.
events.name: Battle of Ösel Island

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Glen Shiel saw British forces defeat the Jacobites and their Spanish allies. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in Scotland during the early 18th century.
events.name: Battle of Glen Shiel

events.enhanced_description: Captain John Perry successfully repaired the Dagenham Breach, a significant engineering achievement that helped to prevent flooding in the surrounding areas. His work was crucial for maintaining the integrity of the local waterways.
events.name: Captain John Perry fixes Dagenham Breach

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Francavilla, the Austrians faced defeat at the hands of the Spanish forces. This battle was part of the larger conflicts involving the Spanish and Austrian powers during this period.
events.name: Battle of Francavilla

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of San Sebastian concluded with the Spanish garrison surrendering to the forces led by the Duke of Berwick. This event was significant in the context of the ongoing conflicts in the Basque region.
events.name: Siege of San Sebastian

events.enhanced_description: Princess Maria Josepha of Austria married Frederick Augustus, Elector of Saxony, just ten days after renouncing her claim to the Austrian throne. This marriage was a strategic alliance within the Habsburg dynasty.
events.name: Marriage of Maria Josepha of Austria

events.enhanced_description: The Opernhaus am Zwinger, one of the largest opera houses of its time, opened in Dresden with a performance of Antonio Lotti's 'Giovi in Argo'. This event marked a significant cultural milestone in the arts.
events.name: Opening of the Opernhaus am Zwinger

events.enhanced_description: Muhammad Shah was crowned as the 12th Mughal Emperor of India at Shahjahanabad, shortly after the death of Shah Jahan II. His ascension marked a new chapter in the Mughal Empire's history.
events.name: Crowning of Muhammad Shah

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1719, Fernando Manuel de Bustillo Bustamante y Rueda, the Spanish Governor-General of the Philippines, was assassinated in a coup d'état orchestrated by supporters of the Archbishop of Manila, whom Bustamante had previously imprisoned. This event marked a significant power struggle within the colonial administration of the Philippines.
figures: Fernando Manuel de Bustillo Bustamante y Rueda

image.caption: Photograph of Félix Resurrección Hidalgo’s *El Asesinato del Gobernador Bustamante*.
image.credit: Félix Resurrección Hidalgo — National Museum of the Philippines
image.date_qualification: Artwork dated ca. 1904; the supplied image is a photograph of the artwork, not a photograph of the 1719 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Fernando Manuel de Bustillo Bustamante y Rueda

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1719, the British Army, commanded by Major General George Wade, invaded and captured the forts of Vigo on the Atlantic coast of Spain. This military action was part of the larger context of the War of the Quadruple Alliance.
events.name: Capture of Vigo

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1719, the Red Canal was inaugurated in Saint Petersburg after seven years of construction, with Tsar Peter the Great in attendance. This engineering feat was part of Peter's efforts to modernize Russia and improve its infrastructure.
events.name: Opening of the Red Canal

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1719, Sweden and Denmark-Norway signed an armistice, effectively halting combat in the Great Northern War. This agreement laid the groundwork for the subsequent Treaty of Frederiksborg in 1720, which formalized peace between the two nations.

image.caption: Commemorative medal depicting Frederik IV and personifications of Denmark and Sweden.
image.date_qualification: The medal commemorates the 1720 treaty; the supplied image date is 2020 and is not the date of the event depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.name: Frederiksborg, Capital Region of Denmark, Denmark

events.name: Armistice between Sweden and Denmark-Norway

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1719, a treaty was signed between Sweden and Hanover at the conclusion of the Great Northern War, whereby Sweden ceded the Duchies of Bremen and Verden to Hanover. This marked a significant territorial loss for Sweden and a gain for Hanover.
events.name: Treaty between Sweden and Hanover

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1719, Andrew Bradford published the American Weekly Mercury, marking it as Pennsylvania's first newspaper. This publication played a crucial role in the dissemination of news and information in the American colonies.
events.name: Publication of the American Weekly Mercury

events.enhanced_description: In May 1720, the Great Plague of Marseille began, marking the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in Western Europe. The epidemic resulted in the deaths of over 100,000 people in the city and surrounding areas.
events.name: Beginning of the Great Plague of Marseille

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, the Tuscarora people began migrating from North Carolina due to the pressures of European colonization. This migration was part of a larger trend of displacement among Native American tribes during this period.
events.name: Tuscarora Migration

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, the Town on Queen Anne's Creek in North Carolina was renamed Edenton in honor of Governor Charles Eden. This renaming was part of the town's development and incorporation, which occurred in 1722.
events.name: Renaming of Edenton

events.enhanced_description: The Guild Regulation of 1720 was introduced in Sweden, aiming to regulate guilds and trade practices within the country. This regulation was part of broader economic reforms during this period.
events.name: Guild Regulation of 1720

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, the Kangxi Emperor announced that all western businessmen in China could only trade in Guangzhou. This policy was part of the Qing Dynasty's efforts to control foreign trade and influence.
events.name: Kangxi Emperor's Trade Announcement

events.enhanced_description: The Academia Real da Historia was founded in Lisbon, Portugal, in 1720. This institution aimed to promote historical studies and preserve the nation's heritage.
events.name: Foundation of Academia Real da Historia

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, Jonathan Swift began major composition work on his satirical novel 'Gulliver's Travels' in Ireland. This work would later become one of the most significant pieces of English literature.
events.name: Jonathan Swift Begins Gulliver's Travels

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, 'Il teatro alla moda', a satirical pamphlet by Benedetto Marcello, was published anonymously in Venice. This work critiqued the theatrical practices of the time.
events.name: Publication of Il teatro alla moda

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, the Royal Cork Yacht Club was founded in Cork, Ireland, marking it as the first yacht club in the world. This establishment played a significant role in the development of sailing and yachting culture.
events.name: Foundation of the Royal Cork Yacht Club

events.enhanced_description: In 1720, France experienced the Mississippi Bubble, parallel to the South Sea Bubble in England. The market shares of the Mississippi Company soared before crashing, leading to widespread financial panic and the eventual flight of John Law, the architect of the Bubble.
events.name: Mississippi Bubble in France

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1720, Sweden and Prussia signed the Treaty of Stockholm, concluding hostilities in the Great Northern War. This treaty marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Northern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Stockholm

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1720, Edmond Halley was appointed as Astronomer Royal for England. His contributions to astronomy and navigation were pivotal during this period, influencing scientific thought.
events.name: Appointment of Edmond Halley as Astronomer Royal

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1720, the Treaty of The Hague was signed between Spain and the Quadruple Alliance, effectively ending the War of the Quadruple Alliance. This treaty reshaped alliances and territorial claims in Europe.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of The Hague

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1720, Spanish forces launched an assault on the British settlement of Nassau in the Bahamas, marking a significant confrontation at the end of the War of the Quadruple Alliance. This battle underscored the ongoing tensions between colonial powers in the Caribbean.
events.name: Battle of Nassau

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1720, Queen Ulrika Eleonora of Sweden abdicated the throne to allow her husband, Frederick I, to take over as king. This decision was influenced by the refusal of the Swedish Riksdag to accept a joint rule.
events.name: Abdication of Queen Ulrika Eleonora of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1720, the Riksdag of the Estates elected Frederick I as the new King of Sweden. This election followed the abdication of his wife, Ulrika Eleonora, and marked a new chapter in Swedish monarchy.
events.name: Election of Frederick I as King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1720, Bajirao I was appointed as the Peshwa of the Maratha Empire by Chhatrapati Shahu, succeeding his father. This appointment marked the beginning of Bajirao's influential leadership and military campaigns that expanded Maratha power.

image.caption: Painting of Bajirao I.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — The Era of Baji Rao: An Account of the Empire of the Deccan Book by Uday S. Kulkarni Original portrait from the 19th century
image.date_qualification: 18th–19th century (as stated in the image metadata); not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Appointment of Bajirao I as Peshwa

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1720, the coronation of King Frederick I of Sweden took place in Stockholm, six weeks after he ascended to the throne. This event was a significant ceremonial occasion in Swedish history.
events.name: Coronation of King Frederick I of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1720, the Treaty of The Hague, signed on February 17, went into effect, concluding the War of the Quadruple Alliance. This treaty involved significant territorial and political changes among the signatory nations.
events.name: Enforcement of the Treaty of The Hague

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1720, the British privateer Speedwell, captained by George Shelvocke, was wrecked on the uninhabited island of Más a Tierra, now known as Robinson Crusoe Island, off the coast of Chile. The crew was marooned for five months before successfully escaping by building a boat from the wreckage.
events.name: Wreck of the Speedwell

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1720, British silversmiths were once again permitted to use sterling silver after 24 years of being restricted to the softer Britannia silver. This change marked a significant moment in the history of British craftsmanship and trade.
events.name: Return to Sterling Silver for British Silversmiths

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1720, the British Parliament approved the Bubble Act, officially known as the Royal Exchange and London Assurance Corporation Act 1719. This legislation prohibited the formation of joint-stock companies without prior royal approval, reflecting the economic turmoil of the time.
events.name: Approval of the Bubble Act

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1720, the Nizam-ul-Mulk of Hyderabad survived an attempted ambush by Mughal forces led by the Sayyid brothers in Burhanpur, Madhya Pradesh. This event was pivotal in the establishment of a rival state in southern India, marking a significant shift in regional power dynamics.
events.name: Ambush of Nizam-ul-Mulk of Hyderabad

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1720, the South Sea Bubble reached its peak, with shares of the South Sea Company priced at £1,060 each. However, this speculative frenzy would soon lead to a dramatic collapse in stock prices, affecting countless investors.
events.name: Peak of the South Sea Bubble

events.enhanced_description: Under the authority of the Bubble Act, the Lords Justices in Great Britain attempted to curb the excesses of the stock markets during the South Sea Bubble. They dissolved numerous petitions for patents and charters, abolishing over 80 dubious joint-stock companies, although these measures had little impact on the ongoing speculative frenzy.
events.name: Bubble Act Enforcement during the South Sea Bubble

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Frederiksborg was signed on July 14, 1720, between Denmark-Norway and Sweden, effectively ending the Great Northern War. This treaty marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Northern Europe, concluding years of conflict.
events.name: Treaty of Frederiksborg

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Grengam, fought on July 27, 1720, in the Ledsund Strait between the Åland Islands, was the last major naval engagement of the Great Northern War. This battle marked the conclusion of Russian and Swedish offensive naval operations in the Baltic Sea.
events.name: Battle of Grengam

events.enhanced_description: The Spanish Villasur expedition, which began on June 16, 1720, aimed to counter French influence on the Great Plains. However, it ended in disaster on August 14, 1720, when the expedition was ambushed by a coalition of Pawnee and Otoe forces.

locations.name: Near North Platte, Nebraska, United States

events.name: Villasur Expedition Ambush

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1720, the English stock market crashed, leading to a significant drop in stock prices for the South Sea Company. This event marked a pivotal moment in financial history, highlighting the dangers of speculative investments.
events.name: South Sea Company Stock Market Crash

events.enhanced_description: On October 8, 1720, Sayyid Hussain Ali Khan Barha, a powerful figure in the Mughal Empire, was assassinated by Turkish nobleman Haider Beg Dughlat. This assassination was orchestrated by Nizam ul-Mulk as retaliation for an earlier ambush attempt.

image.caption: Portrait of Nawab Hussain Ali Khan Barha.
image.credit: Unknown author Unknown author — Mughal portfolio
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the event’s subject, not a depiction of the assassination. The image date is described as early 18th century, but no supported display date is provided.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Assassination of Sayyid Hussain Ali Khan Barha

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1720, Muhammad Ibrahim, a grandson of the late Emperor Bahadur Shah I, was freed from prison and declared Mughal Emperor by conspirators. His reign lasted only 32 days, described as fleeting and insignificant.
events.name: Muhammad Ibrahim Declared Mughal Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On November 13, 1720, Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah defeated his brother Muhammad Ibrahim in a battle at Hasanpur, Uttar Pradesh. Following this defeat, Ibrahim was returned to incarceration in Shahjahanabad, modern-day Delhi.
events.name: Battle of Hasanpur

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1720, the notorious pirate Calico Jack Rackham was tried in Spanish Town, Jamaica, and subsequently hanged at Port Royal. His trial was notable for the involvement of female pirates Mary Read and Anne Bonny, who were spared execution.
events.name: Trial and Execution of Calico Jack Rackham

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1720, Fath-Ali Khan Daghestani was deposed from his position as Grand Vizier of Iran and tortured by Mohammadqoli Khan, the bodyguard of Shah Sultan Husayn. This event marked a significant power shift within the Safavid Empire.
events.name: Deposition of Fath-Ali Khan Daghestani

events.enhanced_description: In 1721, José de Azlor y Virto de Vera established the fort of Presidio La Bahía at its original location, on the ruins of the failed French Fort Saint Louis. This fortification played a crucial role in the Spanish colonial efforts in Texas.
figures: José de Azlor y Virto de Vera

image.caption: Presidio La Bahía in Goliad, Texas.
image.date_qualification: A later photograph of the presidio at its current location, which the article says dates to 1747; it does not depict the fort’s 1721 establishment. Image date is not supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Establishment of Presidio La Bahía

events.enhanced_description: In 1721, regular mail service was established between London and New England, enhancing communication and trade between the two regions. This development was significant for the growing transatlantic relationship.
events.name: Regular mail service established between London and New England

events.enhanced_description: In 1721, under the leadership of the eighth shōgun of Japan, Yoshimune Tokugawa, the concept of a suggestion box was developed. This innovation aimed to improve governance by allowing citizens to voice their opinions and suggestions.
events.name: Suggestion box developed in Japan

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1721, the Committee of Inquiry published its findings on the collapse of the South Sea Company in Great Britain. This investigation was crucial in understanding the causes and consequences of the financial crisis.
events.name: Committee of Inquiry on South Sea Company

events.enhanced_description: James Stanhope, the chief minister of Great Britain, died on February 5, 1721, a day after collapsing while defending his government's actions regarding the South Sea Bubble in Parliament. His death marked a significant political shift during a turbulent time.
events.name: Death of James Stanhope

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1721, Johann Sebastian Bach completed his Brandenburg Concertos, dedicating them to Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg-Schwedt. These works are considered masterpieces of the Baroque period and showcase Bach's innovative compositional style.
events.name: Completion of Bach's Brandenburg Concertos

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1721, Robert Walpole became the first Prime Minister of Great Britain, a title that was more a term of disparagement at the time. His leadership marked the beginning of a new era in British politics.
events.name: Robert Walpole Becomes First Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: The deadliest outbreak of smallpox in Boston's history began on April 21, 1721, when the British ship HMS Sea Horse arrived with infected sailors. Over the next ten months, the outbreak resulted in 5,759 cases and 844 deaths.
events.name: Smallpox Outbreak in Boston

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1721, pirates John Taylor and Olivier Levasseur captured the 700-ton Portuguese galleon Nossa Senhora do Cabo at Réunion. This heist yielded one of the largest pirate hauls in history, valued between £100,000 and £875,000.
events.name: Capture of Nossa Senhora do Cabo

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1721, Pope Innocent XIII was elected as the 244th pope of the Roman Catholic Church, succeeding Pope Clement XI. His papacy would last until his death in 1724, during which he continued the policies of his predecessor.
events.name: Pope Innocent XIII succeeds Pope Clement XI

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1721, Dr. Zabdiel Boylston initiated the first public inoculation campaign against smallpox in Boston, Massachusetts. This groundbreaking effort involved inoculating his own son and others, marking a significant step in the fight against infectious diseases.
events.name: First public inoculation campaign in Boston

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1721, a Spanish expedition led by Governor José de Azlor y Virto de Vera confronted a smaller French force commanded by Louis Juchereau de St. Denis at the Neches River in Texas. Outnumbered, St. Denis retreated, allowing the Spanish to reclaim the territory.
figures: José de Azlor y Virto de Vera
events.name: Spanish expedition encounters French forces at Neches River

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1721, the city of Shamakhi in the Persian Safavid Empire was sacked, marking a significant event in the region's tumultuous history. This event highlighted the instability and conflict prevalent during the Safavid period.
events.name: Sack of Shamakhi

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1721, the Treaty of Nystad was signed, officially ending the Great Northern War. This treaty marked a significant shift in power in Northern Europe, with Sweden ceding territories to Russia.
events.name: Treaty of Nystad signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1721, the Kelantan Sultanate was established in what is now Kelantan, Malaysia. This marked the beginning of a significant political entity in the region, which would play a crucial role in the history of Malaysia.
events.name: Establishment of the Kelantan Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1721, Peter I was proclaimed the first Emperor of All Russia, transitioning the nation from a Tsardom to an Empire. This proclamation marked a pivotal moment in Russian history, setting the stage for future imperial expansion.
events.name: Peter I proclaimed Emperor of All Russia

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1721, Philip V of Spain signed a Royal Decree in Lerma, transforming the Seminary of Saint Rose of Lima in Caracas into the Universidad Real y Pontificia de Caracas. This decree was a significant step in the development of higher education in colonial Venezuela.
events.name: Philip V of Spain signs Royal Decree

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1722, Edenton was incorporated as the county seat of Chowan County, North Carolina. This designation made Edenton the de facto capital of North Carolina until 1746, when the government relocated to New Bern.
events.name: Incorporation of Edenton

events.enhanced_description: In 1722, Peter the Great of Russia established the Table of Ranks, a system that classified military and civil service positions. This reform aimed to modernize the Russian state and reduce the power of the nobility by allowing commoners to rise through the ranks based on merit.
events.name: Creation of the Table of Ranks

events.enhanced_description: In 1722, a group of Bohemian Brethren, known as the 'Hidden Seed,' settled in Herrnhut, on the estate of Count Nicolaus Zinzendorf in Upper Lusatia, Saxony. This settlement became the foundation for the Moravian Church's renewal and a center for religious revival.
events.name: Settlement of Herrnhut

events.enhanced_description: The Chiesa del Purgatorio, a Catholic Church, was constructed in Venafro, Italy, in 1722. This church reflects the architectural and religious developments of the period in the region.
events.name: Construction of Chiesa del Purgatorio

events.enhanced_description: In 1722, Lille Grønnegade Theatre was founded in Copenhagen, marking the establishment of the first public theatre in Denmark. This venue played a crucial role in the development of Danish theatre and culture.
events.name: Foundation of Lille Grønnegade Theatre

events.enhanced_description: In 1722, Jean-Philippe Rameau published his influential work, 'Traitée de l'harmonie réduite à ses principes naturels' (Treatise on Harmony), in Paris. This publication laid the groundwork for modern music theory, significantly impacting the study and practice of music.
events.name: Publication of Rameau's Treatise on Harmony

events.enhanced_description: In 1722, the 'Brown Bess' muzzle-loading smoothbore musket was adopted as the standard infantry firearm for the British Army. This weapon would remain in service for over a century, becoming synonymous with British military power.
events.name: Standardization of the Brown Bess musket

events.enhanced_description: In 1722, Johann Sebastian Bach composed 'The Well-Tempered Clavier,' a seminal work in the history of Western classical music. This collection of preludes and fugues is celebrated for its exploration of musical harmony and structure.
events.name: Composition of The Well-Tempered Clavier

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1722, Daniel Defoe's novel 'Moll Flanders' was published anonymously in London. The novel is considered one of the earliest examples of the English novel and explores themes of morality and survival.
events.name: Publication of Moll Flanders
