events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1722, the Battle of Cape Lopez commenced off the coast of West Africa, near present-day Gabon. The Royal Navy, under Captain Chaloner Ogle, engaged the notorious pirate Bartholomew Roberts, leading to Roberts' death and the capture of his crew.
events.name: Battle of Cape Lopez begins

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1722, Peter the Great announced that his heir would be his four-year-old grandson, Prince Pyotr Alekseivich. This decision was significant for the future of the Russian monarchy and its succession.
events.name: Peter the Great announces heir

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1722, Nasir-ud-Din Muhammad Shah, the Grand Mogul of the Mughal Empire, appointed Nizam-ul-Mulk as his Grand Vizier. This appointment would later lead to Nizam-ul-Mulk's rebellion and the establishment of his own independent state.
events.name: Nizam-ul-Mulk appointed Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1722, the Battle of Gulnabad took place, where the Pashtun forces led by Mahmud Hotak decisively defeated the Persian Safavid dynasty's troops. This victory was instrumental in the decline of the Safavid Empire.

image.caption: Diagram of the Battle of Gulnabad, based on historical descriptions.
image.date_qualification: Illustration created 2021-03-04; it is not a contemporary depiction or photograph of the battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Battle of Gulnabad

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1722, the first Silence Dogood letter, written by Benjamin Franklin, was printed in Philadelphia. This series of letters showcased Franklin's wit and criticism of society, contributing to his reputation as a leading figure in American literature.
events.name: First Silence Dogood letter printed

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1722, Dutch admiral Jacob Roggeveen landed on Easter Island, marking one of the first European encounters with the remote island. This event opened the door to further exploration and eventual colonization of the Pacific islands.
events.name: Jacob Roggeveen lands on Easter Island

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1722, the Pennsylvania colony enacted a statute requiring individuals importing persons previously convicted of sodomy to pay a fine. This law reflected the social attitudes and legal frameworks of the time regarding morality and crime.
events.name: Pennsylvania colony enacts sodomy statute

events.enhanced_description: On May 9, 1722, the British general election concluded with Prime Minister Robert Walpole's Whig Party gaining 48 additional seats in the House of Commons, solidifying their majority. This election was pivotal in shaping the political landscape of Great Britain.
events.name: 1722 British general election closes

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1722, pirate Edward Low and his crew sailed into Port Roseway, near modern Shelburne, Nova Scotia, where they attacked fishing boats. This incident marked a notable act of piracy in the region, showcasing the dangers of the seas during this era.
events.name: Edward Low attacks fishing boats in Port Roseway

events.enhanced_description: On July 25, 1722, Father Rale's War began along the Maine and Massachusetts border, marking a conflict between New England colonists and Native American tribes. This war was part of the larger struggle for control over the region.
events.name: Father Rale's War begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1722, the Russo-Persian War commenced with Peter the Great's campaign into Persia. This conflict marked a significant expansion of Russian influence in the region and set the stage for future confrontations.

image.caption: Hand-drawn map of Rasht, identified on the map as Gilan.
image.date_qualification: A map of Rasht, likely drawn between 1722 and 1734 during the Russian occupation; the saved image date gives only the first half of the 18th century, so no display date is supported.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Russo-Persian War begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1722, Francis Atterbury, the Anglican Bishop of Rochester, was arrested and confined in the Tower of London for treason. He was accused of leading a Jacobite plot to restore the House of Stuart to the throne.
events.name: Francis Atterbury arrested for treason

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1722, Wälättä Giyorgis, a 16-year-old who cared for Emperor Bakaffa during his illness, married the Emperor, marking her rise to power as Empress Mentewab. Following Bakaffa's death, she became regent for their son, Iyasu II.
events.name: Wälättä Giyorgis marries Emperor Bakaffa

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1722, New Orleans, recently established as the capital of the Louisiana Territory by France, was struck by what would later be termed the 'Great Hurricane of 1722.' The storm caused devastating damage, with waves reaching 7 feet and winds exceeding 100 miles per hour, resulting in the destruction of nearly every public building in the city.
events.name: Great Hurricane of 1722

events.enhanced_description: The six-month-long Siege of Isfahan culminated on October 23, 1722, when the Safavid capital surrendered to Afghan rebels. Sultan Husayn abdicated, recognizing Mahmud Hotak as the new Shah of Persia, marking a significant shift in power during a tumultuous period in Persian history.
events.name: Siege of Isfahan

events.enhanced_description: On November 15, 1722, during the Russo-Persian War, Emperor Peter the Great of Russia issued an order to establish the Caspian Flotilla. This strategic move aimed to secure Russian dominance over the Caspian Sea, enhancing naval capabilities in the region.
events.name: Establishment of the Caspian Flotilla

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1722, the Dutch East India Company cargo ship Schoonenberg ran aground in Struis Bay, South Africa. The majority of its crew looted the ship, leading to speculation about whether the wreck was an accident or part of a conspiracy, a mystery that has intrigued historians for nearly 300 years.

locations.name: Struis Bay, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Schoonenberg shipwreck

events.enhanced_description: The Kangxi Emperor, who reigned for 61 years, passed away on December 20, 1722. His death marked the end of an era in Qing dynasty China, leading to the ascension of his son Yinzhen, who became known as the Yongzheng Emperor.
events.name: Death of the Kangxi Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1723, the Province of Carolina incorporated Beaufort as the Port of Beaufort, making it the third incorporated town in the province. This event was significant for the development of local governance in colonial America.
events.name: Incorporation of Beaufort, North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1723, the notorious English-born pirate Edward Low intercepted the Portuguese ship Nostra Signiora de Victoria. After the captain refused to surrender his treasure, Low ordered his brutal execution, marking one of the many atrocities committed by Low during this period.
events.name: Pirate Edward Low's attack

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1723, Yinzhen was crowned as the Yongzheng Emperor, marking the beginning of a new era in Qing dynasty China following the death of his father, the Kangxi Emperor. His reign would be characterized by significant reforms and consolidation of power.
events.name: Coronation of Yongzheng Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1723, King Louis XV of France attained his majority on his 13th birthday, effectively ending the regency of his cousin Philippe II, Duke of Orléans. This transition marked a significant moment in French history as Louis XV began to assume full royal powers.
events.name: King Louis XV attains majority

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1723, the Mapuche Uprising began in Chile as indigenous Mapuche forces, led by Toqui Vilumilla, launched an attack against the city of Tucapel. This conflict would last until February 13, 1726, as the Mapuche fought to resist colonial encroachment.
events.name: Mapuche Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1723, the Russian Empire captured Rasht from the Persian Empire, bringing the city and the Gilan Province under Russian control. This event was part of the broader conflict during the Russo-Persian War.
events.name: Capture of Rasht

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1723, Major Abraham Davel attempted to declare the canton of Vaud independent from the Swiss government, seizing control of Lausanne with 500 men. His rebellion was swiftly suppressed, leading to his arrest and execution for treason.
events.name: Abraham Davel's rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On May 27, 1723, the Black Act came into force in Great Britain, aimed at combating illegal hunting. This legislation significantly expanded the number of crimes punishable by death, reflecting the harsh legal measures of the time.

image.caption: Coat of arms of Great Britain.
image.date_qualification: The arms are described as dating from 1714–1801; image_date 2010-07-20 is the image's original date, not the date of the depicted historical event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True; Restrictions: insignia

events.name: Enactment of the Black Act

events.enhanced_description: On May 30, 1723, Johann Sebastian Bach assumed the position of Thomaskantor in Leipzig, where he presented his first new cantata, 'Die Elenden sollen essen, BWV 75,' at St. Nicholas Church. This marked the beginning of his influential tenure in the city.
events.name: Bach's first cantata performance

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1723, during the Russo-Persian War, Baku surrendered to Russian forces. This event marked a significant territorial gain for Russia in the ongoing conflict with Persia.
events.name: Surrender of Baku

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1723, Johann Sebastian Bach's 'Magnificat' was first performed in Leipzig. This choral work is celebrated for its intricate composition and remains a significant piece in the choral repertoire.
events.name: First performance of Bach's Magnificat

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1723, Christian von Wolff delivered a controversial lecture in Prussia, which led to his banishment on charges of atheism. This incident highlighted the tensions between philosophy and religious orthodoxy in early 18th-century Europe.
events.name: Christian von Wolff's lecture and ban

events.enhanced_description: Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, who had served as the Regent of France for King Louis XV, was appointed Prime Minister on August 10, 1723. His tenure was short-lived as he died less than four months later, marking a significant moment in French political history.
events.name: Philippe II, Duke of Orléans appointed Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1723, the Ostend Company was chartered by merchants and shipowners in Antwerp to establish trade routes in the East and West Indies. This initiative marked a significant step in the economic expansion of the Austrian Netherlands.
figures: Merchants and shipowners of the Austrian Netherlands
events.name: Chartering of the Ostend Company

events.enhanced_description: The Peterhof Palace, often referred to as the 'Russian Versailles', was formally opened on August 15, 1723, just outside Saint Petersburg. This grand palace was commissioned by Peter the Great as a symbol of Russian power and culture.
events.name: Opening of the Peterhof Palace

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Saint Petersburg was signed on September 1, 1723, officially ending the Russo-Persian War (1722–1723). This treaty marked a significant territorial gain for Russia in the region.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Saint Petersburg

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1723, Grand Master António Manoel de Vilhena laid the first stone of Fort Manoel in Malta. This fortification was part of the Knights Hospitaller's efforts to strengthen their defenses in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Laying of the first stone of Fort Manoel

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1723, Emperor Peter the Great authorized the formation of the Serbian Hussar Regiment, aimed at recruiting Serbian men into the Russian Imperial Army. This initiative was part of Peter's broader military reforms.
events.name: Authorization of the Serbian Hussar Regiment

events.enhanced_description: Gian Gastone de' Medici ascended to the title of Grand Duke of Tuscany on October 31, 1723, following the death of his father, Cosimo III. His reign marked the end of the Medici dynasty's rule over Tuscany.
events.name: Gian Gastone de' Medici becomes Grand Duke of Tuscany

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1723, the Province of Carolina officially chartered New Bern, which would later become the capital of North Carolina until the establishment of Raleigh. This event marked a significant development in the colonial governance of the region.
events.name: Chartering of New Bern

events.enhanced_description: Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, died on December 2, 1723, at the Palace of Versailles at the age of 49. His death marked the end of a significant political era in France, having served as regent and Prime Minister.

image.caption: Portrait of Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, in armour, by Jean-Baptiste Santerre.
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated circa 1710–1717, during Philippe II’s lifetime; it is not a depiction of his death.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Philippe II, Duke of Orléans

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1723, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of his Christmas Cantata, 'Darzu ist erschienen der Sohn Gottes, BWV 40', in Leipzig. This work exemplified Bach's deep religious devotion and musical genius.
events.name: First performance of Bach's Christmas Cantata

events.enhanced_description: Jack Sheppard, a notorious highwayman known for his daring escapes from prison, was hanged in London on January 1, 1724. His execution marked the end of a sensational criminal career that captivated the public and highlighted the issues of crime and punishment in early 18th-century England.
events.name: Hanging of Jack Sheppard

events.enhanced_description: Willem Mons, the lover of Catherine I of Russia, was executed in early 1724, with his head preserved in alcohol as a grim trophy. This event underscored the volatile nature of court politics and the dangers faced by those close to power in the Russian Empire.
events.name: Execution of Willem Mons

events.enhanced_description: In 1724, the Nizam of Hyderabad declared Hyderabad as the permanent capital of the Indian princely state. This decision established the city as a significant political and cultural center in Southern India, influencing the region's governance and development.
events.name: Hyderabad becomes capital of the Indian princely state

events.enhanced_description: In 1724, China expelled foreign missionaries, reflecting the growing tensions between Western influences and traditional Chinese values. This expulsion was part of a broader trend of resistance against foreign intervention in Chinese affairs during the Qing Dynasty.
events.name: Expulsion of foreign missionaries from China

events.enhanced_description: The construction of Blenheim Palace was completed in 1724, serving as a monumental gift from the nation to the Duke of Marlborough for his military achievements at the Battle of Blenheim in 1704. This grand estate remains a symbol of British heritage and architectural excellence.

locations.name: Blenheim Palace, Oxfordshire, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Completion of Blenheim Palace

events.enhanced_description: In 1724, the Austrian Netherlands formally agreed to the Pragmatic Sanction, a crucial legal framework aimed at ensuring the succession of Charles VI's daughter, Maria Theresa. This agreement was pivotal in maintaining the Habsburg dynasty's stability in Europe.
events.name: Austrian Netherlands agree to the Pragmatic Sanction

events.enhanced_description: In 1724, Shah Mahmud Hotaki of Afghanistan experienced a mental breakdown, which significantly impacted the political landscape of the region. His instability led to a power vacuum and subsequent struggles for control among rival factions.
events.name: Shah Mahmud Hotaki goes insane

events.enhanced_description: The Kaitokudō academy, a merchant school that would later contribute to the establishment of Osaka University, was founded in Japan in 1724. This institution played a vital role in the education of merchants and the economic development of the region.
events.name: Foundation of Kaitokudō academy

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1724, King Philip V of Spain abdicated the throne in favor of his 16-year-old son, Louis I. This transition marked a significant moment in the Spanish monarchy's history.
events.name: Abdication of King Philip V of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1724, the Dutch East India Company cargo ship Fortuyn departed from the Cape of Good Hope on its maiden voyage to Batavia in the Dutch East Indies. Tragically, the ship was never seen again.
events.name: Departure of the Fortuyn

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1724, Spanish Captain General Bruno Mauricio de Zabala forced the Portuguese to abandon their fortified settlement at what would become Montevideo, Uruguay. This event was pivotal in establishing Spanish control over the region.
events.name: Portuguese abandonment of Montevideo

events.enhanced_description: Saint Petersburg State University was established on January 28, 1724, marking a significant development in higher education in Russia. It became one of the leading educational institutions in the country.
events.name: Establishment of Saint Petersburg State University

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1724, Catherine I was officially named tsaritsa by her husband, Peter the Great. This event solidified her position in the Russian monarchy and marked a significant moment in the history of the Russian Empire.
events.name: Catherine I named Tsaritsa

events.enhanced_description: The premiere of 'Giulio Cesare', an Italian opera by George Frideric Handel, took place in London on February 20, 1724. This opera would go on to become one of Handel's most celebrated works.
events.name: Premiere of Giulio Cesare

events.enhanced_description: Pope Innocent XIII died on March 7, 1724, after less than three years as the Roman Catholic pontiff. His death prompted a papal conclave to elect his successor.
events.name: Death of Pope Innocent XIII

events.enhanced_description: The 1724 papal conclave opened in Rome on March 20, 1724, following the death of Pope Innocent XIII. The conclave deliberated for over two months before electing a new pope.
events.name: Opening of the 1724 papal conclave

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach led the first performance of his 'St John Passion' in Leipzig. This work is noted for its profound theological depth and musical complexity.
events.name: First performance of Bach's St John Passion

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of his cantata 'Erfreut euch, ihr Herzen, BWV 66', composed for Easter in Leipzig. This piece reflects Bach's mastery of choral music.
events.name: First performance of Bach's Easter Cantata

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach led the first performance of his cantata 'Du Hirte Israel, höre, BWV 104' in Leipzig. This work illustrates the theme of the Good Shepherd in pastoral music.
events.name: First performance of Bach's Du Hirte Israel, höre

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1724, Jonathan Swift published the first of the seven Drapier's Letters in Dublin, using the pseudonym 'M. B., Drapier'. These pamphlets aimed to rally public opinion against the British imposition of a privately minted copper coinage.
events.name: Publication of the first Drapier's Letter

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1724, Cardinal Giulio Piazza, the Archbishop of Faenza, came within four votes of being elected the new Pope during the papal conclave in Rome. His near election highlighted the intense political maneuvering within the Church.
events.name: Cardinal Giulio Piazza's near election as Pope

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1724, Cardinal Vincenzo Orsini was unanimously selected by the cardinals at the papal conclave in Rome and accepted the papacy as Pope Benedict XIII. His election marked a new chapter in the papacy.

image.caption: Commemorative plaque for Pope Benedict XIII at the Spanish Steps in Rome.
image.date_qualification: Depicted image dated 2009-02-23; the election occurred in 1724.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Election of Pope Benedict XIII

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the cantata 'O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort' (BWV 20) in Leipzig, marking the beginning of his second cycle of chorale cantatas. This performance was part of his significant contributions to sacred music during his tenure at St. Thomas Church.
events.name: Johann Sebastian Bach leads his cantata O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort (BWV 20)

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Constantinople was signed between the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice, concluding sixteen years of conflict. Venice ceded several territories and agreed to pay an annual tribute, reshaping the balance of power in the Eastern Mediterranean.
events.name: The Treaty of Constantinople is signed

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of his cantata 'Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam' (BWV 7) in Leipzig. This work is part of his chorale cantata cycle, reflecting his deep engagement with Lutheran liturgical music.
events.name: Bach leads the first performance of Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam, BWV 7

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of 'Meine Seel erhebt den Herren' (BWV 10) in Leipzig during the Feast of the Visitation. This cantata is notable for its intricate musical structure and theological depth.

image.caption: Portrait of Johann Sebastian Bach by Elias Gottlob Haussmann; Bach holds a copy of the six-part canon BWV 1076.
image.date_qualification: Portrait made in 1748, decades after the 1724 first performance; it depicts Bach, not the performance.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Bach leads the first performance of Meine Seel erhebt den Herren, BWV 10

events.enhanced_description: The Tumult of Thorn, occurring on July 16, 1724, was a violent religious conflict in Royal Prussia that erupted between Catholic and Protestant communities. This event highlighted the tensions of the time and had lasting implications for religious coexistence in the region.
events.name: Tumult of Thorn

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1724, 'Peter the Wild Boy' was captured near Helpensen, Lower Saxony. This feral child became a subject of fascination in Europe, representing the intersection of nature and civilization.
events.name: "Peter the Wild Boy" is captured

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1724, the Hyderabad State was established in India when Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah appointed Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan as its first Nizam. This princely state played a crucial role in the region's history until India's independence.
events.name: The Hyderabad State is created

events.enhanced_description: In August 1724, Longman, the oldest surviving publishing house in England, was founded in London by Thomas Longman. This establishment has played a significant role in the history of publishing and literature in the UK.
events.name: Longman publishing house is founded

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of 'Nimm von uns, Herr, du treuer Gott' (BWV 101) in Leipzig. This chorale cantata is based on a well-known hymn and showcases Bach's mastery of vocal composition.
events.name: Bach leads the first performance of Nimm von uns, Herr, du treuer Gott, BWV 101

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1724, Louis I of Spain died of smallpox at the age of 17, after a brief reign of just seven months. His death led to the resumption of the throne by his father, Philip V, marking a significant moment in Spanish royal history.

image.caption: Oil portrait of Louis I of Spain by Michel Ange Houasse.
image.credit: Michel Ange Houasse — Unknown source Unknown source
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1717, before Louis I's death in 1724; it is a portrait, not a depiction of his death.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Louis I of Spain dies

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1724, José de Grimaldo resumed his position as Prime Minister of Spain following the return of King Philip V to the throne. Grimaldo's leadership was pivotal during a tumultuous period in Spanish politics.
events.name: José de Grimaldo resumes office as Prime Minister of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of 'Jesu, der du meine Seele' (BWV 78) in Leipzig. This chorale cantata is based on a passion hymn and exemplifies Bach's profound theological and musical insights.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Johann Sebastian Bach by Gebel.
image.date_qualification: The painting is described as dating before 1798; the 2014 timestamp is the image file's recorded original date, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Bach leads the first performance of Jesu, der du meine Seele, BWV 78

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1724, the Paris Bourse, the stock exchange for France, was established by order of King Louis XV, following the advice of Nicolas Ravot d'Ombreval. This institution marked a significant development in the financial landscape of France.
events.name: The Paris Bourse is created

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of 'Herr Gott, dich loben alle wir' (BWV 130) in Leipzig for the feast of archangel Michael. This work is characterized by its rich choral textures and theological themes.
events.name: Bach leads the first performance of Herr Gott, dich loben alle wir, BWV 130

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1724, Muhammad bin Nasir was elected as the new Imam of Oman following the overthrow of his brother, Saif bin Sultan II. This event marked a significant shift in Omani leadership and governance.
events.name: Muhammad bin Nasir is elected as Imam of Oman

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1724, the historic Teatro Nuovo opera house was inaugurated in Naples with the premiere of Antonio Orefice's comic opera 'Lo Simmele'. This venue became a significant cultural landmark in the Italian opera scene.
events.name: Teatro Nuovo opera house is inaugurated

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1724, Yeongjo ascended to the throne as the new Emperor of Korea following the death of his older brother, Gyeongjong. Yeongjo's reign would last nearly 52 years, significantly impacting Korean history.
events.name: Yeongjo becomes Emperor of Korea

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of 'Schmücke dich, o liebe Seele' in Leipzig. This cantata, based on a communion hymn, showcases Bach's intricate musical style and deep spirituality.
events.name: Bach leads the first performance of Schmücke dich, o liebe Seele

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1724, George Frideric Handel's opera 'Tamerlano' premiered in London. This opera is notable for its complex characters and rich musical composition, contributing to Handel's reputation as a leading composer of his time.
events.name: George Frideric Handel's opera Tamerlano premieres

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1724, Joseph Blake, known as 'Blueskin', was hanged in London for his crimes as a highwayman. His execution highlighted the harsh penalties for crime during this period in British history.
events.name: Joseph Blake (alias 'Blueskin') is hanged

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1724, notorious highwayman Jack Sheppard was hanged in London. His life and criminal exploits captured the public's imagination, making him a legendary figure in British folklore.
events.name: Highwayman Jack Sheppard is hanged

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1724, the Dutch East India Company frigate Slot ter Hooge struck rocks and sank off Porto Santo Island, Madeira, resulting in the loss of 221 of the 254 people on board. This maritime disaster underscored the dangers of sea travel during this era.
events.name: Dutch East India Company frigate Slot ter Hooge sinks

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1724, Metropolitan Mojsije Petrović, leader of the Serbian Orthodox Church within the Habsburg monarchy, issued a 57-point decree aimed at purging the church of Turkish influence. This decree was significant in the context of religious and cultural identity in the region.
events.name: Metropolitan Mojsije Petrović issues decree

events.enhanced_description: In 1724, following an attack against Jesuit Catholics, ten Lutheran officials, including Mayor Johann Gottfried Rösner, were publicly executed in Toruń. This brutal act reflected the intense religious conflicts of the time and the precarious position of Protestant leaders in predominantly Catholic regions.
events.name: Execution of Lutheran officials in Thorn

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1724, the Viceroyalty of Zhili was recreated in the Chinese Empire by Emperor Yongzheng, with Li Weijun appointed as the first Viceroy. This administrative change was significant for governance in northern China.
events.name: Viceroyalty of Zhili is recreated

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1724, Francesco Valesio resumed writing his 'Diario di Roma', a detailed account of daily life in Rome, after a 13-year hiatus. His writings provide valuable insights into the social and cultural dynamics of the time.
events.name: Francesco Valesio resumes writing Diario di Roma

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1724, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of his chorale cantata 'Gelobet seist du, Jesu Christ, BWV 91' in Leipzig. This work is based on Martin Luther's Christmas hymn from 1524, showcasing Bach's deep integration of religious themes within his musical compositions.
events.name: First performance of Gelobet seist du, Jesu Christ, BWV 91

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1725, Johann Sebastian Bach conducted the first performance of his chorale cantata 'Jesu, nun sei gepreiset, BWV 41' in Leipzig. This work is celebrated for its intricate musical structure and profound theological themes.
events.name: First performance of Jesu, nun sei gepreiset, BWV 41

events.enhanced_description: In January 1725, the Tokugawa shogunate implemented the Gonin Gumi policy, organizing groups of five households into units responsible for collective behavior. This system aimed to enhance social order and accountability within communities across Japan.
events.name: Implementation of Gonin Gumi policy in Japan

events.enhanced_description: In 1725, the Terengganu Sultanate was established in Terengganu Darul Iman, marking a significant development in the political landscape of the Malay Peninsula. This sultanate played a crucial role in the region's history and governance.
events.name: Establishment of the Terengganu Sultanate

events.enhanced_description: In 1725, during the Qing Dynasty in China, 66 copies of the Complete Classics Collection of Ancient China were printed, requiring the creation of 250,000 movable type characters cast in bronze. This monumental work reflects the rich literary and cultural heritage of China.
events.name: Printing of the Complete Classics Collection of Ancient China

events.enhanced_description: In 1725, Freemasonry was established in France as an English import, marking the beginning of Masonic traditions in the country. This development would influence French society and culture in the years to come.
events.name: Establishment of Freemasonry in France

events.enhanced_description: In 1725, Antonio Vivaldi published The Four Seasons, a set of violin concertos that would become one of the most famous and celebrated works in classical music. This composition showcased Vivaldi's innovative approach to music and his mastery of the violin.
events.name: Publication of The Four Seasons by Vivaldi

events.enhanced_description: In 1725, Johann Joseph Fux published Gradus ad Parnassum, a seminal work on counterpoint that laid out the rules for constructing music. This influential text became a foundational resource for composers and musicians in the study of music theory.
events.name: Publication of Gradus ad Parnassum by Johann Joseph Fux

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1725, Johann Sebastian Bach led the first performance of 'Liebster Immanuel, Herzog der Frommen, BWV 123', a chorale cantata for Epiphany, in Leipzig. This piece reflects Bach's mastery in blending musical artistry with religious devotion.

image.caption: Portrait of Ahasverus Fritsch with a Latin encomium by Johann Christoph Treuner.
image.date_qualification: Portrait of the hymn author associated with the cantata; the image date is 1672, preceding the first performance in 1725.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: First performance of Liebster Immanuel, Herzog der Frommen, BWV 123

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1725, James Macrae, a former captain for the British East India Company, was appointed to administer the Madras Presidency. His tenure marked significant reforms in governance across Southern India, influencing the region's administrative practices.
events.name: James Macrae appointed to administer Madras Presidency

events.enhanced_description: On January 20, 1725, James Figg hosted the first recorded international boxing match in London, featuring English drover Bob Whitaker against Venetian gondolier Alberto di Carni. This event marked a significant moment in the history of boxing, showcasing the sport's growing popularity.
events.name: First recorded international boxing match

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1725, the Spanish corsair Amaro Pargo was granted the title of Hidalgo, signifying his noble status. This recognition highlighted the intersection of piracy and nobility in early 18th-century Spain.

image.caption: Tombstone of Amaro Pargo at the Parish of Santo Domingo de Guzmán in San Cristóbal de La Laguna, Tenerife, Spain.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2015-01-20; the image documents a later site associated with Amaro Pargo, not the 1725 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Amaro Pargo receives title of Hidalgo

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1725, Catherine I ascended to the throne as Empress of Russia following the death of her husband, Peter the Great. Her reign marked a significant transition in Russian history, as she navigated the complexities of leadership in a rapidly changing empire.
events.name: Catherine I becomes Empress of Russia

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1725, the first reported case of white men scalping Native Americans occurred in the New Hampshire colony. This brutal act marked a significant and tragic moment in the history of colonial relations with Indigenous peoples in North America.
events.name: First reported case of scalping in New Hampshire

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1725, Johann Sebastian Bach's chorale cantata 'Wie schön leuchtet der Morgenstern, BWV 1' was first performed during the Feast of the Annunciation, coinciding with Palm Sunday. This work exemplifies Bach's ability to intertwine liturgical themes with musical innovation.
events.name: First performance of Wie schön leuchtet der Morgenstern, BWV 1

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1725, the second performance of Johann Sebastian Bach's 'St John Passion, BWV 245' took place at St. Thomas Church in Leipzig. This performance included movements from his earlier Weimarer Passion, showcasing Bach's evolving style and deepening theological exploration.
events.name: Second performance of St John Passion, BWV 245

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1725, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, and King Philip V of Spain signed the Treaty of Vienna. This treaty was significant in European diplomacy, addressing territorial disputes and alliances in the wake of the War of the Spanish Succession.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1725, the Black Watch was raised as a military company under General George Wade as part of efforts to pacify the Scottish Highlands. This regiment would become one of the most famous and storied units in British military history.
events.name: Formation of the Black Watch

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1725, Empress Catherine I of Russia established the Order of Saint Alexander Nevsky during the grand wedding of her daughter Anna. This order was intended to honor military leaders and became a significant symbol of Russian nobility.
events.name: Creation of the Order of Saint Alexander Nevsky

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1725, Jonathan Wild, a fraudulent 'Thief-Taker General', was hanged at Tyburn in London for his complicity in aiding criminals. His execution highlighted the corruption within law enforcement and the complexities of crime in early 18th-century England.

image.caption: Printed gallows ticket for Jonathan Wild’s hanging at Tyburn.
image.credit: User:.... — Originally uploaded to en: by User:Geogre at October 20, 2004, with the following description: Gallows ticket for the hanging of w:Jonathan Wild . Note that the emblem at the top is Wild's own imprint, showing him in cloth cap and bearing a mace as a symbol of policing. The main illustration bears the emblems of Death (left) and the Grave (right), surmounted by devices of imprisonment. Between Death and the Grave is a small casket. The text invites all criminals, and then ladies and gentlemen, to walk with their friend I--- W--d to the "triple tree," which was Tyburn. The gallows there were a simple L-shaped beams arranged with three together.
image.date_qualification: The image date is not supplied. The ticket is identified as being for the hanging on 24 May 1725; that event date does not establish when the ticket was produced.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Hanging of Jonathan Wild

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1725, the Malt tax riots began in Hamilton, Scotland, in response to increased prices of beer and whisky due to new taxes. The unrest quickly spread throughout Scotland, reflecting widespread discontent with government policies and economic hardship.

locations.name: Hamilton, South Lanarkshire, Scotland, United Kingdom

events.name: Malt tax riots in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1725, the Grand Lodge of Ireland convened its first recorded meeting, establishing itself as the second oldest Grand Lodge in the world and the oldest in continuous existence. This event marked a significant moment in the history of Freemasonry, influencing its development in Ireland and beyond.

image.caption: The Grand Lodge of Ireland building in Dublin.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2018-06-19; the image documents the later site, not the 1725 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Grand Lodge of Ireland holds its first recorded meeting

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1725, Mattheus de Haan was appointed as the Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies, overseeing the Dutch colonial administration until his death in 1729. His tenure was marked by the complexities of colonial governance and trade in Southeast Asia.
events.name: Mattheus de Haan becomes Governor-General of the Dutch East Indies

events.enhanced_description: On July 15, 1725, Sir Richard Everard was appointed as the 4th Governor of North Carolina. His administration faced challenges related to governance and relations with Native American tribes during a period of colonial expansion.
events.name: Sir Richard Everard becomes Governor of North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1725, the civil marriage of King Louis XV of France and Princess Maria Leszczyńska took place in Strasbourg, with the Duke of Orléans acting as proxy for the King. This union strengthened ties between France and Poland and was significant in the context of European dynastic politics.
events.name: Civil marriage of King Louis XV and Princess Maria Leszczyńska

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1725, the French Navy ship Chameau sank off the coast of Nova Scotia due to a storm, resulting in the deaths of at least 216 people. The tragedy highlighted the perils of maritime travel during this period and the ship's valuable cargo was discovered decades later.
events.name: Sinking of the Chameau

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1725, the wedding ceremony of King Louis XV and Maria Leszczyńska took place in Fontainebleau, solidifying her role as Queen Consort of France. Their marriage would endure for nearly 43 years, significantly impacting the French monarchy.
events.name: Wedding of King Louis XV and Maria Leszczyńska

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1725, the Treaty of Hanover was signed between Great Britain, France, and Prussia, aiming to stabilize relations and prevent conflicts in Europe. This treaty was part of the broader diplomatic efforts during the early 18th century.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Hanover

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1725, Joan Paul Schaghen was appointed by the Dutch East India Company as the Governor of Ceylon following the death of Johannes Hertenberg. His leadership was crucial during a time of colonial expansion and competition in the region.
events.name: Joan Paul Schaghen appointed Governor of Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: On October 23, 1725, Russia dispatched 1,500 troops and 120 civilians to its border with China to survey boundaries for a treaty with the Chinese Empire. The mission was led by Serbian adventurer Sava Vladislavich, who aimed to prepare maps for future negotiations.
events.name: Russia dispatches troops to survey border with China

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1725, the fourth and final treaty of the 1725 Peace of Vienna was signed, creating an alliance between Austria and Spain. This treaty was part of the broader diplomatic landscape of Europe during the early 18th century.
events.name: Fourth treaty of the 1725 Peace of Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1725, William Bradford introduced the New-York Gazette, the first newspaper in the Province of New York, marking a significant development in colonial journalism and communication. This publication laid the groundwork for the growth of media in America.

locations.name: New York, New York, United States

events.name: First newspaper in the Province of New York

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1725, Chief Chicagou of the Mitchigamea tribe and chiefs from five other tribes of the Illini Confederation were received as guests by King Louis XV in Paris. Chicagou pledged the support of the Illini for the French presence in North America, highlighting the importance of indigenous alliances.
events.name: Chief Chicagou received by King Louis XV

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1725, British astronomers James Bradley and Samuel Molyneux began observations of stellar parallax at Molyneux's private observatory. These observations were crucial in leading to Bradley's discovery of the aberration of light, a significant advancement in astronomy.
events.name: Observations of stellar parallax by Bradley and Molyneux

events.enhanced_description: On December 12, 1725, Johan Willem Ripperda, the former Dutch Ambassador to Spain, arrived in Madrid claiming to be appointed as the new Prime Minister by King Philip V. His audacious claim was initially accepted, but he was forced to resign after four months.
events.name: Johan Willem Ripperda claims Prime Ministership in Spain

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1725, a treaty was signed by chiefs of four member tribes of the Wabanaki Confederacy and representatives from the British provinces of Massachusetts Bay, New Hampshire, and Nova Scotia, effectively ending Dummer's War. This treaty marked a significant step towards peace in the region.
events.name: Treaty ends Dummer's War

events.enhanced_description: In 1726, Muhammad bin Saud became the head of the House of Saud, marking the beginning of a significant political dynasty in the Arabian Peninsula. His leadership would lay the groundwork for the eventual establishment of the modern Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
events.name: Muhammad bin Saud becomes head of the House of Saud

events.enhanced_description: In 1726, the remaining ruins of Liverpool Castle were finally demolished, marking the end of an era for one of the city's historical landmarks. This demolition reflected the broader trends of urban development and modernization in 18th-century England.
events.name: Demolition of Liverpool Castle

events.enhanced_description: In late 1726, Nader Shah successfully recaptured the city of Mashhad, which had been a significant stronghold in his campaign to consolidate power in Persia. This victory was crucial in establishing his authority and setting the stage for his future conquests.
events.name: Nader recaptures Mashhad

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1726, the Conventicle Act (Konventikelplakatet) was adopted in Sweden, outlawing all non-Lutheran religious meetings outside of church services. This act reflected the state's control over religious practices during this period.
events.name: The Conventicle Act adopted in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1726, the First Treaty of Vienna was signed between Austria, the Holy Roman Empire, and Spain, establishing the Austro-Spanish Alliance in preparation for a potential war against Great Britain. This treaty was a key moment in European diplomatic history.
events.name: First Treaty of Vienna signed

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1726, the Dutch East India Company frigate Aagtekerke set sail from the Dutch Cape Colony on its maiden voyage to the East Indies, but it was never seen again. The loss of the ship and its crew of 200 remains a mystery in maritime history.
events.name: Maiden voyage of the Aagtekerke

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1726, the Supreme Privy Council was established in Russia, serving as an advisory body to the Tsar. This institution played a significant role in the governance of the Russian Empire during the 18th century.
events.name: Establishment of the Supreme Privy Council in Russia

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Negrete marked a significant turning point in the conflict between the Mapuche people and Spanish colonial authorities in Chile, effectively bringing an end to the Mapuche uprising that had persisted from 1723 to 1726. This event underscored the complexities of colonial governance and indigenous resistance in the region.
events.name: The Parliament of Negrete

events.enhanced_description: On March 2, 1726, a night watchman in London discovered a severed head by the River Thames, later identified as that of Catherine Hayes' husband. This gruesome find led to a sensational trial and the eventual execution of Hayes and her accomplice, highlighting the darker aspects of crime and justice in early 18th-century England.
events.name: Discovery of Catherine Hayes' husband's severed head

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1726, Emperor Yongzheng of China issued a special edict to interrogate Qin Daoran regarding a conspiracy involving his brothers, Yintang, Yin-ssu, and Yin-ti, aimed at overthrowing him. This event reflects the intense political intrigue and familial rivalries within the Qing dynasty.
events.name: Yongzheng's edict against his brothers

events.enhanced_description: On March 29, 1726, the slave ship L'Aurore arrived in New Orleans, bringing with it 290 enslaved Africans captured in Gambia. This marked one of the first large-scale shipments of slaves to the region, significantly impacting the demographic and cultural landscape of colonial Louisiana.
events.name: Arrival of L'Aurore in New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: On March 30, 1726, King Haffon of the Kingdom of Whydah permitted Portuguese traders to construct Fort São João Batista in Savi. This event was met with resistance from the Dutch West India Company, which attempted to destroy the fort, illustrating the fierce competition among European powers for control over trade in West Africa.
events.name: Fort São João Batista construction

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1726, Jacques de Campredon, France's first ambassador to Russia, concluded his mission after four years of failed negotiations for a Franco-Russian alliance and an unsuccessful marriage proposal between King Louis XV and Catherine I's daughter. His departure marked a significant moment in Franco-Russian relations during the early 18th century.
events.name: Departure of Jacques de Campredon

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1726, the French philosopher Voltaire began his exile in England, a period that would greatly influence his writings and thoughts on liberty and governance. This exile was a response to his conflicts with the French authorities, and it allowed him to engage with Enlightenment ideas flourishing in Britain.
events.name: Voltaire's exile in England

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1726, King Louis XV dismissed Louis Henri, Duke of Bourbon, from his position as Prime Minister of France, appointing André-Hercule de Fleury in his place. This political shift reflected the ongoing power struggles within the French court and the King's desire for a more stable administration.
events.name: Dismissal of Louis Henri, Duke of Bourbon

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1726, André-Hercule de Fleury was recalled from exile by King Louis XV and subsequently banished Louis Henri, Duke of Bourbon, and Madame de Prie from court. This event marked a significant consolidation of power for Fleury and a shift in the political landscape of France.

image.caption: Portrait of André-Hercule de Fleury, a painting from the workshop of Hyacinthe Rigaud.
image.credit: Workshop of Hyacinthe Rigaud — National Gallery, London
image.date_qualification: Portrait made after 1728; it is not a contemporary depiction of the 1726 political events.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Fleury's return and banishment of Bourbon

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1726, notorious pirate Nicholas Brown was captured near Xtabi, Jamaica. His capture was part of the broader efforts by colonial authorities to suppress piracy in the Caribbean, which had become a significant threat to maritime trade.
events.name: Capture of Pirate Nicholas Brown

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1726, the Portuguese Navy galleon HMFMS Santa Rosa suffered a catastrophic explosion off the coast of Recife, killing nearly all of its 700 passengers and crew. The incident highlighted the dangers of maritime transport during this period, particularly concerning the handling of gunpowder.
events.name: Explosion of HMFMS Santa Rosa

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1726, André-Hercule de Fleury was appointed a Roman Catholic Cardinal by Pope Benedict XIII. This elevation marked a significant step in his ecclesiastical career, which would later lead to his role as Prime Minister of France.
events.name: André-Hercule de Fleury made Cardinal

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1726, the Nanfan Treaty, originally signed in 1701 between the Iroquois Confederacy and the British Province of New York, was amended by both parties. This amendment reflects the ongoing negotiations and complexities of colonial relations with Native American tribes.

locations.name: New York, New York, United States

events.name: Amendment of the Nanfan Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On September 16, 1726, a devastating earthquake struck Palermo, Sicily, resulting in the deaths of 226 people. This natural disaster underscored the vulnerability of urban centers in the region to seismic activity.
events.name: Earthquake in Palermo

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1726, Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI issued an order that restricted the number of Jews who could be legally recognized as legitimate householders. This decree reflected the broader context of Jewish rights and restrictions in early 18th-century Europe.
events.name: Charles VI's order limiting Jewish householders

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1726, Pope Benedict XIII extended permission for the celebration of the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel to the entire Roman Catholic Church. This decision reflected the Pope's efforts to unify and promote Catholic traditions across Europe.
events.name: Pope Benedict XIII extends feast permission

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1726, Juan Bautista de Orendáin y Azpilicueta was reappointed as Secretary of the Universal Bureau, effectively the Prime Minister of Spain, following the retirement of José de Grimaldo. This appointment was significant in the context of Spanish politics during the early 18th century.
figures: Juan Bautista de Orendáin y Azpilicueta
events.name: Juan Bautista de Orendáin y Azpilicueta appointed Secretary

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1726, Grigore II Ghica ascended to the throne as the Prince of Moldavia after Mihai Racoviță stepped aside. His reign would be marked by efforts to navigate the complex political landscape of Eastern Europe during the Ottoman Empire's dominance.

image.caption: Portrait painting of Grigore Ghica II by Theodor Aman.
image.date_qualification: Portrait of Grigore II Ghica, created in 1863, well after his 1726 accession; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Grigore II Ghica becomes Prince of Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: In November 1726, Mary Toft allegedly gave birth to 16 rabbits in Godalming, England, a bizarre claim that later turned out to be a hoax. This incident captivated public attention and raised questions about medical ethics and the gullibility of society.
events.name: Mary Toft's rabbit births hoax

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1726, Jonathan Swift's satirical novel 'Gulliver's Travels' was published anonymously in London, quickly selling out within a week. The novel's sharp critique of human nature and society established Swift as a leading literary figure of his time.
events.name: Publication of Gulliver's Travels

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1726, Callinicus, the Metropolitan of Heraclea, died suddenly just one day after being elected as the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. His unexpected death raised questions about the political machinations surrounding the election process within the Eastern Orthodox Church.
events.name: Death of Callinicus, Metropolitan of Heraclea

events.enhanced_description: On December 21, 1726, Spain's ambassador to Great Britain demanded the return of Gibraltar, accusing Britain of violating the Treaty of Utrecht. This demand escalated tensions, leading to the Thirteenth Siege of Gibraltar that began on February 22, 1727.
events.name: Demand for Gibraltar

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1726, Spanish settlers founded the settlement of Montevideo in the Viceroyalty of Peru. This strategic location would later become a significant port city and a focal point for trade and military operations in the region.
events.name: Founding of Montevideo

events.enhanced_description: In February 1727, Muhammad bin Saud founded the First Saudi State, marking the beginning of a significant political entity in the Arabian Peninsula. This state would lay the groundwork for the future Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
events.name: Founding of the First Saudi State

events.enhanced_description: Janet (Jenny) Horne of Loth, Sutherland, became the last alleged witch in the British Isles to be executed, burned at the stake in Dornoch, Scotland. This event marked a significant moment in the history of witch trials in Britain.
events.name: Execution of Janet (Jenny) Horne

events.enhanced_description: The first Amish settlers moved to North America, marking the beginning of a significant migration that would shape the cultural landscape of the region. This movement was driven by the desire for religious freedom and community.
events.name: First Amish move to North America

events.enhanced_description: Lt. Col. Francisco de Mello Palheta smuggled coffee seeds to Brazil, initiating the country's rise as a major coffee producer. This act laid the groundwork for Brazil's future coffee empire.

image.caption: Map showing Brazilian coffee-growing regions for Arabica and Robusta.
image.credit: jonkerz ♠talk 10:39, 28 April 2013 (UTC) — Own work , based on File:Brazil location map.svg
image.date_qualification: Map dated 2013-04-28; it does not depict the 1727 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Francisco de Mello Palheta smuggles coffee seeds to Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On January 6, 1727, Martin Spanberg and two other members of the First Kamchatka Expedition arrived in Okhotsk after nearly two years of travel from Saint Petersburg. This expedition, led by Vitus Bering, aimed to explore the Arctic and expand Russian territorial claims.
events.name: Arrival of the First Kamchatka Expedition in Okhotsk

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1727, Charité Hospital was established in Berlin, originally converted from an institution built to prepare for a bubonic plague epidemic. Under the orders of King Frederick William I, it became a center for medical research and assistance to the poor.

image.caption: Charité University Hospital Berlin after renovation.
image.date_qualification: A 2016 photograph of the modern hospital site, not a depiction of its establishment in 1727.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Establishment of Charité Hospital

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1727, Abd el-Sayed was enthroned as Pope John XVII of Alexandria, becoming the 105th leader of the Coptic Christian Church. His papacy would last until his death on April 20, 1745, during a time of significant religious and cultural development.
events.name: Enthronement of Pope John XVII of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: On February 2, 1727, Johann Sebastian Bach's solo cantata, Ich habe genug (BWV 82), premiered in Leipzig. This work is celebrated for its profound emotional depth and is a significant contribution to the Baroque music repertoire.
events.name: Premiere of Bach's Ich habe genug

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1727, the German composer George Frideric Handel became a British subject. This pivotal moment allowed him to fully immerse himself in the vibrant musical culture of Britain, leading to his prolific output and lasting legacy.
events.name: George Frideric Handel becomes a British subject

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1727, the Thirteenth Siege of Gibraltar commenced as Spain attempted to recapture the territory from British control. This military engagement marked a significant chapter in the ongoing conflict over Gibraltar, which remains strategically important.
events.name: Thirteenth Siege of Gibraltar begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1727, the Battle of Halidzor took place in Armenia, where a small group of defenders successfully overcame a much larger Ottoman army. This victory was significant in the context of regional resistance against Ottoman expansion.
events.name: Battle of Halidzor

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1727, the Kingdom of Dahomey, under King Trudo Agaja, conquered and annexed the Kingdom of Xwéda after King Haffon was killed in battle. This expansion solidified Dahomey's power in West Africa.
events.name: Dahomey conquers Xwéda

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1727, Ismail Ibn Sharif, who had ruled as Sultan of Morocco for 55 years, died at the age of 81. His death triggered a tumultuous 30-year struggle among his seven sons for succession to the throne.

image.caption: Portrait of Ismail Ibn Sharif, credited to Germain Moüette.
image.credit: Germain Moüette — Histoire des conquestes de Mouley Archy (1683), Datenbank Tripota in der Wissenschaftlichen Bibliothek der Stadt Trier/Stadtarchiv
image.date_qualification: Image date: 1683, as supplied; predates the 1727 death event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Ismail Ibn Sharif

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1727, Johann Sebastian Bach's St Matthew Passion (BWV 244b) premiered at St. Thomas Church in Leipzig. This monumental work is regarded as one of the greatest achievements in Western classical music.
events.name: Premiere of Bach's St Matthew Passion

events.enhanced_description: On May 12, 1727, the Brotherly Agreement was adopted by the Moravian Church community at Herrnhut, influenced by Count Nicolaus Zinzendorf. This agreement marked the beginning of a significant renewal within the church, emphasizing unity and mission.
events.name: Brotherly Agreement of the Moravian Church

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1727, Peter II of Russia was made Emperor at the young age of eleven. His reign was marked by the influence of regents and the challenges of governing a vast empire.
events.name: Peter II of Russia becomes Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1727, the Royal Bank of Scotland was founded by Royal Charter in Edinburgh. This institution would become one of the leading banks in the UK and play a significant role in the development of modern banking.
events.name: Founding of the Royal Bank of Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1727, George, Prince of Wales, ascended to the throne as King George II of Great Britain following the death of his father. His reign would see significant developments in British politics and colonial expansion.
events.name: George II becomes King of Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1727, Spain officially ceased hostilities after its failed attempt to recapture Gibraltar from Britain. A truce was signed the following day, marking the end of a significant military engagement.
events.name: Spain ceases hostilities over Gibraltar

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1727, Uxbridge, Massachusetts, was incorporated as a town. This event marked an important step in the development of local governance in colonial America.
events.name: Incorporation of Uxbridge, Massachusetts

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1727, Shuja-ud-Din Muhammad Khan ascended to the position of Nawab of Bengal following the death of his father-in-law, Murshid Quli Khan. At this time, Bengal was a significant province within the Mughal Empire.
events.name: Shuja-ud-Din Muhammad Khan becomes Nawab of Bengal

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1727, seventeen Ursuline Sisters from France landed in New Orleans, Louisiana. Their arrival marked the beginning of significant Catholic educational and charitable efforts in the region, including the establishment of the Ursuline Academy.
events.name: Ursuline Sisters land in New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1727, the Moravian Church community at Herrnhut experienced a significant Pentecostalist event, which revitalized their spiritual practices and community life. This experience was pivotal in the church's 18th-century renewal.
events.name: Moravian Church undergoes Pentecostalist experience

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1727, elections for the House of Commons commenced in Great Britain, continuing until October 17. This election cycle was crucial in shaping the political landscape of the country.
events.name: Elections for the House of Commons begin

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1727, Anne, the eldest daughter of King George II of Great Britain, was given the title of Princess Royal. This title is traditionally bestowed upon the eldest daughter of the reigning monarch.
events.name: Anne becomes Princess Royal

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1727, a tragic barn fire during a puppet show in Burwell, Cambridgeshire, resulted in the deaths of 78 people, many of whom were children. This incident highlighted the dangers of public gatherings and led to increased safety regulations.
events.name: Burwell barn fire during puppet show

events.enhanced_description: George II of Great Britain was crowned at Westminster Abbey, where Handel's Coronation Anthems, including the famous 'Zadok the Priest', were composed for the occasion. This anthem has since been a staple at every British monarch's coronation.
events.name: George II of Great Britain is crowned

events.enhanced_description: The elections for the British House of Commons concluded with the Whigs, led by Sir Robert Walpole, securing a supermajority by winning 415 out of 558 seats. This marked a significant decrease in the Tories' representation, which fell from 169 to 128 seats.
events.name: British House of Commons elections conclude

events.enhanced_description: The Tabriz earthquake struck Persia, resulting in a catastrophic loss of life, with estimates of around 77,000 fatalities. This disaster had profound effects on the region's population and infrastructure.
events.name: Tabriz earthquake

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Seville was signed by representatives of the Netherlands, marking a significant diplomatic agreement in European politics. This treaty aimed to resolve ongoing conflicts and establish peace among the involved nations.
events.name: The Netherlands signs the Treaty of Seville

events.enhanced_description: The foundation stone of Jerusalem's Church in Berlin was laid, marking the beginning of a significant architectural project that would become a notable landmark in the city. The church reflects the cultural and religious diversity of Berlin.
events.name: Foundation stone of Jerusalem's Church in Berlin is laid

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Bank of Scotland issued its first pound note, marking a significant development in the history of currency in Great Britain. This event highlighted the bank's role in the financial system following the union of England and Scotland.
events.name: Royal Bank of Scotland issues first pound note

events.enhanced_description: The London Evening Post, a conservative newspaper, published its first issue, establishing itself as a significant voice in British media. It continued to operate for 70 years, influencing public opinion and political discourse.
events.name: The London Evening Post publishes its first issue

events.enhanced_description: Voltaire, the prominent French Enlightenment writer, concluded his exile in England, returning to France. His time in England significantly influenced his philosophical views and writings.
events.name: Voltaire Ends Exile in England

events.enhanced_description: English astronomer James Bradley utilized his observations of stellar aberration to calculate the speed of light and noted the nutation of the Earth's axis. His work laid important groundwork for future astronomical studies.
events.name: James Bradley's Observations

events.enhanced_description: The Real y Pontificia Universidad de San Gerónimo de la Habana, the oldest university in Cuba, was founded in Havana. This institution played a crucial role in the education and cultural development of the region.
events.name: Foundation of the Real y Pontificia Universidad de San Gerónimo de la Habana

events.enhanced_description: The coronation of Peter II as Tsar of the Russian Empire took place in Moscow, marking the beginning of his reign. This event was significant in the context of Russian history and the continuation of the Romanov dynasty.
events.name: Coronation of Peter II as Tsar of Russia

events.enhanced_description: The Beggar's Opera, a ballad opera written by John Gay with music arranged by Johann Christoph Pepusch, premiered at the Lincoln's Inn Fields Theatre in London. This production became the most popular theatrical work of the 18th century, satirizing the conventions of Italian opera.
events.name: The Beggar's Opera is performed for the first time

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Palkhed, Maratha Peshwa Bajirao I achieved a decisive victory over the first Nizam of Hyderabad, Nizam-ul-Mulk. This battle was a significant event in the Deccan Wars, showcasing the military prowess of the Maratha Empire.
events.name: Battle of Palkhed

events.enhanced_description: Jean-Jacques Rousseau left Geneva for the first time, marking a pivotal moment in his life that would influence his philosophical writings and ideas. This departure set the stage for his later works that would impact the Enlightenment.

image.caption: Photograph of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s tomb in the Panthéon in Paris.
image.date_qualification: A 2013 photograph of Rousseau’s tomb, a contextual site image rather than a depiction of his departure from Geneva.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau leaves Geneva

events.enhanced_description: Saint Serapion of Algiers, the first Mercedarian of the Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy, was canonized by Pope Benedict XIII. His canonization recognized his contributions to the church and his dedication to the faith.
events.name: Canonization of Saint Serapion of Algiers

events.enhanced_description: John Essington, a member of the British House of Commons, was expelled after a successful petition led to his unseating. His financial troubles ultimately led to his demise in Newgate Prison less than a year later.
events.name: Expulsion of John Essington from the House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: The 82 survivors of the wrecked Dutch East India Company frigate Zeewijk arrived at their original destination of Batavia in the Dutch East Indies, now Jakarta, Indonesia. They had built a new ship, Sloepie, to complete their journey.
events.name: Survivors of the Zeewijk arrive in Batavia

events.enhanced_description: Saint Margaret of Cortona, known as the patron saint of the falsely accused, homeless people, and those suffering from mental illness, was canonized. Her life and works continue to inspire many in the Catholic faith.
events.name: Canonization of Saint Margaret of Cortona

events.enhanced_description: Pope Gregory VII, who served as pontiff from 1073 to 1085, was canonized as a Roman Catholic saint. His papacy was marked by significant reforms and conflicts that shaped the church's role in medieval Europe.
events.name: Canonization of Pope Gregory VII

events.enhanced_description: The Royal Bank of Scotland introduced the overdraft, allowing merchant William Hogg to access cash credit to pay his creditors. This innovation in banking practices had lasting implications for financial transactions.
events.name: Royal Bank of Scotland invents the overdraft

events.enhanced_description: The Congress of Soissons opened in the French town of Soissons to negotiate a treaty between Great Britain and Spain. The discussions would lead to a treaty recognizing territorial claims and establishing peace.
events.name: Congress of Soissons opens

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Kyakhta was signed at the border city of Kyakhta between representatives of Tsar Peter II of Russia and Emperor Yongzheng of China. This treaty established the border between the two empires and facilitated trade.
events.name: Treaty of Kyakhta signed

events.enhanced_description: The First Kamchatka Expedition, led by Vitus Bering, set sail from the Kamchatka Peninsula on the ship Archangel Gabriel. This expedition was crucial for mapping the northern Pacific and exploring new territories.
events.name: First Kamchatka Expedition

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 8, Prince Teruhito, son of Emperor Nakamikado, was named as the Crown Prince of Japan. He would later ascend to the throne as Emperor Sakuramachi at the age of 15, following his father's death.
events.name: Prince Teruhito named Crown Prince of Japan

events.enhanced_description: After a brief reign of only four months, Abdalmalik was deposed as Sultan of Morocco by his half-brother Ahmad ad Dahabi, whom he had previously ousted. Following his deposition, Abdalmalik was captured and executed on March 2, 1729, marking a turbulent period in Moroccan leadership.
events.name: Deposition of Abdalmalik as Sultan of Morocco

events.enhanced_description: The Szeged witch trials concluded with the execution of twelve individuals, six men and six women, who were burned at the stake on Boszorkány Sziget, or 'Witch Island.' This event reflects the intense superstitions and societal fears prevalent in 18th-century Hungary.
events.name: Szeged Witch Trials Execution

events.enhanced_description: Due to advancing Arctic ice, the First Kamchatka Expedition, led by Vitus Bering, was forced to turn back after incorrectly concluding that they had reached the easternmost point of Russia and Asia. The expedition failed to spot the coast of Alaska, highlighting the challenges of Arctic exploration.
events.name: First Kamchatka Expedition Turnaround

events.enhanced_description: The City of Nuuk was founded in Greenland as Fort Godt-Haab by royal governor Claus Paarss. This establishment marked a significant development in the Danish colonial presence in Greenland.
events.name: Founding of Nuuk

events.enhanced_description: Persian physician Mohammad Mehdi ibn Ali Naqi completed his treatise, Zad al-musafirin, which provided guidance for travelers to Persia on maintaining their health. This work reflects the medical knowledge and practices of the time.
events.name: Completion of Zad al-musafirin

events.enhanced_description: John Deane, a colonial administrator of the British East India Company, returned to Kolkata after a two-year absence to resume his role at Fort William, overseeing the Bengal Presidency, which encompassed modern-day West Bengal and Bangladesh.
events.name: John Deane Returns to Calcutta

events.enhanced_description: The Copenhagen Fire of 1728, the largest in the city's history, caused extensive damage and destruction. This catastrophic event had lasting effects on the urban landscape and rebuilding efforts in Copenhagen.
events.name: Copenhagen Fire of 1728

events.enhanced_description: The Maratha Empire's army invaded the Mughal Empire's Malwa province, successfully crossing the Narmada River. This military action culminated in the Battle of Amjhira on November 29, where the Maratha forces defeated the Mughal defenders.
events.name: Maratha Empire Invades Malwa

events.enhanced_description: William Burnet was appointed by King George II as the Governor of the Province of New Hampshire, in addition to his role as Governor of the Province of Massachusetts Bay. This dual governorship lasted until September 7, 1729.
events.name: William Burnet Appointed Governor of New Hampshire

events.enhanced_description: Frederick, the eldest son of King George II of Great Britain, was officially made Prince of Wales at the age of 21. This title marked his formal recognition as the heir apparent to the British throne.
events.name: Frederick Made Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: At just 14 years old, Joseph, Prince of Brazil, married the 10-year-old Princess Mariana Victoria of Spain, the eldest daughter of King Philip V of Spain. This union would later see them ascend to the thrones of Portugal and Spain, respectively.
events.name: Marriage of Joseph, Prince of Brazil

events.enhanced_description: King Philip V of Spain issued a royal cedula aimed at incentivizing families from the Canary Islands to settle in New Spain, specifically north of the Rio Grande in present-day Texas. This initiative was part of broader colonial expansion efforts.
events.name: Royal Cedula by King Philip V

events.enhanced_description: In the city of Resht, leaders from Russia and Afghanistan signed a peace treaty, with General Vasily Levashev representing Russia and Muhammad Saidal Khan for Afghanistan. This agreement aimed to stabilize relations between the two nations.
events.name: Peace Treaty in Resht

events.enhanced_description: James Oglethorpe began his service as Chairman of the Gaols Committee in the British House of Commons, investigating the conditions of jails and prisons following the death of his friend Robert Castell. His findings would later contribute to significant penal reforms in Britain.
events.name: James Oglethorpe's Gaols Committee

events.enhanced_description: Abdallah of Morocco ascended to the throne following the death of his half-brother, Abu'l Abbas Ahmad. His reign lasted five years, during which he faced multiple challenges and was deposed several times before his eventual return to power.
events.name: Abdallah Becomes Sultan of Morocco

events.enhanced_description: Pope Benedict XIII canonized John of Nepomuk, a Bohemian priest who had been tortured and drowned in 1393. His canonization recognized him as the patron saint of Roman Catholics in the Czech Republic, highlighting his enduring legacy.
events.name: Canonization of John of Nepomuk
