events.enhanced_description: On June 16, 1746, Austrian forces achieved a significant victory over French and Spanish troops at the Battle of Piacenza. This battle was part of the larger War of the Austrian Succession, showcasing the shifting alliances and military strategies of the time.
events.name: Battle of Piacenza

events.enhanced_description: On June 18, 1746, Samuel Johnson was contracted to write his seminal work, A Dictionary of the English Language. This dictionary would later become one of the most influential works in the history of English lexicography.
events.name: Contract for A Dictionary of the English Language

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1746, Catherine of Ricci, a prominent figure in the Catholic Church known for her mystical experiences and piety, was canonized. Her canonization reflects the Catholic Church's recognition of her contributions to spirituality and religious life.
events.name: Canonization of Catherine of Ricci

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1746, Father Joachim Royo, the last of five Spanish Catholic missionaries in Fuzhou, China, was captured by Chinese authorities after defying orders to cease evangelizing. His capture highlights the tensions between missionary efforts and local governance during this period.
events.name: Capture of Father Joachim Royo

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1746, King Philip V of Spain died after a reign of more than 45 years. His death marked the end of an era, with his son Ferdinand VI succeeding him, continuing the Bourbon dynasty's influence in Spain.

image.caption: Gold 1 escudo coin depicting Philip V of Spain and Sardinia.
image.date_qualification: The coin is dated 1702; the supplied 2014 timestamp is a photograph/file date, not the depicted date. The event is dated 9 July 1746.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of King Philip V of Spain

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1746, the Dress Act was enacted in Scotland, banning the wearing of the kilt as a measure to suppress Highland culture following the Jacobite Rising. Although the act's effective date was later, its announcement marked a significant cultural repression.
events.name: Dress Act in Scotland

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1746, the Earl of Kilmarnock and Lord Balmerino were executed by beheading in the Tower of London for their roles in the Jacobite uprising. Their deaths symbolized the harsh repercussions faced by those who supported the Jacobite cause.

locations.name: Tower of London, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Executions of Jacobite Lords

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1746, Bonnie Prince Charlie fled to the Isle of Skye from Arisaig after the unsuccessful Jacobite Rising of 1745. His escape marked a significant moment in the aftermath of the rebellion, as he sought refuge from British forces.

locations.name: Isle of Skye, Scotland, United Kingdom

events.name: Bonnie Prince Charlie's Flight

events.enhanced_description: On October 11, 1746, the French army defeated an allied force of Austrian, British, Hanoverian, and Dutch troops at the Battle of Rocoux. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the War of the Austrian Succession, showcasing the shifting dynamics of European warfare.
events.name: Battle of Rocoux

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1746, The College of New Jersey was founded in Princeton, New Jersey. This institution would later be renamed Princeton University and become one of the leading universities in the United States.
events.name: Founding of The College of New Jersey

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1746, a devastating earthquake struck Lima and Callao, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. The earthquake, estimated to have a magnitude of around 8.6, was one of the most powerful in the region's history, leading to significant changes in urban planning and construction in the aftermath.
events.name: An earthquake demolishes Lima and Callao, in Peru

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1746, Anwaruddin Khan, the Nawab of Arcot, led an army of 10,000 soldiers in an attempt to reclaim Madras from French control. However, he was repelled by Captain Louis Paradis of the French Army, marking a significant moment in the struggle for control over southern India during the colonial period.
events.name: Anwaruddin Khan driven back by Captain Louis Paradis

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1746, the citizens of Genoa, inspired by the teenage boy Giovanni Battista Perasso, known as Balilla, revolted against the occupying Austrian forces and their local collaborator, the Marquis of Botta d'Adorno. This uprising temporarily expelled the Austrians from the city-state, although they returned shortly thereafter.
events.name: Citizens of Genoa rise up against Austrian troops

events.enhanced_description: James Lind began his pioneering experiment to determine the effects of citrus fruits on scurvy among sailors. His work laid the foundation for understanding the importance of vitamin C in preventing this debilitating disease, which was a significant issue for long sea voyages.
events.name: James Lind's Scurvy Experiment

events.enhanced_description: During the War of the Austrian Succession, Spanish troops invaded and occupied the coastal towns of Beaufort and Brunswick in North Carolina, an event that became known as the Spanish Alarm. Local militias eventually drove the Spanish forces out, showcasing colonial resistance.
events.name: Spanish Alarm in North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: Samuel Johnson began his monumental work on 'A Dictionary of the English Language' in London. This dictionary would later become one of the most influential works in the history of English lexicography, shaping the language for generations.
events.name: Samuel Johnson's Dictionary Work

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1747, the London Lock Hospital opened as the first clinic dedicated to treating venereal diseases. This establishment marked a significant advancement in public health and the medical treatment of sexually transmitted infections.
events.name: The first venereal diseases clinic opens at London Lock Hospital

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1747, during King George's War, a combined French and Indian force led by Captain Nicolas Antoine II Coulon de Villiers attacked and defeated British troops at Grand-Pré, Nova Scotia. This battle was part of the larger conflict between British and French colonial powers in North America.
figures: Nicolas Antoine II Coulon de Villiers
events.name: King George's War: Attack at Grand-Pré

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1747, Juan de Arechederra, the Spanish Governor-General of the Philippines, allied with Sultan Azim ud-Din I of Sulu to suppress a rebellion by the Moros in the Visayas. This collaboration aimed to maintain Spanish control over the archipelago amidst rising local resistance.
events.name: Juan de Arechederra suppresses Moro rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On March 19, 1747, Simon Fraser, the 79-year-old Scottish Lord Lovat, was convicted of high treason for his role in the Jacobite rising of 1745. Following a seven-day trial, he was sentenced to be hanged, drawn, and quartered, but King George II commuted his sentence to beheading, which was carried out on April 9.
events.name: Simon Fraser convicted of high treason

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1747, Lord Lovat was beheaded at Tower Hill, London, after being convicted of high treason. His execution marked the end of an era for the Jacobite cause, as he was the last person in Britain to be executed by beheading, a method that would not be formally abolished until the 19th century.
events.name: Lord Lovat beheaded at Tower Hill

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1747, during the War of the Austrian Succession, the British Navy achieved a decisive victory over a French fleet at the First Battle of Cape Finisterre. This battle was significant in asserting British naval dominance in the Atlantic during the conflict.
events.name: First battle of Cape Finisterre

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1747, Emperor Momozono ascended to the throne of Japan, succeeding Emperor Sakuramachi. His reign, though short-lived, was marked by the continuation of the Edo period's policies and cultural developments.
events.name: Emperor Momozono ascends to the throne of Japan

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1747, the English ships Dobbs galley and California, captained by William Moore and Francis Smith, explored Hudson Bay. Their expedition revealed that there was no Northwest Passage by this route, contributing to the understanding of North America's geography.
events.name: Exploration of Hudson Bay

events.enhanced_description: On July 2, 1747, during the War of the Austrian Succession, the Battle of Lauffeld took place, where French forces defeated the combined armies of Hanover, Great Britain, and the Netherlands. This battle was a critical moment in the ongoing conflict for European dominance.
events.name: Battle of Lauffeld

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1747, Great Britain, Russia, and the Dutch Republic signed the Convention of Saint Petersburg, which aimed to stabilize relations among the three powers during the ongoing War of the Austrian Succession. This agreement was significant in shaping the diplomatic landscape of Europe.
events.name: Convention of Saint Petersburg signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 24, 1747, Seyyid Abdullah Pasha, the Turkish Governor of Cyprus, was appointed as the new Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire. His tenure lasted until 1750 and was marked by efforts to stabilize the empire amidst internal and external challenges.
events.name: Seyyid Abdullah Pasha becomes Grand Vizier

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1747, during the War of the Austrian Succession, the city of Bergen op Zoom in the Netherlands fell to the French Army after a 70-day siege. This event underscored the ongoing military struggles in Europe and the shifting balance of power.
events.name: Bergen op Zoom falls to the Army of France

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1747, a hurricane struck the Caribbean Sea, sinking 11 British ships, most of which were off the coast of Saint Kitts. This natural disaster highlighted the perils of maritime navigation in the region during hurricane season.
events.name: Hurricane sinks British ships off Saint Kitts

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1747, a loya jirga (grand council) in Kandahar elected Ahmad Shah Durrani as their leader, marking the beginning of the Durrani Empire in Afghanistan. This event was pivotal in unifying various Pashtun tribes under his leadership.
events.name: Ahmad Shah Durrani becomes leader in Afghanistan

events.enhanced_description: On October 21, 1747, King George II appointed Thomas Herring as the new Archbishop of Canterbury, following the death of John Potter. Herring's tenure was marked by efforts to address issues within the Church of England during a time of religious and political change.
events.name: Thomas Herring becomes Archbishop of Canterbury

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1747, a hurricane swept across Saint Kitts, sinking 12 British freighters and one French ship. This event underscored the dangers faced by maritime trade in the Caribbean during hurricane season.
events.name: Hurricane sinks British freighters and one French ship

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1747, the British Navy achieved another victory over a French fleet at the Second Battle of Cape Finisterre during the War of the Austrian Succession. This battle further solidified British naval supremacy in the Atlantic.
events.name: Second battle of Cape Finisterre

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1747, rioters in Amsterdam took to the streets demanding governmental reform. This unrest reflected the growing discontent among the populace regarding political corruption and the need for change in the Dutch Republic.
events.name: Rioters in Amsterdam demand governmental reform

events.enhanced_description: The Knowles Riot erupted in Boston as citizens protested against the impressment of local sailors into the British Royal Navy. This event highlighted the growing tensions between American colonists and British authorities over issues of autonomy and military service.
events.name: Knowles Riot

events.enhanced_description: The Second Stadtholderless Period in the United Provinces ended with Prince William IV of Orange being appointed as stadtholder. This marked a significant shift in the political landscape of the Dutch Republic, restoring a centralized leadership after a period of decentralized governance.
events.name: End of Second Stadtholderless Period

events.enhanced_description: Benjamin Franklin established the Pennsylvania Associators, the first militia in Pennsylvania, in response to the lack of a standing military force due to the pacifistic nature of the Quaker founders. This formation was crucial for the colony's defense during escalating tensions with Britain.
events.name: Formation of the Pennsylvania Associators

events.enhanced_description: The Maryland freighter sloop Endeavour set sail from Annapolis for the West Indies but encountered a devastating hurricane. The ship was severely damaged, drifting for six months before finally reaching Tiree, Scotland, illustrating the perils of maritime travel in the 18th century.
events.name: Endeavour's Ordeal

events.enhanced_description: The Parliament of Great Britain amended the Naturalisation Act of 1740 to extend recognition to all non-Anglican Protestant denominations in its colonies. This legislative change was significant in promoting religious tolerance and inclusion within the British Empire.
events.name: Amendment of Naturalisation Act

events.enhanced_description: José de Escandón was appointed by the Viceroy of New Spain as the first Royal Governor of Nuevo Santander, an area that now encompasses parts of modern-day Texas and Tamaulipas. His leadership was pivotal in the development and governance of this frontier region.
events.name: Royal Governor of Nuevo Santander

events.enhanced_description: The Camberwell beauty butterfly was named after specimens discovered in Camberwell, London. This event reflects the growing interest in entomology and the classification of species during the 18th century.
events.name: Naming of the Camberwell Beauty Butterfly

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, Leonhard Euler published 'Introductio in analysin infinitorum', a foundational text in analytical mathematics that introduced concepts that would shape the field. This work is considered a significant contribution to mathematics, influencing future generations of mathematicians.
events.name: Publication of Introductio in analysin infinitorum

events.enhanced_description: Montesquieu's seminal work, 'De l'esprit des lois', was published in 1748, exploring the relationship between laws and social structures. This influential text laid the groundwork for modern political science and theories of governance.
events.name: Publication of De l'esprit des lois

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, Friedrich Gottlieb Klopstock anonymously published the first three cantos of his epic poem 'Der Messias' in the literary journal Bremer Beiträge in Leipzig. This work marked a significant contribution to German literature and showcased Klopstock's innovative use of hexameter.
events.name: Publication of Der Messias

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, Adam Smith began delivering public lectures in Edinburgh, laying the groundwork for his later influential work, 'The Wealth of Nations'. His lectures focused on moral philosophy and economics, significantly impacting the development of economic thought.
events.name: Adam Smith begins public lectures

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, Eva Ekeblad made history by becoming the first female member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Her contributions to science, particularly in agriculture and chemistry, paved the way for greater inclusion of women in scientific fields.
events.name: Eva Ekeblad becomes first female member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, construction began on the Sveaborg fortification near Helsinki, which would become a crucial naval base for the Swedish Empire. The fortification was designed to protect the city and its waters from potential invasions.
events.name: Construction of Sveaborg fortification begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, the ruins of Pompeii were rediscovered, sparking interest in the ancient Roman city that had been buried under volcanic ash since the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. This rediscovery would lead to significant archaeological studies and insights into Roman life.
events.name: Rediscovery of the ruins of Pompeii

events.enhanced_description: In 1748, Louis XV of France reneged on his promise to abolish the income tax following the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. This led to public outcry and protests from the Parlement of Paris, resulting in a reduction of the tax rate to 5%.
events.name: Louis XV breaks promise on income tax

events.enhanced_description: Ahmad Shah Durrani captured Lahore, a significant city in the Punjab region, marking a pivotal moment in the power struggles of the Indian subcontinent during the 18th century. This event solidified Durrani's influence in the region.
events.name: Ahmad Shah Durrani Captures Lahore

events.enhanced_description: A devastating fire broke out at the prison and barracks in Kinsale, Ireland, resulting in the deaths of 54 prisoners of war. Fortunately, around 500 prisoners were safely evacuated to another facility, highlighting the dangers of overcrowded and poorly maintained prisons.
events.name: Fire at Kinsale Prison

events.enhanced_description: The San Gabriel mission project commenced with the establishment of the San Francisco Xavier mission along the San Gabriel River in what is now Texas. This initiative aimed to spread Catholicism further north in the Viceroyalty of New Spain, but faced challenges from local Indigenous populations.
events.name: San Gabriel Mission Project

events.enhanced_description: In a significant battle near Manupur, Mughal forces led by Prince Ahmad Shah Bahadur achieved victory over Ahmad Shah Durrani. This conflict was part of the larger power struggles in the region during the 18th century.
events.name: Battle near Manupur

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic fire ignited in Change Alley, Cornhill, London, lasting for two days and causing extensive damage estimated at over £1,000,000. Dr. Samuel Johnson later remarked on the horror of such a disaster, which also spurred advancements in fire insurance practices.
events.name: Fire in the City of London

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Maastricht commenced as French forces under Maurice de Saxe attacked the Dutch fortress during the War of the Austrian Succession. The siege lasted for just over three weeks, culminating in the fortress's fall on May 7.
events.name: Siege of Maastricht

events.enhanced_description: A congress convened at Aix-la-Chapelle with the objective of concluding the War of the Austrian Succession. The negotiations led to the signing of a treaty on October 18, marking a significant diplomatic effort to restore peace in Europe.
events.name: Congress at Aix-la-Chapelle

events.enhanced_description: Following the agreement for the Dutch Republic to return control of Maastricht to France, Count Löwendal led the French Army through the city's gates to accept its surrender. This event marked a significant territorial gain for France in the ongoing conflict.

image.caption: Louis-Nicolas Van Blarenberghe’s illustration depicting the surrender of Maastricht.
image.date_qualification: The depicted event is dated 1748; the image itself is dated “late 18th century.”
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Surrender of Maastricht

events.enhanced_description: A catastrophic fire in Moscow resulted in the deaths of 482 people and the destruction of approximately 5,000 buildings. This disaster had a profound impact on the city and its inhabitants, leading to significant changes in urban planning and fire safety regulations.
events.name: Fire in Moscow

events.enhanced_description: Admiral Edward Boscawen arrived at Fort St. David on the southeastern coast of India with a formidable fleet to defend against French attacks. His strategic offensive aimed to eliminate French presence in the region, significantly impacting colonial dynamics in India.

locations.name: Fort St. David, Tamil Nadu, India

events.name: Admiral Edward Boscawen in India

events.enhanced_description: The first Lutheran Church body in America was founded during a conference in Philadelphia, organized by German-born evangelist Henry Muhlenberg. This gathering of Lutheran pastors aimed to unify their practices and establish a common liturgy for worship.
events.name: First Lutheran Church Body in America

events.enhanced_description: Shah Rukh ascended to power as the ruler of Greater Khorasan, an area that played a crucial role in the political and cultural landscape of Persia. His reign was marked by efforts to consolidate power and manage the diverse populations within his territory.
events.name: Shah Rukh Becomes Ruler of Greater Khorasan

events.enhanced_description: On August 13, 1762, the Battle of Havana concluded after a protracted siege, resulting in the surrender of Havana by Spanish forces to the British. This event was a pivotal moment in the Seven Years' War, significantly impacting colonial power dynamics.
events.name: Battle of Havana

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle was signed to officially end the War of the Austrian Succession, with Great Britain gaining control of Madras in India in exchange for the fortress of Louisbourg in Canada. This treaty reshaped colonial holdings and diplomatic relations in Europe.

image.caption: Portrait of Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle-upon-Tyne, by Charles Jervas.
image.credit: Charles Jervas — Historical Portraits Picture Archive, ItemID 711
image.date_qualification: Circa 1735; this is the depicted portrait date, not the date of the treaty.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1748, the Electorate of Hanover issued a decree that expelled all adherents of the Moravian Church from its territory. This action reflected the tensions between different religious groups during a time of increasing state control over religious practices.
events.name: Decree banishing adherents of the Moravian Church

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1748, Austria and Spain signed a second treaty to conclude the War of the Austrian Succession. As part of the agreement, Austria committed to withdrawing its troops from Modena and Genoa, marking a significant step towards stabilizing the region after years of conflict.
events.name: Second Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle

events.enhanced_description: In 1749, the first issue of Berlingske was published in Copenhagen, marking the beginning of Denmark's oldest continually operating newspaper. This publication played a crucial role in the dissemination of news and information in Denmark.
events.name: First issue of Berlingske published

events.enhanced_description: In 1749, a census was conducted in Finland, marking an important step in the administrative organization of the region under Swedish rule.
events.name: Census in Finland

events.enhanced_description: In 1749, the Great Partition land reform began in Sweden, a significant initiative that would reshape land ownership and agricultural practices in the country over the following decades.
events.name: Great Partition Land Reform

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1749, Benning Wentworth issued the first of the New Hampshire Grants, which facilitated the establishment of Vermont. This action was pivotal in the settlement and governance of the region during a time of territorial disputes.
events.name: Benning Wentworth issues New Hampshire Grants

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1749, the Teatro Filarmonico, the main opera theater in Verona, Italy, was destroyed by fire. This event marked a significant loss for the cultural landscape of the city, leading to its reconstruction in 1754.
events.name: Teatro Filarmonico destroyed by fire

events.enhanced_description: In February 1749, the second part of John Cleland's erotic novel 'Fanny Hill' was published in London. This controversial work gained notoriety and contributed to discussions about morality and literature in the 18th century.
events.name: Publication of Fanny Hill (Part 2)

events.enhanced_description: On February 28, 1749, Henry Fielding's comic novel 'The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling' was published in London. This novel is considered a classic of English literature and showcases Fielding's innovative narrative style.
events.name: Publication of The History of Tom Jones

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1749, a 'corpse riot' erupted in Glasgow after a body disappeared from a churchyard in the Gorbals district. The incident sparked public outrage against anatomy students suspected of grave robbing, leading to protests and increased vigilance over graveyards.
events.name: Corpse riot in Glasgow

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1749, composer George Frideric Handel conducted the first performance of his oratorio 'Solomon' at Covent Garden in London. This event marked a significant moment in the history of English music and showcased Handel's mastery of the oratorio form.

locations.name: Covent Garden, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: First performance of Handel's Solomon

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1749, the British Royal Navy ship HMS Namur was wrecked in a storm near Fort St. David, India, resulting in the loss of 520 lives. This tragedy highlighted the dangers faced by naval vessels during the period.

locations.name: Fort St. David, Tamil Nadu, India

events.name: HMS Namur wrecked

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1749, the first official performance of Handel's 'Music for the Royal Fireworks' took place in London but was cut short due to an outbreak of fire. This piece was composed to celebrate the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle, marking the end of the War of the Austrian Succession.
events.name: First performance of Music for the Royal Fireworks

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1749, King George II of Great Britain granted the Ohio Company 200,000 acres of land north of the Ohio River, which encompasses much of modern-day Ohio and parts of West Virginia. This grant was contingent on the company attracting European settlers to the area.
events.name: King George II grants land to Ohio Company

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1749, a devastating fire in Glasgow left 200 families homeless. This incident underscored the challenges of urban living during this period and the need for improved fire safety measures.
events.name: Fire in Glasgow leaves families homeless

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1749, the Conspiracy of the Slaves was revealed in Malta, which was intended to take place on June 29. This event highlighted the tensions between enslaved individuals and their masters, reflecting broader issues of slavery in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Conspiracy of the Slaves revealed in Malta

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1749, the British founded the naval fort at Halifax, Nova Scotia, as a strategic defense against the French fortress of Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island. This fortification played a crucial role in British colonial military strategy in North America.
events.name: Founding of Halifax

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1749, Irish-born trader George Croghan purchased 200,000 acres of land in the Ohio River valley from the Six Nations of the Iroquois Confederacy. This transaction occurred at the Iroquois capital of Onondaga and was significant in the context of colonial expansion and land disputes.
events.name: George Croghan purchases land from Iroquois

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Ambur, fought on August 3, 1749, marked the beginning of the Second Carnatic War. In this conflict, the British-supported Nawab Anwaruddin Khan faced off against the French-supported Chanda Sahib, resulting in a decisive defeat for Anwaruddin, who was killed in battle.
events.name: The Battle of Ambur

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1749, Mary Musgrove Bosomworth, claiming the title of Coosaponakeesa, Queen of the Creek Indians, led a delegation of 200 Creek Indians into Savannah. They confronted British colonial authorities to demand compensation for land taken from the Creek, but were ultimately dismissed as lacking authority.
events.name: Mary Musgrove Bosomworth's March

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1749, four Russian sailors were rescued after being marooned on Edgeøya for over six years. They were the only survivors of a crew of 14, whose vessel had been wrecked by ice in 1743.
events.name: Rescue of Russian Sailors

events.enhanced_description: On August 19, 1749, a significant ceremony took place in San Antonio where four Apache chiefs and Spanish officials symbolically 'buried the hatchet' by placing weapons into a pit, signaling an end to hostilities between the two groups.
events.name: Burying the Hatchet Ceremony

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1749, a delegation comprising 33 members of the Catawba Nation and 73 from the Cherokee Nation arrived in Charleston to negotiate a peace treaty with Governor James Glen, reflecting the ongoing efforts to stabilize relations between Native American tribes and colonial authorities.
events.name: Catawba and Cherokee Delegation

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1749, the first recorded game of baseball took place at Kingston upon Thames, England, featuring Frederick, Prince of Wales. This event marks an important milestone in the history of the sport.
events.name: First Recorded Game of Baseball

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1749, Grand Chief Jean-Baptiste Cope of the Mi'kmaq nation declared war against the British Empire, initiating hostilities by capturing 20 British hostages at Canso, in response to colonial expansion.
events.name: Mi'kmaq War Declaration

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1749, three Russian sailors returned to Archangelsk after being marooned on Edgeøya for over six years. Their return marked the end of a harrowing ordeal that began when their ship was wrecked in 1743.
events.name: Return of Russian Survivors

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1749, Edward Cornwallis, the British Governor of Nova Scotia, issued orders to his militia to target the Mi'kmaq people, offering rewards for their scalps as part of a campaign against the indigenous population.
events.name: Edward Cornwallis's Orders Against Mi'kmaq

events.enhanced_description: On October 4, 1749, King Ferdinand VI of Spain initiated significant clerical reforms by approving a royal cédula that transferred control of Roman Catholic parishes in Latin America from religious orders to the secular clergy, impacting the governance of the church in major cities.
events.name: Clerical Reforms in Spanish America

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1749, a peace treaty was signed in Falmouth (now Portland, Maine) between representatives of Massachusetts Bay and tribal chiefs of the Wabanaki Confederacy, temporarily resolving territorial disputes during King George's War.
events.name: Peace Treaty with Wabanaki Confederacy

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1749, Christopher Gist began his survey of lands along the Ohio River, representing British interests in the region just two months after Pierre Céloron de Blainville's exploration for France, highlighting the escalating competition for territory.
events.name: Christopher Gist's Survey

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1749, the Battle of Penfui occurred on Timor, where a larger Topass army was defeated by the numerically inferior forces of the Dutch East India Company, showcasing the ongoing conflicts in the region.
events.name: Battle of Penfui

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1749, King Louis XV issued an ordinance in response to the rising number of beggars in Paris, mandating their arrest and imprisonment as a measure to control the growing social issue.
events.name: Louis XV's Ordinance on Beggars

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1749, the South Carolina House of Assembly voted to free Caesar Norman, an African-American slave, granting him a pension in exchange for sharing his knowledge of an antidote for snake venom, highlighting the complexities of slavery and knowledge in colonial America.
events.name: Caesar Norman's Freedom

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1749, Sultan Azim ud-Din I, after being ousted from his throne in the Sultanate of Sulu, announced his intention to convert to Christianity and was baptized in Manila, adopting the name Fernando.
events.name: Sultan Azim ud-Din I's Conversion

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1749, Jean-Philippe Rameau premiered his opera Zoroastre at the Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris. Despite its initial failure, the opera would undergo revisions and be revived successfully years later.
events.name: Premiere of Zoroastre

events.enhanced_description: On December 7, 1749, Father Junípero Serra began his missionary work in the New World upon arriving in Veracruz, Mexico. He would go on to establish several missions in California, significantly impacting the region's history.
events.name: Junípero Serra's Missionary Work

events.enhanced_description: On December 30, 1749, Mir Sayyid Muhammad overthrew Shahrokh Shah to briefly restore the Safavid dynasty as Suleiman II. His reign lasted less than three months before Kurdish tribesmen restored Shahrokh to power.
events.name: Mir Sayyid Muhammad's Overthrow

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1750, a group of West African slaves aboard the British slave ship Snow Ann successfully overpowered the crew and navigated the vessel back to Cape Lopez in Gabon. This act of rebellion highlighted the desperate struggle for freedom among enslaved individuals during the transatlantic slave trade.
events.name: Rebellion on the Snow Ann (duplicate)

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Viceroy Juan Francisco de Güemes issued a notice to missionaries in Nuevo Santander, which included parts of modern-day Texas and Tamaulipas, Mexico. The directive aimed to peacefully convert the indigenous Karankawa people to Roman Catholicism, reflecting the colonial efforts to spread Christianity.
events.name: Missionary Notice in Nuevo Santander

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Hannah Snell, a woman who disguised herself as a man to serve in the Royal Marines, revealed her true identity to her fellow soldiers. This act challenged gender norms of the time and brought attention to the roles women could play in military service.
events.name: Hannah Snell reveals her sex

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, the King of Dahomey generated an income of 250,000 pounds from the overseas export of slaves, reflecting the significant role of the transatlantic slave trade in the economy of West African kingdoms. This income was pivotal in maintaining the power and influence of Dahomey during this period.
events.name: King of Dahomey's income from slave trade

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Japanese painter Maruyama Okyo created 'The Ghost of Oyuki', a significant work that exemplified the ukiyo-e style and reflected the cultural fascination with the supernatural in Edo-period Japan. This painting contributed to Okyo's reputation as a master of his craft.
events.name: Maruyama Okyo paints The Ghost of Oyuki

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Britain produced approximately 2% of the world's industrial goods, marking the beginning of its rise as a global industrial power. This output set the stage for the Industrial Revolution that would transform economies and societies in the following decades.

image.caption: Illustration of power-loom weaving.
image.credit: Illustrator T. Allom, Engraver J. Tingle — History of the cotton manufacture in Great Britain by Sir Edward Baines,
image.date_qualification: Dated 1835; this is later than the event’s stated date of 1750 and should be presented as a later illustration of industrial-era textile production.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Britain's industrial output

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Europe saw the abolition of galley slavery, a significant step towards the recognition of human rights and the end of forced labor practices that had persisted for centuries. This change reflected the growing Enlightenment ideals of liberty and justice.
events.name: Abolition of galley slavery in Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, the estimated world population reached 791 million, with significant distributions across continents: Africa had 106 million, Asia 502 million, Europe 163 million, Latin America 16 million, Northern America 2 million, and Oceania 2 million. These figures provide insight into global demographics prior to the major population shifts of the 19th century.
events.name: World population statistics

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Africa's population was estimated at 106 million, reflecting the continent's diverse cultures and societies. This population figure is crucial for understanding the demographic landscape of Africa before the impacts of colonialism and the slave trade.
events.name: Population of Africa

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Asia had an estimated population of 502 million, making it the most populous continent at the time. This demographic data is essential for understanding the historical context of Asian societies and their influence on global affairs.
events.name: Population of Asia

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Europe's population was approximately 163 million, reflecting the continent's complex political and social structures. This figure is significant for understanding the demographic changes that would occur in Europe during the subsequent centuries.
events.name: Population of Europe

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Latin America's population was estimated at 16 million, a reflection of the region's colonial history and the impact of European settlement. This demographic data is crucial for understanding the social and economic dynamics of Latin America during this period.
events.name: Population of Latin America

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Northern America's population was around 2 million, primarily consisting of indigenous peoples and European settlers. This figure is significant for understanding the early demographic landscape of what would become the United States.
events.name: Population of Northern America

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Oceania's population was estimated at 2 million, encompassing a diverse range of cultures and societies across the Pacific Islands. This demographic data is important for understanding the historical context of Oceania before significant European contact.
events.name: Population of Oceania

events.enhanced_description: In 1750, Spain and Portugal agreed that the Uruguay River would serve as the boundary line between their territories in South America. Following this agreement, the Spanish Governor ordered the Jesuits to vacate seven Indian missions along the river, impacting the indigenous communities and the Jesuit missions significantly.
events.name: Boundary Agreement between Spain and Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1750, the Murray-Kean Company, a troupe of actors from Philadelphia, made history by presenting the first performance of a play that had been announced in advance in a newspaper. They staged Shakespeare's 'Richard III' at the Nassau Street Theatre in New York City, marking a significant moment in American theatrical history.
events.name: First Performance of Richard III in New York

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1750, the first number of Samuel Johnson's influential periodical 'The Rambler' was published. This work contributed significantly to English literature and journalism, showcasing Johnson's thoughts on morality, society, and human nature.
events.name: Publication of The Rambler

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1750, Maveeran Alagumuthu Kone, a polygar in Tamil Nadu, launched a rebellion against the East India Company's oppressive tax collection policies. This uprising was part of a broader resistance against colonial rule in India, highlighting the growing discontent among local leaders.

image.caption: Statue of Maveeran Alagumuthu Kone.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2017-05-22; not contemporaneous with the rebellion.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Rebellion led by Maveeran Alagumuthu Kone

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1750, Dr. Thomas Walker and five companions became the first white explorers to traverse the Cumberland Gap, a significant mountain pass in the Appalachian Mountains. Their journey marked the beginning of westward expansion into territories previously inhabited by Native American tribes.
events.name: Cumberland Gap Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1750, a group of West African slaves aboard the British slave ship Snow Ann successfully overpowered the crew and navigated the vessel back to Cape Lopez in Gabon. This act of rebellion highlighted the desperate struggle for freedom among enslaved individuals during the transatlantic slave trade.
events.name: Rebellion on the Snow Ann

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1750, the French army burned the Acadian settlement of Beaubassin in Nova Scotia, forcibly relocating its population. This event was part of the broader territorial disputes between France and Great Britain in North America, particularly regarding the boundaries established by the Missaguash River.
events.name: Destruction of Beaubassin

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1750, riots erupted in Paris following the arrest of teenagers for gambling, fueled by rumors that police were abducting children for blood. The unrest spread across the city, leading to violent confrontations with law enforcement and prompting calls for police reform.
events.name: Riots in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1750, explorers Eggert Ólafsson and Bjarni Pálsson scaled the 4,892-foot-high volcano Hekla in Iceland. This ascent was significant at a time when mountain climbing was still a rare endeavor, showcasing the spirit of exploration during the Age of Enlightenment.
events.name: Climbing of Hekla

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1750, the British Parliament passed the Iron Act, aimed at restricting American iron production by prohibiting new ironworking businesses from producing finished goods. This legislation was part of Britain's broader strategy to control colonial economies and maintain dominance in manufacturing.
events.name: Britain's Iron Act

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1750, an attempt to incite a native uprising against Spanish colonial authorities in Lima was discovered and thwarted. One of the conspirators, Francisco Garcia Jimenez, escaped and later led violent actions against Spaniards, reflecting the tensions in the Viceroyalty of Peru.
events.name: Thwarted Uprising in Lima

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1750, traveller Jonas Hanway departed from St. Petersburg, embarking on a journey back home through Germany and the Netherlands. Later that year, he would reportedly become the first Englishman to adopt the use of an umbrella, a fashion that originated in France.
events.name: Jonas Hanway's Journey

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1750, Halifax, Nova Scotia, suffered a devastating fire that nearly destroyed the city. This catastrophic event had significant implications for the community's development and rebuilding efforts in the years that followed.
events.name: Halifax Fire

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1750, José I ascended to the throne of Portugal following the death of his father, João V. His reign marked significant political changes, including the appointment of the Marquis of Pombal as Chief Minister, who initiated reforms that diminished the power of the Inquisition.
events.name: Ascension of King José I of Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1750, the British Parliament lifted the ban on slavery in the Province of Georgia, allowing for the importation of enslaved Africans. This legislative change marked a significant shift in the colony's economic and social structure as it transitioned to a plantation economy.
events.name: Lifting of Slavery Ban in Georgia

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1750, French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille successfully persuaded the States-General of the Dutch Republic to finance his stellar trigonometry mission to the Cape of Good Hope. This expedition was crucial for advancing astronomical knowledge and mapping the southern skies.
events.name: Lacaille's Stellar Trigonometry Mission

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1750, Crispus Attucks, an African-American slave, escaped from the estate of his owner in Framingham, Massachusetts. His flight from bondage would later lead him to become a notable figure in American history as the first person killed in the Boston Massacre of 1770.
events.name: Crispus Attucks' Escape

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1750, the Louvre Museum was officially created in Paris, following a call by art critic Lafond de Saint-Yenne for the royal art collection to be displayed to the public. The Marquis de Marigny facilitated the arrangement for showcasing 110 paintings, marking a significant cultural development in France.
events.name: Creation of the Louvre Museum

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1750, a riot broke out in Lhasa following the murder of the regent of Tibet. This unrest reflected the political tensions and instability within the region during this period.
events.name: Riots in Lhasa

events.enhanced_description: On May 24, 1862, Westminster Bridge was opened across the River Thames in London, designed by engineer Thomas Page. This new iron bridge replaced an older stone structure and became an important thoroughfare in the city.
events.name: Opening of Westminster Bridge

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1750, what is later described as the first documented presentation of a musical in New York took place at the Nassau Street Theatre. The resident company of actors staged 'The Beggar's Opera,' marking a significant moment in the evolution of American musical theatre.
events.name: First Documented Musical Presentation in New York

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1750, diplomatic relations between Prussia and Russia were severed after Russia refused to cease its support for the Electorate of Saxony. This breakdown in relations foreshadowed the conflicts that would escalate into the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Diplomatic Relations Break Between Prussia and Russia

events.enhanced_description: On December 29, 1750, in Jamaica, two physicians, Dr. John Williams and Dr. Parker Bennet, engaged in a duel with swords and pistols following a heated argument over the treatment of bilious fever. Both men sustained mortal wounds during the confrontation, highlighting the intense rivalries and personal conflicts of the time.
events.name: Duel of Dr. John Williams and Dr. Parker Bennet

events.enhanced_description: In 1751, as the Province of Georgia transitioned from a trustee-operated territory to a Crown colony, the Trustees lifted the prohibition against slavery. This decision marked a significant shift in the colony's demographics and economy, leading to a dramatic increase in the enslaved population over the following decades.
figures: Trustees for the Establishment of the Colony of Georgia
events.name: Lifting of slavery prohibition in Georgia

events.enhanced_description: The Medical School, which would later become part of the University of Pennsylvania, was founded in Philadelphia, marking a significant advancement in medical education in the American colonies. This institution would go on to play a crucial role in the development of medical practices and education in the United States.
events.name: The Medical School is founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1751, the University of Pennsylvania held its first classes, marking a significant development in American higher education. Founded by Benjamin Franklin and other trustees, the institution aimed to provide non-denominational education focused on leadership in various fields.
events.name: University of Pennsylvania's first classes

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1751, the Georgia colony convened its first elected legislature in Savannah, marking a pivotal moment in its governance. The assembly, consisting of 16 representatives, sought to maintain control over the colony's affairs and resist external pressures from neighboring South Carolina.
events.name: Georgia's first elected legislature

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1751, in the aftermath of the Lhasa riot of 1750, Chinese General Ban Di arrived in Tibet to oversee the punishment of rebel leaders. Under the authority of the Qianlong Emperor, he orchestrated the interrogation and execution of the seven imprisoned leaders, demonstrating the harsh measures taken to maintain control over the region.
events.name: Lhasa riot aftermath

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1751, at Lakkireddipalle in southeastern India, the new Nizam of Hyderabad, Subhadar Muzaffar Jang, confronted Nawab Bahadur Khan of Kurnool in a fierce battle. The two leaders engaged in hand-to-hand combat, resulting in the death of both leaders, which marked a significant moment in the regional power struggles.
events.name: Battle of Lakkireddipalle

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1751, English poet Thomas Gray published 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' anonymously in 'The Magazine of Magazines'. The poem, which reflects on mortality and the lives of the rural poor, would later become popularly known as 'Gray's Elegy' and is considered a classic of English literature.
events.name: Publication of Gray's Elegy

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1751, Pierre de Rigaud, the Marquis de Vaudreuil, who served as the Governor of French Louisiana, issued the first police regulations for New Orleans. This initiative aimed to combat rising crime in the city and laid the groundwork for future law enforcement practices.
figures: Pierre de Rigaud, Marquis de Vaudreuil
events.name: First police regulations in New Orleans

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1751, New Year's Day was legally observed for the last time on this date in England and Wales due to the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750. This act transitioned the calendar system, leading to significant changes in how dates were recorded in British territories.
events.name: Last New Year's Day on March 25

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1751, Frederick, Prince of Wales, heir-apparent to the British throne, died at the age of 44 after a game of cricket. His death led to his 12-year-old son, Prince George, becoming the new heir-apparent, who would later ascend to the throne as King George III.

image.caption: Portrait of Frederick, Prince of Wales, painted by Thomas Hudson.
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1750, before Frederick's death on 31 March 1751; this is not an image of the death event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Death of Frederick, Prince of Wales

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1751, King Frederick I of Sweden died at the age of 74, marking the end of the House of Hesse's rule in Sweden due to his lack of legitimate heirs. His death led to the ascension of Prince Adolf Frederick from the House of Holstein-Gottorp as the new king.
events.name: Death of King Frederick I of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1751, the Qianlong Emperor of China visited Nanjing for the first time, accompanied by a large entourage. This visit underscored the emperor's authority and the importance of Nanjing in the imperial hierarchy, as he stayed for four days in the historic southern capital.
events.name: Qianlong Emperor's visit to Nanjing

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1751, 12-year-old Prince George William Frederick was formally invested as the new Prince of Wales, following the death of his father, Frederick, Prince of Wales. This event marked the beginning of his journey towards becoming King George III, which would occur nine years later.

image.caption: Pastel portrait of George, Prince of Wales, by Jean-Étienne Liotard.
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1754, three years after the investiture.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Investiture of Prince George William Frederick

events.enhanced_description: The first recorded cricket match in the American colonies took place in Greenwich Village, where a team of New Yorkers triumphed over a team of Englishmen with a score of 167 to 80. This event marked the introduction of cricket as a popular sport in America.

locations.name: Greenwich Village, Manhattan, New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First cricket match in the American colonies

events.enhanced_description: The Pennsylvania Hospital, the first hospital in the American colonies, was chartered in Philadelphia, granting rights to Benjamin Franklin and Dr. Thomas Bond. This institution would become a cornerstone of medical care in the region.
events.name: Chartering of the Pennsylvania Hospital

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1752, Great Britain and its empire adopted the Gregorian calendar, marking the last use of the Julian calendar in the British territories. This change resulted in the omission of 11 days, with the day following September 2 being designated as September 14, significantly altering the way time was recorded in the English-speaking world.
events.name: Adoption of the Gregorian calendar in Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: The colony of South Carolina reversed a previous law imposing a hefty tax on the purchase of imported African slaves, reducing it significantly. This legislative change effectively revitalized the slave trade in the colony.
events.name: South Carolina reduces tax on imported African slaves

events.enhanced_description: Denis Diderot published the first volume of his monumental work, the Encyclopédie, which aimed to compile and disseminate knowledge across various fields. This publication was a significant contribution to the Enlightenment and the spread of rational thought.

image.caption: Title page of the Encyclopédie, edited by Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d’Alembert.
image.credit: Long List of Contributors to the Encyclopédie — File:ENC 1-NA5 600px.jpeg http://ets.lib.uchicago.edu/ARTFL/OLDENCYC/images
image.date_qualification: Reproduced and retouched title page of the Encyclopédie. The saved date identifies the publication period, not a proven image creation date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Diderot's Encyclopédie

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Kirkhbulakh, the Kingdom of Kartli successfully defeated a large army from the Tabriz Khanate, showcasing the military prowess of Erekle II. This victory was crucial for the stability and independence of the Georgian kingdom.

image.caption: Coat of arms of the Kingdom of Kartli.
image.credit: Jolle Derived work: Carnby — This file was derived from: Coat of arms of Kartli Georgia1.png
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 2014-02-04; it is a modern image of a historical symbol, not a contemporaneous event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Kirkhbulakh

events.enhanced_description: A devastating fire swept through Stockholm, destroying approximately 1,000 houses and leaving many residents homeless. This disaster highlighted the vulnerability of urban areas to fire hazards during this period.
events.name: Fire in Stockholm

events.enhanced_description: The Academy and College of Philadelphia, which would later evolve into the University of Pennsylvania, opened its doors with Benjamin Franklin serving as its first president. This institution played a pivotal role in the development of higher education in America.
events.name: Opening of the Academy and College of Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: The Kalvária Banská Štiavnica, a significant architectural and cultural site, was completed in the Kingdom of Hungary. This site reflects the rich history and religious significance of the region.
events.name: Completion of Kalvária Banská Štiavnica

events.enhanced_description: William V, the three-year-old son of the late William IV, was appointed as the last Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic. His mother, Princess Anne, served as regent during his minority, which lasted until her death in 1759.
events.name: William V becomes Stadtholder of the Dutch Republic

events.enhanced_description: The Hōreki period commenced in Japan, marking a new era in the Edo period characterized by cultural developments and political changes. This period would influence various aspects of Japanese society.
events.name: Beginning of the Hōreki period in Japan

events.enhanced_description: The 50-day siege of the British fort at Trichinopoly was broken when defenders used musket fire to stampede the elephants of the French-backed troops led by Chanda Sahib. This marked a significant turning point in the conflict.
events.name: Siege of Trichinopoly broken

events.enhanced_description: George Washington, then 19 years old, fell seriously ill with smallpox while visiting Barbados during an epidemic. He survived the illness but was bedridden for nearly a month, an experience that would shape his views on health and disease.
events.name: George Washington contracts smallpox

events.enhanced_description: Adolf Frederick was formally crowned as the King of Sweden in a ceremony that took place nearly eight months after he ascended to the throne. This event marked a significant moment in Swedish royal history.
events.name: Coronation of Adolf Frederick as King of Sweden

events.enhanced_description: At the conclusion of the Charlestown Conference, the Cherokee nation signed a treaty with British colonial authorities, represented by Governor James Glen. This agreement was signed by notable Cherokee war chiefs, marking a significant diplomatic engagement.
events.name: Treaty signed between the Cherokee nation and British authorities

events.enhanced_description: In the Battle of Arnee, a British East India Company-led force under Robert Clive defeated a much larger Franco-Indian army commanded by Raza Sahib. This victory was pivotal in the context of the Second Carnatic War.
events.name: Battle of Arnee in the Second Carnatic War

events.enhanced_description: The Theresian Military Academy was founded in Wiener Neustadt, Austria, establishing a significant institution for military education in the Habsburg Empire. This academy would train many future military leaders.
events.name: Founding of the Theresian Military Academy

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1752, the British Empire officially adopted the Gregorian calendar, aligning its calendar system with much of Europe. This reform was part of a broader effort to standardize timekeeping and improve the accuracy of dates in commerce and governance.
events.name: The British Empire adopts the Gregorian calendar

events.enhanced_description: In 1752, the capital of the Kingdom of Burma, Ava, was sacked by the Hanthawaddy Kingdom, led by King Binnya Dala. This event marked a significant conflict in the power struggles of the region.
events.name: Sacking of Ava by Hanthawaddy Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: In June 1752, Benjamin Franklin reportedly conducted his famous kite experiment, demonstrating that lightning is a form of electricity. Although the exact date is debated, the experiment significantly advanced the understanding of electrical phenomena.

image.caption: Alfred Jones’s engraved vignette “Franklin and Electricity,” depicting Benjamin Franklin in an electrical-science context.
image.credit: Alfred Jones, for the Bureau of Engraving and Printing — Restoration by Godot13
image.date_qualification: The image description places the source impression in a Treasury Department presentation album from circa 1902; the supplied 2014 image date is an upload/scan date, not the date depicted.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Franklin's kite experiment

events.enhanced_description: In 1752, the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando was formally established in Madrid, Spain, marking a significant step in the modernization of Spanish art education during the Spanish Enlightenment.
events.name: Establishment of the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1752, Pennsylvania Hospital, the first hospital in the United States, admitted its first patients at a temporary location in Philadelphia. This institution was groundbreaking in providing medical treatment, particularly for the mentally ill, and set a precedent for future healthcare facilities in America.

image.caption: Site photograph of Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2024-02-29; the image does not document the 1752 admission event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Pennsylvania Hospital admits its first patients

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1752, French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered Messier 83, also known as the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy, during his research voyage in the Southern Hemisphere. This discovery was significant as it was the first galaxy cataloged outside the Local Group, expanding the understanding of the universe.

image.caption: Processed astronomical image of Messier 83, the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy.
image.credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab) & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) — The Outskirts of the Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
image.date_qualification: A modern telescope image of the galaxy, not a depiction of its 1752 discovery. The supplied image date is an upload date, not a depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Discovery of Messier 83

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1752, the Virginia Assembly passed a law making maiming a felony, addressing the brutal practice of gouging that was prevalent at the time. This legislation marked a step towards more humane legal standards in colonial America.
events.name: Virginia Assembly passes law against maiming

events.enhanced_description: On February 29, 1752, Alaungpaya, a village chief in Upper Burma, founded the Konbaung Dynasty. His leadership would unify the country within eight years, establishing a significant dynasty in Burmese history.
events.name: Founding of the Konbaung Dynasty

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1752, Shō Kei, the ruler of Okinawa Island and the Ryukyu Kingdom, died at the age of 41 after a reign that began when he was just 13. His death marked a significant transition in the kingdom's leadership to his young son, Shō Boku.
events.name: Death of Shō Kei

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1752, the electors of the Republic of Venice elected Francesco Loredan as their new Doge, following the death of Pietro Grimani. His election was a pivotal moment in Venetian politics, occurring shortly after the previous leader's passing.
events.name: Election of Francesco Loredan as Doge

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1752, The Halifax Gazette was published, marking it as the first newspaper in Canada. This publication played a crucial role in disseminating news and information in the growing colony.
events.name: Publication of The Halifax Gazette

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1752, Spanish Governor Tomás Vélez Cachupín of Santa Fe de Nuevo México initiated peace negotiations with the Comanche tribe in Taos. This marked a significant diplomatic effort to establish relations and peace with the indigenous people.
events.name: Peace negotiations with the Comanche tribe

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1752, the Kingdom of Afghanistan, under Ahmad Shah Durrani, successfully recaptured the city of Lahore from the Sikhs of Punjab. This event was pivotal in the ongoing power struggles in the region.
events.name: Recapture of Lahore by Ahmad Shah Durrani

events.enhanced_description: On April 13, 1752, the Philadelphia Contributionship for the Insurance of Houses from Loss by Fire held its organizational meeting in Philadelphia. This company, founded largely through the efforts of Benjamin Franklin, became the oldest property insurance company in the United States.
events.name: Organizational meeting of the Philadelphia Contributionship

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1752, Adam Smith was unanimously elected as the Professor of Moral Philosophy at the University of Glasgow. His teachings during this period would later influence his seminal work, The Theory of Moral Sentiments.
events.name: Adam Smith elected Professor of Moral Philosophy

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1752, physicist Thomas-François Dalibard successfully conducted the kite experiment proposed by Benjamin Franklin in Marly-la-Ville, France. This experiment was pivotal in demonstrating the connection between lightning and electricity.
events.name: Dalibard conducts Franklin's kite experiment

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1752, the Treaty of Logstown was signed, granting control over lands south and east of the Ohio River to the English. This treaty was a significant diplomatic agreement involving various Native American leaders and colonial representatives.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Logstown

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1752, Pickawillany, the capital of the Miami Indian nation, was attacked and burned by Odawa, Ojibwe, and French soldiers under the command of Odawa War Chief Charles Michel de Langlade. This event marked a significant conflict in the ongoing struggles between Native American nations and colonial powers.
events.name: Attack on Pickawillany

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1752, Divitdar Mehmed Emin Pasha was dismissed from his position as Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire by Sultan Mahmud I. This change in leadership was part of the ongoing political dynamics within the empire.
events.name: Dismissal of Grand Vizier Mehmed Emin Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1752, the first of the Kronstadt canals, conceived by Peter the Great, was completed and opened to maritime traffic. This engineering feat was crucial for enhancing the naval capabilities of Russia.
events.name: Completion of the first Kronstadt canal

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1752, Edward Cornwallis, the British Governor of Nova Scotia, was recalled to Britain after failing to compel the Acadian population to pledge allegiance to the Crown. His replacement, Peregrine Hopson, adopted a more lenient approach.
events.name: Recall of Edward Cornwallis

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1752, a group of Scottish Presbyterians who had fled to America held the first Covenanter communion in the 13 American colonies, marking a significant moment in the religious history of the region. This event symbolized the establishment of a distinct Presbyterian identity in the New World.
events.name: First Covenanter communion in America

events.enhanced_description: On August 25, 1752, the first group of the United Brethren church, known as the Moravians, departed from Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, on a mission to secure land for German emigrants in America. After a 450-mile journey, they arrived in Edenton, North Carolina, where they eventually purchased the Wachovia Tract, establishing a significant settlement.
events.name: Moravian mission to find land

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1752, Benjamin Franklin published an account in the Pennsylvania Gazette describing his famous kite experiment, which he had proposed in his earlier writings. Although he did not claim to be the first to conduct the experiment, it became popularly associated with his name and contributed to the understanding of electricity.
events.name: Franklin's kite experiment description

events.enhanced_description: On November 3, 1752, a devastating hurricane struck Santa Rosa Island, Florida, destroying the Spanish settlement there and leaving only two buildings standing. The surviving residents relocated to the mainland, where they established the Presidio San Miguel de Panzacola, which later became the foundation of Pensacola.

locations.name: Santa Rosa Island, Florida, United States

events.name: Hurricane destroys Spanish settlement

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1752, British Governor Hopson of Nova Scotia and French Governor General of New France, the Marquis Duquesne, reached an agreement to exchange deserters from their respective armies in Canada. This understanding included a commitment that returned deserters would not face execution, reflecting a temporary truce in the ongoing conflicts.
events.name: Deserters exchange agreement

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1752, a peace treaty was signed at Shubenacadie, Nova Scotia, temporarily halting Father Le Loutre's War between British colonists and the Mi'kmaq tribe. Governor Hopson represented the British, while Chief Kopit, the Sakamaw of the Mi'kmaq, signed on behalf of his people, marking a significant moment in colonial relations.
events.name: Peace treaty in Father Le Loutre's War

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1752, the first recorded performance of a Shakespearean play in America took place in Williamsburg, Virginia, where a company of players staged 'The Merchant of Venice'. This event marked a significant cultural milestone in the American theatrical landscape.
events.name: First Shakespearean play in America

events.enhanced_description: In 1753, James Lind authored 'A Treatise of the Scurvy', a groundbreaking work that laid the foundation for understanding the causes and prevention of scurvy, particularly among sailors. His research emphasized the importance of citrus fruits in combating this disease.
events.name: James Lind writes A Treatise of the Scurvy

events.enhanced_description: In 1753, Robert Wood published 'The Ruins of Palmyra; otherwise Tedmor in the Desart', which introduced the ancient city of Palmyra to the Western world. His work combined archaeological observations with artistic illustrations, significantly influencing perceptions of ancient civilizations.

image.caption: View of Palmyra with the Temple of Bel, Syria.
image.date_qualification: A later site view, not an image of Robert Wood publishing his book. Original image date: 2010-04-06.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Robert Wood publishes The ruins of Palmyra

events.enhanced_description: In 1753, the Cramer family established a brewing operation in Warstein, North Rhine-Westphalia, which would later evolve into the renowned Warsteiner brand. This venture marked the beginning of a significant brewing tradition in the region.
events.name: The Cramer family starts brewing operation at Warstein

events.enhanced_description: On January 3, 1753, King Binnya Dala of the Hanthawaddy Kingdom ordered the burning of Ava, the former capital of the Kingdom of Burma. This act was part of a broader conflict and marked a significant moment in the region's tumultuous history.
events.name: Burning of Ava

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1753, Elizabeth Canning returned to her mother's home in London after a month's absence, claiming she had been abducted. Her subsequent trial caused a significant public uproar, highlighting issues of gender and justice in 18th-century England.

image.caption: Portrait of Elizabeth Canning.
image.date_qualification: The portrait is dated circa 1820, roughly 67 years after the event; it is not a contemporary event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Elizabeth Canning's return

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1753, a letter published in Scots' Magazine introduced the concept of electrical telegraphy, suggesting a method for sending electric signals across wires. This early proposal laid the groundwork for future developments in communication technology.
events.name: First concept of electrical telegraphy

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1753, Sweden adopted the Gregorian calendar, skipping 11 days to align with the new system. This significant change in timekeeping marked Sweden's transition into modernity and affected the way dates were recorded in the country.
events.name: Sweden adopts the Gregorian calendar

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1753, the Jewish Naturalisation Act was passed by Britain's House of Lords, allowing Jewish immigrants to England to become naturalized citizens without the requirement of receiving the Sacrament of the Lord's Supper. This act represented a significant step towards religious tolerance in Britain.

locations.name: House of Lords, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Jewish Naturalisation Act 1753

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1753, Carl Linnaeus published 'Species Plantarum', which is recognized as the formal start date of the scientific classification of plants. This work laid the foundation for modern taxonomy and significantly advanced botanical science.
events.name: Species Plantarum published

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1753, the Jewish Naturalisation Act passed the House of Commons and later received royal assent from King George II. This legislation allowed Jewish immigrants to become naturalized citizens, reflecting changing attitudes towards religious minorities in Britain.

locations.name: House of Commons, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Jewish Naturalisation Act receives royal assent

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1753, the Parliament of Great Britain passed Lord Hardwicke's Marriage Act, aimed at preventing clandestine marriages in England and Wales. This act was a significant reform in marriage law, requiring formal registration and public notice.

locations.name: Parliament of Great Britain, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Lord Hardwicke's Marriage Act

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1753, the British Museum was established in London by Act of Parliament, becoming one of the world's first national public museums. It was created to house a collection of artifacts and knowledge, reflecting the Enlightenment ideals of education and public access to culture.
events.name: Establishment of the British Museum

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1753, the Parliament of Great Britain repealed the Jewish Naturalisation Act, which had allowed Jewish immigrants to become naturalized citizens. This repeal reflected the ongoing tensions and challenges faced by religious minorities in Britain.

locations.name: House of Commons, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Repeal of the Jewish Naturalisation Act

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1753, Russian scientist Georg Richmann became the first person to be electrocuted by his own equipment while conducting experiments with a lightning rod. This tragic incident highlighted the dangers of early electrical experimentation and contributed to the understanding of electricity.
events.name: Georg Richmann electrocuted

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1753, the Unity of Brethren, a branch of the Moravian Church, received a grant for the Wachovia Tract in western North Carolina. This land was intended for the benefit of German-speaking immigrants, facilitating their settlement in America.
events.name: Grant of Wachovia Tract to Unity of Brethren

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1753, after receiving warnings about French incursions into Virginia, the cabinet of British Prime Minister Henry Pelham voted to send a warning to colonial governors. This directive aimed to prevent encroachments on British territories by French forces and their Native American allies.
events.name: British cabinet's warning to colonial governors

events.enhanced_description: On September 3, 1753, Tanacharison, a chief of the Oneida tribe, met with French officers in the Ohio region and warned them against advancing further into Iroquois territory. This encounter underscored the tensions between colonial powers and Indigenous nations in North America.
events.name: Tanacharison warns French officers

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1753, Britain's Board of Trade issued a directive to colonial governors, instructing them to send delegates to meet with the Iroquois Confederacy. This meeting aimed to strengthen alliances and address ongoing tensions between colonial settlers and Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Directive for summit meeting with Iroquois

events.enhanced_description: On October 31, 1753, Virginia Lieutenant Governor Robert Dinwiddie commissioned 21-year-old militia Major George Washington to dissuade the French from occupying the Ohio Country. This marked Washington's first significant military assignment, foreshadowing his future role in the French and Indian War.
events.name: George Washington commissioned

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1753, King Fernando VI of Spain issued a set of 25 regulations governing theatrical performances, emphasizing modesty and decorum in the arts. These regulations reflected the cultural values of the time and aimed to control public entertainment.
events.name: Regulations for theatrical performances in Spain
