events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1759, Smeaton's Tower, the Eddystone Lighthouse designed by John Smeaton, was first illuminated. This lighthouse became an engineering marvel of its time and set new standards for lighthouse design.
events.name: Illumination of Smeaton's Tower

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1759, a devastating fire swept through the city of Salonika, destroying approximately 4,000 houses. This disaster had a lasting impact on the city's architecture and urban planning.
events.name: Fire in Salonika

events.enhanced_description: On November 25, 1759, a powerful earthquake struck near Beirut, registering a surface wave magnitude of 7.4. This catastrophic event resulted in the destruction of all villages in the Beqaa Valley and was classified with a maximum Mercalli intensity of IX (Violent).
events.name: Near East Earthquakes of 1759

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1759, Étienne de Silhouette served as Controller-General of France and initiated significant financial reforms aimed at addressing the country's fiscal challenges. His policies, however, were met with resistance and criticism, leading to his eventual downfall.
events.name: Étienne de Silhouette's Financial Reforms

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1759, the British fleet under Sir Edward Hawke decisively defeated a French fleet commanded by Marshal de Conflans in the Battle of Quiberon Bay. This victory effectively crippled the French naval presence and secured British dominance at sea during the Seven Years' War.

image.caption: Oil painting by Dominic Serres depicting the Battle of Quiberon Bay.
image.credit: Dominic Serres — National Maritime Museum, Greenwich
image.date_qualification: Retrospective depiction of the 1759 battle, painted in 1779.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Quiberon Bay

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1759, the Austrian army under Marshal von Daun successfully encircled and forced the surrender of a Prussian force led by Friedrich von Finck at the Battle of Maxen. This defeat was a significant setback for Frederick the Great's forces.
events.name: Battle of Maxen

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1759, Alamgir II, the Mughal Emperor of India, was assassinated in a conspiracy led by his Prime Minister, Imad-ul-Mulk. Following his death, Shah Alam II, a grandson of the previous emperor Aurangzeb, ascended to the throne.
events.name: Assassination of Alamgir II

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1759, the Germantown Union School was founded, which later became known as Germantown Academy. This institution holds the distinction of being America's oldest nonsectarian day school.
events.name: Founding of Germantown Academy

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1759, Shah Jahan III was installed as the puppet ruler of the Mughal Empire, just eleven days after the assassination of Alamgir II. His reign lasted only ten months before he was removed from power.
events.name: Installation of Shah Jahan III

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1759, Arthur Guinness leased the Guinness Brewery at St. James's Gate in Dublin, Ireland. This marked the beginning of what would become one of the most famous breweries in the world, known for its iconic stout.
events.name: Leasing of the Guinness Brewery

events.enhanced_description: In 1760, Abbé Charles-Michel de l'Épée opened the world's first free school for the deaf in Paris, known as the Institut National de Jeunes Sourds de Paris, while Thomas Braidwood established Braidwood's Academy for the Deaf and Dumb in Edinburgh. These institutions marked significant advancements in deaf education and the recognition of the rights of individuals with hearing impairments.
events.name: Establishment of Schools for the Deaf

events.enhanced_description: In 1760, Western countries engaged in extensive trade with China, paying a staggering 3,000,000 ounces of silver for Chinese goods. This trade highlighted the growing economic interdependence between Europe and Asia during the 18th century.
events.name: Western Trade with China

events.enhanced_description: Around 1760, Abu Dhabi was founded, marking the establishment of a settlement that would grow to become the capital of the United Arab Emirates. This founding laid the groundwork for the region's future development and significance.

locations.name: Abu Dhabi, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates

events.name: Founding of Abu Dhabi

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1760, the Battle of Barari Ghat took place, where Afghan forces achieved a decisive victory over the Marathas. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts in the Indian subcontinent during this period.
events.name: Battle of Barari Ghat

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, British General Sir Eyre Coote achieved a significant victory over the French forces led by the Marquis de Bussy-Castelnau at the Battle of Wandiwash in India.
events.name: Battle of Wandiwash

events.enhanced_description: On January 28, 1760, Benning Wentworth created the New Hampshire Grant of Pownal, Vermont. This land grant was part of the colonial expansion and settlement efforts in New England.
events.name: Creation of New Hampshire Grant of Pownal

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1760, the British Royal Navy ship HMS Royal Katherine ran aground off Bolt Head, resulting in the tragic loss of 699 lives. This incident underscored the dangers faced by naval vessels during this era.
events.name: HMS Royal Katherine disaster

events.enhanced_description: On February 26, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, French troops under privateer François Thurot captured the town and castle of Carrickfergus in Northern Ireland. However, they were later defeated in a naval action in the Irish Sea on February 28.
events.name: Battle of Carrickfergus

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1760, during the French and Indian War and the Anglo-Cherokee War, Cherokee natives attacked a North Carolina militia stationed at Fort Dobbs. The militia, commanded by General Hugh Waddell, successfully repelled the attack.
events.name: Cherokee attack on Fort Dobbs

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1760, the Great Fire of Boston erupted, destroying 349 buildings and marking the largest conflagration in the American colonies up to that time. This event had significant implications for urban planning and fire safety in colonial America.
events.name: Great Fire of Boston

events.enhanced_description: On April 3, 1760, Great Britain and Prussia agreed to begin peace negotiations to end the Seven Years' War. This marked a significant step towards resolving one of the largest global conflicts of the 18th century.
events.name: Peace negotiations in the Seven Years' War

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1760, 'Tacky's War', a significant slave rebellion, began in Jamaica and lasted for 18 months. The uprising resulted in the deaths of 60 white residents and over 400 black rebels, highlighting the tensions of slavery in the Caribbean.

image.caption: François-Anne David’s engraving visualizes European fears of slave revolts and most likely depicts Tacky's War.
image.date_qualification: Created in 1800; retrospective illustration, not an image made during the 1760–1761 revolt.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: 'Tacky's War' begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1760, France's Minister of the Navy, Nicolas René Berryer, received permission to send ships to assist French forces in Quebec. A fleet of six ships, commanded by Captain François Chenard de la Giraudais, departed from Bordeaux, although it was too late to prevent the loss of New France to the British.
events.name: French naval assistance to Quebec

events.enhanced_description: On April 11, 1760, the Burmese Army, led by King Alaungpaya, reached the outskirts of Siam's capital, Ayutthaya, but ultimately retreated instead of laying siege to the city. This decision marked a significant moment in the conflict between Burma and Siam.
events.name: Burmese Army's retreat from Ayutthaya

events.enhanced_description: On April 12, 1760, two of six French ships encountered a British blockade led by Admiral Edward Boscawen. This incident exemplified the naval challenges faced by France during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: French ships encounter British blockade

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1760, Marshal François Gaston de Lévis departed from Montreal with 7,000 troops, planning to retake Quebec City from British forces. This maneuver was part of the larger struggle for control of New France during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: French troops depart for Quebec

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1760, Belgian entertainer Joseph Mervin is credited with giving the first demonstration of roller skates at the Carlisle House in London. Unfortunately, the performance ended in disaster, marking a notable moment in the history of recreational activities.
events.name: First demonstration of roller skates

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1760, Marshal Lévis and his troops landed at Saint-Augustin-de-Desmaures, near Quebec City, preparing to lay siege to the British forces occupying the area. This event was a significant step in the ongoing conflict for control of Canada during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Landing of Marshal Lévis at Saint-Augustin-de-Desmaures

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1760, British Army Brigadier General James Murray led a force of 3,500 men toward Saint-Augustin-de-Desmaures to confront Marshal Lévis and the French Army. This maneuver was part of the larger struggle for dominance in North America during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: March of British Army toward Saint-Augustin

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1760, British defenders clashed with the French Army at the Battle of Sainte-Foy, a pivotal encounter in the struggle for Quebec. The British, led by General Murray, suffered significant casualties and were forced to retreat, while the French under Marshal Lévis also incurred heavy losses.
events.name: Battle of Sainte-Foy

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1760, representatives of the remaining Penobscot Indian tribes from Maine and New Brunswick made peace with the British at Fort Pownal in Newfoundland. This agreement marked a significant step in the British efforts to stabilize relations with Indigenous peoples during the colonial conflicts.
events.name: Peace with Penobscot Indian tribes

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1760, Swiss mathematician Daniel Bernoulli presented a groundbreaking paper at the French Academy of Sciences in Paris, where he introduced a mathematical model to study the population dynamics of infectious diseases. This work laid the foundation for future epidemiological studies.

image.caption: Oil portrait of Daniel Bernoulli.
image.credit: Unknown Edited by Bammesk — Basel Historical Museum Link: https://www.hmb.ch/en/museums/objects-in-the-collection/details/s/portraet-des-daniel-bernoulli/
image.date_qualification: The image is dated circa 1720–1725; it does not depict the 1760 presentation.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Daniel Bernoulli's presentation

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1760, King Alaungpaya of Burma died during a retreat from Ayutthaya, having stopped at the village of Kinywa en route to Martaban. His death led to his son Naungdawgyi ascending the throne, marking a significant transition in Burmese leadership.
events.name: Death of King Alaungpaya

events.enhanced_description: On May 16, 1760, three British Royal Navy ships commanded by Commodore Robert Swanton arrived to break the siege of Quebec, thwarting Marshal Lévis's attempts to recapture the city from British control. This event was crucial in maintaining British dominance in the region during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: British Royal Navy breaks siege of Quebec

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1760, Captain Giraudais's French fleet reached the Gaspé Peninsula in northeastern Quebec, capturing seven British merchant ships. However, upon learning that British forces had already moved up the St. Lawrence River, Giraudais diverted his fleet to Chaleur Bay in Newfoundland.
events.name: French fleet captures British merchant ships

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1760, New England planters arrived in Nova Scotia to claim land that had been taken from the Acadians during their expulsion. This event marked a significant demographic and cultural shift in the region.
events.name: Arrival of New England planters in Nova Scotia

events.enhanced_description: On June 11, 1760, Robert Rogers and his Rangers launched a strike from Lake Champlain against French military posts along the Richelieu River, successfully attacking and destroying Fort Sainte-Thérèse. This operation was part of the broader conflict during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Robert Rogers' strike against French military posts

events.enhanced_description: On June 19, 1760, the British established Cumberland County and Lincoln County in Maine, reflecting the administrative changes occurring in the region during the colonial period. This development was part of the broader efforts to organize and govern newly acquired territories.
events.name: Creation of Cumberland and Lincoln Counties

events.enhanced_description: On June 22, 1760, Captain John Byron, commanding HMS Fame, located France's Captain Giraudais but unfortunately ran aground before he could launch an attack. This incident highlights the challenges faced by naval commanders during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Captain John Byron's encounter with Captain Giraudais

events.enhanced_description: On July 3, 1760, a lightning strike caused a major fire at Portsmouth Royal Dockyard in England, resulting in significant damage to the facility. This incident underscored the vulnerabilities of even the most important naval installations of the time.
events.name: Fire at Portsmouth Royal Dockyard

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, the British defeated French forces in the Battle of Restigouche, marking the last naval battle in New France. This victory further solidified British control over the region.
events.name: Battle of Restigouche

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1760, a formal request was made to the Spanish government to allow the founding of what would later become the city of Mayagüez in Puerto Rico. This request was part of the broader colonial expansion efforts in the Caribbean.
events.name: Request to found Mayagüez

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, the Anglo-Hanoverian army led by Ferdinand of Brunswick stormed Warburg, with English commander Lord Granby playing a heroic role in the victory. This battle was significant in the ongoing conflict between Britain and France.
events.name: Battle of Warburg

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1760, the church of Our Lady of Candlemas was founded in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, establishing the basis for the city's future development. This event marked an important cultural milestone in the region.
events.name: Founding of Our Lady of Candlemas Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, British General Jeffery Amherst and his troops captured Montreal from the French, effectively bringing Canada completely under British control. This event marked a significant turning point in North American colonial history.
events.name: Capture of Montreal

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1760, the town of Mayagüez, Puerto Rico, was officially founded. This establishment played a crucial role in the development of the region and its colonial economy.
events.name: Founding of Mayagüez

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1760, the wedding of Princess Isabella of Parma and Prince Joseph of Austria took place at Hofburg Palace's Redoute Hall in Vienna. This royal union was significant in strengthening political alliances in Europe.
events.name: Wedding of Princess Isabella of Parma and Prince Joseph of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, Russian troops entered Berlin, marking a significant moment in the conflict as they advanced into Prussian territory. This event highlighted the shifting dynamics of power in Europe.
events.name: Russian troops enter Berlin

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1760, during the Seven Years' War, Ferdinand of Brunswick faced defeat at the Battle of Kloster-Kamp against a French army. This setback was part of the ongoing struggle for control in the region.
events.name: Battle of Kloster-Kamp

events.enhanced_description: On October 25, 1760, King George II of Great Britain died, leading to the ascension of his 22-year-old grandson, George, Prince of Wales, as King George III. This transition marked the beginning of a long reign that would significantly impact British history.
events.name: Death of George II of Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Torgau, fought on November 3, 1760, was a significant engagement during the Seven Years' War where Frederick II of Prussia achieved a hard-fought victory against the Austrian forces led by Ernst Gideon von Laudon. This battle was notable for its intense combat and strategic importance, as it forced the Austrians to withdraw across the Elbe River.
events.name: Battle of Torgau

events.enhanced_description: On November 29, 1760, Colonel François-Marie Picoté de Belestre of the French Army formally surrendered Fort Detroit to British Army Major Robert Rogers, marking a pivotal moment in the French and Indian War. The raising of the British Union Jack over the fort symbolized the shift of power in the region from French to British control.
events.name: Surrender of Fort Detroit

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1760, British authorities convened a peace conference at Fort Detroit, engaging with Native American delegates from tribes such as the Wyandot and Ottawa. This historic meeting aimed to renew alliances and establish peace following the recent surrender of the fort, symbolized by the presentation of a wampum belt by the Indigenous leaders.
events.name: Native American Peace Conference

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Pondicherry began on December 6, 1760, as British Army Lieutenant General Eyre Coote initiated an assault on the French stronghold in India. This siege was part of the broader conflict of the Seven Years' War and culminated in the eventual surrender of the French forces on January 15, 1761.

image.caption: Engraving depicting the ruins of Pondicherry.
image.date_qualification: The engraving depicts the ruins after the British destruction of Pondicherry; its image date is given as 1762, after the 1760–1761 siege.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Siege of Pondicherry

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1760, the Assembly of the British colony of Jamaica enacted legislation outlawing the African religious practice of obeah, imposing severe penalties including banishment and execution. This law reflected the colonial authorities' fears of rebellion following Tacky's War and aimed to suppress African cultural practices.
events.name: Outlawing of Obeah in Jamaica

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, the Halifax Treaties were concluded between various bands of the Mi'kmaq, other First Nations peoples, and the British, notably marked by the Burying the Hatchet ceremony on June 25. These treaties aimed to establish peace and regulate relations between the British and Indigenous peoples.
events.name: Halifax Treaties concluded

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, a 'state' formed by escaped slaves in Dutch Guyana signed a treaty with the local governor. This event highlighted the struggles for autonomy and recognition by enslaved individuals seeking freedom.
events.name: Treaty signed by escaped slaves in Dutch Guyana

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, the marine chronometer was invented, providing a crucial tool for accurately determining longitude at sea. This invention significantly advanced navigation and maritime exploration.
events.name: Marine chronometer invented

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, Matthew Boulton's Soho Manufactory opened in Birmingham, England, marking a significant development in the Industrial Revolution. This factory became known for producing high-quality metal goods and played a key role in the advancement of manufacturing techniques.
events.name: Matthew Boulton's Soho Manufactory opens

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, the music for "Ah! vous dirai-je, maman" was first published in France by Monsieur Bouin in his book Les Amusements d'une Heure et Demy. This melody later became famous as the tune for the children's song 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.'
events.name: Publication of "Ah! vous dirai-je, maman"

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, the Faber-Castell Company was founded by Kasper Faber in Nuremberg, Germany. This company would go on to become one of the world's leading manufacturers of writing instruments.
events.name: Faber-Castell Company founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, mathematician Johann Heinrich Lambert found a proof that π (pi) is irrational, marking a significant advancement in mathematical theory. This discovery has had lasting implications in mathematics and science.
events.name: Johann Heinrich Lambert proves π is irrational

events.enhanced_description: In 1761, l'Ordre des Chevaliers Maçons Élus Coëns de l'Univers was founded in France, contributing to the development of Masonic traditions and practices. This organization played a role in the broader context of Enlightenment thought and fraternal societies.
events.name: l'Ordre des Chevaliers Maçons Élus Coëns de l'Univers founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1761, the Third Battle of Panipat was fought between the Durrani Empire, led by Ahmad Shah Durrani, and the Maratha Confederacy. This decisive battle resulted in a catastrophic defeat for the Marathas, with over 100,000 soldiers and civilians killed, and it significantly altered the power dynamics in India.
events.name: Third Battle of Panipat

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1761, an earthquake struck London, causing significant damage by breaking chimneys in areas such as Limehouse and Poplar. This event was one of the notable seismic occurrences in the city during the 18th century.
events.name: Earthquake in London

events.enhanced_description: On March 8, 1761, a second earthquake occurred in North London, affecting areas such as Hampstead and Highgate. This seismic event contributed to the growing awareness of geological activity in the region.
events.name: Second Earthquake in North London

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1761, an earthquake measuring 8.5 struck Lisbon, Portugal, with effects felt as far north as Scotland. Despite its magnitude, few deaths were reported, largely due to censorship by the Portuguese government.
events.name: Lisbon Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1761, the Austrian Empire and the Russian Empire signed a new treaty of alliance, strengthening their diplomatic and military ties during a period of significant geopolitical tension in Europe.
events.name: Austrian-Russian Treaty of Alliance

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1761, a severe epidemic of influenza broke out in London, affecting nearly the entire population and leading to a notable increase in miscarriages and premature births among pregnant women. This outbreak highlighted the public health challenges of the time.
events.name: Influenza Epidemic in London

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1761, Thomas Boone was transferred to become the Royal Governor of South Carolina after his tenure as the Royal Governor of New Jersey was marred by difficulties in working with the local assembly. This change reflected the ongoing challenges of colonial governance.
events.name: Thomas Boone's Transfer

events.enhanced_description: On May 4, 1761, a tornado struck Charleston, South Carolina, marking the first recorded multiple death tornado in the 13 American colonies. The storm resulted in the deaths of eight people and the sinking of five ships in the harbor.
events.name: Tornado in Charleston

events.enhanced_description: On June 6, 1761, a transit of Venus was observed from 120 locations around the world, including St. Petersburg, where Mikhail Lomonosov made significant observations. He noted a ring of light around Venus, becoming the first to discover that the planet has an atmosphere.
events.name: Transit of Venus

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1761, the first section of the Bridgewater Canal was opened, facilitating the transportation of coal from local mines to Manchester. This engineering achievement played a crucial role in the Industrial Revolution by improving trade and transportation.
events.name: Opening of the Bridgewater Canal

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1761, the Parlement of Paris voted to close all colleges, associations, and seminaries associated with the Jesuit Order, following a long campaign led by Louis-Adrien Le Paige. This decision reflected the growing tensions between the French government and the Jesuits during the Enlightenment.
events.name: Closure of Jesuit Colleges

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1761, George Washington, then a military officer and politician, advertised a reward in the Maryland Gazette for the capture of four fugitive slaves who had escaped from his estate at Mount Vernon. This advertisement highlights the complexities of slavery and property rights in colonial America.
events.name: George Washington's Fugitive Slaves

events.enhanced_description: On August 15, 1761, the Third Family Compact was executed between King Charles III of Spain and King Louis XV of France, solidifying their alliance and cooperation against common enemies in Europe. This treaty was part of the broader Bourbon family agreements that shaped European politics.
events.name: Third Family Compact

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1761, Cherokee chief Attakullakulla met with British Army officer Major James Grant at Fort Prince George to negotiate an end to the Anglo-Cherokee War. This meeting was crucial in addressing the tensions between the British and Cherokee nations.

locations.name: Fort Prince George, South Carolina, United States

events.name: Anglo-Cherokee War Negotiations

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1761, King George III of Great Britain married Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, a union that would have significant implications for the British monarchy and its relationship with Germany. Their marriage produced 15 children and solidified political alliances.

locations.name: St. James's Palace, London, England, United Kingdom

events.name: Marriage of George III and Charlotte

events.enhanced_description: On September 19, 1761, Portugal officially abolished slavery, marking a significant step in the country's legal and social reforms. This decision reflected the growing Enlightenment ideals regarding human rights and the treatment of individuals.
events.name: Abolition of Slavery in Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1761, George III and his wife Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz were crowned at Westminster Abbey in London. This event marked the beginning of their reign and was significant in establishing the royal family's presence in British society.
events.name: George III and Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz are crowned

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1761, Austrian field marshal Ernst Gideon von Laudon successfully captured the Prussian town of Schweidnitz during the Seven Years' War. This victory was part of a larger campaign that significantly impacted the war's dynamics in Central Europe.
events.name: Ernst Gideon von Laudon captures Schweidnitz

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1761, William Pitt was dismissed from his position as Secretary of State for the Southern Department, marking a significant shift in British politics. His dismissal ended a powerful coalition government with Prime Minister the Duke of Newcastle, leading to changes in policy during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: William Pitt is dismissed

events.enhanced_description: On October 30, 1761, Colonel Henry Bouquet issued a proclamation aimed at curbing Anglo-American settlement on Indian lands in North America. This proclamation was a response to increasing tensions between settlers and Native American tribes.
events.name: Henry Bouquet issues proclamation against Anglo-American settlement

events.enhanced_description: On November 7, 1761, the New London Harbor Light was first lit, serving as a crucial navigational aid for ships entering the Connecticut harbor. This lighthouse is notable for being one of the earliest in the United States and has been in continuous operation for over 250 years.
events.name: New London Harbor Light is first lit

events.enhanced_description: On November 11, 1761, the Earl of Egremont, as Secretary of State for the Southern Department, initiated a policy that prohibited land grants to white settlers in territories occupied by American Indian tribes. This decision was part of the British government's efforts to manage relations with Native Americans.
events.name: Earl of Egremont forbids land grants to settlers

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1761, a separate peace treaty was signed between the Cherokee Indians and the Colony of Virginia, effectively bringing the Anglo-Cherokee War to a close. This treaty aimed to restore peace and regulate relations between the settlers and the Cherokee.
events.name: Peace treaty signed between Cherokee Indians and Virginia

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1761, a 500-man force from the Army of Spain captured the Yucatán village of Cisteil, effectively ending the revolt of Mexico's Maya population. The Spanish forces faced significant resistance, resulting in heavy casualties among the Maya defenders.
events.name: Spanish Army ends Maya revolt

events.enhanced_description: On December 16, 1761, Russian forces under General Pyotr Rumyantsev captured the Prussian fortress of Kolberg after a four-month siege during the Seven Years' War. This victory was significant in the context of the war, altering the balance of power in the region.
events.name: Russians take Kolberg

events.enhanced_description: In 1762, the Cock Lane ghost became a sensational topic in London, attracting public attention and debate over the existence of spirits. The case involved claims of haunting and led to a trial that questioned the intersection of belief, superstition, and rational inquiry in 18th-century England.
events.name: Cock Lane ghost

events.enhanced_description: In 1762, Empress Go-Sakuramachi succeeded to the throne of Japan following the death of her brother, Emperor Momozono. Her reign lasted for eight years, during which she navigated the complexities of the imperial court.

image.caption: A published portrait of Empress Go-Sakuramachi.
image.credit: Published by 三英舎 (San'ei-sha) — "御歴代百廿一天皇御尊影"
image.date_qualification: Portrait published in 1894, long after her 1762 accession; it is not a contemporary depiction of the accession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Empress Go-Sakuramachi ascends to the throne

events.enhanced_description: In 1762, the North Carolina General Assembly designated Kingston, named after King George III, as the county seat of Dobbs County. The name was later shortened to Kinston in 1784, reflecting the evolving identity of the town.
figures: King George III of the United Kingdom
events.name: Incorporation of Kingston as the county seat of Dobbs County

events.enhanced_description: The town of Charlottesville was founded in 1762 in Virginia, later becoming notable for its historical significance and as the home of the University of Virginia, founded by Thomas Jefferson.
events.name: Founding of Charlottesville, Virginia

events.enhanced_description: In 1762, the Plymouth Synagogue was built in Plymouth, England, becoming the oldest synagogue built by Ashkenazi Jews in the English-speaking world. It stands as a testament to the Jewish community's history in Britain.
events.name: Construction of the Plymouth Synagogue

events.enhanced_description: In 1762, Jean-Jacques Rousseau published two seminal works, The Social Contract in Amsterdam and Emile in The Hague. These texts sparked significant philosophical debate and were subsequently banned in Rousseau's native Geneva.
events.name: Publication of The Social Contract and Emile

events.enhanced_description: James Stuart and Nicholas Revett published their architectural treatise, Antiquities of Athens, in 1762, which significantly influenced neoclassical architecture and the study of ancient Greek structures.
events.name: Publication of Antiquities of Athens

events.enhanced_description: In 1762, Paisius of Hilendar completed the Istoriya Slavyanobolgarskaya, a significant work that documented the history of the Bulgarian people and contributed to the revival of Bulgarian national consciousness.
events.name: Completion of Istoriya Slavyanobolgarskaya

events.enhanced_description: Around 1762, Shaikh Mohamed bin Khalifa Al Khalifa founded Zubarah on the northwestern shore of the Qatari Peninsula, establishing a city-state that became a significant trading hub and center of authority over local tribes.
figures: Shaikh Mohamed bin Khalifa Al Khalifa
events.name: Foundation of Zubarah

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1762, Britain declared war against Spain and Naples, following their recent alliance with France during the ongoing Seven Years' War. This declaration marked a significant escalation in the conflict and expanded the war's geographical scope.
events.name: Britain declares war against Spain and Naples

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1762, Empress Elisabeth of Russia died and was succeeded by her nephew Peter III. His ascension to the throne marked a shift in Russian foreign policy, as he sought peace with Prussia.
events.name: Empress Elisabeth of Russia dies

events.enhanced_description: On January 16, 1762, British forces under General Robert Monckton landed on the French island of Martinique in the Caribbean. This operation was part of the broader military campaigns during the Seven Years' War.

image.caption: Dominic Serres’s retrospective depiction of the Capture of Martinique.
image.date_qualification: The image depicts the 1762 capture but is a later artwork dated 1766, not a contemporary event photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: British forces land on Martinique

events.enhanced_description: On February 5, 1762, the Great Holocaust of the Sikhs was carried out by the forces of Ahmed Shah Abdali in Punjab, resulting in the deaths of approximately 30,000 men, women, and children. This brutal campaign marked a significant moment in the history of Sikh resistance against invasions.
events.name: Great Holocaust of the Sikhs

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1762, French forces on Martinique surrendered to the British during the ongoing Seven Years' War. The island was subsequently returned to France as part of the Peace of Paris, which concluded the conflict.

image.caption: Dominic Serres’s painting *The Capture of Martinique, 11 February 1762*.
image.date_qualification: The artwork is dated 1766 in the supplied metadata, so it is not a contemporary photograph or an image made during the event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: French forces on Martinique surrender to the British

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1762, a Royal Navy fleet with 16,000 men departed from Spithead, England, setting sail toward Cuba to seize strategic Spanish possessions in the Americas. This military operation was part of the broader conflict of the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Royal Navy fleet departs for Cuba

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1762, Jean Calas, a 68-year-old French merchant, was unjustly executed on the orders of the Parlement of Toulouse due to religious differences. His brutal execution sparked outrage and became a pivotal case in the fight against judicial injustice in France.
events.name: Jean Calas executed

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1762, the first Saint Patrick's Day Parade took place in lower Manhattan, New York City, inaugurating an annual tradition that celebrates Irish culture. This event has grown to become one of the largest parades in the world, attracting hundreds of thousands of participants.
events.name: First Saint Patrick's Day Parade in New York City

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1762, Samuel Farley launched The American Chronicle, a weekly newspaper in New York City. This publication was significant as it was the seventh newspaper to be established in the city, contributing to the growing landscape of American journalism.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Launch of The American Chronicle

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1762, a powerful earthquake struck the border region between modern-day Bangladesh and Myanmar, triggering a tsunami in the Bay of Bengal. This disaster resulted in the tragic loss of at least 200 lives.
events.name: Earthquake and Tsunami in the Bay of Bengal

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1762, France enacted a new ordinance requiring all black and mixed-race individuals to register their identity with the Admiralty Court. This law, influenced by adviser Guillaume Poncet de la Grave, aimed to document both free and enslaved individuals, reflecting the complexities of race and identity in colonial France.
events.name: Ordinance for Black and Mixed-Race Frenchmen

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1762, the Treaty of Saint Petersburg was signed, effectively ending the war between Russia and Prussia. The treaty resulted in the return of all territorial conquests made by Russia back to Prussia, marking a significant shift in the balance of power in Eastern Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Saint Petersburg

events.enhanced_description: On May 22, 1762, the Treaty of Hamburg was signed, which officially removed Sweden from the conflict against Prussia during the Seven Years' War. This treaty was part of the broader negotiations that sought to stabilize the region after years of warfare.
events.name: Treaty of Hamburg

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1762, King George III dismissed Prime Minister Duke of Newcastle due to dissatisfaction with the progress of the French and Indian War. He appointed his former tutor, John Stuart, 3rd Earl of Bute, as his successor, marking a significant political shift in British leadership.
events.name: Dismissal of Duke of Newcastle

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1762, Marco Foscarini was elected as the new Doge of the Republic of Venice following the death of Francesco Loredan, who had served for a decade. Foscarini's election marked a continuation of Venice's unique political traditions.
events.name: Marco Foscarini becomes Doge of Venice

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1762, Cherokee war chief Ostenaco, along with aides Standing Turkey and Pouting Pigeon, was received by King George III in London. Their visit aimed to discuss peace terms with the British government, reflecting the complex relations between Native American tribes and colonial powers.
events.name: Ostenaco meets King George III

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1762, the Anglo-Hanoverian army led by Ferdinand of Brunswick achieved a decisive victory over French forces at the Battle of Wilhelmsthal in Westphalia. This battle was a significant event in the ongoing conflicts of the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Wilhelmsthal

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1762, Catherine II orchestrated a coup to overthrow her husband, Tsar Peter III, and ascended to the throne as Empress of Russia. This event marked the beginning of her influential reign, which would significantly shape Russian history.
events.name: Catherine II becomes Empress of Russia

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1762, Frederick II of Prussia achieved victory over Austrian forces led by Marshal Daun at the Battle of Burkersdorf in Silesia. This battle was one of Frederick's last major engagements during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Burkersdorf

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1762, King Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha successfully conquered Makwanpur, furthering his campaign to unify Nepal. This conquest was part of his broader efforts to establish a centralized state in the region.
events.name: Conquest of Makwanpur

events.enhanced_description: On September 15, 1762, British troops defeated the French at the Battle of Signal Hill, marking the last battle of the North American theatre of the Seven Years' War. This victory solidified British control over Newfoundland.

locations.name: St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada

events.name: Battle of Signal Hill

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1762, British troops of the East India Company captured Manila from Spanish forces during the Seven Years' War. This event led to the British occupation of Manila and its designation as an open port, altering the colonial landscape in the region.
events.name: Battle of Manila

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1762, Christoph Willibald Gluck's opera Orfeo ed Euridice premiered in Vienna. This work is considered a landmark in the development of opera, emphasizing emotional expression and dramatic coherence.
events.name: First performance of Orfeo ed Euridice

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1762, the Siege of Schweidnitz concluded with Prussia capturing the strategic fortress from Austria. This victory was crucial for Prussia's military position in Silesia during the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Siege of Schweidnitz

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1762, Prince Henry of Prussia achieved a significant victory over the Austrian army led by Marshal Serbelloni at the Battle of Freiberg. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts of the Seven Years' War.
events.name: Battle of Freiberg

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1762, Catherine II announced a manifesto welcoming foreigners to settle in Russia, waiving previous religious requirements for immigration. However, the manifesto notably excluded Jews, reflecting the complex social dynamics of the time.
events.name: Catherine II's Immigration Manifesto

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1762, Catherine II issued an invitation to Europeans to settle in southern Russia along the Volga River, promising free travel expenses and rights guarantees. This initiative aimed to promote agricultural development in the region.
events.name: Catherine II's Invitation to European Settlers

events.enhanced_description: In August 1763, a devastating fire swept through Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey), destroying approximately 2,600 houses and leaving many residents homeless, highlighting the vulnerability of urban centers in the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: Fire in Smyrna

events.enhanced_description: In 1763, Little Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, Turkey, suffered significant damage due to an earthquake, highlighting the vulnerability of historical structures in seismically active regions.
events.name: Little Hagia Sophia earthquake damage

events.enhanced_description: In 1763, composer Joseph Haydn wrote his Symphony No. 13, contributing to the development of classical music during the late 18th century.
events.name: Joseph Haydn's Symphony No. 13

events.enhanced_description: The Russo-Circassian War began in 1763 as the Russian Empire sought to annex Circassia, leading to a protracted conflict that would last for decades and significantly impact the region's demographics and politics.
events.name: Russo-Circassian War begins

events.enhanced_description: On January 27, 1763, the seat of colonial administration in the Viceroyalty of Brazil was moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, marking a significant shift in the political landscape of colonial Brazil.
events.name: Relocation of colonial administration in Brazil

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1763, colonial authorities in North Carolina established Mecklenburg County from the western portion of Anson County, named in honor of Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, the wife of King George III.

locations.name: Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, United States
Anson County, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Establishment of Mecklenburg County

events.enhanced_description: On February 10, 1763, the Treaty of Paris was signed, officially ending the French and Indian War. This treaty resulted in France ceding Canada and significant territories to Great Britain, reshaping the colonial landscape of North America.
events.name: Treaty of Paris ends the French and Indian War

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1763, the Treaty of Hubertusburg was signed, bringing an end to the Seven Years' War between Prussia and Austria, along with their respective allies. This treaty solidified Prussia's status as a major European power.
events.name: Treaty of Hubertusburg ends the Seven Years' War

events.enhanced_description: On February 23, 1763, the Berbice Slave Uprising began in the former Dutch colony of Berbice. This revolt was a significant event in the history of slavery in the Americas, highlighting the struggles for freedom among enslaved people.
events.name: Berbice Slave Uprising begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1763, Charles Townshend was appointed President of the Board of Trade in the British government, a position that would influence colonial policy leading up to the American Revolution.
events.name: Charles Townshend becomes President of the Board of Trade

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1763, the Théâtre du Palais-Royal, which had served as the home of the Paris Opera for nearly 90 years, was destroyed in an accidental fire, marking a significant loss in French cultural heritage.

image.caption: The Théâtre du Palais-Royal in Paris, France.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2011-11-26; not contemporary with the 1763 destruction.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Destruction of the Théâtre du Palais-Royal

events.enhanced_description: On April 16, 1763, George Grenville took office as the Prime Minister of Great Britain, succeeding the Earl of Bute amid criticism over the concessions made in the Treaty of Paris.
events.name: George Grenville becomes Prime Minister of Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On April 18, 1763, Marie-Josephte Corriveau was hanged near her home in Saint-Vallier, Quebec, after being found guilty of murdering her husband. Her story became a part of French Canadian folklore as 'la Corriveau'.
events.name: Execution of Marie-Josephte Corriveau

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1763, Teedyuscung, known as the 'King of the Delaware Indians', was assassinated by arsonists who burned down his home in Pennsylvania. This act was seen as retaliation for his signing of the Treaty of Easton.
events.name: Assassination of Teedyuscung

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1763, John Wilkes published Issue 45 of his satirical newspaper The North Briton, which criticized King George III's speech praising the end of the Seven Years' War. This led to his arrest for libel, becoming a landmark case for freedom of speech.
events.name: Publication of The North Briton Issue 45

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1763, Pontiac, chief of the Odawa people, convened a conference near Detroit, rallying leaders from 17 nations to unite against British control of former French territories in North America.
events.name: Pontiac convenes conference to attack British outposts

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1763, Pontiac initiated Pontiac's War by launching a surprise attack on the British garrison at Fort Detroit. However, the plan was compromised by a young native girl who alerted the British.
events.name: Beginning of Pontiac's War

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1763, during Pontiac's War, Chippewa warriors captured Fort Michilimackinac by distracting the garrison with a game of lacrosse, showcasing their strategic ingenuity.

image.caption: Aerial photograph of the reconstructed Fort Michilimackinac historic site.
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the reconstructed site, not the 1763 capture; image date: 2022-10-11.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Capture of Fort Michilimackinac

events.enhanced_description: On June 28, 1763, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck Hungary and Slovakia, causing significant shaking and resulting in 83 fatalities, although damage was limited.
events.name: Earthquake in Hungary and Slovakia

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1763, the British East India Company declared Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal, to be deposed, marking a significant moment in the consolidation of British power in India.
events.name: Deposition of Mir Qasim

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1763, the Mozart family embarked on a grand tour of Europe, significantly raising the profile of child prodigy Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and showcasing his musical talents across the continent.
events.name: The Mozart family grand tour of Europe

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1763, Mir Qasim was routed at Odwa Nala, leading to his retreat to Patna where he massacred the English garrison, but ultimately faced defeat in subsequent battles.
events.name: Mir Qasim routed at Odwa Nala

events.enhanced_description: The Amsterdam banking crisis of 1763 was marked by the spectacular bankruptcies of prominent bankers Leendert Pieter de Neufville and Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky, leading to a financial contagion that affected merchants across major European cities including Amsterdam, Hamburg, Berlin, and Stockholm.
events.name: Amsterdam banking crisis

events.enhanced_description: On August 5, 1763, during Pontiac's War, British forces led by Colonel Henry Bouquet achieved a decisive victory against Chief Pontiac's Native American coalition at the Battle of Bushy Run, securing British control over the western frontier.
events.name: Battle of Bushy Run

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1763, Empress Catherine II of Russia endorsed Ivan Betskoy's plans for establishing a Foundling Home in Moscow, a significant step towards social reform and the care of abandoned children in the Russian Empire.
events.name: Foundling Home in Moscow

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1763, King George III issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763, which restricted British colonists from settling west of the Appalachian Mountains in an effort to stabilize relations with Indigenous peoples and prevent further conflicts.
events.name: Royal Proclamation of 1763

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1763, Thomas Bayes' groundbreaking work on probability theory was first announced, laying the foundation for what is now known as Bayes' theorem, which has profound implications in statistics and decision-making.
events.name: Bayes' theorem announcement

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1763, Touro Synagogue in Newport, Rhode Island, was dedicated, becoming the oldest surviving synagogue in North America and a symbol of religious freedom and tolerance in the New World.
events.name: Dedication of Touro Synagogue

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1763, the Paxton Boys massacred six Conestoga Indians in their homes in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. The violence escalated when they later killed 16 survivors sheltered in a workhouse, reflecting the tensions between settlers and Native Americans during this period.
events.name: Paxton Boys massacre

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1764, the Siculicidium was carried out, resulting in the massacre of hundreds of the Székely minority in Transylvania by the Austrian Army at Mădăraș, reflecting the ethnic tensions and conflicts in the region.
events.name: Siculicidium

events.enhanced_description: On January 19, 1764, John Wilkes was expelled from the House of Commons of Great Britain for seditious libel, an event that highlighted the tensions between freedom of speech and government authority in the period leading up to the American Revolution.
events.name: John Wilkes expelled from House of Commons

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1764, the settlement of St. Louis was established, which would grow to become a major city and a key hub for trade and westward expansion in the United States.
events.name: Establishment of St. Louis

events.enhanced_description: On March 15, 1764, French explorer and scholar Anquetil Du Perron returned to Paris after a nine-year mission and presented a complete copy of the Zoroastrian sacred text, the Zend Avesta, to the Bibliothèque Royale, marking a significant moment in the study of Eastern religions in Europe.
events.name: Presentation of Zend Avesta

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1764, Francisco Javier de la Torre arrived in Manila to assume the role of Spanish Governor-General of the Philippines, a position that would influence colonial administration in the region.
events.name: Arrival of Francisco Javier de la Torre

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1764, following the British victory in the French and Indian War, a British expedition led by Major Arthur Loftus was attacked by Tunica warriors while exploring newly acquired territories east of the Mississippi River, forcing the soldiers to retreat under fire.
events.name: British expedition attacked by Tunica warriors

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1764, following lobbying by Governor George Johnstone, Britain's Lords of Trade recommended a northern boundary for the new province of West Florida, significantly expanding its jurisdiction and impacting colonial governance.
events.name: Boundary recommendation for West Florida

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1764, the prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire cast their last vote as Emperor Francis I's health declined, approving his son Joseph as King of the Romans, a pivotal moment in the transition of power within the empire.
events.name: Last vote of prince-electors

events.enhanced_description: On March 31, 1764, a mutual defense treaty was signed in Saint Petersburg between Empress Catherine the Great of Russia and King Frederick the Great of Prussia, committing both nations to support each other militarily for eight years.
events.name: Mutual defense treaty between Russia and Prussia

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1764, the British Parliament passed the Sugar Act, which imposed duties on sugar and molasses imported into the American colonies, a significant legislative move that would contribute to rising tensions leading up to the American Revolution.
events.name: Sugar Act passed

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1764, residents of French Louisiana were informed that they would come under Spanish rule due to a secret agreement between France and Spain, marking a significant shift in colonial governance in North America.
events.name: Spanish rule in Louisiana announced

events.enhanced_description: On April 27, 1764, eight-year-old prodigy Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart performed a private concert for King George III and Queen Charlotte in London, showcasing his extraordinary talent and marking an early highlight in his illustrious career.
events.name: Mozart's concert for King George III

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1764, Baden, a member state of the Confederation of Switzerland, declared a policy of neutrality in future conflicts, a stance that would influence the broader Swiss policy of neutrality established in 1815.
events.name: Baden declares neutrality

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1764, the Quebec Gazette was established in Quebec City, becoming the oldest surviving newspaper in North America and a significant development in the region's media landscape.
events.name: Quebec Gazette established

events.enhanced_description: On June 29, 1764, one of the strongest tornadoes ever recorded struck Woldegk, a small town in northeastern Germany. This tornado is notable for its intensity and the destruction it caused, contributing to the study of severe weather phenomena in Europe.
events.name: One of the strongest tornadoes ever recorded hits Woldegk, Germany

events.enhanced_description: On July 6, 1764, the last British troops departed from Havana, Cuba, two years after capturing the city from Spain during the Seven Years' War. This withdrawal was part of a treaty that saw Spain cede West Florida to Great Britain in exchange for the return of Havana.
events.name: The last British troops depart Havana, Cuba

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on July 8, 1764, the Niagara Conference was convened by Sir William Johnson, the British Superintendent of Indian Affairs, to negotiate peace with Native American tribes following the French and Indian War. This significant gathering included around 2,000 representatives from various tribes across North America.

locations.name: Niagara Falls, New York, United States

events.name: The Niagara Conference begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1764, King George III approved the conditional repatriation of Acadians who had taken up arms against British rule during the French and Indian War. The Privy Council's order allowed those willing to pledge allegiance to the British Crown to settle in Nova Scotia, albeit dispersed across various locations.

image.caption: Thomas Davies’s painting depicts the plundering and burning of Grimross.
image.credit: Thomas Davies — National Gallery of Canada #6270
image.date_qualification: The painting is dated 1758 and depicts an earlier episode of the Acadian Expulsion, not the 1764 repatriation order.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Conditional repatriation of the Acadians in Canada

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1764, King George III issued a Royal Determination regarding the disputed boundary between the colonial provinces of New York and New Hampshire. This declaration established the Connecticut River as the boundary line, resolving a long-standing territorial dispute.

locations.name: Connecticut River, New Hampshire/Vermont, United States

events.name: Royal Determination of the boundary between New York and New Hampshire

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1764, a tragic incident occurred near Greencastle, Pennsylvania, when a group of four Delaware Indians invaded a schoolhouse, resulting in the deaths of ten schoolchildren and their teacher, Enoch Brown. This event is often cited as the first documented school shooting in the United States, occurring amidst the tensions of Pontiac's War.
events.name: First documented United States school shooting

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1764, Sir William Johnson arrived at the Niagara River site to meet with representatives of various Indian nations. This meeting was part of the ongoing efforts to negotiate peace following the French and Indian War.

locations.name: Niagara Falls, New York, United States

events.name: Johnson arrives at the Niagara River site

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1764, the Treaty of Fort Niagara was signed between Great Britain and 44 North American Indian nations, effectively ending hostilities that had persisted since the French and Indian War. Sir William Johnson represented Britain, while various tribal leaders signed on behalf of their nations.

locations.name: Fort Niagara, New York, United States

events.name: The Treaty of Fort Niagara is signed

events.enhanced_description: On September 7, 1764, Stanisław August Poniatowski was elected as the King of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. His reign would be marked by attempts at reform and modernization amidst the challenges posed by neighboring powers.
events.name: Stanisław August Poniatowski is elected King

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1764, Edward Gibbon conceived the idea for his monumental work, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, while reflecting amid the ruins of the Capitol in Rome. This work would become a cornerstone of historical literature.
events.name: Edward Gibbon conceives The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: On October 22, 1764, the British East India Company achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Buxar against the combined forces of Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Bengal, the Nawab of Awadh, and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. This battle solidified British control over Bengal and marked a significant turning point in Indian history.
events.name: Battle of Buxar

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1764, Mary Campbell, a captive of the Lenape during the French and Indian War, was turned over to forces commanded by Colonel Henry Bouquet. This event was part of the broader context of conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers.
events.name: Mary Campbell is turned over to Colonel Henry Bouquet

events.enhanced_description: On December 1, 1764, a small group of 30 Sikhs defended the holy site of the Golden Temple (Darbar Sahib) in Amritsar against a massive force of 30,000 Afghans. This siege is remembered as a significant event in Sikh history, showcasing the community's resilience.
events.name: Siege of Darbar Sahib (1764)

events.enhanced_description: In 1765, Frederick the Great, King of Prussia, issued a decree abolishing the historic punishments against unmarried women for alleged 'sex crimes', particularly the humiliating practices known as Hurenstrafen. This reform marked a significant shift in the legal treatment of women in Prussia.
events.name: Decree Abolishing Punishments for Unmarried Women

events.enhanced_description: In early 1765, Isaac Barré, a member of the British House of Commons, coined the term 'Sons of Liberty' in response to Charles Townshend's derogatory remarks about American colonists during discussions of the Stamp Act. This term would later be adopted by American colonists as a rallying cry for resistance against British oppression.
events.name: Coining of the Term 'Sons of Liberty'

events.enhanced_description: Dr. James Baker establishes the first chocolate factory in the Thirteen Colonies in Dorchester, Massachusetts, marking a significant development in the American food industry. This factory would pave the way for the popularization of chocolate in the colonies and later the United States.
events.name: The first chocolate factory in the Thirteen Colonies is established

events.enhanced_description: The first true restaurant opens in Paris, founded by a tavern-keeper named Boulanger, who offers cooked dishes in an all-night establishment on the Rue Bailleul. This innovation in dining would influence culinary culture and the restaurant industry worldwide.
events.name: The first true restaurant opens in Paris

events.enhanced_description: The auto-da-fé parade, a public ceremony often used as a pretext for violence against Jews and alleged heretics, is abolished in Lisbon. This decision reflects a significant shift in societal attitudes towards religious tolerance and the treatment of minority groups.
events.name: The auto-da-fé parade is abolished in Lisbon

events.enhanced_description: The Desai Atash Behram, a Zoroastrian fire temple, is established in Navsari, India. This temple serves as a significant religious center for the Parsi community, reflecting the enduring traditions and cultural heritage of Zoroastrianism in India.
events.name: Desai Atash Behram is established in Navsari, India

events.enhanced_description: Catherine the Great establishes the Novodevichii Institute in Saint Petersburg, the first secondary education school for non-noble females in Russia. This initiative marks a significant step towards women's education and empowerment in the Russian Empire.
events.name: Catherine the Great establishes the Novodevichii Institute

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1765, Spain's five-member special junta, appointed by Prime Minister Jerónimo Grimaldi, presented a report aimed at addressing the stagnation of Spain's commerce with its colonies and foreign nations. The report provided detailed directives for José de Gálvez, the visitador general in charge of New Spain, to implement reforms to enhance trade efficiency.
events.name: Report of the Special Junta

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1765, following a public campaign led by the writer Voltaire, judges in Paris posthumously exonerated Jean Calas, who had been wrongfully executed for the alleged murder of his son in 1762. This landmark decision highlighted the issues of justice and religious intolerance in France during this period.
events.name: Exoneration of Jean Calas

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1765, royal assent was granted to the Duties in American Colonies Act, commonly known as the Stamp Act, marking the first direct tax imposed by Great Britain on the thirteen American colonies. This act required colonists to purchase stamps for legal documents and various goods, inciting widespread protest and resistance among the colonists.
events.name: Royal Assent to the Stamp Act

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1765, Great Britain enacted the Quartering Act, which mandated that private households in the thirteen American colonies provide housing and provisions for British soldiers. This legislation was met with resentment and contributed to the growing tensions between the colonies and the British government.
events.name: Passage of the Quartering Act

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1765, representatives of the British Empire and the Choctaw Indian tribe signed a peace treaty at Fort Tombecbe, near present-day Epes, Alabama. This treaty established boundaries between Choctaw lands and those designated for British settlers, and included provisions for British support in local governance.
events.name: Treaty at Fort Tombecbe

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1765, English surveyors Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon commenced the survey of the boundary between Pennsylvania and Maryland, following the completion of the semi-circular boundary with Delaware. This survey would later become known as the Mason-Dixon Line, a significant demarcation in American history.
events.name: Mason-Dixon Line Survey Begins

events.enhanced_description: On April 14, 1765, in response to the recently passed Stamp Act, American colonists invaded a British Army arsenal near New York City Hall, sabotaging weapons by spiking them. This act of defiance was part of the growing unrest against British taxation and control in the colonies.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Colonial Sabotage of British Arsenal

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1765, German engineer Christian Kratzenstein presented a perfected version of the arithmetical machine originally invented by Gottfried Leibniz to the Russian Academy of Sciences in Saint Petersburg. This machine addressed previous flaws in calculations, although it was not further developed.
events.name: Presentation of Arithmetical Machine

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1765, an accidental fire devastated one quarter of Montreal, shortly after British rule was established over the formerly French colony of Quebec. This disaster highlighted the challenges faced by the new administration in managing the city and its infrastructure.
events.name: Fire in Montreal

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1765, while strolling in Glasgow Green, Scottish engineer James Watt experienced a moment of inspiration that led to a breakthrough in the development of the steam engine. He conceptualized a method to improve the efficiency of steam engines, which would later revolutionize industry and transportation.

image.caption: Interior of James Watt’s garret workshop, preserved in the Science Museum, London.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2008-05-30; it does not depict the event itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: James Watt's Inspiration for the Steam Engine

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1765, the Isle of Man was brought under British control through the Isle of Man Purchase Act, which confirmed HM Treasury's acquisition of the feudal rights of the Dukes of Atholl. This act marked a significant step in consolidating British authority over the island.
events.name: Isle of Man Purchase Act

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1765, King George III dismissed George Grenville from his position as Prime Minister of Great Britain, appointing Charles Watson-Wentworth, Lord Rockingham, as his successor. This change in leadership reflected the shifting political landscape in Britain during a time of increasing colonial unrest.
events.name: Dismissal of George Grenville

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1765, under the orders of Chief Pontiac, War Chief Wahpesah of the Kickapoo people released British Indian Affairs negotiator George Croghan after 35 days of detention. This event was part of broader negotiations among Native American tribes and the British following the French and Indian War.
events.name: Release of George Croghan

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1765, Qianlong, the Emperor of China, issued a decree mandating the creation of copper engravings to depict his military victories. This initiative was part of a broader effort to promote Chinese culture and history, while also fostering diplomatic relations with Britain and France.
events.name: Qianlong's Decree on Copper Engravings

events.enhanced_description: On July 21, 1765, Karim Khan Zand returned to Shiraz after eliminating his rivals for leadership of Persia. He established Shiraz as his capital and initiated the construction of citadels, mosques, schools, and other significant buildings, marking the beginning of a cultural and architectural renaissance in the region.
events.name: Construction of Citadels in Shiraz

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1765, a party led by Odawa Chief Pontiac and British negotiator George Croghan traveled along the Wabash River to secure the release of all white prisoners of war held by the Miami people and Odawa tribes. This event underscored the ongoing negotiations and tensions in the Great Lakes region following the French and Indian War.
events.name: Release of White Prisoners of War

events.enhanced_description: On July 30, 1765, eight students at Yale College attacked the residence of President Thomas Clap in protest against his promotion of 'New Light' Calvinist doctrine. The incident involved vandalism and public disorder, leading to the students pleading guilty and Clap's eventual resignation.
events.name: Attack on Yale President's Residence

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1765, Empress Catherine II of Russia issued a decree authorizing a new method for producing vodka through freezing. This innovation reflected the growing importance of vodka in Russian culture and economy.
events.name: Catherine II's Vodka Production Decree

events.enhanced_description: On August 14, 1765, in a demonstration against the Stamp Act, Bostonians attacked the home of Andrew Oliver, a customs official. This act of violence was part of the broader colonial resistance to British taxation and control.
events.name: Attack on Andrew Oliver's Home

events.enhanced_description: On August 16, 1765, the Treaty of Allahabad was signed, marking the beginning of British political and constitutional involvement in India. This treaty established the foundation for British rule in the region and significantly altered the political landscape of India.
events.name: Signing of the Treaty of Allahabad

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1765, Joseph II ascended to the throne as Holy Roman Emperor. His reign would be marked by significant reforms and attempts to modernize the empire, reflecting the Enlightenment ideals of the time.
events.name: Joseph II Becomes Holy Roman Emperor

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1765, in a further protest against the Stamp Act, Bostonians destroyed the home of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson. This act of violence underscored the growing tensions and resistance among colonists against British authority.
events.name: Destruction of Thomas Hutchinson's Home

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1765, a mob attacked the house of philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau in Switzerland, reflecting the contentious political climate of the time and the backlash against Enlightenment thinkers. This incident highlighted the tensions between revolutionary ideas and traditional societal norms.
events.name: Mob Attack on Rousseau's House

events.enhanced_description: François Antoine, a local hunter, claims to have killed the infamous Beast of Gévaudan, a creature that terrorized the region and was responsible for numerous attacks on livestock and humans. This event sparked widespread interest and fear, leading to various theories about the beast's identity and nature.
events.name: François Antoine announces he has killed the Beast of Gévaudan

events.enhanced_description: The Pennsylvania Gazette reports the resignation of Mr. McCullough, the Distributor of Stamps for North Carolina, in protest against the unpopular Stamp Act imposed by the British Parliament. This act of defiance reflects the growing unrest in the American colonies regarding British taxation policies.
events.name: The Pennsylvania Gazette reports that a Mr. McCullough resigns in protest at the Stamp Act

events.enhanced_description: The Stamp Act, a direct tax imposed by the British Parliament, goes into effect across the thirteen American colonies, requiring all printed materials to carry a tax stamp. This legislation ignites widespread protests and resistance among colonists, laying the groundwork for future revolutionary actions.

image.caption: Newspaper-style posting of the Stamp Act.
image.credit: British Parliment 1765 — Library of Congress , Gwillhickers
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 1765; this dates the document, not a recorded moment of enactment or posting.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Stamp Act goes into effect in the thirteen American colonies

events.enhanced_description: In a report by The Pennsylvania Gazette, Dr. Huston, who was appointed as the Distributor of Stamps for North Carolina, resigns in protest against the Stamp Act. His resignation underscores the growing dissent against British taxation in the colonies.
events.name: The Pennsylvania Gazette reports that Dr. Huston resigns in protest at the Stamp Act

events.enhanced_description: Charles Edward Stuart, known as 'Bonnie Prince Charlie', declares himself King Charles III, becoming the new Stuart claimant to the British throne and a figurehead for the Jacobite movement. His claim symbolizes the ongoing struggle for the restoration of the Stuart monarchy in Britain.

image.caption: Portrait of Prince Charles Edward Stuart, painted by Allan Ramsay.
image.date_qualification: Portrait dated 1745; it depicts Charles Edward Stuart, not his 1766 accession as the Stuart claimant.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Charles Edward Stuart becomes King Charles III

events.enhanced_description: In February, a series of ferocious wolf attacks occur in France, notably attributed to the Beast of Gévaudan. These incidents capture public attention and lead to widespread fear and speculation about the nature of the beast.

image.caption: Engraving of la Bête du Gévaudan, published in The London Magazine.
image.date_qualification: The engraving is dated 1765, during the period of attacks described in the article; it is a contemporary depiction, not a photograph of an attack.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Ferocious wolf attacks occur in France

events.enhanced_description: In 1766, the sloop Mary Brow arrived in Savannah, marking the first direct importation of African slaves into the colony of Georgia. This event signified a pivotal moment in the colony's economic development and the entrenchment of slavery in the southern United States.
events.name: First importation of African slaves into Georgia

events.enhanced_description: In 1766, American botanist John Bartram completed his first extensive exploration and cataloging of North American plants, contributing significantly to the field of botany and the understanding of North American flora.
events.name: John Bartram's exploration of North American plants

events.enhanced_description: In 1766, Childsburgh, the seat of Orange County, North Carolina, was renamed Hillsborough in honor of Wills Hill, 1st Marquess of Downshire. This change reflected the evolving political landscape in the American colonies.
events.name: Renaming of Childsburgh to Hillsborough

events.enhanced_description: In 1766, Dr. James Fordyce published his two-volume work, Sermons to Young Women, in London. This influential text aimed to guide young women in moral and religious conduct, reflecting the societal values of the time.

image.caption: Engraved portrait of James Fordyce, by T. Trotter from a model by J. Flaxman.
image.credit: Engraved by T.Trotter from a model by J. Flaxman. — http://ihm.nlm.nih.gov/images/B12050
image.date_qualification: The image date is given as 1786, twenty years after the work’s publication in 1766.
image.image_date: Published in London. by T. Cadel in 1786.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Publication of Sermons to Young Women

events.enhanced_description: Christian VII ascends to the throne as King of Denmark-Norway, marking the beginning of his reign during a period characterized by political intrigue and the influence of his court physician, Johann Friedrich Struensee.
events.name: Christian VII becomes King of Denmark-Norway
