events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1787, Captain William Bligh set sail from Portsmouth, England, aboard the HMS Bounty, embarking on a mission to collect breadfruit plants from Tahiti. This voyage would later become infamous due to the mutiny that occurred during the journey.
events.name: Captain William Bligh sets sail from England for Tahiti, on HMS Bounty

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1788, the first edition of The Times, originally known as The Daily Universal Register, was published in London. This newspaper would go on to become one of the most influential publications in the world.
events.name: The first edition of The Times is published in London

events.enhanced_description: In 1788, British iron production reached an impressive 68,000 tons, reflecting the industrial advancements of the time. This increase in production was a key factor in the burgeoning Industrial Revolution in Britain.
events.name: Annual British iron production reaches 68,000 tons

events.enhanced_description: On January 2, 1788, Georgia ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the fourth state to do so. This ratification was a crucial step in the establishment of the new federal government.
events.name: Georgia ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1788, Connecticut ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the fifth state to join the Union. This event underscored the growing acceptance of the Constitution among the states.
events.name: Connecticut ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On January 18, 1788, the leading ship of Captain Arthur Phillip's First Fleet arrived at Botany Bay, marking the beginning of British colonization in Australia. This event was significant for both British history and the indigenous peoples of Australia.
events.name: The leading ship of Captain Arthur Phillip's First Fleet arrives at Botany Bay

events.enhanced_description: On January 22, 1788, the Congress of the Confederation elected Cyrus Griffin as its last president, marking the end of this governing body as the United States moved towards a new constitutional framework. Griffin's presidency was symbolic of the transitional period in American governance.
events.name: The Congress of the Confederation elects Cyrus Griffin as its last president

events.enhanced_description: On January 24, 1788, the La Perouse expedition arrived off Botany Bay, coinciding with Captain Arthur Phillip's efforts to establish a colony. This encounter highlighted the international interest in the Pacific region during this era.
events.name: The La Perouse expedition arrives off Botany Bay

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1788, the First Fleet, led by Captain Arthur Phillip, landed at Sydney Cove, establishing the first permanent European settlement in Australia. This event is commemorated as Australia Day and marks the beginning of British colonization.

image.caption: Indigenous art titled “Dawn Reflections” projected on the Sydney Opera House.
image.date_qualification: Contemporary Australia Day event imagery from 2023, not a depiction of the 1788 First Fleet landing; the original image date is recorded as 26 January 2023, 05:34:01 (according to Exif data).
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Australia Day: First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove

events.enhanced_description: On January 31, 1788, Henry Benedict Stuart was recognized as the new Stuart claimant to the British throne, taking the title King Henry IX. He became a figurehead for the Jacobite movement, which sought to restore the Stuart dynasty.
events.name: Henry Benedict Stuart becomes the new Stuart claimant to the throne

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1788, Isaac Briggs and William Longstreet patented a steamboat, contributing to the evolution of maritime transportation. This innovation paved the way for the development of steam-powered vessels in the United States.
events.name: Isaac Briggs and William Longstreet patent a steamboat

events.enhanced_description: On February 6, 1788, Massachusetts ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the sixth state to do so. This ratification was crucial for the Constitution's acceptance and the establishment of the federal government.
events.name: Massachusetts ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On February 7, 1788, Sydney was named and founded by the British Colony of New South Wales. This city would grow to become one of Australia's largest and most significant urban centers.
events.name: Sydney is named and founded by the British Colony of New South Wales

events.enhanced_description: On February 9, 1788, Austria entered the Russo-Turkish War (1787–1792) and launched an attack on Moldavia. This conflict was part of a larger struggle for power in Eastern Europe and had significant implications for the region.
events.name: Austria enters the Russo-Turkish War and attacks Moldavia

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1788, the uninhabited Lord Howe Island was discovered by the brig HMS Supply, commanded by Lieutenant Ball. This discovery occurred while en route to Norfolk Island to establish a penal settlement.
events.name: Lord Howe Island is discovered by HMS Supply

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1788, the La Perouse expedition departed from Sydney Cove for New Caledonia, never to be seen again. This mysterious disappearance remains one of the great maritime mysteries of the age.
events.name: The La Perouse expedition leaves Sydney Cove for New Caledonia

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1788, the Edinburgh Evening Courant published a notice offering a £200 reward for the capture of William Brodie, a town councilor who led a double life as a burglar. This incident highlighted the stark contrast between his public persona and criminal activities.
events.name: The Edinburgh Evening Courant carries a notice of £200 reward for the capture of William Brodie

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1788, the Great New Orleans Fire devastated the city, killing approximately 25% of the population and destroying 856 buildings, including significant structures like St. Louis Cathedral and The Cabildo. The fire left much of the town in ruins, prompting a reevaluation of fire safety measures.
events.name: The Great New Orleans Fire

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1788, American pioneers established Marietta in present-day Ohio, marking it as the first permanent American settlement outside the original Thirteen Colonies. This settlement played a crucial role in westward expansion and the development of the Northwest Territory.
events.name: Establishment of Marietta

events.enhanced_description: Beginning on April 13, 1788, the 'Doctors' Mob' riot erupted in Manhattan as residents protested against grave robbers who were stealing bodies for medical dissection. The unrest highlighted tensions between the medical community and the public, culminating in a violent response that was suppressed by authorities on April 15.
events.name: America's first recorded riot, the 'Doctors' Mob'

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1788, Maryland ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the seventh state to do so. This ratification was a significant step in the establishment of the new federal government and the framework of American democracy.
events.name: Maryland ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1788, the Royal Dramatic Theatre (Kungliga Dramatiska Teatern) was founded in Stockholm, Sweden. This institution became the national theatre of Sweden, playing a pivotal role in the development of Swedish drama and performing arts.
events.name: Foundation of the Royal Dramatic Theatre

events.enhanced_description: The Australian frontier wars began on May 15, 1788, marking a series of conflicts between European settlers and Indigenous Australians. These confrontations arose as settlers expanded their territories, leading to significant cultural and social upheaval.
events.name: Beginning of the Australian frontier wars

events.enhanced_description: On May 23, 1788, South Carolina ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the eighth state to join the Union. This event was crucial in solidifying the framework of governance for the newly independent states.
events.name: South Carolina ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1788, the Day of the Tiles occurred in Grenoble, France, an event that some historians consider the beginning of the French Revolution. Citizens protested against royal authority, leading to violent clashes with troops and a significant escalation of political tensions.
events.name: Day of the Tiles

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1788, the African Association was founded in London, England, with the aim of exploring the Niger River and locating the fabled city of Timbuktu. This organization played a significant role in the European exploration of Africa.
events.name: Foundation of the African Association

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1788, English captains Thomas Gilbert and John Marshall, while returning from Botany Bay, became the first Europeans to encounter the Gilbert Islands in the Pacific Ocean. They also charted other islands in the region, contributing to the mapping of the Pacific.
events.name: Encounter with the Gilbert Islands

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1788, New Hampshire ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the ninth state to do so. This ratification was pivotal in allowing the Constitution to go into effect, leading to the establishment of the new federal government.
events.name: New Hampshire ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On June 25, 1788, the Virginia Ratifying Convention ratified the United States Constitution, making Virginia the tenth state to join the Union. This event was crucial for the Constitution's acceptance and the establishment of the federal government.
events.name: Virginia Ratifying Convention ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On June 26, 1788, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart completed his antepenultimate symphony, now known as Symphony No. 39 in E-flat. This work is celebrated for its innovative orchestration and emotional depth, contributing to Mozart's legacy as a master composer.
events.name: Mozart completes Symphony No. 39

events.enhanced_description: On June 27, 1788, the Russo-Swedish War broke out following a staged attack on Swedish troops in Puumala, present-day Finland. This conflict marked a significant escalation in tensions between Russia and Sweden, leading to a prolonged military engagement.
events.name: Russo-Swedish War begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1788, a devastating hailstorm swept across France and the Dutch Republic, producing hailstones 'as big as quart bottles' that took 'three days to melt.' The storm caused immense damage to crops and property, exacerbating the economic difficulties of the time.
events.name: Hailstorm in France and the Dutch Republic

events.enhanced_description: On July 24, 1788, Governor General Lord Dorchester issued a proclamation from the Chateau St. Louis in Quebec City, dividing the British Province of Quebec into five districts: Gaspé, Nassau, Lunenburg, Mecklenburg, and Hesse. This administrative change aimed to improve governance in the province.
events.name: Governor General Lord Dorchester divides Quebec

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1788, New York ratified the United States Constitution, becoming the eleventh state to do so. This ratification was crucial for the Constitution's implementation and the establishment of the new federal government.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: New York ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On July 28, 1788, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart completed his penultimate symphony, now known as Symphony No. 40 in G Minor. This symphony is renowned for its emotional intensity and innovative structure, solidifying Mozart's reputation as a leading composer of the Classical era.
events.name: Mozart completes Symphony No. 40

events.enhanced_description: On August 8, 1788, King Louis XVI of France agreed to convene the Estates-General for May 1789, marking the first meeting since 1614. This decision was a response to the financial crisis and social unrest, setting the stage for the French Revolution.

image.caption: Map of electoral subdivisions represented at the Estates-General of 1789, traced from Brette’s 1904 atlas.
image.date_qualification: Map created 2021-01-02; depicts the electoral subdivisions for the Estates-General of 1789, not the 1788 decision.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: King Louis XVI agrees to convene the Estates-General

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1788, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart completed his final symphony, known as Symphony No. 41 in C Major, later nicknamed 'The Jupiter' after his death. This symphony is celebrated for its grandeur and complexity, representing the culmination of Mozart's symphonic achievements.
events.name: Mozart completes his final symphony

events.enhanced_description: On August 12, 1788, the Anjala conspiracy was signed, a secret agreement among Swedish officers to negotiate peace with Russia during the Russo-Swedish War. This conspiracy reflected the growing discontent within the Swedish military regarding the war's direction.
events.name: The Anjala conspiracy is signed

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1788, the trial of Deacon William Brodie for burglary began in Edinburgh, Scotland. Brodie, who had led a double life as a respected town councilor and a burglar, was ultimately sentenced to death by hanging, highlighting the complexities of his character.
events.name: Trial of Deacon William Brodie begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1788, the United States Congress of the Confederation passed an act that established a timeline for voting in the first presidential election under the new Constitution. This act was a critical step in the transition to a functioning federal government.
events.name: U.S. Congress passes act for presidential voting timeline

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1788, during the Austro-Turkish War, the Battle of Karánsebes occurred, marked by a tragic friendly-fire incident within the Austrian army that resulted in mass casualties. This chaotic event underscored the challenges of military coordination during wartime.
events.name: Battle of Karánsebes

events.enhanced_description: The Theater War commenced on September 24, 1788, when the forces of Denmark-Norway invaded Sweden, marking the beginning of a conflict that would last until 1790. This war was largely influenced by the political tensions in Northern Europe and the ambitions of King Gustav III of Sweden.

image.caption: Anthon Christoffer Rüde’s illustration of the Affair at Quistrumbro.
image.date_qualification: The supplied image date is 1790-01-01; it does not depict the war’s beginning in 1788.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Theater War begins

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1788, William Brodie, a prominent Edinburgh cabinetmaker and the inspiration for Robert Louis Stevenson's character Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, was hanged at the Tolbooth in Edinburgh. His execution was a significant event reflecting the social and moral issues of the time.
events.name: William Brodie is hanged

events.enhanced_description: In October 1788, King George III of the United Kingdom began to exhibit signs of derangement, leading to the onset of the Regency Crisis. This crisis raised questions about the monarchy's stability and the role of Parliament, ultimately resulting in the appointment of a regent.
events.name: Regency Crisis of 1788 begins

events.enhanced_description: The 14th and final session of the Continental Congress was adjourned on October 21, 1788, marking the end of an era in American governance under the Articles of Confederation. This session was significant as it transitioned power to the newly established federal government.
events.name: Continental Congress adjourned

events.enhanced_description: On November 8, 1788, voting took place in the 11 states that had ratified the United States Constitution to elect the first U.S. Senators. In Virginia, Richard Henry Lee and William Grayson, both anti-federalists, received the highest votes, reflecting the political divisions of the time.
events.name: Voting for first U.S. Senators

events.enhanced_description: Cyrus Griffin completed his term as the last President of the Congress of the Confederation on November 15, 1788. His presidency marked the conclusion of the Congress under the Articles of Confederation, paving the way for the new federal government.
events.name: Cyrus Griffin completes service as President of Congress

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1788, Prime Minister William Pitt presented the first formal report to the Houses of Parliament regarding King George III's mental illness. This report led to a two-week adjournment of Parliament as they awaited further examinations by royal physicians.
events.name: Report on King George III's mental illness

events.enhanced_description: From November 25, 1788, France experienced fifty consecutive days of temperatures below freezing, a record that would remain unbroken for over 200 years. This extreme weather had significant impacts on agriculture and daily life in the country.
events.name: Cold weather in France

events.enhanced_description: In December 1788, Scottish poet Robert Burns wrote his famous version of the poem 'Auld Lang Syne', which would later become a traditional song for New Year's celebrations around the world. This work reflects the cultural heritage and literary significance of Scotland.
events.name: Robert Burns writes Auld Lang Syne

events.enhanced_description: On December 6, 1788, during the Russo-Turkish War, the Ottoman fortress of Özi fell to Russian forces after a prolonged siege. The siege was marked by harsh winter conditions, including a severe storm that dropped temperatures to -23°C (-9°F).
events.name: Siege of Özi

events.enhanced_description: King Charles III of Spain died on December 14, 1788, after a reign that saw significant reforms and modernization in Spain. He was succeeded by his son, Charles IV, marking a transition in Spanish monarchy during a tumultuous period in European history.
events.name: Death of King Charles III of Spain

events.enhanced_description: In January 1789, Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès published the influential pamphlet 'What Is the Third Estate?' which argued for the rights of the common people in France. This work played a crucial role in shaping the discourse leading up to the French Revolution.
events.name: Publication of What Is the Third Estate?

events.enhanced_description: In March 1789, the first version of a graphic description of the slave ship Brookes was issued by the English Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade. This document played a crucial role in raising awareness about the horrors of the slave trade.
events.name: Graphic description of slave ship issued

events.enhanced_description: The Second Xhosa War, also known as the War of the Axe, began in 1789 as tensions escalated between the Xhosa people and European settlers in the Eastern Cape region of South Africa. This conflict was part of a series of frontier wars that arose from land disputes and colonial expansion.
events.name: Second Xhosa War begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Paris faced a significant economic crisis, with an estimated 150,000 of its 600,000 residents unemployed. This widespread unemployment contributed to the social unrest that fueled the French Revolution.
events.name: An estimated 150,000 of Paris's 600,000 people are without work

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, the Storofsen flood struck Norway, causing widespread devastation. This natural disaster had significant impacts on the local population and infrastructure.
events.name: Storofsen flood in Norway

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, the National Assembly at Versailles reconstituted itself as the National Constituent Assembly, marking a pivotal moment in the French Revolution as it began drafting a new constitution for France.
events.name: At Versailles, the National Assembly reconstitutes itself as the National Constituent Assembly

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, the Theatre War officially concluded in Scandinavia, marking the end of hostilities between Sweden and Russia. This conflict had significant implications for the balance of power in Northern Europe.
events.name: The Theatre War officially ends in Scandinavia

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, survivors of the mutiny on the Bounty, including Captain William Bligh, reached Timor after a perilous 4,000-mile journey in an open boat. This remarkable feat of navigation and endurance highlighted the challenges faced by seafarers in the 18th century.
events.name: Survivors of the mutiny on the Bounty reach Timor

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, the United States Department of the Post Office was established, facilitating communication across the growing nation. This development was crucial for the expansion of postal services and the dissemination of information.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The United States Department of the Post Office is established

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Joseph II, Holy Roman Emperor, issued a decree converting all peasant labor obligations into cash payments. This reform aimed to modernize the agrarian economy and alleviate the burdens on peasants, reflecting Joseph's broader efforts to implement enlightened absolutism.
events.name: Joseph II decrees peasant labor obligations be converted into cash payments

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, the Qajar dynasty established itself as the ruling dynasty of Iran, marking the beginning of a new era in Persian history. Under Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, the dynasty sought to consolidate power and modernize the state amidst regional challenges.
events.name: The Qajar dynasty establishes themselves as rulers in Iran

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Antoine Lavoisier published the Traité Élémentaire de Chimie, which is considered the first modern chemistry textbook. This work laid the foundation for modern chemical nomenclature and principles, significantly advancing the field of chemistry.
events.name: The Traité Élémentaire de Chimie is published

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth discovered the element uranium while studying the mineral pitchblende. This discovery was significant in the field of chemistry and later played a crucial role in nuclear science.
events.name: Martin Heinrich Klaproth discovers uranium

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, the Bengal Presidency established a penal colony in the Andaman Islands, marking the beginning of British colonial administration in this remote region. This move aimed to manage convicts and assert control over the strategically important islands.
events.name: The Bengal Presidency establishes a penal colony in the Andaman Islands

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Thomas Jefferson returned from Europe, bringing with him the first macaroni machine to the United States. This introduction of pasta-making technology contributed to the culinary landscape of America and reflected Jefferson's appreciation for French cuisine.
events.name: Thomas Jefferson returns from Europe with the first macaroni machine

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, influenced by Benjamin Rush's arguments against excessive alcohol consumption, about 200 farmers in a Connecticut community formed a temperance movement. This grassroots initiative aimed to promote moderation and reduce the social issues associated with alcohol.
events.name: Temperance movement forms in Connecticut

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Fort Washington was constructed in Cincinnati, Ohio, to protect early U.S. settlements in the Northwest Territory. This fortification played a crucial role in the defense and expansion of American territories during a period of westward migration.
events.name: Fort Washington is built in Cincinnati

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Olaudah Equiano's autobiography, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano, was published in London. This work is one of the earliest published narratives by a black writer and played a significant role in the abolitionist movement.
events.name: Olaudah Equiano's autobiography is published

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, Peggy, the world's oldest surviving private yacht, was built in Castletown, Isle of Man. This vessel represents a significant part of maritime history and showcases the craftsmanship of the time.

locations.name: Castletown, Isle of Man, United Kingdom

events.name: Peggy of Castletown is built

events.enhanced_description: In 1789, two Frenchmen, Blanchard and Maguier, invented the pedal-powered tricycle. This innovation represented a significant advancement in personal transportation and laid the groundwork for future developments in cycling.
events.name: The pedal-powered tricycle is invented

events.enhanced_description: The 1788-89 United States presidential election and House of Representatives elections were held, marking a pivotal moment in American history as the nation established its first federal government. This election set the stage for the presidency of George Washington.
events.name: 1788-89 United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1789, the Treaty of Fort Harmar was reaffirmed, which included terms from previous treaties with Native American tribes. This treaty was significant in the context of U.S. expansion and relations with indigenous peoples.
events.name: Treaty of Fort Harmar

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1789, 'The Power of Sympathy or the Triumph of Nature Founded in Truth', the first American novel, was printed in Boston, Massachusetts. Written by William Hill Brown, this novel marked a significant milestone in American literature.
events.name: First American novel printed

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1789, Georgetown University was founded in Georgetown, Maryland, which is now part of modern-day Washington, D.C. It became the first Roman Catholic college in the United States, playing a vital role in higher education.
events.name: Georgetown University founded

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1789, Emperor Quang Trung of Vietnam achieved a decisive victory against the Chinese Qing forces at Ngọc Hồi-Đống Đa. This battle is celebrated as one of the greatest military successes in Vietnamese history, solidifying national pride.
events.name: Ngọc Hồi-Đống Đa victory

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1789, George Washington was unanimously elected as the first president of the United States by the United States Electoral College. His election marked a foundational moment in the establishment of the U.S. government and its democratic principles.
events.name: George Washington elected president

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1789, King Gustav III of Sweden enforced the Union and Security Act, effectively dismantling Sweden's 70-year-old parliamentary system in favor of absolute monarchy. This act significantly altered the political landscape of Sweden.
events.name: Union and Security Act enforced

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1789, the 1st United States Congress convened at Federal Hall in New York City, officially declaring the new United States Constitution to be in effect. This meeting marked the beginning of the legislative branch of the U.S. government.
events.name: 1st United States Congress meets

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1789, the Menashi-Kunashir rebellion began in Japan, involving conflict between the Ainu people and Japanese settlers. This rebellion highlighted the tensions between indigenous populations and expanding Japanese influence.
events.name: Menashi-Kunashir rebellion begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1789, a catastrophic explosion occurred at the Venetian arsenal on the island of Corfu, resulting in the deaths of 180 bystanders and the destruction of a seawall. This incident underscored the dangers associated with military stockpiles.
events.name: Explosion at Venetian arsenal

events.enhanced_description: On April 1, 1789, the United States House of Representatives achieved its first quorum at Federal Hall in New York City, marking a significant step in the establishment of the new government. Congressman Frederick Muhlenberg was elected as the first Speaker of the House, setting a precedent for future legislative leadership.
events.name: First Quorum of the U.S. House of Representatives

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1789, the United States Senate attained its first quorum at Federal Hall in New York City, electing John Langdon as its first President pro tempore. This event coincided with the joint session of Congress where electoral votes were counted, officially certifying George Washington as President-elect and John Adams as Vice President-elect.
events.name: First Quorum of the U.S. Senate

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1789, Selim III succeeded Abdul Hamid I as the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire. His reign would be marked by attempts at modernization and reform in response to the challenges facing the empire during a time of significant internal and external pressures.
events.name: Selim III becomes Sultan

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1789, George Washington received a warm welcome in Trenton, New Jersey, as the president-elect. This event was a significant moment in the early history of the United States, reflecting the public's support for Washington as a leader.
events.name: George Washington's reception at Trenton

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1789, John Adams was inaugurated as the first Vice President of the United States at Federal Hall in New York City. He began presiding over the Senate, playing a crucial role in the early legislative processes of the new nation.

image.caption: Engraved Bureau of Engraving and Printing portrait of John Adams.
image.credit: The Bureau of Engraving and Printing — Restoration by Godot13
image.date_qualification: Portrait; not a contemporary image of the event. The supplied image date is 2014-06-19 17:22:32.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: John Adams takes office as Vice President

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1789, Fletcher Christian led a mutiny against Captain William Bligh aboard the British Royal Navy ship HMS Bounty in the Pacific Ocean. This event became one of the most famous mutinies in naval history, driven by discontent over harsh treatment and the crew's desire for a better life.
events.name: Mutiny on the Bounty

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1789, George Washington was inaugurated as the first President of the United States at Federal Hall in New York City. This historic event marked the beginning of the new federal government under the Constitution and set the precedent for future presidential inaugurations.
events.name: George Washington's Inauguration

events.enhanced_description: On May 5, 1789, the Estates-General convened for the first time in 175 years at Versailles, France, marking the beginning of the French Revolution. This assembly brought together representatives from the three estates of the realm and highlighted the growing discontent with the monarchy.
events.name: Estates-General convenes

events.enhanced_description: In June 1789, the Inconfidência Mineira emerged as the first significant attempt at Brazilian independence from Portuguese rule. This movement was driven by local elites in Minas Gerais who sought greater autonomy and was ultimately suppressed by colonial authorities.

image.caption: Flag of the Inconfidentes, depicted in an image by Carlos Oswald.
image.date_qualification: Image dated circa 1939; the depicted flag image is retrospective, not contemporaneous with the 1789 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Inconfidência Mineira

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1789, representatives of the Third Estate at the Estates-General declared themselves the National Assembly in Versailles, asserting their authority and signaling a pivotal shift in the political landscape of France. This act was a key moment leading up to the French Revolution.
events.name: National Assembly declared

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1789, members of the National Assembly took the Tennis Court Oath in Versailles, pledging not to disband until a new constitution was established for France. This oath became a symbol of the revolutionaries' determination to create a government that represented the people.
events.name: Tennis Court Oath

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1789, King Louis XVI of France delivered a conciliatory speech urging reforms during a joint session of the Estates-General. He ordered the three estates to meet together, a move that reflected the growing pressure for change in the face of revolutionary fervor.
events.name: Louis XVI's conciliatory speech

events.enhanced_description: In July 1789, it was reported that approximately 150,000 of Paris's 600,000 residents were unemployed, highlighting the economic distress that contributed to the social unrest leading up to the French Revolution. This situation exacerbated tensions between the populace and the monarchy.
events.name: Unemployment in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On July 1, 1789, the comic ballet La fille mal gardée, choreographed by Jean Dauberval, premiered at the Grand Théâtre de Bordeaux. This ballet is notable for its innovative choreography and remains a classic in the repertoire of ballet companies worldwide.
events.name: La fille mal gardée premiere

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1789, the U.S. Congress passed its first bill, which set out tariffs. This legislation was crucial for establishing the financial framework of the new nation and marked the beginning of federal economic policy.

locations.name: United States Congress, New York City

events.name: First U.S. Tariff Bill

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1789, the National Assembly reconstituted itself as the National Constituent Assembly in Versailles, beginning preparations for what would become the French Constitution of 1791. This marked a significant step in the revolutionary process.
events.name: National Constituent Assembly formed

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1789, explorer Alexander Mackenzie reached the Mackenzie River Delta, becoming the first recorded person to cross North America from east to west. His journey contributed significantly to the mapping and understanding of the Canadian landscape.
events.name: Alexander Mackenzie reaches the Mackenzie River Delta

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1789, King Louis XVI dismissed his popular Chief Minister Jacques Necker, a decision that sparked outrage among the populace and contributed to the growing unrest leading to the French Revolution. Necker's dismissal was seen as a direct threat to the financial reforms he had championed.
events.name: Louis XVI dismisses Jacques Necker

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1789, an angry crowd in Paris, incited by journalist Camille Desmoulins, protested against King Louis XVI's decision to dismiss Minister Jacques Necker. This demonstration was a pivotal moment in the lead-up to the French Revolution, reflecting the public's growing discontent with the monarchy.
events.name: Parisian crowd protests Necker's dismissal

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1789, the people of Paris began seizing arms in preparation for the defense of the city against potential royalist forces. This act of defiance was part of the escalating tensions that would soon culminate in the storming of the Bastille.
events.name: Seizure of arms in Paris

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1789, citizens of Paris stormed the fortress of the Bastille, freeing the seven prisoners held there. This event is widely regarded as the symbolic start of the French Revolution, representing the uprising against tyranny and the demand for liberty.
events.name: Storming of the Bastille

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1789, the citizens of Paris stormed the fortress of the Bastille, a symbol of royal tyranny, freeing seven prisoners. This event marked a turning point in the French Revolution and ignited widespread revolutionary fervor across France.
events.name: French Revolution: Storming of the Bastille

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1789, the U.S. Congress established the Department of Foreign Affairs, which would later be renamed the Department of State. This marked the creation of the first federal agency responsible for managing international relations in the United States.

locations.name: United States Congress, New York City

events.name: Establishment of the Department of Foreign Affairs

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1789, members of the Constituent Assembly in France took an oath to abolish feudalism and renounce their privileges. This decision was a crucial step in the revolutionary process, reflecting the desire for equality and justice among the populace.

image.caption: Engraving depicting the National Assembly renouncing privileges at Versailles.
image.credit: Charles Monnet / Isidore Helman (graveur) — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b6943988b/f1
image.date_qualification: Retrospective illustration of the night of 4–5 August 1789; image date is circa 1789.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Oath to end feudalism

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1789, the U.S. Congress established the Department of War, which was responsible for overseeing military affairs in the new nation. This agency played a vital role in shaping the defense and military policy of the United States.

locations.name: United States Congress, New York City

events.name: Establishment of the Department of War

events.enhanced_description: On August 18, 1789, the Liège Revolution erupted in the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, a significant uprising against the ruling authorities. This revolution was part of a broader wave of revolutionary movements across Europe during this period.
events.name: Liège Revolution breaks out

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1789, the United States House of Representatives adopted a proposal for a Bill of Rights, which would later become the first ten amendments to the Constitution. This significant step was aimed at ensuring individual liberties and limiting government power.
events.name: A proposal for a Bill of Rights is adopted by the United States House of Representatives

events.enhanced_description: The first naval battle of the Svensksund commenced on August 24, 1789, in the Gulf of Finland, marking a significant engagement during the Russo-Swedish War. The battle showcased naval tactics and the strategic importance of the Baltic Sea.
events.name: The first naval battle of the Svensksund begins in the Gulf of Finland

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1789, the French Constituent Assembly proclaimed the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, a fundamental document of the French Revolution that articulated the principles of individual and collective rights. This declaration laid the groundwork for modern human rights.
events.name: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is proclaimed in France by the Constituent Assembly

events.enhanced_description: On August 28, 1789, astronomer William Herschel discovered Enceladus, one of Saturn's moons, expanding the understanding of the solar system. This discovery was part of Herschel's broader contributions to astronomy, including the discovery of Uranus.

image.caption: Cassini spacecraft view of Enceladus’s cratered and fractured surface.
image.credit: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) / Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — PIA17202 from the NASA/JPL Photojournal
image.date_qualification: A spacecraft image of Enceladus taken in 2015, long after Herschel’s 1789 discovery; it depicts the moon, not the discovery event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: William Herschel discovers Enceladus, one of Saturn's moons

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1789, the United States Department of the Treasury was established, tasked with managing the nation's finances. Alexander Hamilton was appointed as its first Secretary, laying the foundation for the modern financial system.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The United States Department of the Treasury is founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1789, Alexander Hamilton was appointed as the first Secretary of the Treasury of the United States. His leadership and financial policies were instrumental in establishing the economic framework of the new nation.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Alexander Hamilton is appointed as the first United States Secretary of the Treasury

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1789, during the Russo-Turkish War, General Alexander Suvorov achieved a decisive victory at the Battle of Rymnik, defeating a significantly larger Turkish force. This battle solidified Suvorov's reputation as one of Russia's greatest military leaders.
events.name: Battle of Rymnik: Alexander Suvorov roundly defeats 100,000 Turks

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1789, the Judiciary Act was enacted, establishing the federal judiciary and the United States Marshals Service. This act laid the groundwork for the American legal system and the enforcement of federal laws.

image.caption: First page of the Judiciary Act of 1789.
image.credit: United States Congress — Scan from the original work
image.date_qualification: Document date: 1789-09-24; the image depicts the Act’s first page, not the enactment ceremony.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The Judiciary Act of 1789 establishes the federal judiciary, and the United States Marshals Service

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1789, the United States Congress proposed a set of 12 amendments to the Constitution, aimed at protecting individual rights. This proposal would eventually lead to the ratification of the Bill of Rights in 1791.
events.name: The United States Congress proposes a set of 12 amendments to the U.S. Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On September 26, 1789, Thomas Jefferson was appointed as the first Secretary of State of the United States. His role was crucial in shaping foreign policy and establishing diplomatic relations in the early years of the republic.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Thomas Jefferson is appointed as the first U.S. Secretary of State

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1789, the U.S. Department of War established the nation's first regular army, consisting of several hundred men. This move was essential for the defense and security of the newly formed United States.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The U.S. Department of War establishes the nation's first regular army

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1789, the Women's March on Versailles saw thousands of market women march to the palace to demand bread and confront King Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette. This pivotal event in the French Revolution highlighted the growing unrest among the populace and the demand for political reform.
events.name: Women's March on Versailles

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1789, physician Joseph-Ignace Guillotin proposed to the French National Assembly the adoption of more humane forms of capital punishment, including the use of the guillotine. This proposal reflected the revolutionary ideals of equality and justice.
events.name: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin proposes humane capital punishment

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1789, Brabant revolutionaries crossed the border from the Dutch Republic into the Austrian Netherlands, publicly reading the Manifesto of the People of Brabant, which declared their independence. This event was a significant moment in the struggle for autonomy in the region.
events.name: Brabant Revolution: Declaration of independence

events.enhanced_description: On October 27, 1789, the Brabant revolutionaries achieved a significant victory over the Austrian army at the Battle of Turnhout. This battle was a key moment in the Brabant Revolution, showcasing the effectiveness of the revolutionary forces.
events.name: Battle of Turnhout: Brabant revolutionaries defeat the Austrian army

events.enhanced_description: On November 2, 1789, the National Constituent Assembly passed a decree placing the goods of the clergy at the disposal of the Nation. This decision was part of the broader reforms during the French Revolution aimed at reducing the power of the Church.
events.name: Decree on the goods of the clergy passed by the National Constituent Assembly

events.enhanced_description: On November 6, 1789, Pope Pius VI established the first diocese in the United States at Baltimore, appointing John Carroll as its first bishop. This event marked a significant moment in the history of Catholicism in America.
events.name: Pope Pius VI creates the first diocese in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1789, New Jersey became the first state to ratify the United States Bill of Rights, a crucial step in the establishment of individual liberties in the new nation. This action reflected the state's commitment to protecting the rights of its citizens and set a precedent for other states to follow.
events.name: New Jersey ratifies the United States Bill of Rights, the first state to do so

events.enhanced_description: On November 21, 1789, North Carolina ratified the United States Constitution, officially becoming the 12th state of the Union. This ratification was significant as it helped to solidify the framework of the federal government and demonstrated the state's support for a stronger national government.
events.name: North Carolina ratifies the United States Constitution, and becomes the 12th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On November 26, 1789, a national Thanksgiving Day was observed in the United States, as recommended by President George Washington. This event marked the first official Thanksgiving celebration, emphasizing gratitude and unity in the newly formed nation.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: A national Thanksgiving Day is observed in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On December 11, 1789, the University of North Carolina was founded, becoming the first public university in the United States. This institution played a pivotal role in the development of higher education in the country and continues to be a leading educational establishment.

locations.name: Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States

events.name: The University of North Carolina is founded

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1789, a leaflet circulated in Paris accusing the Marquis de Favras of conspiring to rescue the royal family during the tumultuous period of the French Revolution. This incident highlighted the growing tensions and suspicions surrounding royalist sympathizers in revolutionary France.
events.name: A leaflet circulates in France accusing the Marquis de Favras of plotting to rescue the royal family

events.enhanced_description: In 1790, the first specialized rescue lifeboat was tested on the River Tyne in England, designed by Henry Greathead. This innovation significantly improved maritime safety and rescue operations at sea.
events.name: The first boat specialized as a rescue lifeboat is tested

events.enhanced_description: In 1790, the Olowalu Massacre occurred when American Captain Simon Metcalfe opened fire on Hawaiian villagers in canoes, resulting in the deaths of approximately one hundred Hawaiians. This tragic event highlighted the violent encounters between indigenous populations and foreign settlers.
events.name: Olowalu Massacre

events.enhanced_description: In July 1790, King Louis XVI of France accepted the establishment of a constitutional monarchy, a significant shift in governance during the French Revolution. This acceptance was part of the broader struggle between royal authority and revolutionary ideals.
events.name: Louis XVI accepts a constitutional monarchy

events.enhanced_description: From October to December 1790, Vincent Ogé led a rebellion of freed blacks in Saint-Domingue against colonial authorities. The uprising was ultimately suppressed, and Ogé was executed, highlighting the tensions surrounding slavery and freedom in the colony.
events.name: Vincent Ogé's Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On January 8, 1790, President George Washington delivered the first State of the Union address in New York City. This address set a precedent for future presidents and emphasized the importance of communication between the executive branch and Congress.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: George Washington gives the first State of the Union address

events.enhanced_description: On January 11, 1790, the 11 minor states of the Austrian Netherlands signed a Treaty of Union, creating the United States of Belgium. This political union was a response to the Brabant Revolution and aimed to establish a more cohesive governance structure.
events.name: Treaty of Union creates the United States of Belgium

events.enhanced_description: On January 14, 1790, U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton submitted his proposed plan for the payment of American debts, which included significant amounts for foreign and domestic obligations. This plan was crucial in establishing the financial credibility of the new nation.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Alexander Hamilton submits debt payment plan

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1790, Fletcher Christian and eight mutineers from the HMS Bounty landed on Pitcairn Island after their famous mutiny. This event marked the beginning of a new settlement that would remain isolated for many years.
events.name: Fletcher Christian and mutineers land on Pitcairn

events.enhanced_description: On January 26, 1790, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's opera Così fan tutte premiered in Vienna. This work is celebrated for its intricate music and exploration of themes related to love and fidelity.
events.name: Mozart's opera Così fan tutte premieres

events.enhanced_description: On January 30, 1790, the first boat specialized as a rescue lifeboat was tested on the River Tyne in England. This innovation marked a significant advancement in maritime safety and rescue operations.
events.name: First rescue lifeboat tested on the River Tyne

events.enhanced_description: On February 1, 1790, the Supreme Court of the United States convened for the first time in New York City. This event marked the establishment of the highest court in the nation, which would play a crucial role in interpreting the Constitution.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The Supreme Court of the United States convenes for the first time

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1790, King Louis XVI of France declared to the National Assembly his intention to uphold the constitutional laws. This declaration was significant in the context of the French Revolution, as it reflected the king's attempt to navigate the changing political landscape.
events.name: Louis XVI declares to the National Assembly

events.enhanced_description: In 1790, two Quaker delegates, John Woolman and Anthony Benezet, presented a petition to the United States Congress advocating for the abolition of slavery. This marked one of the early organized efforts by religious groups to influence national policy regarding slavery.
events.name: Two Quaker delegates petition the United States Congress for the abolition of slavery

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1790, North Carolina ceded its western territories, which would later become the state of Tennessee, to the federal government. This decision was part of the broader effort to organize and govern the newly acquired lands in the post-Revolutionary United States.

image.caption: Map of the Tennassee State, an early map of Tennessee.
image.date_qualification: A map dated 1796, six years after the 1790 cession; it is contextual evidence, not a depiction of the cession itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: North Carolina cedes its western territories to the federal government

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1790, the United States Congress authorized the first national census, which was crucial for determining representation in Congress and the allocation of federal funds. Thomas Jefferson, as Secretary of State, played a significant role in overseeing the census process.
events.name: The first United States Census is authorized

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1790, France was reorganized into 83 départements, a move aimed at dismantling the feudal system and regional loyalties that had persisted under the old regime. This administrative change was part of the broader reforms initiated during the French Revolution.
events.name: France is divided into 83 départements

events.enhanced_description: On March 6, 1790, the New York legislature agreed to the admission of Vermont into the Union, contingent upon resolving land disputes. This decision was significant in shaping the political landscape of the early United States.
events.name: New York legislature consents to Vermont's admission to the Union

events.enhanced_description: On March 21, 1790, Thomas Jefferson reported to President George Washington in New York City as the newly appointed Secretary of State. This marked the beginning of Jefferson's influential role in shaping the early policies of the United States.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: Thomas Jefferson reports to President George Washington

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1790, the United States Congress established the patent system, aimed at encouraging innovation and protecting inventors' rights. This foundational legislation laid the groundwork for the modern intellectual property system in the U.S.
events.name: The United States patent system is established

events.enhanced_description: On May 13, 1790, the Battle of Reval took place when Gustav III of Sweden attempted to eliminate a Russian squadron wintering in Reval (modern-day Tallinn, Estonia). The battle resulted in significant losses for the Swedish fleet, with 130 Swedes killed and many captured.
events.name: Battle of Reval

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1790, the Battle of Andros occurred when an Ottoman-Algerian fleet destroyed the fleet of the Greek privateer Lambros Katsonis. This battle was part of the ongoing conflicts during the Greek War of Independence.
events.name: Battle of Andros

events.enhanced_description: On May 26, 1790, Congress passed an act to govern the creation of states from the Southwest Territory, which would eventually lead to the formation of Tennessee, Alabama, and Mississippi. This legislation was crucial for the expansion and organization of the United States.
events.name: Congress passes an act to govern the creation of states from the Southwest Territory

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1790, Rhode Island became the last of the original thirteen states to ratify the United States Constitution. This ratification was a significant milestone in the establishment of the federal government and the rule of law in the new nation.
events.name: Rhode Island ratifies the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1790, royal assent was granted for the establishment of the port of Milford Haven in Wales. This development was significant for trade and maritime activities in the region.

locations.name: Milford Haven, Pembrokeshire, Wales, United Kingdom

events.name: Royal assent is given to establishment of the port of Milford Haven

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1790, the Compromise of 1790 was reached between Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and Alexander Hamilton, resolving key issues regarding the federal assumption of state debts and the location of the national capital. This agreement was pivotal in shaping the financial and political landscape of the early United States.
events.name: Compromise of 1790

events.enhanced_description: On June 23, 1790, the alleged London Monster was arrested in London, later receiving a 40-year sentence for multiple assaults. This case captured public attention and reflected the social anxieties of the time.

image.caption: Isaac Cruikshank’s hand-coloured etching depicting a man cutting a woman’s dress, associated with the alleged London Monster attacks.
image.credit: Print made by: Isaac Cruikshank Published by: S W Fores — https://www.britishmuseum.org/collection/object/P_1868-0808-5931
image.date_qualification: Dated 1790; the etching depicts an attack, not the arrest itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The alleged London Monster is arrested

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1790, the Second Battle of Svensksund occurred during the Russo-Swedish War, where the Swedish Navy achieved a decisive victory over the Russian fleet. This battle was one of the largest naval engagements of the war, with significant casualties on both sides.
events.name: Second Battle of Svensksund

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1790, the U.S. House of Representatives narrowly voted to approve the creation of the District of Columbia, which would serve as the national capital. This decision was a critical step in the establishment of the federal government.
events.name: U.S. House of Representatives votes to create the District of Columbia

events.enhanced_description: On July 12, 1790, during the French Revolution, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy was enacted, which restructured the Catholic Church in France and aimed to bring it under state control. This legislation was part of the revolutionary government's efforts to secularize French society.
events.name: Civil Constitution of the Clergy is passed

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1790, the Fête de la Fédération was celebrated in Paris, marking the unity of the French people and the national reconciliation following the revolution. This event symbolized the aspirations of the revolutionaries for a new France.
events.name: Fête de la Fédération

events.enhanced_description: On July 16, 1790, President George Washington signed the Residence Act into law, establishing the site along the Potomac River as the future capital of the United States. This act was a pivotal moment in the establishment of Washington, D.C.
events.name: George Washington signs the Residence Act

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1790, Alexander Hamilton's Assumption Bill was passed by Congress, allowing the federal government to assume the debts of the states. This legislation was crucial for stabilizing the nation's finances and establishing federal authority.
events.name: Alexander Hamilton's Assumption Bill is passed

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1790, the Convention of Reichenbach was signed between Prussia and Austria, marking a diplomatic agreement aimed at stabilizing relations in Central Europe during a period of tension.
events.name: The Convention of Reichenbach is signed

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1790, inventor Samuel Hopkins was granted the first U.S. patent for an improved method of making potash. This milestone marked the beginning of the American patent system and encouraged innovation.
events.name: Samuel Hopkins becomes the first to be issued a U.S. patent

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1790, the U.S. Congress passed a tariff act that established a system of revenue cutters for enforcing customs laws. This act laid the groundwork for what would later become the United States Coast Guard, a vital maritime security service.
events.name: U.S. Tariff Act Creates Revenue Cutters

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Värälä, signed on August 14, 1790, marked the end of the Russo-Swedish War (1788-1790). The treaty restored the status quo ante bellum, reaffirming the territorial boundaries between the two nations.
events.name: Treaty of Värälä

events.enhanced_description: On September 25, 1790, the Peking Opera was born when the Four Great Anhui Troupes introduced Anhui opera to Beijing in celebration of the Qianlong Emperor's 80th birthday. This event marked a significant cultural development in Chinese performing arts.
events.name: Birth of Peking Opera

events.enhanced_description: Leopold II ascended to the throne as Holy Roman Emperor on September 30, 1790. His reign was marked by efforts to reform the empire and manage the challenges posed by revolutionary movements in Europe.

image.caption: Portrait of Leopold II, Holy Roman Emperor, by Anton Hickel.
image.credit: Anton Hickel — Dorotheum : Info about artwork
image.date_qualification: 18th century; this is a portrait, not a depiction of his 1790 accession.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Leopold II Begins Reign

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1790, commissioners from New York announced the successful conclusion of negotiations with Vermont regarding disputed land claims. This agreement paved the way for Vermont's admission as the 14th state of the United States.
events.name: New York and Vermont Negotiations

events.enhanced_description: On October 10, 1790, a devastating earthquake and tsunami struck Oran, Algeria, resulting in the deaths of at least 3,000 people and the destruction of the city. This disaster significantly impacted the region and its governance.
events.name: Oran Earthquake and Tsunami

events.enhanced_description: The Harmar Campaign concluded on October 20, 1790, with a significant defeat for U.S. Army General Josiah Harmar and Colonel John Hardin against the Western Confederacy of Indians, led by Chief Mihšihkinaahkwa of the Miami tribe and Weyapiersenwah of the Shawnee at Kekionga.

image.caption: A map titled “Harmar Campaign,” attributed to Benson J. Lossing.
image.credit: Benson J. Lossing — The Pictorial Field-Book of the War of 1812
image.date_qualification: Map of the Harmar Campaign credited to The Pictorial Field-Book of the War of 1812. It provides campaign context; the saved metadata does not establish its creation date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Harmar Campaign Defeat

events.enhanced_description: On November 24, 1790, France's Constituent Assembly passed a law requiring all Roman Catholic priests to swear an oath of acceptance of the new French Constitution. This law was a significant step in the secularization of the French state during the Revolution.
events.name: Civil Constitution of the Clergy

events.enhanced_description: On November 27, 1790, President George Washington and First Lady Martha Washington arrived in Philadelphia, the temporary capital of the United States, and took residence at the President's House, marking a significant moment in the early governance of the nation.
events.name: Washington Arrives in Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1790, Holy Roman Empire forces recaptured Brussels, effectively ending the short-lived United States of Belgium and restoring the Austrian Netherlands. This event underscored the ongoing struggles for independence in Europe.
events.name: Recapture of Brussels

events.enhanced_description: The United States Congress opened its first session in the new temporary capital of Philadelphia on December 6, 1790. This marked a pivotal moment in the establishment of the legislative framework of the United States.
events.name: First Session of U.S. Congress

events.enhanced_description: The Hawkesbury and Nepean Wars began on December 10, 1790, in New South Wales, Australia, as tensions escalated between Indigenous Australians and European settlers due to increasing colonization and land disputes.
events.name: Hawkesbury and Nepean Wars Begin

events.enhanced_description: On December 17, 1790, the Aztec calendar stone was discovered at El Zócalo in Mexico City. This significant archaeological find provided insight into the rich history and culture of the Aztec civilization.
events.name: Discovery of the Aztec Calendar Stone

events.enhanced_description: On December 22, 1790, during the Russo-Turkish War, the Turkish fortress of Izmail was stormed and captured by Russian General Alexander Suvorov. This victory resulted in the loss of approximately 26,000 Turkish soldiers and marked a significant turning point in the war.
events.name: Capture of Izmail

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1790, Louis XVI publicly assented to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, a pivotal moment during the French Revolution that aimed to bring the Catholic Church under state control and redefine the relationship between church and state.

image.caption: Map of France showing the percentage of priests who swore allegiance to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy.
image.credit: Marmelad / — Own work based on: Carte des prêtres assermentés en France en 1791.png and Départements de France-simple.svg
image.date_qualification: The map represents data from 1791; the image itself is dated 2007-09-09.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Louis XVI Assents to Civil Constitution

events.enhanced_description: In January 1791, Austrian composer Joseph Haydn arrived in England to perform a series of concerts. His visit significantly influenced the musical landscape of the time and solidified his reputation as one of the leading composers of the Classical era.
events.name: Joseph Haydn Arrives in England

events.enhanced_description: In March 1791, during the French Revolution, the National Constituent Assembly accepted the recommendation of its Commission of Weights and Measures to adopt the metric system, standardizing measurements across the nation. This decision marked a significant shift towards modern scientific practices and influenced measurement systems worldwide.
events.name: Adoption of the Metric System

events.enhanced_description: In 1791, the National Constituent Assembly enacted the abolition of guilds in France, dismantling the traditional trade associations that regulated crafts and commerce. This move was part of broader revolutionary reforms aimed at promoting free enterprise and individual rights.
events.name: Abolition of Guilds

events.enhanced_description: In 1791, Claude Chappe demonstrated a mechanical semaphore line in Paris, which allowed for rapid long-distance communication through visual signals. This innovation laid the groundwork for future telecommunication systems and significantly improved information dissemination.
events.name: Demonstration of the Semaphore Line

events.enhanced_description: In 1791, significant translations of Voltaire's works were undertaken, reflecting the Enlightenment's impact on literature and philosophy. Voltaire's ideas on civil liberties and criticism of established institutions continued to influence revolutionary thought.
events.name: Translation of Voltaire

events.enhanced_description: In 1791, the Priestley Riots erupted in Birmingham, England, targeting dissenters and supporters of Joseph Priestley, a prominent Unitarian minister and scientist. The riots reflected the growing tensions between traditional Anglicans and dissenting religious groups during a period of political upheaval.
events.name: Priestley Riots

events.enhanced_description: During the Third Anglo-Mysore War, the Battle of Tellicherry occurred when a British Royal Navy patrol forced a French convoy bound for Mysore to surrender. This event marked a significant naval engagement in the conflict between British and French colonial interests in India.
events.name: Battle of Tellicherry

events.enhanced_description: In 1791, Olympe de Gouges wrote the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, responding to the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. This document advocated for women's rights and equality, marking a significant moment in feminist literature.
events.name: Declaration of the Rights of Woman

events.enhanced_description: The School for the Indigent Blind was founded in Liverpool, England, by Edward Rushton, a blind ex-merchant seaman and abolitionist. Established in 1791, it is recognized as the oldest continuously operating specialist school for the blind in the world.
events.name: School for the Indigent Blind founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1791, Camembert cheese was reputedly first made by Marie Harel, a farmer from Normandy. This cheese has since become one of France's most famous and beloved dairy products, known for its creamy texture and rich flavor.
events.name: Camembert cheese first made

events.enhanced_description: The Dar Hassan Pacha, a palace located in the Casbah of Algiers, was completed in 1791. This architectural marvel reflects the rich history and culture of Algeria during the Ottoman period.
events.name: Dar Hassan Pacha completed

events.enhanced_description: The first printed manuscript of Dream of the Red Chamber, one of the classic Chinese novels written by Cao Xueqin, began publication posthumously in 1791. This work is considered a masterpiece of Chinese literature and offers profound insights into 18th-century Chinese society.
events.name: Dream of the Red Chamber begins publication

events.enhanced_description: The Big Bottom Massacre on January 2, 1791, marked the beginning of the Northwest Indian War in the Ohio Country. This violent conflict arose from tensions between American settlers and Native American tribes over land and sovereignty.
events.name: Big Bottom Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On January 12, 1791, Holy Roman troops reentered Liège, signaling the end of the Liège Revolution and the restoration of its Prince-Bishops. This event reflected the broader struggles of the time between revolutionary ideals and traditional authority.
events.name: End of the Liège Revolution

events.enhanced_description: On January 25, 1791, the British Parliament passed the Constitutional Act 1791, which divided the Province of Quebec into Upper and Lower Canada. This act was a significant step in the governance of Canada and laid the groundwork for its future political structure.
events.name: Constitutional Act 1791

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1791, the Bank of the United States was incorporated in Philadelphia with a 20-year charter and an initial capital of $10,000,000. This institution played a crucial role in stabilizing the American economy and establishing a national financial system.
events.name: Incorporation of the Bank of the United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1791, the United States established diplomatic relations with Portugal, marking an important step in expanding its international presence and fostering relationships with European nations.
events.name: U.S. Opens Diplomatic Relations with Portugal

events.enhanced_description: The French Revolution began on March 2, 1791, as a response to widespread discontent with the monarchy and social inequalities. This pivotal event would reshape France and have lasting impacts on the world.
events.name: French Revolution Begins

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1791, Vermont was admitted as the 14th state of the United States. This admission was significant as it represented the first state to join the Union after the original thirteen colonies.
events.name: Vermont Admitted as 14th State

events.enhanced_description: On March 13, 1791, the first part of Thomas Paine's influential work 'Rights of Man' was published in London. This publication argued for individual rights and government accountability, significantly impacting political thought during the revolutionary period.
events.name: Publication of Rights of Man

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1791, the first of forty boundary markers for the original District of Columbia was laid at Jones Point Light in Alexandria, Virginia. This marked the formal delineation of the nation's capital, which was established to serve as the seat of the federal government.
events.name: Boundary Markers of the District of Columbia

events.enhanced_description: On May 3, 1791, the Sejm of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth proclaimed the Constitution of May 3, the first modern codified constitution in Europe. This landmark document aimed to reform the political system and strengthen the central government, reflecting Enlightenment ideals.
events.name: Proclamation of the Constitution of May 3

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1791, the brigantine Lady Washington, captained by John Kendrick, along with the brig Grace, became the first American ships to reach Japan, docking in Nagasaki. This event marked the beginning of formal trade relations between the United States and Japan.
events.name: First American Ships Reach Japan

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1791, during the French Revolution, King Louis XVI and his family attempted to flee Paris in disguise but were captured in Varennes-en-Argonne. This event significantly undermined the monarchy's credibility and escalated tensions between the royalists and revolutionaries.
events.name: Flight to Varennes

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1791, the Ordnance Survey was founded in Great Britain, tasked with producing detailed maps of the country. This initiative was crucial for military planning and later became essential for civil administration and land use.
events.name: Founding of the Ordnance Survey

events.enhanced_description: On July 8, 1791, Austrian composer Joseph Haydn was awarded an honorary doctorate of music at the University of Oxford during his visit to England. This recognition underscored Haydn's significant contributions to classical music and his influence on subsequent composers.
events.name: Honorary Doctorate for Joseph Haydn

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1791, the ashes of the philosopher Voltaire were transferred to the Panthéon in Paris, symbolizing his enduring legacy and the revolutionary ideals of liberty and reason. This act was part of a broader movement to honor Enlightenment thinkers.
events.name: Transfer of Voltaire's Ashes

events.enhanced_description: On July 14, 1791, the Priestley Riots erupted in Birmingham, England, as a violent backlash against dissenters and supporters of Joseph Priestley. The riots reflected the growing tensions between traditional Anglicans and dissenting religious groups during a period of political upheaval.

image.caption: Johann Eckstein’s retrospective illustration depicts a mob burning Joseph Priestley’s house during the Priestley Riots.
image.credit: Johann Eckstein — Norton Anthology of English Literature
image.date_qualification: The saved image_date gives only the year 1791; it does not establish when the artwork was created. The scene represents an event from 14–17 July 1791.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Priestley Riots Against Dissenters

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1791, the Champ de Mars massacre occurred in Paris when the National Guard opened fire on a crowd demanding the abdication of King Louis XVI. This tragic event highlighted the increasing violence and polarization during the French Revolution.
events.name: Champ de Mars Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On August 4, 1791, the Treaty of Sistova was signed, officially ending the Ottoman–Habsburg wars. This treaty marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Eastern Europe and established a period of relative peace between the two empires.
events.name: Treaty of Sistova

events.enhanced_description: On August 6, 1791, the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin was completed, serving as a neoclassical monument symbolizing peace and unity. It has since become one of Germany's most iconic landmarks and a symbol of the country's tumultuous history.
events.name: Completion of the Brandenburg Gate

events.enhanced_description: On August 7, 1791, George Hammond was appointed as Great Britain's first minister to the United States, marking a significant step in diplomatic relations between the two countries following the American Revolutionary War.
events.name: Appointment of George Hammond

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1791, a slave rebellion broke out in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, marking the beginning of the Haitian Revolution. This uprising ultimately led to the establishment of Haiti as the first independent black republic and the first nation to abolish slavery.
events.name: Haitian Revolution Begins

events.enhanced_description: On August 26, 1791, John Fitch was granted a patent for the steamboat in the United States, a pivotal development in transportation technology. This invention revolutionized river travel and commerce, paving the way for the expansion of trade and settlement.
events.name: Patent for the Steamboat

events.enhanced_description: On August 27, 1791, the Declaration of Pillnitz was issued by Frederick William II of Prussia and Leopold II, Holy Roman Emperor, expressing their desire to intervene in France to restore the monarchy. This declaration heightened tensions leading to the War of the First Coalition against revolutionary France.
events.name: Declaration of Pillnitz

events.enhanced_description: On September 5, 1791, an ordinance was written in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, barring the game of baseball within 80 yards of the Meeting House, marking the first known reference to baseball in North America.
