This reflects the early development of organized sports in American culture.
events.name: Baseball Ordinance in Pittsfield

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1791, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's opera seria, La clemenza di Tito, premiered at the Estates Theatre in Prague to mark the coronation of Leopold II as King of Bohemia. This opera is notable for its exploration of themes of mercy and justice.
events.name: Premiere of La clemenza di Tito

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1791, the capital of the United States was officially named Washington, D.C., in honor of George Washington, the first President. This designation solidified the city's role as the political center of the nation.
events.name: Naming of Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: The Døtreskolen af 1791 was the first serious secondary education school for girls in Denmark, marking a significant step towards gender equality in education. Founded in Copenhagen, it laid the groundwork for future educational reforms for women in the country.
events.name: Døtreskolen af 1791 founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 13, 1791, King Louis XVI of France accepted the final version of the constitution, which established a constitutional monarchy. This acceptance was a pivotal moment during the French Revolution, as it represented a shift of power from the monarchy to the National Assembly.
events.name: Louis XVI accepts constitution

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1791, the Papal States lost control of Avignon to Revolutionary France, a significant territorial loss during the tumultuous period of the French Revolution. This event symbolized the diminishing power of the papacy in the face of revolutionary ideals.
events.name: Papal States lose Avignon

events.enhanced_description: Founded on September 25, 1791, by Basque Franciscan Father Fermín Lasuén, Mission Santa Cruz became the 12th mission in the California mission chain. It played a crucial role in the Spanish colonization of California and the spread of Christianity among Native Americans.
events.name: Mission Santa Cruz founded

events.enhanced_description: On September 28, 1791, the French Revolution led to the promulgation of the law on Jewish emancipation, marking the first such legislation in modern Europe. This law granted civil rights to Jews, significantly altering their status in society.
events.name: Law on Jewish emancipation promulgated

events.enhanced_description: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's singspiel opera, The Magic Flute (Die Zauberflöte), premiered on September 30, 1791, at the Freihaus-Theater auf der Wieden in Vienna. This opera is celebrated for its rich musical composition and profound themes, becoming one of Mozart's most beloved works.
events.name: The Magic Flute premieres

events.enhanced_description: The Legislative Assembly of France convened on October 1, 1791, marking a new phase in the French Revolution. This assembly replaced the National Assembly and was tasked with drafting laws and governing the nation during a time of significant political upheaval.
events.name: Legislative Assembly convenes

events.enhanced_description: Founded on October 9, 1791, by Father Fermín Lasuén, Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad became the 13th mission in the California mission chain. It served as a vital center for the Spanish mission system and contributed to the cultural exchange between Spanish settlers and Native Americans.

image.caption: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad, a Spanish mission in Soledad, California.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 30 January 2015, more than two centuries after the mission’s founding.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 3.0; Copyrighted: True

locations.historical_name: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad
locations.name: Soledad, California, United States

events.name: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad founded

events.enhanced_description: On October 19, 1791, the Treaty of Drottningholm was signed between the Russian Empire and Sweden, establishing an alliance between the two powers. This treaty was significant in the context of European diplomacy and military alliances during the period.
events.name: Treaty of Drottningholm signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 28, 1791, the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen was published in France, advocating for women's rights and equality. This publication was a landmark moment in the feminist movement and challenged the existing gender norms of the time.
events.name: Declaration of the Rights of Woman published

events.enhanced_description: On November 4, 1791, St. Clair's Defeat occurred in modern-day Mercer County, Ohio, where U.S. forces led by General Arthur St. Clair faced a devastating defeat against Miami fighters led by Chief Mihsihkinaahkwa (Little Turtle) and Shawnee warriors commanded by War Chief Weyapiersenwah (Blue Jacket). This battle resulted in the loss of over 600 U.S. soldiers, marking it as one of the worst defeats for the United States Army against Native Americans.
events.name: St. Clair's Defeat

events.enhanced_description: On November 20, 1791, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart became bedridden due to a serious illness that would lead to his death just fifteen days later. This marked a tragic moment in the life of one of history's greatest composers, whose works continue to influence music today.
events.name: Mozart bedridden

events.enhanced_description: On December 4, 1791, the first issue of The Observer was published in London, marking it as the world's first Sunday newspaper. This publication set a precedent for future newspapers and contributed to the evolution of journalism.
events.name: First issue of The Observer published

events.enhanced_description: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, the prolific Austrian composer, died on December 5, 1791, in Vienna. His death marked the end of an era in classical music, leaving behind a legacy of compositions that continue to influence musicians and composers worldwide.
events.name: death of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart

events.enhanced_description: On December 5, 1791, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart died at the age of 35 at his home in Vienna, likely due to acute rheumatic fever. His death marked the end of a prolific career that left an indelible mark on classical music.
events.name: Mozart dies

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1791, the ratification of the first ten amendments to the United States Constitution was completed, creating the United States Bill of Rights. This landmark achievement ensured fundamental rights and liberties for American citizens.
events.name: U.S. Bill of Rights ratified

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1791, the Pale of Settlement was established by Catherine the Great, designating specific areas within the Russian Empire where Jews were permitted to reside permanently. This policy had lasting implications for Jewish communities in Russia.

image.caption: Map showing the percentage of the Jewish population in the Pale of Settlement.
image.credit: Central Statistical Committee of the Russian Empire — https://scalar.usc.edu/works/let-me-get-there/media/pale-of-settlement-1884
image.date_qualification: Map represents population distribution in 1884, decades after the Pale was established in 1791; it is contextual, not a depiction of the establishment event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Pale of Settlement established

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle composed 'La Marseillaise' in Strasbourg, which would later become the national anthem of France. The song, originally written as a revolutionary march, symbolizes the fight for freedom and the spirit of the French Revolution.
events.name: La Marseillaise, the French national anthem, is composed by Claude Joseph Rouget de Lisle

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, British explorer George Vancouver became the first European to navigate into Burrard Inlet, an important waterway in present-day British Columbia, Canada. This exploration contributed significantly to the mapping and understanding of the Pacific Northwest coast.
events.name: Vancouver becomes the first European to enter Burrard Inlet

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Prussia declared war against France, marking a significant escalation in the conflicts arising from the French Revolution. This declaration was part of the broader War of the First Coalition, where various European monarchies sought to suppress revolutionary movements in France.
events.name: Prussia declares war against France

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Tipu Sultan, the ruler of the Kingdom of Mysore, attempted to invade Kerala but faced strong resistance and was ultimately repulsed. This event was part of the larger conflicts during the Anglo-Mysore Wars, which shaped the political landscape of southern India.
events.name: Tipu Sultan's invasion of Kerala

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Hungarian astronomer Franz Xaver von Zach published 'The Tables of the Sun', an essential work that provided crucial data for navigation. This publication contributed significantly to the field of astronomy and navigation during the Age of Enlightenment.
events.name: Publication of The Tables of the Sun

events.enhanced_description: Claude Chappe successfully demonstrated the first semaphore line in 1792, connecting Paris to Lille. This innovation in communication technology allowed for rapid transmission of messages over long distances, revolutionizing communication in France.
events.name: First semaphore line demonstration

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Scottish engineer William Murdoch began his experiments with gas lighting, which would eventually lead to the widespread use of gas for illumination. His pioneering work laid the foundation for modern gas lighting systems.
events.name: William Murdoch's gas lighting experiments

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, George Anschutz constructed the first blast furnace in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, marking a significant advancement in iron production technology. This development played a crucial role in the industrialization of the region.
events.name: Construction of the first blast furnace

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Mary Wollstonecraft published 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman', one of the earliest works advocating for women's rights and education. This groundbreaking text laid the foundation for feminist thought and activism in the years to come.
events.name: Publication of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Barthélemy Catherine Joubert was appointed as a sub-lieutenant in the French army, marking the beginning of his military career. He would later rise to prominence as a general during the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Barthélemy Catherine Joubert becomes sub-lieutenant

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger was appointed Kapellmeister in Vienna, a prestigious position that allowed him to influence the musical landscape of the city. His contributions to music theory and composition were significant during this period.
events.name: Johann Georg Albrechtsberger becomes Kapellmeister

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, the State Street Corporation was founded in Boston, Massachusetts, marking the establishment of one of the oldest financial institutions in the United States. This corporation has played a significant role in the development of the financial services industry.
events.name: Founding of the State Street Corporation

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, the Insurance Company of North America, which would later become Chubb, was founded in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. This company became one of the first insurance firms in the United States, contributing to the growth of the insurance industry.
events.name: Founding of the Insurance Company of North America

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, the Shiloh Meeting House, the predecessor of the Shiloh United Methodist Church, was founded in Lynchburg, Virginia. This establishment played a significant role in the religious community of the area.
events.name: Founding of Shiloh Meeting House

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, the University of Cambridge held the first written examinations in Europe, marking a significant development in academic assessment practices. This innovation set a precedent for future educational standards.
events.name: First written examinations at the University of Cambridge

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, composer Ludwig van Beethoven moved to Vienna from Bonn to study with Joseph Haydn, marking the beginning of his influential career in music. He would remain in Vienna for the rest of his life, becoming one of the most celebrated composers in history.
events.name: Ludwig van Beethoven moves to Vienna

events.enhanced_description: In 1792, explorer James Johnstone established that Vancouver Island is indeed an island, contributing to the mapping and understanding of the Pacific Northwest region of North America. His explorations were vital in the context of European interests in the area.
events.name: James Johnstone establishes Vancouver Island

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1792, the Treaty of Jassy was signed, concluding the war between the Russian Empire and the Ottoman Empire over Crimea. This treaty marked a significant shift in power dynamics in Eastern Europe and the Black Sea region.
events.name: Treaty of Jassy signed

events.enhanced_description: The London Corresponding Society was established to promote political reform and represent the interests of the working class in Britain. It became a significant organization advocating for universal suffrage and parliamentary reform during a time of political unrest.
events.name: The London Corresponding Society is founded

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Holcroft's comedy 'The Road to Ruin' premiered in London, reflecting the social issues of the time, particularly the consequences of gambling and the moral dilemmas faced by individuals. The play was notable for its satirical approach and commentary on contemporary society.
events.name: Thomas Holcroft produces the comedy The Road to Ruin in London

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1792, President George Washington signed the Postal Service Act, which established the United States Post Office Department. This act laid the foundation for a national postal system, facilitating communication across the growing nation.
events.name: The Postal Service Act is signed by President George Washington

events.enhanced_description: Francis II ascended to the throne as the last Holy Roman Emperor on March 1, 1792. His reign marked the end of the Holy Roman Empire's influence in Europe, which would dissolve in 1806 amidst the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor, takes office

events.enhanced_description: On March 7, 1792, a settlement was established in Sierra Leone as a colony for freed slaves from Britain and other parts of the world. This initiative was part of a broader movement to provide a safe haven for formerly enslaved individuals and promote their resettlement.
events.name: A settlement is formed in Sierra Leone as a home for freed slaves

events.enhanced_description: King Gustav III of Sweden was shot by Jacob Johan Anckarström during a masquerade ball at the Royal Opera in Stockholm on March 16, 1792. Although he survived for several weeks, he ultimately succumbed to his injuries, leading to significant political changes in Sweden.
events.name: Assassination of Gustav III

events.enhanced_description: On March 20, 1792, Raleigh was established as the capital of North Carolina after State Senator William Christmas submitted his design for the city. The city was named in honor of Sir Walter Raleigh and was strategically chosen for its central location.
events.name: Establishment of Raleigh as the capital of North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Croix-des-Bouquets on March 22, 1792, marked a significant victory for Black slave insurgents during the Haitian Revolution. This battle was one of the first major confrontations in the fight against colonial rule and slavery in Saint-Domingue.

image.caption: Historical flag of Haiti from the Haitian Revolution.
image.credit: Saul ip — Own work based on: https://www.crwflags.com/fotw/flags/ht-hist.html
image.date_qualification: A symbolic representation of Haiti during the revolution era, not a depiction of the Battle of Croix-des-Bouquets. The image date is 2008-08-08.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Haitian Revolution: Battle of Croix-des-Bouquets

events.enhanced_description: On March 25, 1792, the National Legislative Assembly of France officially sanctioned the use of the guillotine for judicial executions. This decision reflected the revolutionary spirit of the time and the desire for a more humane method of execution.
events.name: The National Legislative Assembly agrees to use the guillotine for executions

events.enhanced_description: The Coinage Act, passed on April 2, 1792, established the United States Mint, which was crucial for creating a standardized currency system in the young nation. This act laid the groundwork for the U.S. monetary system and the production of coins.
events.name: The Coinage Act is passed, establishing the United States Mint

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1792, President George Washington exercised his veto power for the first time, rejecting a bill that aimed to apportion representatives among the states. This event marked a significant moment in the establishment of presidential authority in the United States.
events.name: George Washington vetoes a bill for apportioning representatives

events.enhanced_description: On April 20, 1792, France declared war on Austria, initiating the French Revolutionary Wars. This declaration was a pivotal moment in European history, leading to widespread conflict and the eventual rise of Napoleon Bonaparte.
events.name: France declares war against Austria

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1792, Tiradentes, a prominent figure in the Inconfidência Mineira conspiracy against Portuguese rule in Brazil, was executed in Rio de Janeiro. His martyrdom inspired future generations in the struggle for Brazilian independence.

locations.name: Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

events.name: Execution of Tiradentes in Rio de Janeiro

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1792, highwayman Nicolas Pelletier was executed by guillotine, marking the first use of this method in France. This event symbolized the revolutionary changes in the French justice system and the shift towards more public and systematic executions.
events.name: Nicolas Pelletier becomes the first person executed by guillotine in France

events.enhanced_description: On May 11, 1792, Captain Robert Gray, aboard the Columbia Rediviva, became the first European to navigate the mouth of the Columbia River. This expedition was significant for the exploration and mapping of the Pacific Northwest, paving the way for future settlements.
events.name: Robert Gray's Columbia River expedition

events.enhanced_description: On May 17, 1792, the Buttonwood Agreement was signed by 24 stockbrokers in New York City, marking the founding of what would become the New York Stock Exchange. This agreement established rules for trading securities and laid the groundwork for modern financial markets.

image.caption: Francis Guy’s oil painting depicts the Tontine Coffee House, Merchant’s Coffee House, and Wall Street.
image.date_qualification: Painting dated 1797, five years after the agreement was signed in 1792.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: The Buttonwood Agreement is signed

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1792, Russia invaded Poland, igniting the War in Defence of the Constitution. This invasion was part of a larger conflict involving the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and marked a significant moment in the struggle for Polish sovereignty.
events.name: Russia invades Poland

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1792, a catastrophic earthquake and subsequent tsunami struck Kyushu, Japan, resulting from the collapse of an old lava dome due to volcanic activity from Mount Unzen. This disaster led to the deaths of approximately 14,300 people and highlighted the region's vulnerability to natural disasters.
events.name: 1792 Unzen earthquake and tsunami

events.enhanced_description: On May 29, 1792, the Great Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was disbanded following the Russian invasion of Poland. This event marked a significant turning point in Polish history, leading to the eventual partitions of Poland.
events.name: The Great Sejm is disbanded

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1792, Kentucky was admitted as the 15th state of the United States. This event marked a significant expansion of the nation and reflected the westward movement of settlers during this period.
events.name: Kentucky becomes the 15th state of the United States

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1792, Captain George Vancouver claimed Puget Sound for Great Britain during his exploration of the Pacific Northwest. This claim was part of Vancouver's larger expedition to map the coastline and establish British presence in the region.
events.name: Captain George Vancouver claims Puget Sound for Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On June 13, 1792, Captain George Vancouver became the first European to enter Burrard Inlet, a significant geographical feature in British Columbia, Canada. This exploration contributed to the mapping and understanding of the coastal regions of North America.
events.name: Vancouver enters Burrard Inlet

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1792, during the Polish–Russian War, the Battle of Dubienka saw soldiers of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, led by Tadeusz Kościuszko, bravely resist an overwhelming attack from the Imperial Russian Army. Despite being outnumbered, their defense showcased the resilience of Polish forces.
events.name: Battle of Dubienka

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1792, during the French Revolution, the Tuileries Palace in Paris was stormed by revolutionary forces, leading to the arrest of King Louis XVI. This pivotal event marked a significant turning point in the revolution, as it effectively ended the monarchy's power in France.
events.name: Insurrection of 10 August 1792

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1792, Louis Collenot d'Angremont became the first person executed by guillotine for political reasons during the French Revolution. His execution symbolized the radical turn of the revolution and the increasing use of the guillotine as a tool of political repression.
events.name: Execution of Louis Collenot d'Angremont

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1792, during the War of the First Coalition, the Battle of Verdun saw Prussian forces defeat French troops led by General Nicolas-Joseph Beaurepaire. This battle was part of the larger conflict between revolutionary France and the coalition of European monarchies.
events.name: Battle of Verdun

events.enhanced_description: In September 1792, George Macartney, 1st Earl Macartney, set sail from Portsmouth as the first official envoy from Great Britain to China. This mission aimed to establish diplomatic relations and trade agreements with the Qing Dynasty, marking a significant moment in British-Chinese relations.
events.name: Macartney Embassy

events.enhanced_description: On September 2, 1792, during the French Revolution, the September Massacres occurred as rampaging mobs slaughtered three Roman Catholic bishops, over 200 priests, and at least 1,000 other prisoners. This violent episode reflected the intense paranoia and revolutionary fervor of the time.
events.name: September Massacres

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1792, a group of six men stole some of the former French Crown Jewels from a warehouse where the revolutionary government had stored them. This theft highlighted the chaos and lawlessness that characterized the early years of the French Revolution.
events.name: Theft of French Crown Jewels

events.enhanced_description: On September 12, 1792, Governor Joaquín Alós y Bru founded the town of Fort Borbon, which is now known as Fuerte Olimpo in Paraguay. This establishment was part of the Spanish colonial efforts to secure and administer territories in South America.
events.name: Foundation of Fort Borbon

events.enhanced_description: On September 14, 1792, radical antimonarchist Thomas Paine fled from England to France after being indicted for treason. His move to France was significant as he became involved in the revolutionary movement and continued to advocate for democratic ideals.
events.name: Thomas Paine flees to France

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1792, the Battle of Valmy marked a crucial victory for the French revolutionary army against the Prussians under the Duke of Brunswick. This battle is often credited with saving the French Revolution and bolstering the morale of the revolutionary forces.
events.name: Battle of Valmy

events.enhanced_description: On September 21, 1792, the French National Convention proclaimed the abolition of the monarchy, leading to the establishment of the French First Republic. This momentous decision marked a radical shift in French governance and the end of centuries of monarchical rule.
events.name: Abolition of the monarchy and establishment of the French Republic

events.enhanced_description: On September 22, 1792, the French Revolutionary Calendar was introduced, marking the beginning of a new era in France. This calendar was part of the revolutionary government's efforts to break from the past and establish a new societal order.

image.caption: Engraved French Republican calendar for Year III, attributed to Philibert-Louis Debucourt.
image.credit: Philibert-Louis Debucourt — Bibliothèque nationale de France
image.date_qualification: Dated 1794; later than the calendar’s introduction in 1792.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Beginning of the French Republican Calendar

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1792, the Chickamauga Cherokee launched an attack on Middle Tennessee, aiming to exterminate white settlers. They were met with resistance at Buchanan's Station near Nashville, marking a significant conflict in the ongoing struggles between Native Americans and settlers.
events.name: Chickamauga Cherokee attack

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1792, the Baptist Missionary Society was founded in Kettering, England, marking a significant development in the history of Christian missions. This organization aimed to spread the Christian faith and support missionary work around the world.
events.name: Foundation of the Baptist Missionary Society

events.enhanced_description: On October 3, 1792, a militia departed from the Spanish stronghold of Valdivia to quell a Huilliche uprising in southern Chile. This military action was part of the broader colonial efforts to maintain control over indigenous populations in the region.
events.name: Militia departs from Valdivia

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1792, the first Columbus Day celebration in the United States was held in New York City, commemorating the 300th anniversary of Christopher Columbus's arrival in the New World. This event marked the beginning of a tradition that would evolve over the centuries.

locations.name: New York City, New York, United States

events.name: First Columbus Day celebration in the United States

events.enhanced_description: On October 13, 1792, the cornerstone of the United States Executive Mansion, later known as the White House, was laid in Washington, D.C. This event marked a significant step in the establishment of the nation's capital and its government.
events.name: Foundation of Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On October 29, 1792, Lieutenant William Broughton of the Vancouver Expedition named Mount Hood after British Admiral Lord Hood while exploring the Pacific Northwest. This naming contributed to the European understanding and mapping of the region.
events.name: Naming of Mount Hood

events.enhanced_description: The second United States presidential election took place in 1792, where incumbent President George Washington was unanimously re-elected, receiving all 132 electoral votes. Vice President John Adams was also re-elected, solidifying the early political landscape of the United States.
events.name: Second United States presidential election

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Jemappes, fought on November 6, 1792, marked a significant victory for the French Revolutionary Army against the Austrian forces led by Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen. This battle was pivotal in the War of the First Coalition, showcasing the effectiveness of the French military strategies during the early phases of the Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Battle of Jemappes

events.enhanced_description: On November 19, 1792, France's National Convention passed a resolution pledging support for the overthrow of foreign governments. This declaration was part of the revolutionary ideology that sought to spread revolutionary principles across Europe.
events.name: French National Convention resolution

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1792, George Washington was re-elected as president of the United States, continuing his leadership during the formative years of the nation. His presidency was marked by efforts to establish a stable government and navigate the challenges of a young republic.
events.name: George Washington re-elected president

events.enhanced_description: On December 26, 1792, the trial of Louis XVI of France began, marking a critical moment in the French Revolution. The trial ultimately led to his execution, symbolizing the end of the monarchy and the rise of revolutionary ideals in France.
events.name: Trial of Louis XVI begins

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, the Republic of Mainz was declared by Andreas Joseph Hofmann, marking the establishment of the first republican state in Germany. This event was part of the broader revolutionary movements sweeping across Europe during this period.
events.name: The first republican state in Germany, the Republic of Mainz, is declared

events.enhanced_description: In August 1793, during the tumult of the French Revolution, France declared all slaves in Saint-Domingue free, marking a significant step towards the abolition of slavery in the French colonies. This decree was part of a broader strategy to gain support from the enslaved population against colonial powers and was a precursor to the Haitian Revolution.
events.name: France decrees all the slaves on Saint-Domingue to be free

events.enhanced_description: Beginning in November 1793, Philadelphia was struck by a devastating yellow fever epidemic that resulted in the deaths of approximately 5,000 people. The outbreak led to widespread panic and the temporary abandonment of the city by many residents, including government officials.
events.name: The yellow fever epidemic of 1793 hits Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: In early 1793, crowds in Paris engaged in the symbolic act of burning monarchist emblems, reflecting the revolutionary fervor and the rejection of the old regime. This act was part of the broader movement to dismantle the monarchy and establish a republic.
events.name: Crowds in Paris burn monarchist emblems

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, the Louvre in Paris was opened to the public as an art museum, showcasing the nation's artistic heritage and the treasures acquired during the French Revolution. This marked a significant cultural shift, making art accessible to the general public.
events.name: The Louvre opens as an art museum

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin, a device that revolutionized the cotton industry by significantly speeding up the process of separating cotton fibers from seeds. This invention had profound economic implications, leading to a resurgence of slavery in the Southern United States.

image.caption: Cotton gin on display at the Eli Whitney Museum.
image.credit: Tom Murphy VII — Taken by uploader, user:brighterorange .
image.date_qualification: Museum display photograph, not documentation of Whitney’s 1793 invention; photographed in 2007.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Eli Whitney invents the cotton gin

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, Lawrence Academy was chartered in Groton, Massachusetts, as a private preparatory school. It became one of the earliest institutions of its kind in the United States, contributing to the education of many prominent individuals.
events.name: Lawrence Academy chartered

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, Dominique Jean Larrey, chief surgeon of the French Revolutionary Army, established the first battlefield 'flying ambulance' service, which aimed to provide immediate medical care to wounded soldiers on the battlefield. This innovation significantly improved the survival rates of injured combatants.
events.name: Dominique Jean Larrey creates the first battlefield 'flying ambulance' service

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, the Al Bu Falah tribe moved to Abu Dhabi, marking a significant moment in the history of the emirate. This migration played a crucial role in the development of Abu Dhabi as a prominent settlement in the region.
events.name: The Al Bu Falah move to Abu Dhabi

events.enhanced_description: In 1793, the United States Mint commenced regular production, marking a significant step in the establishment of a national currency. The minting of the half cent coin represented the first step towards a standardized monetary system in the fledgling nation.
events.name: The first year of regular production begins for the United States Mint, and the half cent is minted for the first time

events.enhanced_description: At the age of 11, Niccolò Paganini made his debut as a violin virtuoso in Genoa, showcasing his extraordinary talent. His performances would later revolutionize violin playing and establish him as one of the most celebrated musicians of the Romantic era.
events.name: Niccolò Paganini debuts as a violin virtuoso at age 11 in his birthplace of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On January 7, 1793, the Ebel riot occurred in Sweden, reflecting the social and political tensions of the time. This event was part of a series of disturbances that highlighted the unrest in Swedish society during the late 18th century.
events.name: Ebel riot

events.enhanced_description: On January 9, 1793, Jean-Pierre Blanchard became the first person to fly in a gas balloon in the United States, marking a significant milestone in the history of aviation. This event demonstrated the potential of ballooning as a means of exploration and entertainment.
events.name: Jean-Pierre Blanchard's gas balloon flight

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1793, Nicolas Jean Hugon de Bassville, a representative of Revolutionary France, was lynched by a mob in Rome. This incident highlighted the tensions between revolutionary ideals and the established order in Europe during the French Revolution.
events.name: Lynching of Nicolas Jean Hugon de Bassville

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1793, Louis XVI of France was guillotined after being found guilty of treason by the French National Convention. His execution marked a turning point in the French Revolution, symbolizing the end of monarchy and the rise of republicanism in France.
events.name: Execution of Louis XVI

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1793, the Second Partition of Poland occurred, where the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia partitioned the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. This event further diminished Polish sovereignty and set the stage for future conflicts in the region.

image.caption: The treaty document associated with the Second Partition of Poland.
image.date_qualification: Document dated 1793-09-25, after the event date given as 1793-01-23.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Second Partition of Poland

events.enhanced_description: In February 1793, an incident in Manchester, Vermont, involved the wife of a captain falling ill, leading to local superstitions about a vampire causing her sickness. This event reflects the cultural beliefs and practices of the time regarding illness and supernatural explanations.
events.name: Illness in Manchester, Vermont

events.enhanced_description: In February 1793, the French First Republic declared war on Great Britain, the Dutch Republic, and later Spain, escalating the French Revolutionary Wars. This declaration marked a significant expansion of the conflict and involved multiple European powers.
events.name: French Revolutionary Wars declaration of war

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1793, a French fleet under Admiral Laurent Truguet debarked troops near Cagliari in Sardinia as part of a military expedition. This operation was aimed at expanding French influence in the Mediterranean during the Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: French expedition to Sardinia

events.enhanced_description: On February 22, 1793, a small French and Corsican force briefly occupied the island of La Maddalena before withdrawing to Corsica, with 23-year-old lieutenant Napoleon Buonaparte serving as second-in-command. This event marked one of the early military actions involving Napoleon during the Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Occupation of La Maddalena

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1793, George Washington convened the first Cabinet meeting in Philadelphia, marking a significant moment in the establishment of the executive branch of the United States government. This meeting set the precedent for future Cabinet meetings and the role of advisors in the presidency.
events.name: George Washington holds the first Cabinet meeting as President of the United States

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1793, the Giles Resolutions were introduced in the House of Representatives, calling for a condemnation of Alexander Hamilton's financial policies. This event highlighted the growing political divisions in the early United States and the contentious nature of Hamilton's fiscal strategies.
events.name: The Giles Resolutions are introduced to the United States House of Representatives

events.enhanced_description: On March 1, 1793, John Langdon was appointed as President pro tempore of the United States Senate. His role was crucial in maintaining the Senate's operations during the absence of the Vice President, reflecting the evolving structure of the U.S. government.
events.name: John Langdon serves as President pro tempore of the United States Senate

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1793, George Washington was sworn in for his second term as President of the United States in Philadelphia. This event underscored Washington's pivotal role in the early republic and his commitment to the principles of democracy and governance.
events.name: George Washington is sworn in as the president of the United States for his second term

events.enhanced_description: On March 5, 1793, Austrian forces successfully defeated French troops and recaptured the city of Liège during the War of the First Coalition. This battle was part of the broader conflict between revolutionary France and a coalition of European monarchies.
events.name: French troops are defeated by Austrian forces, and Liège is recaptured

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1793, the Second Battle of Neerwinden took place, where a coalition army of Habsburg monarchy and Dutch Republic troops repulsed attacks from French Republican forces. This battle was significant in the context of the French Revolutionary Wars, showcasing the military struggles of the time.
events.name: Second Battle of Neerwinden

events.enhanced_description: On March 18, 1793, the Second Battle of Neerwinden took place, where a coalition army of Habsburg monarchy and Dutch Republic troops repulsed attacks from French Republican forces. This battle was significant in the context of the French Revolutionary Wars, showcasing the military struggles of the time.
events.name: Second Battle of Neerwinden (duplicate)

events.enhanced_description: On April 6, 1793, the Committee of Public Safety was established in France, with Georges Danton as its head. This committee became a powerful governing body during the French Revolution, tasked with protecting the Republic from internal and external threats.
events.name: Committee of Public Safety is established in France

events.enhanced_description: On April 9, 1793, Edmond-Charles Genêt, France's new Minister to the United States, arrived in Charleston, South Carolina. His arrival marked the beginning of a controversial diplomatic mission that would test U.S. neutrality during the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Edmond-Charles Genêt arrives at Charleston, South Carolina

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1793, George Washington signed the Neutrality Proclamation, declaring the United States neutral in the conflict between France and Great Britain. This proclamation was a pivotal moment in U.S. foreign policy, emphasizing the nation's desire to avoid entanglement in European wars.
events.name: George Washington signs the Neutrality Proclamation

events.enhanced_description: On April 25, 1793, the pioneer parishes of New Orleans and Louisiana were erected, marking the establishment of organized Catholic communities in the region. This incorporation into the Roman Catholic Diocese of Louisiana and the Two Floridas reflected the growing influence of the Catholic Church in the American South.
events.name: Pioneer parishes of New Orleans and Louisiana are erected

events.enhanced_description: On May 25, 1793, the last French troops occupying the small Sardinian island of San Pietro surrendered to a Spanish fleet. This event marked a significant moment in the Mediterranean theater of the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: French expedition to Sardinia: Last French troops surrender

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1793, regular troops under the command of François Hanriot demanded the expulsion of the Girondins from the National Convention. This event was part of the escalating tensions during the French Revolution, leading to significant political shifts.
events.name: French Revolution: Regular troops demand Girondins' expulsion

events.enhanced_description: In June 1793, the Macartney Embassy, led by George Macartney, reached Canton, China, aiming to establish diplomatic relations and trade agreements. However, the mission was rebuffed by the Qianlong Emperor, highlighting the challenges of Western diplomacy in China during this period.
events.name: The Macartney Embassy reaches Canton

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1793, the Girondins were overthrown during the French Revolution, marking a significant shift in power towards the more radical Jacobins. This event intensified the political turmoil and violence that characterized this revolutionary period.
events.name: French Revolution: The Girondins are overthrown

events.enhanced_description: On June 10, 1793, the National Convention established the Jardin des Plantes and the Muséum national d'histoire naturelle in Paris. These institutions played a crucial role in the advancement of natural sciences and public education in France.
events.name: French Revolution: Jardin des Plantes and Muséum national d'histoire naturelle are created

events.enhanced_description: On June 20, 1793, during the Haitian Revolution, French Republican troops and black slave insurgents defeated Royalist and slave owner settlers in the Battle of Cap-Français. This battle was a pivotal moment in the struggle for freedom and independence in Haiti.
events.name: Haitian Revolution: Battle of Cap-Français

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1793, the town of Hamilton was incorporated in Massachusetts. This event marked the establishment of a new community in the early United States, reflecting the growth and development of towns during this period.
events.name: The town of Hamilton, Massachusetts, is incorporated

events.enhanced_description: On July 9, 1793, the Act Against Slavery was passed in Upper Canada, marking a significant step towards the abolition of slavery in the region. This legislation reflected the growing abolitionist sentiment in North America during the late 18th century.
events.name: The Act Against Slavery is passed in Upper Canada

events.enhanced_description: On July 13, 1793, Charlotte Corday assassinated the radical revolutionary leader Jean-Paul Marat in his bath. This act was motivated by her opposition to the violence of the Revolution and had significant repercussions, leading to her execution and further political turmoil.
events.name: Charlotte Corday kills Jean-Paul Marat

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1793, Charlotte Corday was executed by guillotine for the assassination of Jean-Paul Marat. Her trial and execution became emblematic of the radical phase of the French Revolution and the intense political strife of the era.
events.name: Charlotte Corday is executed

events.enhanced_description: On July 20, 1793, Scottish explorer Alexander Mackenzie completed his Peace River expedition, reaching Bella Coola, British Columbia. This achievement made him the first known person to complete a transcontinental crossing of northern North America, contributing significantly to the exploration of the region.
events.name: Alexander Mackenzie's Peace River expedition reaches Bella Coola

events.enhanced_description: On July 29, 1793, John Graves Simcoe decided to establish a fort and settlement at Toronto after sailing into the bay. This decision laid the groundwork for the future development of Toronto as a major city in Canada.
events.name: John Graves Simcoe decides to build a fort and settlement at Toronto

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1793, Oulu Castle in Finland was destroyed in an explosion following the burning of a powder cellar. This incident marked a significant event in the region's military history during a time of conflict.
events.name: Oulu Castle is destroyed in an explosion

events.enhanced_description: On August 10, 1793, the Feast of Unity was celebrated in Paris as part of the French Revolution, symbolizing the unity of the French people in their struggle against monarchy. This event was marked by public festivities and was intended to reinforce the revolutionary ideals of liberty and fraternity.
events.name: French Revolution – Feast of Unity

events.enhanced_description: On August 23, 1793, the National Convention enacted a universal conscription decree, calling upon young men to join the military and urging all citizens to contribute to the war effort. This decree was a response to the external threats facing the nascent French Republic during the Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: French Revolution: Universal conscription decree enacted

events.enhanced_description: The Reign of Terror began on September 5, 1793, as the National Convention took drastic measures to eliminate perceived enemies of the revolution. Under the leadership of figures like Maximilien Robespierre, thousands were executed, and fear permeated French society.
events.name: French Revolution: Reign of Terror begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 8, 1793, the first Círio de Nazaré was celebrated in Belém, Brazil, marking the beginning of a significant religious festival honoring Our Lady of Nazareth. This event has since evolved into one of the largest religious celebrations in Brazil.
events.name: First Círio de Nazaré celebrated

events.enhanced_description: On September 17, 1793, the Army of the Eastern Pyrenees, a French Revolutionary force, achieved a decisive victory against Spanish troops at the Battle of Peyrestortes. This battle was part of the larger conflict between revolutionary France and its neighboring monarchies.
events.name: Battle of Peyrestortes

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1793, President George Washington dedicated the cornerstone of the United States Capitol, symbolizing the establishment of a new government and the nation's commitment to democracy. This event marked a significant milestone in the construction of the Capitol building, which would become a symbol of American governance.
events.name: Cornerstone of the United States Capitol dedicated

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1793, British troops from Jamaica landed in Saint-Domingue to support the counter-revolutionary forces against the French Republic and its newly-freed slaves. This intervention marked a significant escalation in the conflict surrounding the Haitian Revolution.
events.name: British troops land in Saint-Domingue

events.enhanced_description: On October 5, 1793, during the War of the First Coalition, the British Royal Navy conducted a raid on the neutral port of Genoa, boarding and capturing French warships. This action exemplified the naval conflicts that characterized the war against revolutionary France.
events.name: Raid on Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1793, a French Republican force commanded by General Jean-Baptiste Jourdan compelled a Habsburg Austrian Coalition army to retreat at the Battle of Wattignies. This victory was crucial for the French in maintaining their revolutionary government amid external threats.
events.name: Battle of Wattignies

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1793, Marie Antoinette, the former queen consort of Louis XVI, was executed by guillotine in the Place de la Révolution in Paris following a brief trial. Her execution symbolized the radical turn of the French Revolution and the end of the monarchy in France.
events.name: Execution of Marie Antoinette

events.enhanced_description: On October 24, 1793, the National Convention adopted the French Republican Calendar, a radical change aimed at de-Christianizing the society and reflecting revolutionary ideals. This calendar replaced the Gregorian calendar and was used until 1806.
events.name: French Republican Calendar adopted

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1793, the dechristianization movement during the French Revolution reached a peak with the celebration of the Goddess of Reason in Notre-Dame Cathedral. This event symbolized the revolutionary rejection of traditional religious practices and the embrace of secularism.
events.name: Celebration of the Goddess of Reason

events.enhanced_description: On November 12, 1793, Jean Sylvain Bailly, the first Mayor of Paris, was guillotined in the Place de la Révolution. His execution was part of the broader Reign of Terror, which targeted many former revolutionaries and political leaders.
events.name: Execution of Jean Sylvain Bailly

events.enhanced_description: On December 8, 1793, Madame du Barry, the last mistress of King Louis XV, was executed by guillotine in the Place de la Révolution. Her death marked the end of an era associated with the French monarchy and highlighted the radical changes brought about by the Revolution.
events.name: Execution of Madame du Barry

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1793, Noah Webster established the American Minerva, New York City's first daily newspaper. This publication played a significant role in shaping public opinion and disseminating information during a formative period in American history.
events.name: American Minerva established

events.enhanced_description: On December 18, 1793, French forces under General Dugommier captured the port city of Toulon from royalist and British forces led by Vice Admiral Lord Hood. This victory was significant for the French Revolutionary government, as it secured a strategic naval base.
events.name: Capture of Toulon

events.enhanced_description: On December 23, 1793, the Battle of Savenay was fought, where a Republican force decisively defeated the counter-revolutionary Catholic and Royal Army, effectively ending the Virée de Galerne. This battle was a crucial moment in the War in the Vendée, solidifying the Republican control over the region.
events.name: Battle of Savenay

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Kerman in 1794 was a critical military engagement where Qajar forces besieged the capital of the Zand Dynasty. This conflict was part of the larger power struggle in Persia, leading to the eventual rise of the Qajar dynasty.
events.name: Siege of Kerman

events.enhanced_description: In 1794, Niels Lund established the Stibo Group in Aarhus, Denmark, as a printing company. This company would grow to become a significant player in the publishing and technology sectors, influencing the printing industry for centuries.
events.name: The Stibo Group is founded by Niels Lund as a printing company in Aarhus (Denmark)

events.enhanced_description: The Ayrshire Yeomanry, a British cavalry regiment, was formed at Culzean Castle, reflecting the growing militarization and local defense initiatives in response to the revolutionary fervor in Europe.
events.name: Formation of the Ayrshire Yeomanry

events.enhanced_description: The Oban distillery was established in Scotland, contributing to the region's reputation for producing high-quality whisky and becoming a significant part of Scottish cultural heritage.
events.name: Construction of the Oban distillery

events.enhanced_description: On January 13, 1794, the U.S. Congress enacted a law to create a flag featuring 15 stars and 15 stripes, reflecting the admission of Vermont and Kentucky as states. This law highlighted the evolving identity of the United States as it expanded.
events.name: U.S. Congress enacts a law providing for a United States flag of 15 stars and 15 stripes

events.enhanced_description: On January 21, 1794, King George III addressed Parliament, advocating for the continuation of Britain's war against France. His speech underscored the ongoing conflict that characterized European politics during the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: King George III delivers speech opening Parliament recommending continuation of war with France

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1794, during the French Revolution, the National Convention abolished slavery in the French colonies. This landmark decision was a significant step towards human rights and reflected the revolutionary ideals of liberty and equality.
events.name: French Revolution: The National Convention abolishes slavery

events.enhanced_description: On February 8, 1794, the Wreck of the Ten Sail occurred off the coast of Grand Cayman, involving a fleet of ships that met disaster during a storm. This event is notable in maritime history and is often cited in local lore.
events.name: Wreck of the Ten Sail on Grand Cayman

events.enhanced_description: On February 11, 1794, the United States Senate held its first session open to the public, marking a significant step towards transparency in government. This event allowed citizens to witness the legislative process firsthand.
events.name: The first session of the United States Senate is open to the public

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1794, Congress passed the Eleventh Amendment to the United States Constitution, which aimed to limit the ability of individuals to sue states in federal court. This amendment was a crucial development in the evolution of American constitutional law.
events.name: The Eleventh Amendment to the United States Constitution is passed by Congress

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1794, the Pennsylvania General Assembly chartered Canonsburg Academy, which would later evolve into Washington & Jefferson College. This institution played a significant role in the education of early American leaders.
events.name: Canonsburg Academy is chartered by the Pennsylvania General Assembly

events.enhanced_description: On March 12, 1794, General Antoni Madaliński defied orders from the Russian Empire and Kingdom of Prussia to demobilize his troops, advancing instead from Ostrołęka to Kraków. This act of defiance was a precursor to the Kościuszko Uprising.
events.name: General Antoni Madaliński disobeys demobilization order and advances troops

events.enhanced_description: On March 14, 1794, Eli Whitney was granted a patent for his invention of the cotton gin, a device that revolutionized the cotton industry in the United States. This invention significantly increased the efficiency of cotton processing and had profound economic implications.
events.name: Eli Whitney is granted a United States patent for the cotton gin

events.enhanced_description: On March 22, 1794, Congress enacted a law prohibiting American ships from supplying slaves to any nation other than the United States. This legislation was part of the complex legal framework surrounding slavery and trade during this period.
events.name: Congress prohibits American ships from supplying slaves to any nation other than the United States

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1794, British forces captured Martinique from the French during the ongoing conflicts of the French Revolutionary Wars. This victory was part of Britain's broader strategy to control key territories in the Caribbean.
events.name: British troops capture Martinique from the French

events.enhanced_description: On March 24, 1794, Tadeusz Kościuszko proclaimed the start of the Kościuszko Uprising against the Russian Empire and Kingdom of Prussia in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. This uprising aimed to secure Polish independence and reform the government.
events.name: Tadeusz Kościuszko makes proclamation starting the Kościuszko Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On March 26, 1794, the United States imposed a 60-day embargo on all shipping to and from Great Britain. This action reflected the growing tensions between the two nations and the challenges faced by American trade.
events.name: The U.S. lays a 60-day embargo on all shipping to and from Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1794, the United States Government authorized the construction of the first six vessels for the United States Navy. This decision laid the foundation for the future naval power of the United States.
events.name: The United States Government authorizes the building of the first six United States Navy vessels

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1794, the Battle of Racławice took place, where Polish forces supporting the Kościuszko Uprising achieved a significant victory over the Russian Empire. This battle was a pivotal moment in the struggle for Polish independence.
events.name: Battle of Racławice: Polish supporters of the Kościuszko Uprising defeat forces of the Russian Empire

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1794, during the Reign of Terror, prominent revolutionary leaders Georges Danton and Camille Desmoulins were executed. Their deaths marked a turning point in the radical phase of the French Revolution.
events.name: Reign of Terror: Georges Danton and Camille Desmoulins are executed

events.enhanced_description: On April 17, 1794, during the Kościuszko Uprising, Polish forces successfully overthrew the Russian garrison in Warsaw. This victory was a significant moment in the struggle for Polish independence and national identity.
events.name: Kościuszko Uprising – Warsaw Uprising: The Polish people overthrow the Russian garrison in Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: On April 19, 1794, Britain, Prussia, and the Netherlands signed a treaty of alliance against France. This alliance was part of the broader conflict during the French Revolutionary Wars, as European powers sought to counter French expansion.
events.name: Britain, Prussia and the Netherlands sign a treaty of alliance against France

events.enhanced_description: On April 28, 1794, the Sardinian Vespers took place in Cagliari, where the local populace successfully ousted the viceroy and his Piedmontese officials. This uprising was part of a broader movement for autonomy in Sardinia.
events.name: Sardinian Vespers: The people of Cagliari in Sardinia oust the viceroy and his Piedmontese functionaries

events.enhanced_description: On April 29, 1794, the Battle of Boulou occurred, where French forces defeated Spanish and Portuguese troops. This battle was part of the larger conflict during the French Revolutionary Wars, showcasing the military strategies of the time.
events.name: Battle of Boulou: The French defeat the Spanish and Portuguese forces

events.enhanced_description: On May 7, 1794, Maximilien Robespierre established the Cult of the Supreme Being as the state religion of the French First Republic, promoting deism and civic virtue in an attempt to replace the Catholic Church's influence.
events.name: Robespierre establishes the Cult of the Supreme Being

events.enhanced_description: On May 8, 1794, renowned chemist Antoine Lavoisier was tried and executed during the Reign of Terror in Paris, alongside 27 co-defendants, marking a tragic loss for the scientific community.
events.name: Execution of Antoine Lavoisier

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1794, during the War of the First Coalition, French troops led by General Jean-Baptiste Jourdan achieved a significant victory over British forces at the Battle of Tourcoing, bolstering French morale.
events.name: Battle of Tourcoing

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1794, the French Revolutionary Government decided to centralize the Reign of Terror, closing provincial tribunals and mandating that all trials be held in Paris, intensifying the atmosphere of fear and repression.
events.name: Centralization of the Terror

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1794, the British Royal Navy, under Admiral Richard Howe, secured a tactical victory over the French fleet in the Battle of Ushant, although the French merchant convoy managed to reach safety in France.
events.name: The Glorious First of June (Battle of Ushant)

events.enhanced_description: On June 4, 1794, British troops captured Port-au-Prince in Haiti from the French during the Battle of Port-Républicain, marking a significant moment in the struggle for control over the Caribbean.
events.name: Battle of Port-Républicain

events.enhanced_description: On June 17, 1794, the Anglo-Corsican Kingdom was established, a short-lived political entity that resulted from British control over Corsica during the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Establishment of the Anglo-Corsican Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On June 24, 1794, Bowdoin College was founded in Brunswick, Maine, becoming one of the earliest institutions of higher education in the United States and a significant center for liberal arts education.
events.name: Founding of Bowdoin College

events.enhanced_description: In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius erupted catastrophically, burying the cities of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Stabiae, and Oplontis under volcanic ash. The Roman navy, commanded by Pliny the Elder, undertook rescue operations, although Pliny ultimately perished due to inhaling toxic fumes.
events.name: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius

events.enhanced_description: On July 17, 1794, the sixteen Carmelite Martyrs of Compiègne were guillotined in Paris, marking one of the last executions of the Reign of Terror and symbolizing the extreme measures taken during this tumultuous period.
events.name: Execution of the Carmelite Martyrs

events.enhanced_description: The Coup of 9 Thermidor on July 26, 1794, led to the arrest and execution of Maximilien Robespierre, marking a significant turning point in the French Revolution. This event effectively ended the Reign of Terror and shifted the political landscape of revolutionary France.
events.name: Coup of 9 Thermidor

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1794, during the Thermidorian Reaction, Maximilien Robespierre and his ally Louis Antoine de Saint-Just were arrested by the French National Convention, leading to their execution the following day and effectively ending the Reign of Terror.
events.name: Arrest of Robespierre and others

events.enhanced_description: In August 1794, Colombian revolutionary Antonio Nariño was denounced as a traitor after he translated and published the French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, highlighting the influence of Enlightenment ideas in Latin America.
events.name: Denouncement of Antonio Nariño

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1794, Swedish aristocrats gathered to mourn the demise of coffee after it was forbidden by royal decree, reflecting the tensions between the monarchy and the populace over personal freedoms.
events.name: Coffee Mourning in Sweden

events.enhanced_description: On August 9, 1794, Napoleon Bonaparte was arrested and placed under house arrest in Nice due to his association with the Robespierres during their fall, marking a significant moment in his early political career.
events.name: Napoleon's House Arrest

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1794, American troops led by General Anthony Wayne defeated Native American tribes of the Western Confederacy at the Battle of Fallen Timbers, a pivotal moment in the Northwest Indian War that opened up the Ohio territory for settlement.
events.name: Battle of Fallen Timbers

events.enhanced_description: On August 21, 1794, British troops captured Corsica following a bombardment led by Admiral Horatio Nelson, consolidating British control over the island during the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Capture of Corsica

events.enhanced_description: On August 29, 1794, Stonyhurst College was established as a Roman Catholic school in Lancashire, England, continuing a tradition of education that had previously spanned several European locations.
events.name: Establishment of Stonyhurst College

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1794, during the Kościuszko Uprising, Polish forces led by Tadeusz Kościuszko resisted a siege by the armies of the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Prussia, showcasing Polish determination for independence.
events.name: Siege of Warsaw

events.enhanced_description: On September 10, 1794, the University of Tennessee was established in Knoxville, becoming a significant institution for higher education in the southern United States.
events.name: Establishment of the University of Tennessee

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1794, French forces occupied Aachen during the War of the First Coalition, further extending their control in the region and demonstrating the ongoing conflict between revolutionary France and its European adversaries.
events.name: Occupation of Aachen

events.enhanced_description: In a strategic move during the War of the First Coalition, Austria, Britain, and Russia formed an alliance against Revolutionary France, aiming to restore the monarchy and counter the spread of revolutionary ideals across Europe.
events.name: Austria, Britain and Russia ally against France

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Aldenhoven was fought between French forces and the Austrian army during the War of the First Coalition, marking a significant confrontation in the ongoing struggle for dominance in Europe.
events.name: Battle of Aldenhoven

events.enhanced_description: In a historic moment, President George Washington personally led federal troops to suppress the Whiskey Rebellion, demonstrating the federal government's resolve to maintain order and enforce tax laws.
events.name: George Washington leads troops against the Whiskey Rebellion

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Maciejowice was a decisive engagement during the Kościuszko Uprising, where Russian forces defeated Polish troops, leading to the capture and wounding of the Polish leader Tadeusz Kościuszko.
events.name: Battle of Maciejowice

events.enhanced_description: Fort Wayne was established as a military fortification in present-day Indiana, serving as a strategic point for the United States during the expansion into the Northwest Territory.
events.name: Fort Wayne founded

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Praga saw Russian General Alexander Suvorov lead a brutal assault on the suburb of Warsaw, resulting in significant civilian casualties and marking a pivotal moment in the suppression of the Kościuszko Uprising.
events.name: Battle of Praga

events.enhanced_description: The Franklin Literary Society held its inaugural meeting at Canonsburg Academy, which later became Washington & Jefferson College, fostering literary and intellectual discussions among its members.

locations.name: Washington & Jefferson College, Canonsburg, Pennsylvania, United States

events.name: First meeting of the Franklin Literary Society

events.enhanced_description: The Kościuszko Uprising, a national revolt against foreign domination, concluded with the defeat of Tadeusz Kościuszko and his forces, leading to further partitions of Poland.
events.name: End of the Kościuszko Uprising

events.enhanced_description: The Jay Treaty was signed between the United States and Great Britain, addressing unresolved issues from the American Revolutionary War and establishing a decade of peaceful trade between the two nations.
events.name: Signing of the Jay Treaty

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of St-Laurent-de-la-Muga was fought between French and Spanish forces, reflecting the ongoing conflicts during the Revolutionary Wars in Europe.

events.name: Battle of St-Laurent-de-la-Muga

events.enhanced_description: The St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans was dedicated, becoming a significant religious and cultural landmark in the city, reflecting its French colonial heritage.

locations.name: St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans, Louisiana, United States

events.name: Dedication of St. Louis Cathedral

events.enhanced_description: January 1795 marked the coldest month ever recorded in Central England, according to Central England Temperature records dating back to 1659, highlighting significant climatic conditions of the period.
events.name: Coldest month recorded in Central England

events.enhanced_description: In March 1795, English Benedictine monks expelled from Douai were permitted to proceed to England, reflecting the turbulent religious and political climate of the time.
events.name: Expulsion of English Benedictine monks

events.enhanced_description: Warren Hastings, the former Governor-General of India, was acquitted by the British House of Lords of misconduct, a significant event in British political history that reflected the complexities of colonial governance.
events.name: Warren Hastings acquitted

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, Sweden became the first monarchy to officially recognize the French Republic, a significant diplomatic move that reflected the shifting political landscape in Europe during the revolutionary period.
events.name: Sweden recognizes the French Republic

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, British forces landed off the coast of Quiberon to support the royalist revolt in Brittany, an action that underscored the ongoing conflict between revolutionary France and its opponents.
events.name: British forces land off Quiberon

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, French troops successfully recaptured the island of Saint Lucia, which had been contested during the ongoing conflicts of the French Revolutionary Wars, highlighting the strategic importance of Caribbean territories.
events.name: French troops recapture St. Lucia

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, the Hudson's Bay Company constructed Fort Edmonton, which would eventually lead to the establishment of the city of Edmonton, Alberta. This trading post played a crucial role in the fur trade and the development of the region.
events.name: Construction of Fort Edmonton

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, the British Royal Navy made the use of lemon juice mandatory for sailors to prevent scurvy, a common and deadly disease caused by vitamin C deficiency. This decision significantly improved the health and survival rates of naval crews during long voyages.
events.name: Mandatory use of lemon juice in the Royal Navy

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, a significant harvest failure occurred in Munich, Bavaria, leading to food shortages and economic distress in the region. This event highlighted the vulnerabilities of agrarian societies to climatic and environmental changes.
events.name: Harvest failure in Munich

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, Daniel McGinnis discovered the supposed Money Pit on Oak Island, Nova Scotia, which has since become the focus of numerous treasure hunts and theories about buried treasure. This discovery sparked intrigue and speculation that continues to this day.
events.name: Discovery of the Money Pit

events.enhanced_description: In 1795, Jim Beam was founded as Old Jake Beam Sour Mash in Bardstown, Kentucky. This distillery would go on to become one of the most recognized bourbon brands in the world, contributing significantly to American whiskey culture.
events.name: Foundation of Jim Beam

events.enhanced_description: The University of North Carolina opened its doors to students in Chapel Hill, becoming the first state university in the United States and setting a precedent for public higher education.

locations.name: Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States

events.name: Opening of the University of North Carolina

events.enhanced_description: During the War of the First Coalition, French forces occupied Utrecht, marking a significant advance in their military campaign in the Netherlands and altering the balance of power in the region.
events.name: French occupation of Utrecht

events.enhanced_description: Amidst the Batavian Revolution, William V, Prince of Orange, fled Amsterdam, marking a pivotal moment in the transition from the Dutch Republic to the Batavian Republic.
events.name: Flight of William V, Prince of Orange

events.enhanced_description: The Batavian Republic was proclaimed in Amsterdam, effectively ending the Dutch Republic and establishing a new government aligned with revolutionary ideals.
events.name: Proclamation of the Batavian Republic

events.enhanced_description: French troops entered Amsterdam, solidifying their control over the Netherlands during the War of the First Coalition and marking a significant shift in European power dynamics.
events.name: Entry of French troops into Amsterdam

events.enhanced_description: On January 23, 1795, French forces successfully captured the Dutch fleet at Den Helder, a strategic victory during the ongoing conflicts of the French Revolutionary Wars. This event demonstrated the effectiveness of French military strategy and altered the balance of naval power in Europe.
events.name: Capture of the Dutch fleet at Den Helder

events.enhanced_description: The Eleventh Amendment to the United States Constitution was passed, addressing the judicial power of the United States and limiting the ability of individuals to sue states in federal court.
events.name: Passage of the Eleventh Amendment

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Genoa was a naval engagement during the War of the First Coalition, where British and Neapolitan fleets achieved victory over the French, impacting control of the Mediterranean.
events.name: Battle of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: Ludwig van Beethoven made his public debut in Vienna, performing his Second Piano Concerto under the direction of his teacher Antonio Salieri, marking the beginning of his illustrious career as a composer.
events.name: Ludwig van Beethoven's public debut

events.enhanced_description: The Peace of Basel, signed on April 5, 1795, marked a significant diplomatic agreement between France and Prussia, concluding hostilities and establishing a temporary peace during the tumultuous period of the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: The Peace of Basel is signed, between France and Prussia

events.enhanced_description: On April 7, 1795, France officially adopted the metric system, a revolutionary change in measurement that aimed to standardize units across the nation and later influenced global measurement systems.
events.name: The metric system is adopted in France

events.enhanced_description: On April 8, 1795, George, Prince of Wales, married Caroline of Brunswick in a politically motivated union that would later become infamous due to the couple's tumultuous relationship and public scandal.
events.name: George, Prince of Wales, marries Caroline of Brunswick

events.enhanced_description: On April 23, 1795, Warren Hastings, the former Governor-General of India, was acquitted by the British House of Lords after a lengthy trial that scrutinized his administration in India, marking a significant moment in British political history.
events.name: Warren Hastings is acquitted by the British House of Lords of misconduct

events.enhanced_description: On May 1, 1795, the Battle of Nuʻuanu took place, where Kamehameha I defeated the forces of Kalanikūpule, solidifying his control over Oʻahu and paving the way for the unification of the Hawaiian Islands under his rule.
events.name: Battle of Nuʻuanu

events.enhanced_description: In May and June of 1795, the Battle of Richmond Hill occurred in New South Wales, where the indigenous Darug people engaged British colonial forces in a conflict that highlighted the tensions between colonizers and native populations.
events.name: Battle of Richmond Hill

events.enhanced_description: On May 31, 1795, the Revolutionary Tribunal, a key institution during the Reign of Terror, was suppressed, marking a significant shift in the French Revolution as the government sought to stabilize after years of extreme measures.
events.name: French Revolution: Revolutionary Tribunal suppressed

events.enhanced_description: On June 3, 1795, the Dialectic and Philanthropic Societies were founded at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, becoming influential student organizations that fostered debate and intellectual discourse.
events.name: Dialectic and Philanthropic Societies founded

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1795, a devastating fire broke out in Copenhagen, starting in a naval warehouse and ultimately destroying 941 houses, leading to significant loss and prompting changes in fire safety regulations.

events.name: Copenhagen Fire of 1795

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1795, Louis XVII, the titular King of France, died in captivity at the Temple Prison, a tragic end to the life of a boy who was never able to ascend to the throne, leading to widespread speculation and controversy regarding his death.

image.caption: Portrait of Louis XVII (Louis-Charles), by Alexander Kucharsky.

events.name: Death of Louis XVII
