events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Zurich concluded with a victory for Archduke Charles and the Austrian army over the French forces led by André Masséna. This battle was pivotal in the context of the War of the Second Coalition, influencing the strategic landscape of Europe.
events.name: First Battle of Zurich

events.enhanced_description: Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies was restored to his throne following the collapse of the Parthenopean Republic. This restoration marked a significant moment in the political landscape of Italy during the tumultuous period of the late 18th century.
figures: Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies
events.name: Restoration of Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of the Trebbia marked the beginning of a significant defeat for Étienne Macdonald's French army against the forces led by Alexander Suvorov. This battle was a crucial moment in the War of the Second Coalition, highlighting the shifting tides of power in Europe.
events.name: Battle of the Trebbia

events.enhanced_description: In the Action of 18 June 1799, a French frigate squadron under Rear-admiral Perrée was captured by the British fleet commanded by Lord Keith off the coast of Toulon. This engagement was part of the naval operations during the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Action of 18 June 1799

events.enhanced_description: Ranjit Singh's forces took strategic positions outside Lahore, setting the stage for his eventual capture of the city. This maneuver was a key step in establishing the Sikh Empire and solidifying Singh's power in the region.
events.name: Ranjit Singh's positioning outside Lahore

events.enhanced_description: Ranjit Singh successfully captured Lahore from the Bhangi Misl, marking a pivotal moment in the establishment of the Sikh Empire. This victory solidified his position as Maharaja of the Punjab and laid the foundation for a unified Sikh state.

image.caption: Illustration of Maharaja Ranjit Singh by Colonel James Skinner.
image.date_qualification: 1830-06-10; later than the 1799 event and not an event image.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Capture of Lahore by Ranjit Singh

events.enhanced_description: In the Egyptian port city of Rosetta, French Captain Pierre Bouchard discovered the Rosetta Stone, a key artifact that would later enable scholars to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs. This discovery was instrumental in the field of Egyptology and significantly advanced our understanding of ancient Egyptian civilization.
events.name: Discovery of the Rosetta Stone

events.enhanced_description: At the Battle of Aboukir, Napoleon Bonaparte's forces defeated 10,000 Ottoman Mamluk troops commanded by Mustafa Pasha. This victory further solidified French control in Egypt and showcased Napoleon's military prowess during the campaign.
events.name: Battle of Aboukir

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Novi resulted in the defeat of Barthélemy Joubert's French army by the combined Austrian-Russian forces under Alexander Suvorov. This battle was a significant event in the War of the Second Coalition, impacting the French military position in Italy.
events.name: Battle of Novi

events.enhanced_description: The Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland involved Britain and Russia sending an expedition to the Batavian Republic, aiming to counter French influence in the region. This military action was part of the broader conflicts of the War of the Second Coalition.
events.name: Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland

events.enhanced_description: Pope Pius VI, the longest-reigning Pontiff of the Roman Catholic Church, died as a prisoner of war in the citadel of Valence after 24½ years of rule. His death marked a significant moment in the history of the papacy during the tumultuous period of the French Revolutionary Wars.
events.name: Death of Pope Pius VI

events.enhanced_description: During the Vlieter Incident, a squadron of the Batavian Republic's navy, commanded by Rear-Admiral Samuel Story, surrendered to the British Royal Navy without engaging in battle. This incident highlighted the challenges faced by the Batavian Republic during the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland.

image.caption: Robert Dodd aquatint depicting the Batavian fleet surrendering to the British fleet during the Vlieter Incident.
image.date_qualification: Published 1800; depicts the event of 30 August 1799. The image date is not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Vlieter Incident

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Krabbendam was a defensive engagement where the Russo-British expedition force successfully repelled attacks by Franco-Dutch forces. This battle was part of the larger context of the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland during the War of the Second Coalition.
events.name: Battle of Krabbendam

events.enhanced_description: On September 18, 1799, Archduke Charles led the Austrian army to a decisive victory against the French forces commanded by General Jacques Léonard Muller at the Battle of Mannheim. This battle was part of the War of the Second Coalition, which saw various European powers unite against Revolutionary France.
events.name: Victory of Archduke Charles at the Battle of Mannheim

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1799, Frederick North, the Governor of British Ceylon, issued a proclamation that mandated the enforcement of Dutch laws in the newly conquered territory until new laws could be established. This marked a significant administrative transition following British control.
events.name: Proclamation by Frederick North in Ceylon

events.enhanced_description: On September 29, 1799, the Second Roman Republic, established by the French Army after the occupation of Rome, was dissolved just 19 months after its formation. This event marked the end of a brief period of republican governance in the city.
events.name: Dissolution of the Second Roman Republic

events.enhanced_description: On September 30, 1799, during Suvorov's Swiss campaign, the Battle of the Muottental resulted in a significant rout of the French troops led by André Masséna by the Russian forces under Alexander Suvorov. This battle was a key moment in the struggle against French expansion in Europe.
events.name: Battle of the Muottental

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1799, the Battle of Alkmaar saw the Russo-British expedition force achieve a small tactical victory over the Franco-Dutch forces during the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland. This battle contributed to the ongoing military engagements in the region.
events.name: Battle of Alkmaar

events.enhanced_description: On October 6, 1799, the Battle of Castricum resulted in a defeat for the Russo-British expedition force at the hands of the Franco-Dutch forces. This battle was part of the larger conflict during the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland.
events.name: Battle of Castricum

events.enhanced_description: On October 9, 1799, HMS Lutine, a British warship, sank in the West Frisian Islands. The ship is famously known for its treasure, which has led to numerous salvage attempts over the years.
events.name: Sinking of HMS Lutine

events.enhanced_description: On October 12, 1799, Jeanne Geneviève Labrosse made history by becoming the first woman to jump from a balloon with a parachute, descending from an altitude of 900 meters (3,000 feet). This event marked a significant milestone in the history of aviation and parachuting.
events.name: Jeanne Geneviève Labrosse's parachute jump

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1799, the British Royal Navy captured a Spanish treasure convoy off the coast of Vigo, valued at over £54,000,000. This action was a significant naval engagement during the ongoing conflicts of the period.
events.name: Action of 16 October 1799

events.enhanced_description: On October 18, 1799, the Anglo-Russian expedition forces surrendered in North Holland, marking a significant defeat for the coalition forces during the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland. This event underscored the challenges faced by the allies against the Franco-Dutch forces.
events.name: Surrender of Anglo-Russian expedition forces

events.enhanced_description: On November 5, 1799, HMS Sceptre was driven ashore and wrecked in a storm in Table Bay, South Africa, resulting in the loss of 349 crew members, with only 41 survivors. This disaster highlighted the perils faced by naval vessels during the era.

locations.name: Table Bay, Western Cape, South Africa

events.name: Wreck of HMS Sceptre

events.enhanced_description: On November 9, 1799, Napoleon Bonaparte executed a coup d'état known as the Coup of 18 Brumaire, effectively overthrowing the French Directory and bringing an end to the French Revolution. This pivotal moment led to Napoleon's rise to power as First Consul.
events.name: Coup of 18 Brumaire

events.enhanced_description: On November 10, 1799, a remnant of the Council of Ancients in France abolished the Constitution of the Year III and established the French Consulate, appointing Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul. This marked a significant shift in the governance of France.

image.caption: Retrospective depiction of the three French consuls in 1799.
image.date_qualification: Depicts the Consulate in 1799; the supplied 2018 date is the file’s recorded image date, not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Abolition of the Constitution of the Year III

events.enhanced_description: On November 30, 1799, the 1799–1800 Papal conclave opened at the San Giorgio Monastery in Venice. This conclave was convened to elect a new pope following the death of Pope Pius VI.
events.name: Opening of the 1799–1800 Papal conclave

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1799, during the War of the Second Coalition, Austrian Lieutenant Field Marshal Anton Sztáray achieved victory over the French forces at the Battle of Wiesloch. This battle was part of the ongoing struggle between the Austrian Empire and Revolutionary France.
events.name: Battle of Wiesloch

events.enhanced_description: On December 10, 1799, France officially adopted the metre as its unit of length, standardizing measurements across the nation. This decision was part of a broader movement towards metrication that would influence many countries worldwide.
events.name: Adoption of the metre in France

events.enhanced_description: On December 14, 1799, George Washington, the first President of the United States, passed away at his estate in Mount Vernon, Virginia, at the age of 67. His death marked the end of an era in American history and prompted national mourning.
events.name: Death of George Washington

events.enhanced_description: On December 31, 1799, the Batavian Republic allowed the charter of the Dutch East India Company to expire, marking the end of an era for one of the most powerful trading companies in history. This decision reflected the changing political landscape in the Netherlands.
events.name: Expiration of the Dutch East India Company's charter

events.enhanced_description: The Action of 1 January 1800 was a naval engagement during the Quasi-War between the United States and France, occurring off the coast of Haiti. The battle involved U.S. merchant vessels and the naval schooner USS Experiment, facing off against Haitian pirates commanded by General André Rigaud, resulting in an indecisive outcome.
events.name: Quasi-War: Action of 1 January 1800

events.enhanced_description: On 7 February 1800, a public plebiscite in France overwhelmingly confirmed Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul, solidifying his power following the tumultuous years of the French Revolution. This event marked a significant step in Napoleon's rise to dictatorial authority in France.
events.name: Plebiscite confirming Napoleon as First Consul

events.enhanced_description: On 11 February 1800, astronomer Sir William Herschel discovered infrared radiation while experimenting with sunlight and prisms. This groundbreaking discovery expanded the understanding of the electromagnetic spectrum and laid the foundation for future developments in physics and astronomy.
events.name: Discovery of Infrared Radiation

events.enhanced_description: On 22 February 1800, the British Board of Ordnance selected the Baker rifle, designed by Ezekiel Baker, as a new standard firearm for the British Army. This rifle was notable for its accuracy and range, significantly impacting military tactics in the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Selection of the Baker Rifle

events.enhanced_description: On 14 March 1800, Cardinal Barnaba Chiaramonti was elected as Pope Pius VII during the papal conclave of 1799-1800. His election marked a significant moment in the Catholic Church's history, as he would lead the Church through the turbulent times of the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Papal Conclave: Election of Pius VII

events.enhanced_description: On 17 March 1800, the British Royal Navy ship HMS Queen Charlotte caught fire off the coast of Capraia, resulting in the tragic loss of 673 lives. This incident highlighted the dangers faced by naval crews during this period.
events.name: HMS Queen Charlotte Fire

events.enhanced_description: On 20 March 1800, Alessandro Volta described his invention of the voltaic pile, the first chemical battery, in a letter to the Royal Society of London. This invention was pivotal in the development of electrochemistry and electrical engineering.
events.name: Invention of the Voltaic Pile

events.enhanced_description: On 26 March 1800, British Royal Navy officer Henry Waterhouse first charted the Antipodes Islands, located southeast of New Zealand. This exploration contributed to the mapping of the region and enhanced knowledge of its geography.
events.name: Charting of the Antipodes Islands

events.enhanced_description: On 2 April 1800, Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 1 premiered at the Burgtheater in Vienna. This event marked a significant moment in the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era in music.
events.name: Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 1 Premiere

events.enhanced_description: On 3 April 1800, the first indirect voting began in the 1800 United States presidential election, as voters in New York selected their state legislature. This legislature would later vote for the state's presidential electors, marking a pivotal moment in American electoral history.
events.name: First Voting in the 1800 U.S. Presidential Election

events.enhanced_description: On 6 April 1800, during the War of the Second Coalition, General André Masséna was surrounded by 40,000 Austrian troops under Field Marshal Michael von Melas and blockaded by a British squadron led by Lord Keith in the Siege of Genoa. This siege was a critical moment in the conflict, showcasing the strategic challenges faced by the French forces.
events.name: Siege of Genoa

events.enhanced_description: On 24 April 1800, the U.S. Library of Congress was founded in Washington, D.C., establishing a crucial institution for the preservation of knowledge and culture in the United States. It would grow to become one of the largest libraries in the world.

image.caption: Color photograph of the exterior of the Library of Congress James Madison Memorial Building in Washington, D.C.
image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith — Library of Congress Catalog: http://lccn.loc.gov/2007687169 Image download: https://cdn.loc.gov/master/pnp/highsm/03100/03169a.tif Original url: http://hdl.loc.gov/loc.pnp/highsm.03169
image.date_qualification: Photographed 5 October 2007; the image documents the site long after the founding in 1800.
image.image_date: Taken on 5 October 2007, 10:21 (according to Exif data)
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Founding of the U.S. Library of Congress

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Marengo, fought on June 14, 1800, was a decisive engagement in the War of the Second Coalition where Napoleon Bonaparte's forces defeated the Austrian army led by General Michael von Melas. This victory solidified Napoleon's control over northern Italy and marked a significant turning point in the campaign against Austria.
events.name: Battle of Marengo

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1800, French general Jean-Baptiste Kléber was assassinated in Cairo by Suleiman al-Halabi, a Syrian Kurdish student. Kléber had been a key figure in the French campaign in Egypt, and his death marked a significant moment in the struggle between French forces and local resistance.
events.name: Assassination of Jean-Baptiste Kléber

events.enhanced_description: On 15 June 1800, the Convention of Alessandria, also known as the Armistice of Marengo, was signed, leading Austria to agree to evacuate much of Italy. This agreement marked a significant diplomatic achievement for Napoleon and the French Republic.
events.name: Convention of Alessandria

events.enhanced_description: On 19 June 1800, during the War of the Second Coalition, General Jean Victor Marie Moreau led French forces to victory at the Battle of Höchstäd, opening the Danube passageway to Vienna. This victory was crucial for the French campaign in the region.
events.name: Battle of Höchstäd

events.enhanced_description: On 27 June 1800, during the War of the Second Coalition, General Claude Lecourbe led French forces to victory at the Battle of Neuburg, securing control of the Danube from Austrian forces. This victory further solidified French dominance in the region.
events.name: Battle of Neuburg

events.enhanced_description: The Union with Ireland Act 1800, passed on July 2, 1800, by the Parliament of Great Britain, initiated the legislative union of Great Britain and Ireland, leading to the abolition of the Parliament of Ireland. This act was a pivotal moment in British-Irish relations, reshaping the political landscape of the British Isles.

locations.name: Parliament of Great Britain, London, England

events.name: Union with Ireland Act 1800

events.enhanced_description: On July 10, 1800, Lord Wellesley, the British Governor-General of India, established Fort William College in Kolkata to promote the study of Bengali, Hindi, and other vernacular languages of the Indian subcontinent. This institution played a crucial role in the education and administration of British India.

locations.name: Fort William College, Kolkata, West Bengal, India

events.name: Establishment of Fort William College

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1800, King George III granted royal assent to the second Act of Union, which united the Kingdom of Great Britain and the Kingdom of Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, effective January 1, 1801. This act marked a significant shift in the governance of the British Isles.

image.caption: Coat of arms of Great Britain, used from 1714 to 1801.
image.date_qualification: The image is dated 2010-07-20; the arms are described as having been used from 1714 to 1801. This is not an event-date photograph.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True; Restrictions: insignia

locations.name: Kingdom of Great Britain, United Kingdom

events.name: Royal Assent to the Act of Union

events.enhanced_description: On August 30, 1800, Gabriel Prosser, an enslaved African-American blacksmith, planned a slave uprising in Richmond, Virginia, but the plot was thwarted by a heavy rainstorm and the betrayal of two conspirators. This event highlighted the tensions surrounding slavery in the United States and the desperate measures taken by enslaved people seeking freedom.
events.name: Gabriel Prosser's Slave Rebellion Plot

events.enhanced_description: On September 4, 1800, the French garrison in Valletta surrendered to British troops, concluding the Siege of Malta, which had lasted for two years. This victory allowed the British to establish control over Malta, which became a strategic naval base in the Mediterranean.
events.name: Siege of Malta

events.enhanced_description: The Convention of 1800, signed on September 30, 1800, between France and the United States, formally ended the Quasi-War, a conflict characterized by naval engagements and diplomatic tensions. This treaty marked a significant step towards stabilizing Franco-American relations after years of hostility.
events.name: Convention of 1800

events.enhanced_description: On October 1, 1800, the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso was signed, wherein Spain ceded Louisiana back to France in exchange for the Tuscan territories. This treaty was pivotal in reshaping colonial territories in North America and set the stage for future conflicts.
events.name: Third Treaty of San Ildefonso

events.enhanced_description: On October 7, 1800, French privateer Robert Surcouf led a successful attack against the British East Indiaman Kent in the Indian Ocean, capturing the heavily armed vessel with a crew of 437. This event underscored the fierce naval engagements between France and Britain during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Capture of the Kent

events.enhanced_description: On November 1, 1800, John Adams became the first President of the United States to reside in the Executive Mansion, which would later be known as the White House. This marked a significant moment in American history, symbolizing the establishment of a permanent presidential residence.

locations.name: Executive Mansion (White House), Washington, D.C., United States

events.name: John Adams moves into the Executive Mansion

events.enhanced_description: On November 17, 1800, the United States Congress held its first session in the newly constructed Capitol Building in Washington, D.C. This event marked the beginning of a new era in American governance, as the capital moved from Philadelphia to the newly established city.

locations.name: Capitol Building, Washington, D.C., United States

events.name: First Congress in Washington, D.C.

events.enhanced_description: On November 22, 1800, hostilities resumed in the War of the Second Coalition as tensions escalated between French forces and their adversaries. This marked a renewed phase of conflict that would continue to shape European politics and warfare.
events.name: Resumption of Hostilities in the War of the Second Coalition

events.enhanced_description: On December 3, 1800, the Battle of Hohenlinden took place, where the French army, commanded by General Jean Moreau, achieved a decisive victory over the Habsburg and Bavarian troops. This battle was a critical moment in the War of the Second Coalition, leading to significant territorial gains for France.
events.name: Battle of Hohenlinden

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1800, an assassination attempt known as the Plot of the rue Saint-Nicaise failed to kill Napoleon Bonaparte. This event highlighted the political tensions and threats faced by Napoleon during his rise to power in France.

image.caption: Retrospective engraving depicting the Plot of the rue Saint-Nicaise, an assassination attempt on Napoleon Bonaparte.
image.credit: Unknown engraver — This file comes from Gallica Digital Library and is available under the digital ID btv1b8413005b/f1
image.date_qualification: The event is dated 24 December 1800 in the article excerpt and image description; no depicted or creation date is supplied.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Plot of the rue Saint-Nicaise

events.enhanced_description: On December 25, 1800, the Armistice of Steyr was signed between French and Imperial forces in Austria, marking a temporary cessation of hostilities in the War of the Second Coalition. This armistice set the stage for subsequent negotiations and military maneuvers.
events.name: Armistice of Steyr

events.enhanced_description: The legislative union of Great Britain and Ireland was completed on January 1, 1801, under the Act of Union 1800. This act resulted in the formation of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and the dissolution of the Parliament of Ireland.

image.caption: Heraldic coat of arms of Great Britain used from 1714 to 1801.
image.date_qualification: A modern digital rendering of a historical royal symbol, not a depiction of the union’s enactment. Image date: 2010-07-20.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True; Restrictions: insignia

locations.historical_name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
locations.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Act of Union 1800 completed

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1801, Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi discovered the asteroid and dwarf planet Ceres, marking a significant milestone in the field of astronomy. Ceres was the first object to be identified in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
events.name: Giuseppe Piazzi discovers Ceres

events.enhanced_description: In 1801, France conducted its first continuous series of censuses, a significant step in the collection of demographic data that would influence policy and governance. This initiative laid the groundwork for modern statistical practices in the country.
events.name: First continuous census in France

events.enhanced_description: In 1801, Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, began the controversial removal of the Elgin Marbles from the Parthenon in Athens, claiming they were at risk of destruction. This act sparked ongoing debates about cultural heritage and ownership that continue to this day.
events.name: Removal of the Elgin Marbles begins

events.enhanced_description: Philippe Pinel published his influential work, 'Traité médico-philosophique sur l'aliénation mentale; ou la manie', in 1801, advocating for humane treatment of the mentally ill. This publication significantly impacted psychiatric practices and attitudes towards mental health in Europe and America.
events.name: Publication of Traité médico-philosophique

events.enhanced_description: In 1801, Johann Wilhelm Ritter discovered ultraviolet radiation, expanding the understanding of the electromagnetic spectrum. This discovery had profound implications for both science and technology, influencing fields such as chemistry and photography.
events.name: Discovery of ultraviolet radiation

events.enhanced_description: The magnum opus 'Disquisitiones Arithmeticae' by Carl Friedrich Gauss was published in 1801, laying the groundwork for modern number theory. This work is considered one of the most important contributions to mathematics and has influenced countless areas of study.
events.name: Publication of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae

events.enhanced_description: In 1801, the Supreme Council, Scottish Rite (Southern Jurisdiction, USA) was founded in Charleston, South Carolina, marking a significant development in the history of Freemasonry in the United States. This organization played a crucial role in the expansion and organization of Masonic practices.
events.name: Founding of the Supreme Council, Scottish Rite

events.enhanced_description: William Pitt the Younger resigned as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on February 4, 1801, marking a significant shift in British politics. His resignation came amidst political turmoil and opposition to his policies, particularly regarding the ongoing conflicts in Europe.
events.name: William Pitt the Younger resigns as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Lunéville, signed on February 9, 1801, concluded the War of the Second Coalition, solidifying French territorial gains in Europe. Under the treaty, Austria recognized the annexation of territories by France and acknowledged the establishment of several republics in the region.
events.name: The Treaty of Lunéville ends the War of the Second Coalition between France and Austria

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1801, the United States House of Representatives resolved an electoral tie between Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr, electing Jefferson as the third President of the United States. This event marked a pivotal moment in American politics, leading to the first peaceful transfer of power between political parties.
events.name: Electoral tie resolved; Jefferson elected President

events.enhanced_description: On February 27, 1801, Washington, D.C. was officially placed under the jurisdiction of the United States Congress, establishing it as the nation's capital. This decision was crucial in defining the governance and political landscape of the newly formed capital.
events.name: Washington, D.C. placed under Congressional jurisdiction

events.enhanced_description: Thomas Jefferson was sworn in as the third President of the United States on March 4, 1801. His inauguration symbolized a significant shift in American politics, as he was the first president from the Democratic-Republican Party, moving away from Federalist policies.
events.name: Thomas Jefferson sworn in as President

events.enhanced_description: The first census in Great Britain was conducted on March 10, 1801, revealing a population of approximately 8.9 million in England and Wales. This census marked a significant development in demographic studies and governance, providing essential data for future planning and representation.
events.name: First census held in Great Britain

events.enhanced_description: Henry Addington was appointed as First Lord of the Treasury and Chancellor of the Exchequer on March 14, 1801, effectively becoming Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. His leadership came during a period of political transition following Pitt's resignation.

image.caption: James Gillray’s hand-colored etching shows Britannia with political figures Henry Addington, William Pitt, and Charles James Fox.
image.credit: James Gillray — Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, LC-USZC4-8794 (color film copy transparency), uncompressed archival TIFF version (49 MB) , level color (pick white and black point), rotated, cropped, and converted to JPEG (quality level 88) with the GIMP 2.4.5.
image.date_qualification: Published 20 May 1804; retrospective to the 14 March 1801 event.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Henry Addington becomes Prime Minister

events.enhanced_description: The Battle of Alexandria took place on March 21, 1801, where British forces defeated the French troops. Despite the victory, British commander Sir Ralph Abercromby succumbed to wounds sustained during the battle, marking a significant loss for the British leadership.

image.caption: William Faden’s plan of British operations in Egypt, including the Battle of Alexandria.
image.credit: William Fadden, Geographer to His Majesty & to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales — As stated on the map: Published by W. Fadden, Geographer to His Majesty & to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, Charing Cross, May 28th 1801.
image.date_qualification: Published 28 May 1801, after the battle; this is a contemporary map, not a photograph of the battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Battle of Alexandria

events.enhanced_description: On March 23, 1801, Tsar Paul I of Russia was murdered, leading to the ascension of his son, Alexander I. This event marked a significant turning point in Russian history, as Alexander I would go on to implement various reforms and navigate the complexities of European politics.
events.name: Murder of Tsar Paul I of Russia

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Copenhagen occurred on April 2, 1801, where the British Royal Navy, led by Admiral Sir Hyde Parker and Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson, forced the Royal Dano-Norwegian Navy to accept an armistice. This battle was a significant naval engagement during the War of the Second Coalition.
events.name: First Battle of Copenhagen

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1801, Ranjit Singh was invested as Maharaja of Punjab, establishing a significant Sikh empire in the region. His leadership marked the beginning of a new era in Punjab's history, characterized by military strength and cultural flourishing.
events.name: Ranjit Singh invested as Maharaja of Punjab

events.enhanced_description: On May 6, 1801, during the French Revolutionary Wars, the British Royal Navy brig HMS Speedy captured the Spanish frigate El Gamo off the coast of Barcelona. This engagement showcased the bravery and tactical prowess of the British forces despite being outnumbered.
events.name: Action of 6 May 1801 off Barcelona

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1801, the Pascha of Tripoli, Yusuf Karamanli, declared war on the United States by chopping down the flagpole at the U.S. consulate. This act initiated the First Barbary War, highlighting tensions between the U.S. and North African states over piracy and tribute.
events.name: Pascha of Tripoli declares war on the United States

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of Badajoz was signed on June 7, 1801, effectively ending the War of the Oranges between Portugal and Spain. As a result of the treaty, Portugal ceded the city of Olivenza to Spain, reshaping territorial boundaries in the Iberian Peninsula.

image.caption: Castillo de Olivenza in Badajoz, Spain.
image.date_qualification: Image date unknown; upload metadata records 2006-11-24, which is not the depicted date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Treaty of Badajoz ends War of the Oranges

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1801, a tragic incident occurred during a bullfight in Madrid when a bull broke through barriers, resulting in the deaths of two spectators, including the mayor of Torrejón de Ardoz. This event raised concerns about safety regulations in public spectacles.
events.name: Bullfight tragedy in Madrid

events.enhanced_description: The Siege of Cairo concluded on June 27, 1801, with British troops capturing the city from French forces. This victory was part of the broader military campaign during the Egyptian campaign of the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Siege of Cairo ends

events.enhanced_description: The First Battle of Algeciras took place on July 6, 1801, where the French fleet achieved a decisive victory over the British fleet. This battle was part of the ongoing naval engagements during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: First Battle of Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: On July 7, 1801, Toussaint Louverture promulgated a reforming constitution for Santo Domingo, declaring himself emperor for life and nominally abolishing slavery. This constitution aimed to establish a new order in the former French colony and was a significant step in the Haitian Revolution.
events.name: Toussaint Louverture promulgates constitution for Santo Domingo

events.enhanced_description: The Second Battle of Algeciras occurred on July 12, 1801, where the British fleet successfully defeated the combined French and Spanish fleets. This battle was a crucial naval engagement during the Napoleonic Wars, showcasing British naval superiority.
events.name: Second Battle of Algeciras

events.enhanced_description: On July 18, 1801, Napoleon Bonaparte signed a Concordat with Pope Pius VII, re-establishing the Catholic Church in France after years of revolutionary secularism. This agreement aimed to reconcile the church with the state and restore religious order in the nation.
events.name: Napoleon signs Concordat with Pope Pius VII

events.enhanced_description: On August 1, 1801, during the First Barbary War, the United States Navy schooner USS Enterprise captured the Tripolitan corsair polacca Tripoli off the North African coast. This engagement highlighted the U.S. Navy's efforts to combat piracy and protect American shipping interests.

image.caption: William Bainbridge Hoff’s drawing depicts the schooner Enterprise capturing the Tripolitan corsair Tripoli.
image.date_qualification: Depicts the 1801 engagement; the drawing dates to circa 1878.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Action of 1 August 1801

events.enhanced_description: On September 9, 1801, Tsar Alexander I of Russia confirmed the privileges of the Baltic provinces, ensuring their autonomy and rights within the Russian Empire. This decision was part of Alexander's broader strategy to stabilize and integrate the diverse regions of his empire.
events.name: Alexander I confirms privileges of Baltic provinces

events.enhanced_description: On September 24, 1801, Joseph Marie Jacquard exhibited his innovative loom at the National Exposition in Paris, which utilized punched cards to control the weaving pattern. This invention revolutionized the textile industry and laid the groundwork for modern computing.
events.name: Joseph Marie Jacquard exhibits new loom invention

events.enhanced_description: The Treaty of London, signed on September 30, 1801, marked a preliminary peace agreement between the French First Republic and the United Kingdom, effectively ending hostilities that had persisted during the French Revolutionary Wars. This treaty set the stage for further negotiations and the eventual Treaty of Amiens in 1802.
events.name: The Treaty of London is signed

events.enhanced_description: On October 17, 1801, a coup d'état occurred in the Batavian Republic, leading to significant political changes within the government. This event was part of the broader context of instability in the region following the French Revolutionary Wars.
figures: Johan van der Capellen tot den Pol
events.name: A coup d'état is staged in the Batavian Republic

events.enhanced_description: The first edition of the New-York Evening Post was printed on November 16, 1801, marking the establishment of one of the oldest newspapers in the United States. Founded by William Coleman, it played a significant role in American journalism and public discourse.
events.name: The first edition of the New-York Evening Post is printed

events.enhanced_description: On December 15, 1801, Hadži Mustafa Pasha, an Ottoman commander and politician, was assassinated in Belgrade by Kučuk-Alija. This event highlighted the political turmoil and power struggles within the Ottoman Empire during this period.
events.name: Assassination of Hadži Mustafa Pasha

events.enhanced_description: On December 19, 1801, South Carolina College was established in Columbia, South Carolina, serving as a precursor to what is now known as the University of South Carolina. This institution played a crucial role in the higher education landscape of the southern United States.
events.name: Establishment of South Carolina College

events.enhanced_description: On December 24, 1801, engineers Richard Trevithick and Andrew Vivian successfully demonstrated the 'Puffing Devil', a steam-powered road locomotive, in Camborne, Cornwall. This event marked a significant milestone in the development of steam power and transportation technology.
events.name: Demonstration of the Puffing Devil

events.enhanced_description: In February 1802, Colonel Tomkyns Hilgrove Turner brought the Rosetta Stone to England, arriving at Portsmouth aboard the captured French frigate L'Egyptiane. This artifact would later become crucial in deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs and understanding ancient Egyptian civilization.
events.name: Arrival of the Rosetta Stone in England

events.enhanced_description: In May 1802, Madame Marie Tussaud first exhibited her wax sculptures in London. Having gained fame for creating death masks during the Reign of Terror in France, her exhibition marked the beginning of what would become a world-renowned attraction.
events.name: First Exhibition of Madame Tussaud's Wax Sculptures

events.enhanced_description: In June 1802, Humphry Davy published the first account of Thomas Wedgwood's experiments in photography in the Journal of the Royal Institution in London. Although the images could not be fixed and quickly faded, these experiments laid the groundwork for future developments in photography.
events.name: Publication of Thomas Wedgwood's Photography Experiments

events.enhanced_description: In 1802, shortly before his conquest of Tonkin, Nguyen Anh was crowned as Emperor Gia Long in Huế, marking the establishment of the Nguyễn dynasty in Vietnam. This event solidified his rule and the unification of Vietnam under his leadership.
events.name: Crowning of Emperor Gia Long

events.enhanced_description: On January 5, 1802, Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, continued the removal of the Elgin Marbles from the Parthenon in Athens, claiming they were at risk of destruction. This act initiated a long-standing debate over cultural heritage and the ownership of historical artifacts.
events.name: Removal of the Elgin Marbles continues

events.enhanced_description: On January 15, 1802, Canonsburg Academy was chartered by the Pennsylvania General Assembly, which later evolved into Washington & Jefferson College. This institution played a significant role in the education of young men in the region.
events.name: Chartering of Canonsburg Academy

events.enhanced_description: On January 29, 1802, General Charles Leclerc led a French expedition of 40,000 troops to Saint-Domingue in an attempt to restore colonial rule following the Haitian Revolution. This military action was a direct response to Toussaint Louverture's declaration of independence and control over Hispaniola.
events.name: French Saint-Domingue expedition

events.enhanced_description: On February 3, 1802, General Charles Leclerc and the first 5,000 of 20,000 troops arrived at Cap-François (modern Cap-Haïtien) as part of the French expedition to reclaim control over Saint-Domingue. This marked the beginning of a significant military campaign against the Haitian forces.
events.name: Arrival of Leclerc's troops at Cap-François

events.enhanced_description: On February 17, 1802, the remains of Pope Pius VI were returned to the Vatican by France, following his death in captivity in Valence on August 29, 1799. This event marked a significant moment in the relationship between the Papacy and France during the tumultuous period of the French Revolution.
events.name: Return of Pope Pius VI's remains

events.enhanced_description: On March 3, 1802, Ludwig van Beethoven published his Piano Sonata No. 14, commonly known as the 'Moonlight Sonata', in Vienna. This piece has since become one of Beethoven's most celebrated works and a staple of classical music repertoire.
events.name: Publication of Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata

events.enhanced_description: On March 11, 1802, the Rosetta Stone was presented to the Society of Antiquaries of London, which subsequently donated it to the British Museum. This event marked a significant moment in the study of ancient Egypt and the understanding of hieroglyphics.

image.caption: The Rosetta Stone displayed at the British Museum.
image.date_qualification: Photograph of the stone at the British Museum, not a depiction of its 1802 presentation. Original image date: 21 November 2007.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Presentation of the Rosetta Stone to the Society of Antiquaries

events.enhanced_description: On March 16, 1802, the United States Army Corps of Engineers was re-established, and the United States Military Academy at West Point, New York, was opened under its management. This institution has since played a vital role in training military leaders and engineers.
events.name: Re-establishment of the United States Army Corps of Engineers

events.enhanced_description: On March 27, 1802, the Treaty of Amiens was signed, officially ending the War of the Second Coalition and the French Revolutionary Wars. This treaty temporarily restored peace between France and the United Kingdom, allowing for a brief period of stability in Europe.
events.name: Treaty of Amiens signed

events.enhanced_description: On March 28, 1802, H. W. Olbers discovered the asteroid Pallas, the second asteroid to be discovered after Ceres. This discovery contributed to the growing field of astronomy and the understanding of celestial bodies in our solar system.
events.name: Discovery of asteroid Pallas

events.enhanced_description: On April 10, 1802, the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India commenced with the measurement of a baseline near Madras (modern Chennai). This monumental project aimed to survey the entire Indian subcontinent and laid the foundation for modern geodesy.
events.name: Beginning of the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India

events.enhanced_description: On April 21, 1802, approximately 12,000 Wahhabi Sunnis, led by Abdul-Aziz bin Muhammad, attacked and sacked Karbala, resulting in the deaths of 2,000 to 5,000 inhabitants and the plundering of the tomb of Husayn ibn Ali. This event was a significant episode in the conflict between Wahhabi forces and Shia Muslims.
events.name: Sack of Karbala by Wahhabi forces

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1802, Napoleon Bonaparte signed a general amnesty allowing most émigrés from the French Revolution to return to France. This act was a strategic move to reconcile with various factions of the Ancien Régime and solidify his own power.
events.name: General Amnesty by Napoleon

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1802, Napoleon Bonaparte established the French Legion of Honour, a prestigious order of merit that recognized military and civil service. This institution was part of Napoleon's efforts to create a new aristocracy based on merit rather than birth.
events.name: Establishment of the French Legion of Honour

events.enhanced_description: On May 20, 1802, Napoleon Bonaparte enacted the Law of 20 May 1802, which reinstated slavery in French colonies, reversing the abolition that had occurred during the French Revolution. This decision was met with significant opposition and had lasting implications for colonial policies.
events.name: Reinstatement of Slavery in French Colonies

events.enhanced_description: On June 1, 1802, the United States Patent and Trademark Office was established within the Department of State. This marked a significant step in the protection of intellectual property rights in the United States.
events.name: Establishment of the United States Patent and Trademark Office

events.enhanced_description: On June 2, 1802, Pemulwuy, a prominent Indigenous Australian leader of resistance against European settlement, was shot dead by settler Henry Hacking. His death marked a significant moment in the ongoing conflict between Indigenous Australians and European settlers.
events.name: Death of Pemulwuy

events.enhanced_description: On June 8, 1802, Haitian revolutionary leader Toussaint Louverture was captured by French troops and imprisoned at Fort de Joux. This event marked a turning point in the struggle for Haitian independence.
events.name: Capture of Toussaint Louverture

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1802, parliamentary elections began in the United Kingdom, concluding on August 28. The Tories, led by Henry Addington, emerged victorious, gaining control of the House of Commons.
events.name: Parliamentary Elections in the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On July 19, 1802, Éleuthère Irénée du Pont founded E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company near Wilmington, Delaware. Initially established as a gunpowder manufactory, it would grow into one of the largest chemical companies in the world.
events.name: Founding of E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company

events.enhanced_description: On July 22, 1802, Emperor Gia Long captured Hanoi, completing his unification of Vietnam. This victory solidified his rule and marked the establishment of the Nguyễn dynasty's dominance over the region.
events.name: Gia Long Captures Hanoi

events.enhanced_description: On July 31, 1802, poet William Wordsworth, while traveling from London to Dover, was inspired by the early morning scene at Westminster Bridge, which he later captured in his famous sonnet 'Composed upon Westminster Bridge.'
events.name: William Wordsworth's Sonnet

events.enhanced_description: On August 2, 1802, a plebiscite confirmed Napoleon Bonaparte as the First Consul of France. This event solidified his authority and marked a significant step in his rise to power.
events.name: Napoleon Confirmed as First Consul

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1802, the Italian region of Piedmont was officially incorporated into the French First Republic. This annexation was part of Napoleon's broader strategy to expand French influence in Europe.
events.name: Piedmont Becomes Part of France

events.enhanced_description: On October 2, 1802, the war between Sweden and Tripoli officially ended. Although the United States also negotiated peace, tensions remained regarding compensation issues.
events.name: End of War between Sweden and Tripoli

events.enhanced_description: On October 15, 1802, French Army General Michel Ney entered Switzerland with 40,000 troops on orders from Napoleon Bonaparte. This military maneuver was part of Napoleon's efforts to assert control over the region.
events.name: Michel Ney Enters Switzerland

events.enhanced_description: On October 16, 1802, the port of New Orleans and the lower Mississippi River were closed to American traffic by order of the Spanish administrator Juan Ventura Morales. This action threatened the economy of the western United States and highlighted the need for the Louisiana Purchase.
events.name: Closure of New Orleans Port

events.enhanced_description: On October 26, 1802, a powerful 7.9 magnitude earthquake struck the Vrancea district of Romania, destroying hundreds of buildings and triggering landslides. This earthquake is considered one of the strongest to have affected Europe, resulting in four fatalities.
events.name: Vrancea Earthquake

events.enhanced_description: On November 16, 1802, King George III inaugurated the newly elected British House of Lords, emphasizing his commitment to peace while also acknowledging the complexities of European politics. His speech reflected the tensions of the time.
events.name: Inauguration of the British House of Lords

events.enhanced_description: On November 23, 1802, the East Indiaman Vryheid, serving the Batavian Republic, was shipwrecked in a gale off Hythe, Kent. Of the 472 people on board, only 18 survived, marking one of the significant maritime disasters of the era.
events.name: Shipwreck of the Vryheid

events.enhanced_description: On December 2, 1802, the Health and Morals of Apprentices Act came into effect in the United Kingdom, regulating conditions for child labor in factories. Although poorly enforced, it was a pioneering step towards labor reform.
events.name: Health and Morals of Apprentices Act

events.enhanced_description: In 1803, the first edition of Alexandre Balthazar Laurent Grimod de La Reynière's 'Almanach des gourmands' was published in Paris. This work is considered the first guide to restaurant cooking, influencing culinary practices in France and beyond.
figures: Alexandre Balthazar Laurent Grimod de La Reynière
events.name: Publication of Almanach des gourmands

events.enhanced_description: On January 1, 1803, Ohio was officially admitted as the 17th state of the United States. This event marked a significant milestone in the westward expansion of the nation and the establishment of new governance structures in the frontier regions.
events.name: Ohio is admitted as the 17th U.S. state

events.enhanced_description: On January 4, 1803, William Symington demonstrated the Charlotte Dundas, recognized as the first practical steamboat, in Scotland. This innovation marked a significant advancement in maritime technology.
events.name: Demonstration of the Charlotte Dundas

events.enhanced_description: In early 1803, U.S. diplomats James Monroe and Robert R. Livingston sailed to Paris to negotiate the purchase of New Orleans, a critical port for American trade. Their discussions led to the Louisiana Purchase, which doubled the size of the United States and significantly expanded its territory.
events.name: Monroe and Livingston sail for Paris to discuss, and possibly buy, New Orleans; they end up completing the Louisiana Purchase

events.enhanced_description: On February 19, 1803, Napoleon Bonaparte issued an Act of Mediation that restructured the political landscape of Switzerland, replacing the Helvetic Republic with a more decentralized Swiss Confederation. This act allowed for greater autonomy among the cantons and established a framework for modern Swiss governance.
events.name: An Act of Mediation establishes the Swiss Confederation

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1803, during the Kandyan Wars, a British detachment captured the city of Kandy in Ceylon (modern-day Sri Lanka). This marked a significant step in the British campaign to control the island, which was characterized by fierce resistance from the local Kandyan kingdom.
events.name: Kandyan Wars: Kandy, Ceylon is taken by a British detachment

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1803, Edward Despard and six co-conspirators were executed in London for their involvement in a plot to assassinate King George III and destroy the Bank of England. This event highlighted the tensions and unrest in Britain during a time of political upheaval.
events.name: Edward Despard and six others are hanged and beheaded for plotting to assassinate King George III

events.enhanced_description: On February 24, 1803, the Supreme Court of the United States, led by Chief Justice John Marshall, ruled in Marbury v. Madison, establishing the principle of judicial review. This landmark decision empowered the judiciary to invalidate laws that conflicted with the Constitution, shaping the balance of power in the U.S. government.
events.name: Marbury v. Madison: The Supreme Court establishes the principle of judicial review

events.enhanced_description: On February 25, 1803, the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss was enacted, leading to a significant redistribution of territorial sovereignty within the Holy Roman Empire. This act was part of the broader reorganization of German territories following the Napoleonic Wars.

image.caption: Title page of the Reichsdeputationshauptschluss.
image.credit: Original uploader was Känsterle at nl.wikipedia — Transferred from nl.wikipedia ; transferred to Commons by User:Krinkle using CommonsHelper (all following user names refer to nl.wikipedia): 2004-08-21 15:15 Känsterle 346×400 (17838 bytes) Exemplaar van de voorpagina van de Reichsdeputationshauptschluss
image.date_qualification: The title page is dated 25 February 1803; 21 August 2004 is the original upload date, not the depicted document’s date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Reichsdeputationshauptschluss enacts redistribution of territorial sovereignty within the Holy Roman Empire

events.enhanced_description: In March-April 1803, the franc germinal was introduced in France as a new currency standard. This reform aimed to stabilize the French economy following the tumultuous years of the Revolution and establish a reliable monetary system.

image.caption: A French 20-franc gold coin from the National Numismatic Collection.
image.credit: National Museum of American History — National Numismatic Collection, National Museum of American History
image.date_qualification: The saved image date is 1803. The coin is a contemporaneous monetary artifact relevant to the franc germinal, not a depiction of the reform itself.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: The franc germinal is introduced in France

events.enhanced_description: On March 9, 1803, the canton of Aargau was officially established in Switzerland as part of the restructuring initiated by Napoleon's Act of Mediation. This event marked a significant step in the formation of the modern Swiss Confederation.
events.name: Aargau becomes a Swiss canton

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1803, the L'Aigle meteorite fell in Normandy, France, marking a pivotal moment in the study of meteorites. This event shifted scientific opinion regarding the origin of meteorites, leading to increased interest and research in the field of meteoritics.
events.name: The L'Aigle meteorite falls in Normandy

events.enhanced_description: On April 30, 1803, the United States finalized the Louisiana Purchase from France, acquiring approximately 828,000 square miles of territory. This monumental deal, negotiated by Thomas Jefferson's envoys James Monroe and Robert R. Livingston, effectively doubled the size of the nation and opened vast lands for exploration and settlement.
events.name: The Louisiana Purchase is made from France by the United States

events.enhanced_description: In May 1803, Napoleon Bonaparte, as First Consul of France, began preparations for an invasion of England. This military buildup was part of his broader strategy to assert French dominance in Europe and counter British influence.
events.name: First Consul of France, Citizen Bonaparte, begins making preparations to invade England

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1803, the Napoleonic Wars officially began when the United Kingdom declared war on France. This declaration followed France's refusal to withdraw from Dutch territory, marking the start of a series of conflicts that would reshape Europe.
events.name: The Napoleonic Wars begin

events.enhanced_description: On May 19, 1803, Master Malati, a Coptic Christian leader, was beheaded by a Muslim mob in Cairo, Egypt. This tragic event underscored the religious tensions and conflicts present in the region during this period.
events.name: Master Malati is beheaded by a Muslim mob in Cairo, Egypt

events.enhanced_description: On June 5, 1803, the Convention of Artlenburg was signed, agreeing to a ceasefire after the French invasion of Hanover. This agreement allowed many members of the former Hanoverian Army to go into exile and join the King's German Legion.
events.name: Convention of Artlenburg agrees a ceasefire following the French Invasion of Hanover

events.enhanced_description: On June 7, 1803, Indiana Territory governor William Henry Harrison signed treaties at Fort Wayne with representatives from several Native American tribes. These treaties aimed to secure land for American settlers and were ratified by the U.S. Senate later that year.
events.name: Indiana Territory governor William Henry Harrison signs treaties at Fort Wayne

events.enhanced_description: On June 14, 1803, Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the establishment of five military camps along the French coast to prepare for potential conflict with Britain. Each camp was to house thousands of troops, reflecting the growing tensions between the two nations.
events.name: Napoleon Bonaparte orders the establishment of military camps to defend the coast of France

events.enhanced_description: On July 4, 1803, President Thomas Jefferson announced the Louisiana Purchase to the American public, revealing the acquisition of vast territories from France. This announcement marked a pivotal moment in U.S. history, emphasizing the nation's expansionist ambitions.
events.name: The Louisiana Purchase is announced to the American people

events.enhanced_description: On July 5, 1803, the Convention of Artlenburg resulted in the French occupation of Hanover, a territory previously ruled by the British king. This occupation was part of the broader conflict of the Napoleonic Wars and marked a significant shift in territorial control in Europe.
events.name: The convention of Artlenburg leads to the French occupation of Hanover

events.enhanced_description: On July 23, 1803, Robert Emmet initiated an uprising in Ireland against British rule. This rebellion, although ultimately unsuccessful, became a symbol of Irish nationalism and resistance.
events.name: Robert Emmet's uprising in Ireland begins

events.enhanced_description: On July 26, 1803, the wagonway connecting Wandsworth and Croydon was opened, marking the first public railway line in England. This development represented a significant advancement in transportation and set the stage for the future of rail travel.
events.name: The wagonway between Wandsworth and Croydon is opened

events.enhanced_description: On August 3, 1803, the British launched the Second Anglo-Maratha War against the Scindia Dynasty of Gwalior. This conflict was part of the broader struggle for control over India and marked a significant escalation in British military efforts in the region.
events.name: The British begin the Second Anglo-Maratha War

events.enhanced_description: On August 31, 1803, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, on their expedition to explore the newly acquired Louisiana Territory. This journey would provide valuable information about the geography, biology, and indigenous peoples of the vast lands west of the Mississippi River.

image.caption: Map of the Lewis and Clark Expedition.
image.credit: Goszei , from original by User:Sardon — Own work
image.date_qualification: The image depicts the expedition of 1804–1806; the supplied image_date, 2021-03-12, is the map’s date, not the event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 3.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Lewis and Clark Expedition begins

events.enhanced_description: On September 6, 1803, British scientist John Dalton began using symbols to represent the atoms of different elements, laying the groundwork for modern atomic theory. His work significantly advanced the field of chemistry and changed the understanding of matter.
events.name: John Dalton begins using symbols to represent the atoms of different elements

events.enhanced_description: On September 11, 1803, during the Second Anglo-Maratha War, British troops under General Lake achieved a decisive victory against the Maratha forces commanded by General Louis Bourquin in the Battle of Delhi. This battle was pivotal in establishing British dominance in northern India.
events.name: Second Anglo-Maratha War: Battle of Delhi

events.enhanced_description: On September 20, 1803, Irish nationalist Robert Emmet was executed at Kilmainham Gaol in Dublin for his role in the failed rebellion against British rule. His speech before execution became a rallying cry for Irish nationalism.
events.name: Execution of Robert Emmet

events.enhanced_description: On September 23, 1803, the British-led forces, commanded by Arthur Wellesley, defeated the Maratha army at the Battle of Assaye during the Second Anglo-Maratha War. This victory was crucial in consolidating British power in India.
events.name: Second Anglo-Maratha War: Battle of Assaye

events.enhanced_description: On October 14, 1803, following the Second Anglo-Maratha War, the British East India Company occupied the region of Orissa, which is now part of modern-day Odisha, India. This occupation was formalized in the Treaty of Deogaon, signed later that year.
events.name: British occupation of Orissa

events.enhanced_description: On October 20, 1803, the United States Senate ratified the Louisiana Purchase Treaty, which effectively doubled the size of the nation by acquiring vast territories from France. This monumental event was a significant step in the westward expansion of the United States.
events.name: Ratification of the Louisiana Purchase Treaty

events.enhanced_description: On November 18, 1803, the Haitian army, led by Jean-Jacques Dessalines, achieved a decisive victory over the French forces at the Battle of Vertières. This battle was a critical moment in the Haitian Revolution, leading to Haiti's independence.

image.caption: Monument to the heroes of the Battle of Vertières.
image.date_qualification: The image date is 2021-06-01; this is a later photograph of a monument, not a photograph of the 1803 battle.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Haitian Revolution: Battle of Vertières

events.enhanced_description: In early 1803, the Balmis Expedition was initiated in Spain to combat smallpox through vaccination efforts in Spanish America and the Philippines. Led by Dr. Francisco Javier Balmis, this expedition aimed to protect millions from the deadly disease.
events.name: The Balmis Expedition

events.enhanced_description: On December 9, 1803, Congress approved the proposed Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution, which aimed to clarify the electoral process for the presidency and vice presidency. This amendment was a response to the electoral issues faced in the 1800 election.
events.name: Proposed Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution

events.enhanced_description: On December 20, 1803, the formal transfer of the Louisiana Territory from France to the United States was completed in St. Louis. This event marked the culmination of the Louisiana Purchase, which significantly expanded the territory of the United States.
events.name: Completion of the Louisiana Purchase

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, Haiti declared its independence from France, becoming the first black republic in the world and the only nation to successfully conduct a slave revolt. This monumental event reshaped the landscape of colonialism and slavery.

image.caption: 19th-century engraving by Jean-Jacques Frilley, after Auguste Raffet, depicting fighting between Saint-Domingue insurgents and French troops.
image.credit: Auguste Raffet — Archives territoriales de Martinique (patrimoines-martinique.org)
image.date_qualification: Depicted fighting is dated 1802–1803; the engraving is identified as 19th century. The supplied image_date gives a 19th-century date, not a more precise creation date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Haiti gains independence from France

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, John Wedgwood established the Royal Horticultural Society in London, aiming to promote the science and practice of horticulture. This organization has since played a pivotal role in the advancement of gardening and plant cultivation in the UK and beyond.
events.name: John Wedgwood founds the Royal Horticultural Society

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, Thomas Charles played a key role in establishing the British and Foreign Bible Society in London, which aimed to promote the distribution of the Bible in various languages and translations. This organization has significantly contributed to the spread of Christianity and literacy worldwide.
events.name: Thomas Charles is instrumental in founding the British and Foreign Bible Society

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, Emperor Gia Long of the Nguyễn dynasty officially changed the name of his country from Đại Việt to Việt Nam, marking a significant shift in national identity and governance. This change reflected a desire to unify the country under a single name and to assert its sovereignty.
events.name: Gia Long changes country's official name

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, Friedrich Sertürner, a German pharmacist, successfully isolated morphine from the opium poppy, marking a pivotal moment in the field of pharmacology. This discovery paved the way for the development of modern pain management and the use of opiates in medicine.
events.name: Morphine is first isolated

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, explorer Matthew Flinders proposed that the land known as New Holland be renamed Australia, deriving the name from the Latin term 'australis', meaning 'of the south'. This recommendation was significant in shaping the national identity of Australia.

image.caption: Bass and Flinders Point in Cronulla, New South Wales, Australia.
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2010-07-19; the depicted date is not the 1804 event date.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: Public domain; UsageTerms: Public domain; Copyrighted: False

events.name: Matthew Flinders recommends renaming New Holland

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, Shimizu-gumi was established in the Kanda region of Edo, which is modern-day Tokyo. This company would eventually evolve into Shimizu Corporation, one of Japan's leading construction firms, playing a crucial role in the country's infrastructure development.
events.name: Shimizu-gumi is founded

events.enhanced_description: In 1804, the world population reached an estimated 1 billion people, a significant milestone in human history. This demographic shift marked the beginning of rapid population growth that would continue into the 19th and 20th centuries.
events.name: World population reaches 1 billion

events.enhanced_description: On February 4, 1804, the Sokoto Caliphate was founded in West Africa by Usman dan Fodio, following a successful jihad against the Hausa kingdoms. This caliphate became a significant Islamic state in the region, promoting education and trade.
events.name: Founding of the Sokoto Caliphate

events.enhanced_description: On February 14, 1804, the First Serbian Uprising began against Ottoman rule, led by Karageorge Petrović. This uprising marked the beginning of the Serbian Revolution, which ultimately led to Serbia's autonomy from the Ottoman Empire.
events.name: First Serbian Uprising

events.enhanced_description: On February 15, 1804, New Jersey became the last northern state in the United States to abolish slavery. This legislative action was a significant step towards the eventual end of slavery in the United States.
events.name: New Jersey abolishes slavery

events.enhanced_description: On February 16, 1804, during the First Barbary War, Stephen Decatur led a daring raid to burn the captured USS Philadelphia in Tripoli harbor, preventing its use by Barbary pirates. This bold action was a significant moment in U.S. naval history.
events.name: First Barbary War: Raid on USS Philadelphia

events.enhanced_description: On February 18, 1804, Ohio University was chartered by the Ohio General Assembly, becoming the first institution of higher education in the Northwest Territory. This marked a significant development in American education.
events.name: Chartering of Ohio University

events.enhanced_description: On February 20, 1804, Hobart was established as a permanent settlement in Van Diemen's Land (modern-day Tasmania) as a British penal colony. This marked the beginning of significant European settlement in the region.
events.name: Establishment of Hobart

events.enhanced_description: On February 21, 1804, Richard Trevithick's Penydarren steam locomotive made its first successful run on the Merthyr Tramroad in South Wales, marking a significant milestone in the development of railway technology.
events.name: First locomotive operation

events.enhanced_description: On March 4, 1804, the Castle Hill convict rebellion broke out in New South Wales, led by Irish convicts. This uprising was a significant event in Australian colonial history, reflecting the discontent among convicts.
events.name: Castle Hill convict rebellion

events.enhanced_description: On March 10, 1804, a formal ceremony was held in St. Louis to transfer ownership of the Louisiana Territory from France to the United States, marking a pivotal moment in American history known as Three Flags Day.
events.name: Louisiana Purchase, Three Flags Day

events.enhanced_description: On March 17, 1804, Friedrich Schiller's play 'Wilhelm Tell' premiered in Weimar, directed by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. This performance marked a significant contribution to German literature and theater.
events.name: First performance of Wilhelm Tell

events.enhanced_description: The Napoleonic Code, officially known as the Civil Code of the French, was enacted on March 21, 1804, establishing a comprehensive set of civil laws that influenced legal systems worldwide. It emphasized clearly written and accessible law, replacing feudal laws and promoting the principles of the French Revolution, such as equality before the law.

image.caption: The Napoleonic Code on display at the Historical Museum of the Palatinate.
image.date_qualification: Museum display of the code, not a depiction of its 1804 adoption; photograph dated 2010-12-19.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY-SA 4.0; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0; Copyrighted: True

events.name: The Napoleonic Code is adopted as French civil law

events.enhanced_description: On April 2, 1804, a convoy of merchant ships led by the British frigate HMS Apollo tragically ran aground off the coast of Portugal, resulting in the loss of forty merchant vessels and considerable loss of life. This incident highlighted the dangers of naval warfare and maritime navigation during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Forty merchantmen are wrecked when a convoy led by British frigate HMS Apollo runs aground off Portugal

events.enhanced_description: On April 4, 1804, the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge embarked on a journey aboard The Speedwell to the Mediterranean. During his time in Malta, he secured a position as a public official, which influenced his literary work and thoughts on nature and society.
events.name: Samuel Taylor Coleridge sets sail on The Speedwell for the Mediterranean

events.enhanced_description: On April 5, 1804, the High Possil meteorite, the first recorded meteorite to fall in Scotland in modern times, landed in the area of High Possil. This event sparked interest in meteorites and contributed to the scientific understanding of these celestial phenomena.
events.name: The High Possil meteorite falls at High Possil

events.enhanced_description: On April 22, 1804, the Haiti massacre occurred, an ethnic cleansing aimed at eradicating the white population in Haiti following the revolution. This event highlighted the intense racial tensions and the aftermath of the successful slave revolt.
events.name: Haiti Massacre

events.enhanced_description: On April 26, 1804, Henry Addington resigned from his position as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, a role he had held since 1801. His resignation marked a significant shift in British politics during a tumultuous period characterized by the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Henry Addington resigns as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On May 10, 1804, William Pitt the Younger commenced his second term as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. His leadership during this period was crucial in navigating the challenges posed by the ongoing Napoleonic Wars and domestic issues.
events.name: William Pitt the Younger begins his second term as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom

events.enhanced_description: On May 14, 1804, the Lewis and Clark Expedition, led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, set out from Camp Dubois, Illinois, to explore the newly acquired Louisiana Territory. This journey was pivotal in expanding the United States' knowledge of the western frontier and its indigenous peoples.
events.name: The Lewis and Clark Expedition departs from Camp Dubois

events.enhanced_description: On May 18, 1804, Napoleon Bonaparte was proclaimed Emperor of the French by the French Senate, marking a significant shift in French governance and the establishment of the First French Empire. This event solidified his power and set the stage for his ambitious expansion across Europe.
events.name: Napoleon Bonaparte is proclaimed Emperor of the French

events.enhanced_description: On May 21, 1804, Père Lachaise Cemetery was opened in Paris, becoming the first garden cemetery in the city. It has since become a significant cultural landmark, known for its beautiful landscaping and as the final resting place of many notable figures.

image.caption: Chemin Errazu at Père Lachaise Cemetery.
image.credit: Peter Poradisch — Peter Poradisch (Drfine); own photography
image.date_qualification: Photographed 2006-08-09; the image postdates the cemetery's 1804 opening.
image.rights_statement: LicenseShortName: CC BY 2.5; UsageTerms: Creative Commons Attribution 2.5; Copyrighted: True

events.name: Père Lachaise Cemetery is opened

events.enhanced_description: On June 9, 1804, Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 in E-flat major, known as the 'Eroica,' premiered in Vienna. This symphony is considered a landmark in the history of music, marking the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era.
events.name: Beethoven's Symphony No. 3 premieres in Vienna

events.enhanced_description: On June 15, 1804, New Hampshire ratified the Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution, which reformed the electoral process for the President and Vice President. This amendment was crucial in addressing issues that arose during the elections of the early republic.
events.name: The Twelfth Amendment to the United States Constitution is ratified by New Hampshire

events.enhanced_description: On June 21, 1804, chemist Smithson Tennant announced the discovery of the elements iridium and osmium to the Royal Society in London. Shortly thereafter, William Hyde Wollaston revealed himself as the discoverer of palladium, marking significant advancements in the field of chemistry.
events.name: Smithson Tennant announces the discovery of iridium and osmium

events.enhanced_description: On July 11, 1804, Vice President Aaron Burr fatally shot former Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton during a duel in Weehawken, New Jersey. This event had profound political ramifications and marked a significant moment in American history.
events.name: Aaron Burr shoots Alexander Hamilton in a duel

events.enhanced_description: On July 27, 1804, Tennessee ratified the Twelfth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which clarified the electoral process for the President and Vice President. This ratification helped solidify the amendment's status and addressed previous electoral complications.
events.name: The Twelfth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution is ratified by Tennessee

events.enhanced_description: On August 11, 1804, in response to Napoleon's proclamation as Emperor of the French, Francis II declared himself Emperor of Austria, adding to his existing title as Holy Roman Emperor. This move signified the shifting political landscape in Europe during the Napoleonic Wars.
events.name: Francis II assumes the title of Emperor of Austria

events.enhanced_description: On August 20, 1804, during the Lewis and Clark Expedition, Sergeant Charles Floyd became the only member of the Corps of Discovery to die on the journey, reportedly from acute appendicitis. His death underscored the challenges faced by the expedition as they explored the uncharted territories of the Louisiana Purchase.

locations.name: Near Sioux City, Iowa, United States

events.name: Lewis and Clark Expedition: Sergeant Charles Floyd dies

events.enhanced_description: On September 1, 1804, German astronomer Karl Ludwig Harding discovered the asteroid Juno, marking a significant advancement in the field of astronomy.
